title: ICE officer has been charged after striking a man with a car in Houston
text:
HOUSTON (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston was indicted by a grand jury Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, prosecutors said.
The officer, Mario Alberto Morales, was driving an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10 when he struck and ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, who was running away during a pursuit through a parking lot, according to the Harris County District Attorney’s Office. Parra Hernandez broke his leg and remains in federal custody at a rehabilitation facility, said District Attorney Sean Teare, who announced the indictment at a news conference that included body camera video of the encounter and a recording of Morales calling 911.
ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that Teare said is contradicted by video.
“The evidence we have in this case is as clear as any that I’ve ever prosecuted or investigated,” Teare said.
Morales, 33, is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, although other encounters have come under investigation, including a fatal shooting by an ICE officer this summer in Houston.
Morales’ attorney, David Lindenmuth, said his client didn’t commit a crime and he accused Teare of indicting Morales “for political gain.” Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth said.
“Mr. Morales is truly a good man, a former member of our military, who has given his entire life to public service either for his country or in or adjacent to law enforcement,” Lindenmuth told The Associated Press. “To have him charged for what was so clearly just an accident — the DA’s office, the DA himself, has invented a crime out of thin air.”
Teare hinted at concerns over Morales’ background but would not provide details.
Morales, who is charged with a second-degree felony, was not in custody Friday and a warrant will be issued for his arrest, according to Teare.
ICE asserted that local officials do not have the authority to investigate federal officers acting in the course of their duties.
“Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE,” the agency said in a statement.
The district attorney played Morales’ body camera footage
Teare has said video clearly contradicts the ICE account. Surveillance video shows a Jeep Cherokee speed over a median and drive toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away. During a news conference Friday, he played Morales’ body camera footage, which shows him driving and talking about pursuing someone.
The video shows Morales making a few sharp moves with the steering wheel before the SUV shakes. Morales stops the vehicle, then gets out and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is several feet away. The video then shows Parra Hernandez on the ground and grabbing his leg, and yelling in pain.
Morales is heard saying, “He got hit with a car, bro.” It is not clear to whom he is talking.
“I was coming in and I hit him with the car,” Morales says.
Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation
Parra Hernandez has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years and did not have a deportation order or criminal background, according to Teare.
Other aspects of ICE’s account have also been called into question.
After Parra Hernandez was taken into custody, ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day. ICE said he was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him. FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston that has been working with the family, said Mendoza-Cervantes’ daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017.
Teare’s office has previously said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE’s statement.
ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for years.
Fatal summer Houston shooting also under investigation
Teare has said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence “either intentionally or through gross negligence.” He has said Morales left the scene before the vehicle could be impounded.

title: Letter to the Editor: Susan Collins is a bad deal for Maine
‘She’s a miracle’: Family says 2-year-old is healing after crash that killed her parents
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) — A fatal head-on collision on an Alaska highway last week killed a Fairbanks couple.
According to Alaska State Troopers, 38-year-old Sasha Hart and her husband, 41-year-old David Hart, were killed in the Oct. 19 crash on the Parks Highway near Trapper Creek.
According to troopers, Sasha Hart was driving a Subaru Forester south on the Parks Highway when she crossed the center line and collided head-on with a northbound Ford F-250.
Their 2-year-old daughter, Paige, was also in the Subaru and survived.
“She’s a miracle. Aren’t you?” Shery Elterman-Hart, David Hart’s sister, said as she held her niece during an interview.
A life built in Fairbanks
According to the Hart family, the couple just celebrated their 10-year anniversary. They built a life together in Fairbanks, where they blended Sasha’s Jamaican and David’s Alaskan lifestyles.
“She just became one of us. We were really close with David before they met, but then when she came, she just sort of lumped right in,” Elterman-Hart said.
The family said the two enjoyed traveling and watching hockey. They also shared a love for food, the family said.
Above all, they loved being parents to their daughter.
“She was their entire world,” Katie Ragsdale, David Hart’s sister, said. “I don’t know if it’s Paige’s house or their house.”
Paige’s recovery
The family said certain traits of David and Sasha are seen in Paige, including the same “stink” face as her mother and her father’s sweet tooth.
“You still have a piece of them, a living piece of them still on Earth,” Ragsdale said.
According to the family, Paige is healing fast after suffering six broken bones from the crash.

title: Letter: Ignore billionaires and attack ads trying to sway your vote
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
As someone who has been following elections for a long time, I have been struck by both the number and the toxicity of this year’s TV ads. I’d be curious to know how much this non-stop assault affects the outcome of our elections. Most people knew who they were voting for a year ago, and those who don’t at this point probably won’t bother to vote. I expect a lot of mute buttons are getting a workout.
Still, the amount of money spent — wasted? — on these ads is staggering. Once again, immigrant Elon Musk, is weighing in with another $366 million contribution to fund the mudslinging. This is on top of the roughly $300 million in the last election cycle. That’s pocket change for him, of course, but what does this “tech bro” have to offer conservative voters, aside from money? His one brief stint in government as the DOGE guy was an absolute disaster that will end up costing much more than it saved.
There is way too much money coming in from out-of-state billionaires for these elections. Nearly 100 billionaires and their spouses have donated to reelect Sen. Collins, including the head of the private equity firm that bought and closed the Jay and Bucksport paper mills.
None of these inescapable ads is addressing problems that matter like the $40 trillion national debt that is growing by more than $40 billion a week, or the precarious finances of Social Security and Medicare.
I urge Maine voters to ignore these self-serving billionaires and their lying ads and learn the facts before you vote.
Peter Pfeiffer
Solon

title: Former Lewiston city councilor Iman Osman arrested again
text:
Former Lewiston, Maine, city councilor Iman Osman arrested again
Former Lewiston city councilor Iman Osman has been arrested again.
The Lewiston Police Department confirms that Osman, 37, turned himself in to officers at the Lewiston Police station on Thursday afternoon. According to court documents, Osman is charged with tampering with a victim and violation of condition of release.
Osman, who was facing gun theft charges, resigned in January, less than 72 hours after being sworn into office.
According to court documents, on Oct.17, a woman contacted police and said Osman had asked her to sign a written statement regarding the weapons charges. The woman, who is Somali, said she had no knowledge of the gun in question, but that Osman asked her to sign something saying he had permission to have or take the gun. According to court documents, the woman had been in a relationship with the late owner of the gun and had a child with him. According to court documents, the woman told police she never gave Osman permission to take anything from her late-boyfriend's apartment.
According to court documents, Osman and the executive director of the Somali Bantu Community Association told her she would not get in any trouble "and to just sign the document so Osman can be 'saved' from this charge."
According to court documents, the woman said Osman contacted her again a few days before she went to police and told her he was sending her a document that she needed to sign, without saying what it was.
According to court documents, the woman said Osman had not delivered that document but that she was worried he was going to submit a document with her signature forged.
Osman, who served on the Lewiston School Committee for a year, won the Nov. 4, 2025, election for the Ward 5 City Council seat against incumbent Councilor Eryn M. Soule-Leclair by 35 votes, according to the city's municipal election results.
In his resignation letter, Osman claimed he faced "racist opposition" during his campaign for City Council and "vicious personal attacks" during his time in public office.
On Dec. 1, 2025, Osman was indicted by an Androscoggin County grand jury on charges of receiving stolen property and theft by unauthorized taking. According to the court documents, the charges are connected to firearms or explosive devices obtained from two different estates between Nov. 15, 2023, and Oct. 11, 2024.
Osman has denied all criminal charges against him.

title: Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a US general election
text:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV has become the first pontiff to vote in a U.S. general election, casting a mail-in ballot in a contest that will decide America’s political future as the Trump era slowly comes to an end.
The Vatican confirmed Friday that the Chicago-born pontiff had submitted a mail-in ballot in the city ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, citing his long-standing belief in civic participation.
Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen” as he has done “whenever he was eligible to do so,” the Holy See press office said.
The statement said he had also voted while living in Peru, where he lived as a missionary priest and bishop for over 20 years.
“The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” it added.
Leo holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship, and is also the head of state of a foreign country, the Holy See. The city-state is an absolute monarchy with no political elections.
U.S. federal law allows citizens living abroad, even those working for foreign governments, to vote via absentee ballot. Americans working for foreign governments aren’t automatically at risk of forfeiting their U.S. citizenship, though the U.S. State Department says on its website that it may “actively review” the citizenship status of Americans who “serve as a foreign head of state, foreign head of government, or foreign minister.”
This election, Illinois voters are deciding whether to elect Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to his third term, and they’re also filling an open U.S. Senate seat after longtime Catholic Democrat Dick Durbin’s retirement. There are no statewide issues on the Illinois ballot. President Donald Trump is not on the ballot, but he has campaigned hard to try to preserve Republican control of the U.S. House and Senate for the final two years of his second term.
The pope, registered at a New Lenox, Illinois, address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3, said Kim Fladhammer, chief of staff to the Will County clerk, on Friday. The Chicago Sun-Times first reported the request.
The request was made just 10 days before Leo underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Leo has been slowly resuming his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital Oct. 17.
It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. The pope’s older brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St. Jude’s, an Augustinian-run parish in New Lenox, Illinois. The elder Prevost attends Mass there, and Leo gave a talk at the parish in 2024 while still a cardinal.
Prevost’s past votes have gone Democratic and Republican
Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections.
The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a primary ballot. No such declaration is required in general elections.
While registered in heavily Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative suburban Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.
The records also show that he submitted ballots in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022.
Clashes with Trump
Since becoming pope, Leo has drawn criticism from Trump for repeatedly condemning the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran and calling for dignified treatment of immigrants, following the Trump administration’s crackdown and mass deportation program.
Earlier this year, Trump called Leo “weak” and captive to the “radical left,” kicking off a remarkable back-and-forth public argument that dominated Leo’s April trip to Africa.
Responding to Trump, Leo told reporters en route to Algeria: “I’m not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the church works for.”
The public dispute has subsided in recent months.
“We try to let things pass if there are misunderstandings,” the Vatican foreign minister, Archbishop Richard Paul Gallagher, told reporters this week. “With anybody, we would be looking to approach it and say, ‘OK, there may be a misunderstanding, let’s move on and try to rebuild trust and confidence.’”
Leo and Trump have not spoken by phone since the pope’s May 2025 election. Last week, however, Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the humanitarian crisis in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
Asked why Trump and Leo haven’t spoken, Gallagher said the Holy See has found a capable conduit in the U.S. ambassador to the Holy See, Brian Burch, and hadn’t needed to elevate any issue higher.
A pope who follows US politics closely
Leo has made clear on several occasions that he follows local and national U.S. politics closely and is not afraid to intervene.
Recently, Leo reiterated official church teaching declaring the death penalty “inadmissible.” He made the pronouncement in a social media post on the World Day Against the Death Penalty, which came as the U.S. announced plans to livestream an execution by firing squad. The plans were later scrapped.
In 2025, Leo intervened in a debate over abortion, after Chicago Cardinal Blase Cupich announced plans to give a lifetime achievement award to Sen. Durbin. The plans drew objection from some conservative U.S. bishops given the powerful Democratic senator’s support for abortion rights. Leo called for respect for both sides, but he also pointed out the contradiction between people who call themselves “pro-life” but also support the death penalty.
Also in 2025, Leo said he was “very disappointed” that his home state of Illinois approved a law allowing medically assisted dying, which is condemned by the Catholic Church.
The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, in a note commenting on the confirmation of Leo’s midterm vote, urged Catholics to put “our faith before our politics” and uphold human dignity and the common good.
“As Catholics and Americans, we are blessed to be able to participate in our nation’s political and public life,” said the conference’s director of public affairs, Chieko Noguchi. “In voting, our Holy Father sets the example that encourages each citizen to exercise their civic responsibility.”
___
Associated Press writers Holly Meyer in Nashville, Tennessee, and Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin, contributed to this report.

title: ICE officer charged after striking a man with a car in Houston
text:
ICE officer charged after striking a man with a car in Houston
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston was charged Friday with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, prosecutors said.
The Harris County District Attorney's office says Mario Alberto Morales was behind the wheel of an unmarked black vehicle on Oct. 10 when it struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, who was running away. Parra Hernandez was later placed in custody with a broken leg.
Few federal officers during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown have faced criminal charges for their actions in the field, although some encounters have come under investigation.
The case in Houston was brought by District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, who is also investigating the fatal shooting of a Mexican homebuilder in July that set off protests in the nation’s fourth-largest city.
ICE did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment about the indictment charging Morales.
ICE has said Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the car and called accusations that the officer intentionally struck him false and “reckless.” Teare has said the surveillance footage clearly contradicts the ICE account.
In the video, a Jeep Cherokee speeds over a median and drives toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away. The video does not show the car hitting him — that view is blocked by another vehicle — but it shows the SUV inches away from him. The footage then shows Parra Hernandez on the ground.
Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation
Other aspects of ICE's account have also been called into question.
ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day and was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him. FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston, said Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017. She also said his real name is Jose Hector Jimenez.
Teare's office has also said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE's statement.
ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for nearly a decade.
Parra Hernandez has been in the country for more than 30 years. He was living in the U.S. without authorization, according to FIEL, which has been working with his family.
Fatal summer Houston shooting also under investigation
Teare said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence “either intentionally or through gross negligence.” He said the ICE officer who drove the SUV that struck Parra Hernandez fled the scene before the vehicle could be impounded.
In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his requests for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his van. DHS has said Salgado Araujo had “weaponized his vehicle” before the shooting and that an officer fired in self-defense. Other passengers in the van have disputed that account.
Teare has not given a timetable for when his office's investigation into the shooting will be complete. In September, a witness to the shooting was seen entering a courthouse area reserved for grand jury proceedings.

title: Early Darkness And Trick-or-treaters In Eastern Maine Neighborhoods Call For Extra Caution This Weekend
text:
There are a ton of fun activities happening in Eastern Maine this weekend, as folks celebrate Halloween. Between Trunk-or-treats and regular trick-or-treating, authorities are expecting an uptick in both regular traffick and foot-traffic the next two nights, especially in the Bangor area.
That coupled with the time change and the skies getting darker earlier has local law enforcement agents reminding motoritist to keep an eye on the roads, and pedestrians to dress with visibility in mind, and to travel with a flashlight if possible.
Read More: How To Keep Trick-or-treaters Safe On Maine Streets
The Bangor Police Department took to Facebook to encourage people to stay safe this weekend.
"Keep your eyes peeled for little ghosts and goblins who will be out in force. We recommend all trick or treaters wear reflective items to enhance visibility and motorists should drive with extra care. Please, be extra cautious around crosswalks and in neighborhoods."
They also pointed out that there will be officers attending some of the holiday events this weekend.
Read More: Bangor Touch-A-Truck & Treat at Cross Insurance Center Today
They include the big Bangor Parks and Recreation Touch a Trunk or Treat will be happening from 5:30 PM to 7:30 PM tonight at the Cross Insurance Center, and the event at the Trunk or Treat & Touch a Truck taking place Saturday morning from 10 AM to noon at the Crosspoint Church Bangor, 1476 Broadway.
The Maine DOT is also reminding folks to make a plan to get a ride home if you plan to have some adult fun this Halloween.
"If you’re seeing ghosts in your headlights, stay out of the driver’s seat! Plan a sober ride home this Halloween. If You Feel Different, You Drive Different."
Designate a driver before you head out for the night, and stay safe!

title: Prosecutors drop felony charge against rapper Rick Ross in domestic violence case
text:
MIAMI BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her, court records said.
The Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office filed paperwork Thursday to drop a felony charge of battery by strangulation because of “insufficient evidence.” Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, still faces a misdemeanor charge of battery domestic violence.
Ross, 50, has pleaded not guilty to all charges, and his attorney said Friday that his client would continue to defend himself against the allegations. Ross surrendered at the Miami Beach police station on Oct. 1, two days after the woman filed a report with police, officials said. He was freed on bail several hours later.
According to an arrest report, a woman told Miami Beach detectives that she had been living with Ross when he accused her of cheating on him and struck her multiple times on Aug. 28. She said Ross also choked her with the collar of her shirt and slammed her into a wall. The woman said she was eventually able to leave the home and returned later — after Ross left — to collect her belongings.
Ross previously pleaded no contest to aggravated assault in 2017 after he was accused of forcing a man into a guesthouse at his suburban Atlanta mansion in 2015 and beating him with a handgun, according to Georgia court records. Under a Georgia first-time offender program, the court issued an order exonerating Ross of guilt on that felony count.
Ross is a longtime South Florida resident who gained prominence in 2006 with his debut single “Hustlin’.”
The rapper and entrepreneur helped put Miami on the musical map in the early 2000s, when most hip-hop fans looked to Atlanta and Houston as Southern rap headquarters. “Hustlin’” was certified platinum twice by the Recording Industry Association of America and sparked a bidding war for Ross. He eventually signed with Def Jam Records, headed by Jay-Z.
Ross’ debut album, “Port of Miami,” also went platinum, debuting at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart. It was the first in a series of chart-toppers, including 2008’s “Trilla” and 2009’s “Deeper Than Rap.” He has been nominated for nine Grammy Awards.
In 2008, he founded the influential label Maybach Music Group, boosting the careers of signees like Wale, Meek Mill and French Montana.
His most recent album, “Set In Stone,” was released in July.

title: Maine’s first Senate election was steeped in political chaos
text:
110 years ago, Mainers went to the polls, and for the first time in the state’s history, cast ballots for their next U.S. senator. They’d elect not one, but two representatives to the upper chamber in 1916.
In that tempest of a campaign, voters turned out in four separate statewide elections, dramatically expanding the democratic process. And just like this election season, the eyes of the nation were on Maine.
Prior to 1914, the role of picking senators fell solely on state legislatures. This changed with the passage of the 17th Amendment in 1913, which mandated the regular election of senators by popular democracy. (Which, of course, in Maine, like most of the country, meant just men.)
The first group of popularly chosen senators were elected in the 1914 midterms, with Mainers slated to cast their first ballots two years later in 1916.
The elections could hardly have come at a more pivotal time for the politics of the day.
Facing the backdrop of World War I, rising racial tensions, the height of the women’s suffrage movement and a rapidly evolving federal government, even observers at the time knew the 1916 elections would be a pivotal moment in American history. Just like today, Maine was a key bellwether.
Throwing out the old guard
Despite decades of dominance, the Maine Republican Party was dealt a significant electoral blow in 1910. Voters upended 60 years of precedent when they ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Bert M. Fernald in favor of Augusta Democrat Frederick W. Plaisted.
But more critical to national politics, Democrats were able to flip the state Legislature, giving them the power to pick Maine’s next U.S. senator.
The man they picked was Charles F. Johnson, a former mayor and state representative from Waterville.
“Keen and logical in debate, wise in council and astute in politics, he was looked upon as the Democratic leader in the House,” a Bangor Daily Commercial article said of Johnson after his election. “His speeches were among the best delivered at Augusta during those winters, and he never arose to speak without the respectful attention, not only of the members of his… party, but of his Republican political opponents as well.”
Republicans found their footing in 1912, taking back both the governorship and the Legislature, meaning they could pick their own candidate, former governor Edwin C. Burleigh, as the state’s next senator. Burleigh would be Maine’s last senator to be elected by the Legislature.
But just as it looked like Maine was ready to return to one-party rule, things got weird.
First, Republicans fumbled away the governorship.
A different dynamic
To say the electoral dynamics of the early 1900s were different from today’s would be a massive understatement.
Neither the Democratic or Republican parties had a claim to any major ideology. Left-right, progressive-conservative, liberal-nativist, both major parties made their plays for voters from across the wide political spectrum of early 20th-century America. U.S. President Woodrow Wilson’s nativist positions may have appealed to anti-immigrant fervor, but his policy of neutrality amid World War I through his first term also won over German and Irish immigrants wary of an alliance with Great Britain.
The Republican Party, which included members like the popular progressive President Theodore Roosevelt as well as socialist Rep. Fiorello La Guardia, also served as the political home to opponents of organized labor and the champions of unfettered commerce. The most prominent activists within the women’s suffrage movement often aligned with the GOP, and yet the western states that expanded the vote to women years before the 19th Amendment was passed were largely Democratic strongholds.
The contradicting coalitions created by alliances of incoherent ideologies were as fragile as the peace that shattered across the Atlantic Ocean two years earlier. That factional fraying is what allowed Wilson – facing reelection in 1916 – to ascend to the presidency in the first place.
In 1912, Teddy Roosevelt, nearly four years removed from his White House tenure, made the controversial decision to challenge his former vice president, then-President William Howard Taft, accusing his one-time political protege of abandoning the progressive movement. When Taft and the more moderate factions of the party successfully beat back the challenge, Roosevelt opted to form a new party dedicated to a more liberal vision of America. Roosevelt and his backers built the Progressive Party, widely known as the Bull Moose Party, in an effort to surge past the unpopularity of the Democrats and Republicans.
They failed.
In the end, the Progressives and Republicans split the vote, and Wilson and the Democrats coasted into office winning 435 electoral college votes, despite finishing with 100,000 fewer votes than the party’s nominee in 1908.
National politics affect Maine
Back in Maine, the same split would throw a wrench into the 1914 gubernatorial election.
In the same year Wilson was elected president, William T. Haines and a united Republican Party at the state level successfully unseated Gov. Plaisted.
But two years later, that GOP unity wavered. In 1914, Maine Progressive Party candidate Halbert P. Gardner pulled nearly 13% of the vote in the governor’s race, much of that seemingly coming from Haines’ base of support, and paving the way for another Democrat, Oakley C. Curtis, to take power.
With Democrats riding high and Republicans limping forward, few could have predicted the political calamity on the horizon.
‘The curtain raiser’
Adding another layer of drama to 1916 was Maine’s unusual election timing. Until the late 1950s, Maine was one of only two states to hold its state elections (everything but the presidency) in September, two months before the rest of the country voted.
This led to heightened national attention and the perception of Maine results as a bellwether for the upcoming nationwide races. In the leadup to the Sept. 11 election, GOP presidential nominee Charles Evans Hughes visited Maine to campaign extensively with state Republicans, seeking to boost his own candidacy at the same time.
Teddy Roosevelt also traveled to Maine to campaign for Republicans as the elections neared, delivering a rousing speech at an event in Lewiston that the Daily Sun called the state’s “greatest ever staged” demonstration.
“Maine is our political forecaster,” the Boston Globe wrote in a September editorial. “The outcome in Maine is the curtain raiser for the big show two months hence.”
With Roosevelt back to supporting the GOP and Wilson’s popularity teetering, a reunited Republican Party smelled blood, and was ready to test its strength in northern New England.
But picking the right candidates wouldn’t be as simple as in the past.
Directly electing a senator wasn’t the only change for Maine voters that year. In 1916, the state held its first primary elections for federal and statewide races, abandoning the less democratic nominating process of party meetings and conventions.
The Democratic incumbents, Governor Curtis and Senator Johnson, faced no official opposition en route to their nominations, but a deep field of Republican candidates lined up for these top positions.
“Senatorial and gubernatorial candidates of Maine’s finest material,” in the words of a Daily Kennebec Journal headline, would draw tens of thousands to the polls in Maine’s first-ever statewide primary on June 20.
But just days before the primary, the political world was rocked by the sudden and unexpected passing of a Maine political mainstay.
A parade of primaries
Republican Sen. Burleigh died in Augusta after falling ill earlier in the afternoon. The cause of death was “acute indigestion,” according to an article in the Lewiston Daily Sun.
Respected by people in both parties, Burleigh’s death stunned the public.
But for Republicans, the tragedy also compounded the stakes for 1916. Burleigh had been the only statewide Republican left standing. He was a prominent presence in Maine politics for decades, and his was the only major race where the party expected to have the incumbency advantage. In the U.S. Senate, Burleigh’s death brought the GOP’s caucus down 39 members, matching their lowest count in decades.
To fill the seat, the state would need to hold a separate primary, since it was too soon to incorporate a special election into the June 20 race. So, a month after Maine’s first-ever statewide primary, it hosted its second-ever statewide primary.
Two days after Burleigh’s death, Maine Republicans picked the bulk of their ticket.
Former Maine Senate President Carl Milliken, of Pittsfield, handily won the primary for governor. Meanwhile, Frederick Hale, a former U.S. representative and member of a prominent political family in the Pine Tree State, came out on top in a tight three-way race with former-Gov. Bert Fernald and state Sen. Ira G. Hersey.
Finishing closely behind Hale, Fernald resurrected his campaign and entered the special race to replace Burleigh. He went on to comfortably win the July 24 primary, claiming the second Republican nomination for U.S. Senate.
On the Democratic side, Bowdoin College professor Kenneth C. Sills threw his hat in the ring to replace Burgleigh, with the party clearing the field for him like they did for their other statewide candidates.
Suffragists’ say
Despite being shut out by a repressive political system, women’s rights groups would make their mark on the 1916 elections.
Neither party had the inherent support of the feminist movement. But when, after securing the Republican presidential nomination, Hughes came out in support of a Constitutional amendment for women’s suffrage, the choice for advocates became clear.
Wilson and the Democrats claimed to support women voting, but insisted that it was an issue best left to the states. While suffrage groups worked to expand the vote in individual states, a Federal amendment had been the preferred path of the most prominent activist groups.
Two years earlier, a women’s suffrage amendment had been rejected in the Senate. Johnson, now seeking reelection, voted against it.
“We women in Maine are terribly behind the times,” author and activist Florence Brooks Whitehouse said in early 1916 during an event in Lewiston, the Daily Sun reported.
Whitehouse, an Augusta native who later moved to Portland, was the face of movement in Maine. In the runup to 1916, Whitehouse helped launch the state’s branch of the National Woman’s Party, a political organization at the suffrage movement’s radical vanguard that would be instrumental in winning passage of the 19th Amendment.
In 1916 Maine suffragists attended both parties’ state conventions, where they questioned candidates and pushed for their support. At the GOP convention in Portland, equal-suffrage supporters were so well-represented that they spilled over from their allotted convention space.
“Both morning and afternoon, the solid phalanx of women behind the suffrage banner, wearing suffrage colors, massed in the balcony opposite the stage,” Whitehouse wrote in a column featured in the Lewiston Evening Journal. “When the suffrage-plank in the platform was read, the women showed their appreciation in peals of applause.”
At the Democratic convention in Bangor, the party’s perceived “avowed antipathy” toward suffragists diminished the activists’ enthusiasm. But they were able to press candidates and officials on their enfranchisement position.
Sen. Johnson, who gave a “splendid speech” to the convention, according to Whitehouse, spoke with suffragists after the event, echoing the president’s position of supporting expanding the vote to women, but getting to it through action from the individual state governments.
After Hughes declared his support for a federal amendment, the National Woman’s Party concentrated its effort on defeating Wilson and the Democrats.
At the national level, their electoral effort to mobilize voters against the incumbent administration in equal-suffrage states ultimately failed, with Hughes losing all but one state where women had the ballot.
But in Maine, where a slate of Republican candidates far more receptive to the suffragists’ cause were on the verge of regaining power, the prospects were better.
‘A Republican landslide’
The Associated Press reported that in the final 24 hours of the Maine campaign, prominent speakers on both sides combined for 292 speeches in “every city and sizable town.”
On Election Day, returns weren’t coming in long before suspense evaporated and the Republican victory materialized.
Hale beat the incumbent Johnson by nearly 10,000 votes (or about 6.5%). In the race to replace the late Burleigh, Fernald outran Sills by more than 13,000 votes.
“Republicanism is triumphant in the state of Maine,” declared the front page of the Daily Kennebec Journal.
“It’s a Republican landslide,” echoed the Lewiston Evening Journal.
It was even worse down the ballot for Democrats. Incumbent Gov. Oakley Curtis lost to Republican Carl Milliken by a margin of over 9%. But Curtis was gracious in defeat.
“The best man won,” Curtis said, according to a story in the Lewiston Evening Journal, “and there are no bones broken.” He added that his party “got a good licking, and that’s all there is to it.”
Republicans swept four U.S. House races as well, including a flip of the 2nd District, which covered much of Androscoggin County and western Maine.
An article in the Lewiston Evening Journal summed up the scope of Democrats’ collapse in Maine: “In the election of Monday, which marked the end of one of the liveliest and most hotly contested campaigns in the state’s history, the Republicans elected their governor, two United States senators, four representatives to Congress, 28 out of the 31 members of the state Senate, and, probably, 112 members of the state House of Representatives.”
Looking at a wipeout, Democrats still sought to spin the results into their favor, claiming that, even in defeat, they had “materially reduced” the usually large Republican majority.
“The results of the election in Maine indicates a sweeping Democratic victory in November,” said Vance C. McCormick, Woodrow Wilson’s 1916 campaign manager and party chairman. “I have never claimed that we would win in Maine because I realized that to carry such a rock-ribbed Republican stronghold in a presidential year would be practically impossible.”
Republicans, naturally, said the sweep would reflect a victory for Charles Evans Hughes and the GOP. In October, Hersey told a group of Republican editorial editors and publishers that “the verdict of Maine will be the verdict of this nation,” the Kennebec Journal reported at the time.
But Maine was a bad bellwether.
Democrats rebound in November
Two months after Maine’s slate of state elections, voters returned to the polls to have their say in the presidential race. And while things appeared to be going Republicans’ way early, a closer look at Maine’s results showed an electorate dramatically shifting toward Wilson and the Democrats.
Turnout from September to November dropped by around 15,000 votes, and the GOP’s comfortable margins from earlier in the year was nearly halved, with a little over 5,000 ballots separating Hughes and Wilson.
Some missed the signs.
Doing their own “Dewey defeats Truman” 32 years earlier, the Portland Daily Press declared an erroneous result across their front page.
“Hughes elected president,” the headline read.
In reality, Wilson had squeaked by in one of America’s closest elections. If a couple thousand votes in California had gone the other way, Hughes would have become the 29th President of the United States.
However, it wasn’t all bad for all Republican supporters. Wilson eventually came around on suffrage, and by 1918 he was calling on Congress to pass a federal amendment. A vote that year came up just short, with Maine’s senators diverging: Fernald voting in favor, and Hale voting against.
Over the next year, Florence Brooks Whitehouse headed an effort to press Hale into supporting the amendment. Eventually, when it was clear which way the wind was blowing, Hale relented and joined the rest of the Maine delegation to pass the 19th Amendment to the United States Constitution. After calling a special session to ratify the amendment, Gov. Milliken signed it in the company of prominent Maine suffragists, including Whitehouse.
“Maine has been worthy of her best tradition today, and in a measure justified her motto by leading the second half of the ratification states,” Whitehouse said after the signing, according to an article in the Lewiston Evening Sun. “She has tipped the scales in favor of the enfranchisement of American women, and it is safe to predict all the states which have arranged for special sessions will hurry to be counted.”

title: Suspect caught on video confessing to killing family, college professor, prosecutor says
text:
LORAIN COUNTY, Ohio (WOIO/Gray News) - Moments after a celebrated college professor and his wife were shot to death inside their Ohio home, prosecutors say the suspect knocked on a stranger’s door and asked to be recorded on video confessing to the killings.
Asia Nguyen-Duy, 31, of Ashland, Oregon, appeared in court Thursday, being carried in by several police officers, placed in a chair and rolled to the defense table.
Nguyen-Duy previously went by Daniel Jones. Court records show they legally changed their name in 2025. During Thursday’s hearing, Nguyen-Duy said they are gender-neutral and prefer to be called Asia Nguyen-Duy.
They are facing six counts of murder, four counts of felonious assault and one count of tampering with evidence in the deaths of 64-year-old Pipo Nguyen-Duy and 56-year-old Thi Tran Phong.
During the hearing, prosecutors revealed that Nguyen-Duy, covered in scratches and blood, approached a nearby resident. They asked them to record a video, and admitted to killing their family, claiming they were “escaping a cult” and taking full responsibility for the acts.
Police were first alerted Wednesday morning after finding a smoldering, modified vehicle registered to Nguyen-Duy in an Oberlin College parking lot containing loose ammunition and magazine packaging.
Officers found Nguyen-Duy nearby and conducted a welfare check at the victims’ home, discovering both dead from multiple gunshot wounds.
Pipo Nguyen-Duy was an internationally exhibited photographer and longtime studio art professor at Oberlin College.
A judge set bond at $3 million, and the case has been bound over to county common pleas court.

title: Chadbourne Road Crash In Standish Highlights Dangers Of Drowsy Driving On Maine Roads
text:
Maine State Police Say Drowsy Driver Hit Maine DOT Trailer In Standish After Falling Asleep At The Wheel
Maine DOT workers at a job site in Standish got quite a scare Thursday afternoon, after a man allegedly fell asleep behind the wheel and hit a trailer.
Read More: Halloween Safety In Eastern Maine This Weekend
According to the Maine State Police, the incident happened just before 2 PM on the Chadbourne Road.
"The preliminary investigation indicates that 32-year-old Merlin Maston of New Gloucester was traveling southbound in a Chevrolet Cruze when he fell asleep at the wheel and struck the rear of a MaineDOT trailer. At the time, MaineDOT employees were conducting roadway work. One MaineDOT employee who was outside the truck was struck by the vehicle but reported no injuries."
There was another Maine DOT employee who was also impacted by the crash. Both individuals were evaluated at the scene.
Authorities say they are still looking into the incident.
According to the Maine Driver Handbook, drowsy drivers account for a significant number of crashes each year.
"Drowsiness is tied to as many as 240,000 crashes a year...Micro-sleeps last only 4 to 5 seconds, but at 55 mph even that can be fatal."
They suggest that drivers should take periodic breaks if they start to feel sleepy.
"Take a break every 2 hours or 100 miles, and a 15 to 20 minute nap if you feel danger signs of fatigue."
The National Sleep Foundation echoes the concern about drowsy drivers on Maine roadways.
"Just like drunk, drugged, and distracted driving, drowsy driving is a real public health issue, causing thousands of car crashes each year and killing an estimated 6,400 people in the U.S. alone according to the AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety. 95% of Americans recognize that drowsy driving is dangerous yet nearly two-thirds of Americans report that they have driven while drowsy."
They say younger drivers between the ages of 16 and 25 and shift workers are in a high-risk category for falling asleep while driving.

title: Milford man pleads not guilty in toddler’s death
text:
A Milford man pleaded not guilty Friday in the death of his toddler.
Shane McLaughlin, 37, pleaded not guilty to one felony count manslaughter, as well as three counts of child endangerment, Friday in Penobscot County Superior Court. His 1-year-old daughter, Eleanora Ray McLaughlin, died of hypothermia at the family’s home on Dec. 28.
Eleanora was living with her twin sister and an older brother at their father’s house at the time of her death.
McLaughlin was arrested Wednesday after a grand jury indicted him. No further information was available in his court case file.
McLaughlin is held at the Penobscot County Jail on a $250,000 bail. A bail hearing will be held next week at the request of his defense attorney, Seth Levy.

title: In Alaska race, Trump targets a long, sometimes sordid political tradition of 'spoiler' candidates
text:
By investigating an Alaska Democratic Senate hopeful over her campaign’s reported involvement in recruiting a candidate with the same name as the Republican incumbent, President Donald Trump’s administration is targeting a political trick that has been used in American politics for decades.
The practice goes back at least to 1946, when a four-term Boston city councilman named Joe Russo ran in a Democratic primary for a congressional seat against a 27-year-old janitor with the same name. He was recruited to the ticket by supporters of the third candidate in the race and its eventual winner, John F. Kennedy.
In Alaska, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is facing three other challengers on the state’s final ballot in a race that could determine control of the Senate — Democrat Mary Peltola, who was previously the state’s lone House member, and two candidates who have barely campaigned, including a retired school teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.
Alaska Republicans have long suspected the second Sullivan of being a Democratic plant, and the Trump administration took the unusual step last week of suing to prevent certification of a possible Peltola victory until it could be determined if voters were confused.
The New York Times this week reported that internal campaign texts and communications showed the Peltola campaign recruited the second Sullivan, leading the president to call for the Democrat’s prosecution and his Justice Department to issue a flurry of subpoenas in a criminal investigation.
Peltola has denied involvement in the scheme, as has the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.
Trump has targeted adversaries with the Justice Department, critics say
Critics say Trump has used the Justice Department as an extension of his own personal political operation, targeting his enemies with investigations and indictments and intervening in the election in ways not seen before in modern memory.
The Justice Department has historically avoided taking overt investigative actions within 60 days of an election. But there has been a burst of activity in politically sensitive matters in recent weeks, including the search of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home. Trump’s Justice Department has defended the timing of its recent investigative moves, saying in a statement Wednesday that it is “following the facts and the law, not anyone’s political timetable.”
Justin Levitt, a Justice official during the Biden administration, said that appeared unlikely given how often campaigns recruit or boost so-called spoilers.
“It may be distasteful, but it happens all the time,” said Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Marymount University in Los Angeles. “There is no behavior that has been disclosed that is in violation of federal law.”
Using such candidates is a tactic that Trump’s own political operation has employed in this very election.
In Ohio’s Senate race, a group tied to the president’s political operation is urging voters to support a socialist candidate to pull votes from the Democrat challenging that state’s Republican incumbent. In Nevada, a political operation with ties to Republicans is boosting an independent candidate for governor named Danielle Ford, who has the same last name as the Democratic candidate challenging that state’s GOP governor. Trump’s allies tried to recruit Kanye West onto the 2020 presidential ballot as a third-party candidate.
The New York Times story detailed an effort reaching back to 2025 to recruit another Dan Sullivan to the Alaska Senate ballot. The story detailed the use of a Democratic strategist from outside Alaska who was paid by a political organization backing Peltola, who announced her Senate run in January 2026.
In Peltola’s 2024 reelection bid for the House, Republicans supported keeping on the ballot a New York inmate who was a registered Democrat and filed to run in Alaska. Peltola lost that race.
A system potentially prone to manipulation
Jason Torchinsky, a veteran Republican campaign finance attorney and former Justice Department official, said in an interview that the Times story pointed to possible crimes involving the financing of the operation to run the second Sullivan.
But the bigger point, he argued, is that Alaska’s unusual ranked-choice voting system is particularly prone to manipulation. Anyone who pays a $100 filing fee can end up on a lengthy primary ballot, and the top four finishers make it to November, where voters can rank three of them.
“This is just Exhibit A for how ranked-choice voting systems can be manipulated by various actors,” said Torchinsky, noting that in traditional systems candidates must secure the nomination of a political party that already has access to the ballot, gathering sometimes tens of thousands of voter signatures.
Still, defenders of Alaska’s voting system, which Republicans have supported trying to repeal through a ballot measure this election, contend that it is harder to manipulate because voters can simply pick both Sullivans and not Peltola. That is what Sullivan’s own campaign is urging Alaskans to do.
In states with more traditional voting methods, a vote for a third-party candidate is one fewer for a Democrat or Republican. That’s why many in the GOP this year are concerned about Libertarian candidates pulling votes from their Senate candidates, and why the Republican Party often advocates on behalf of Green Party candidates fighting to get on the November ballot in various states.
Identical names are one variation
Finding candidates with the same name is a variant on the trick, and it can have criminal consequences.
In Florida in 2020, a Democratic state senator named Jose Javier Rodriguez faced a challenge from a Republican and another candidate named Alex Rodriguez. The second Rodriguez won 6,382 votes as an independent, and the Democrat Rodriguez lost his seat to his Republican challenger by 32 votes.
A Republican former state senator, Frank Artiles, was later convicted of illegal campaign contributions and falsifying a candidate form for his role in helping the second Rodriguez run. Artiles was sentenced to 60 days in jail. The Republican victor in the state Senate race, Ileana Garcia, denied any knowledge of Artiles’ scheme. She remains in that seat.
David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research in Washington, said he expects a judge will very soon reject the Justice Department’s “frivolous” lawsuit seeking to stop certification if Sen. Sullivan doesn’t win.
“If both parties wanted to come together in Congress and try to figure out a way to regulate these kinds of things so that neither party does them and they constantly do them both,” Becker said, “that wouldn’t be the worst thing in the world.”
___
Associated Press writer Marc Levy in Harrisburg, Pa., contributed.

title: Doctor says time outdoors can support physical and mental health
text:
(Aging Untold) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine.
Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it.
“Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Our genetic roots are in the outdoors and the surroundings that we see around us right now,” Mann said.
Doctor cites human history outdoors
Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments.
Asked whether people should be prescribed time outside the way they are prescribed medicine, Mann said, “I absolutely think we should.”
He said he is personally an advocate for holistic health.
Sunlight and physical health
Mann said sunlight benefits the body, including through vitamin D development.
“Sunlight is beneficial for your body for vitamin D development and has links to improved cancer rates and decreased infections, and a whole host of other medical problems that are directly connected to your interaction with the sun,” Mann said.
Exercising outside can also have physical benefits.
Outdoor time and mental health
Mann said there is a lot of data and research on the psychological effects of being outdoors.
Mann said people spend a lot of time on screens, including phones, tablets and TV, and screen time is directly linked to anxiety and other psychological conditions.
Time outdoors does not require a long hike
Mann said time outdoors does not have to involve a long hike.
“It doesn’t have to be a hike seven miles in the woods,” Mann said. “We know that based on literature and data that even just 10 or 15 minutes outdoors, working in your garden or mowing your lawn or spending time on your back porch can equally yield significant benefits.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers discusses benefits of outdoor time
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said that when people get less sunlight, vitamin D levels go down and people start to see affective disorders.
“Sometimes one of the simplest prescriptions for the body and the brain is to step outside,” Rogers said.

title: Former Miss America to have a street named after her in her hometown

title: Prosecutors drop felony charge against rapper Rick Ross in domestic violence case
text:
Prosecutors drop felony charge against rapper Rick Ross in domestic violence case
Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her, court records said.
The Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office filed paperwork Thursday to drop a felony charge of battery by strangulation because of “insufficient evidence.” Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, still faces a misdemeanor charge of battery domestic violence.
Ross, 50, has pleaded not guilty to all charges, and his attorney said Friday that his client would continue to defend himself against the allegations. Ross surrendered at the Miami Beach police station on Oct. 1, two days after the woman filed a report with police, officials said. He was freed on bail several hours later.
Related video above: Police: Man shouted 'I don't care who your daddy is' before attacking Rick Ross' son
According to an arrest report, a woman told Miami Beach detectives that she had been living with Ross when he accused her of cheating on him and struck her multiple times on Aug. 28. She said Ross also choked her with the collar of her shirt and slammed her into a wall. The woman said she was eventually able to leave the home and returned later — after Ross left — to collect her belongings.
Ross previously pleaded no contest to aggravated assault in 2017 after he was accused of forcing a man into a guesthouse at his suburban Atlanta mansion in 2015 and beating him with a handgun, according to Georgia court records. Under a Georgia first-time offender program, the court issued an order exonerating Ross of guilt on that felony count.
Ross is a longtime South Florida resident who gained prominence in 2006 with his debut single “Hustlin'.”
The rapper and entrepreneur helped put Miami on the musical map in the early 2000s, when most hip-hop fans looked to Atlanta and Houston as Southern rap headquarters. “Hustlin'” was certified platinum twice by the Recording Industry Association of America and sparked a bidding war for Ross. He eventually signed with Def Jam Records, headed by Jay-Z.
Ross’ debut album, “Port of Miami,” also went platinum, debuting at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart. It was the first in a series of chart-toppers, including 2008’s “Trilla” and 2009’s “Deeper Than Rap.” He has been nominated for nine Grammy Awards.
In 2008, he founded the influential label Maybach Music Group, boosting the careers of signees like Wale, Meek Mill and French Montana.
His most recent album, “Set In Stone,” was released in July.

title: Sunny, Cool, & Breezy Halloween. Nice Day Sunday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Rain showers across northern and western Maine will fizzle out by midnight. A few light snow showers will also be possible in the higher elevations. Skies turn mostly clear with lows ranging from the upper 20s in the north to the mid to upper 30s along the coast. Northwest winds will stay gusty, reaching near 30 mph at times.
Halloween: Dry & Breezy
Saturday brings dry conditions and mostly sunny skies with seasonable afternoon highs reaching into the 40s to low 50s. Breezy northwest winds gusting to 25 mph will gradually subside by early afternoon, but temperatures will drop swiftly after sunset into the 30s.

- Clock Reminder: Remember to set your clocks back one hour before heading to bed Saturday night. Daylight Saving Time ends Sunday morning, giving everyone an extra hour of sleep while shifting sunrise and sunset times an hour earlier. Sunday: Pick of the Weekend
Sunday features mostly sunny skies and pleasant fall conditions to wrap up the weekend. Highs will be in the 50s with lighter westerly winds.

title: Tour company sues over fees for international visitors to national parks, including Acadia
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
An Arizona tour company has sued the federal government over increased fees for international visitors to national parks, including Acadia.
The National Park Service implemented the new pricing structure at the start of 2026. The America the Beautiful annual digital park pass stayed $80 for U.S. residents but jumped to $250 for nonresidents. International visitors aged 16 and older without the annual pass now pay $100 per person on top of the standard entrance fee at Acadia and 10 of the other busiest parks.
Phoenix-based Across Arizona Tours filed the lawsuit in September, arguing that the Trump administration did not have the authority to change the fees. The company operates van tours in the Grand Canyon. The complaint says the co-owner has spoken with 80 to 90 people who decided not to reserve a tour with the company, mostly because of the increased fees.
“As a result of the new fees, Across Arizona Tours has suffered a decline in business over the past year among nonresident customers,” the complaint says. “Given the potential for hundreds of dollars of additional fees for a family visiting, many potential customers have chosen to forgo visiting the Grand Canyon entirely, opting instead to visit different destinations in the U.S. or to plan to visit and spend their money on other countries.”
It is not clear how the change is impacting Acadia National Park. The park reported more than 3.3 million recreational visits this year through the end of September, slightly less than the same period last year, but did not say how many of those are nonresidents.
No one responded to an email to the general media inbox for Acadia on Thursday evening. A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of the Interior did not answer questions about how the fee has impacted international visitation at Acadia but touted the policy in a written statement.
“Thanks to President Donald J. Trump, U.S. residents, who already fund the National Park System through federal taxes, are continuing to enjoy affordable pricing, while foreign tourists are paying higher entrance fees to help maintain our parks and improve visitor experiences,” the statement said. “This administration will continue to put American families first — making parks more accessible, more affordable and more efficient for future generations.”
In August, Secretary Doug Burgum posted on X that the policy had generated $20 million in new funding for national parks.
The federal government has not yet filed a response to the complaint in court. The plaintiffs argue that Congress has never authorized the National Park Service to impose higher entrance fees for nonresidents.
“The federal defendants ignore both the explicit and implicit limitations on their authority,” the complaint says. “In doing so, they presume a boundless authority to impose whatever fees they deem fit. That elastic view of their authority is wrong — not least because it would violate separation of powers for Congress to delegate an unbounded authority to impose different fees for any group, or for any reason.”
Other parks subject to the $100 surcharge for international visitors are Bryce Canyon, Everglades, Glacier, Grand Teton, Rocky Mountain, Sequoia and Kings Canyon, Yellowstone, Yosemite and Zion.

title: Woman who killed best friend’s newborn said she had a years-long compulsion to hurt children, reports say
text:
ALLEGHENY COUNTY, Pa. (Gray News) - A woman admitted to killing her best friend’s 6-week-old son and injuring his twin brother while babysitting in Pennsylvania, prosecutors said.
Nicole Virzi, 32, pleaded guilty Wednesday to third-degree murder and other charges, avoiding a potential death penalty trial. She was sentenced to 35 to 80 years in prison.
In 2024, Virzi was visiting Pittsburgh to assist her longtime friend, Savannah Roberts, with newborn twins Leon and Ari Katz, NBC News reported.
When the parents took Ari to a hospital to treat unexplained injuries, Virzi offered to watch Leon.
Later that night, Virzi called 911 claiming Leon fell from a baby bouncer. He was rushed to a children’s hospital, where he died.
An autopsy revealed Leon died from blunt force trauma to the head, with investigators concluding the catastrophic injuries could not have resulted from a bouncer fall.
Detectives also determined Virzi caused Ari’s initial injuries. Prosecutors revealed in court that Virzi told investigators she “always had a compulsion she could not control to harm kids.”
In a letter to Allegheny County Common Pleas Judge Jill E. Rangos, Roberts said Virzi’s betrayal shattered her trust, writing, “I could’ve never imagined that a person, let alone my best friend, was capable of the cruelty or violence Nicole displayed.”

title: Netanyahu claims that Arab-led parties ‘stole’ the election as his bloc loses majority in Israel
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — Israel’s final election results confirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority and that weeks of difficult negotiations among very different parties, from ultra-Orthodox Jewish to secular to Arab-led, lie ahead.
The results released early Friday showed Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday’s election. The main opposition bloc won 48. Arab-led parties secured the other 19, a historic showing. Now parties must meet, bargain and seek a way to team up for at least 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, remains in charge.
“Now comes the truly hard part,” centrist politician Yair Lapid said on X, urging patience and adding: “If you want to know if something’s happening behind the silence you’re hearing now, the answer is yes.”
The president will task someone with forming a government
Difficult decisions lie ahead. Will the main opposition parties that campaigned hard to unseat the divisive Netanyahu make the politically sensitive choice to partner with Arab-led ones? Or will they toss their vows aside to team up with Netanyahu in a potentially fractious unity government?
Friday is when much of Israel starts winding down for Shabbat, and it was not clear who might be meeting with whom. Israelis debated possible coalitions and challenges, as some expressed traditional wariness around Arab parties and others insisted it was time for Israel to take a deep breath and embrace them.
“There are options for all of this, not like in the United States, where there are only two parties,” said Beny Engalrd, a resident of Tel Aviv.
The election results still need to be certified and submitted to the president next Wednesday. Then President Isaac Herzog will task someone with forming the new government. That could be the leader of the party that received the most votes — Netanyahu — or whoever leaders of the various parties believe is best suited.
If multiple attempts to form a government fail, Israel faces a new election early next year. Herzog this week said he will do everything in his power to avoid that scenario.
Netanyahu and Likud target Arab parties without evidence
In the hours before final results were announced, Netanyahu and his Likud party amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance.
The opposition quickly accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population, which makes up 20% of the population and showed up at the polls like never before in outrage over Netanyahu’s far-right allies like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. His party lost seats.
In Netanyahu’s first public comment Friday, he posted on X asserting it is forbidden to form a coalition with Arab parties.
The head of Israel’s election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, had said “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him. In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims but asked the agency to investigate.
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu’s party were accusing Qatar of involvement — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group. Qatar issued a denial, calling the allegations “ridiculous and dangerous.”
As it announced results, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. Acting Director General Dean Livne did not elaborate but warned that reports about the investigation had been “entirely unfounded.”
“It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population,” he said.
By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be trying to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab-led parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for chief rival Gadi Eisenkot or others to join with them.
The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to “cast aspersions” on an entire section of the population that “exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner.”
The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament, saying that “allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless.”
The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week.
Opposition could assert control in the upcoming Knesset
Even as coalition negotiations begin, the new Knesset is expected to be sworn in Nov. 10. Once it convenes, Eisenkot’s bloc could join forces with the Arab parties to elect a new Knesset speaker, giving them control over the parliamentary agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.
Already, hundreds of Israelis have been holding rallies urging Eisenkot and others to join forces with the Arab-led parties, a step that has happened only once before, briefly, in 2021.
“I believe we should join forces and cooperate with the Arab parties, a legitimate population in the state of Israel,” said Miri Sklair, a resident of Jaffa.
If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over yearslong corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into security failures before the devastating Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

title: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls.
It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores.
Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option.
Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access.
In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. The network encourages locals to eat healthy produce grown by themselves or their neighbors.
Aisha Ellis, farm manager for the network, said she has seen a difference in the 20 years the network has been in operation.
“You would start seeing people more regulated health wise. You’ll see people come back to life, participating. And you start creating different food traditions in your home,” Ellis said.
Through a local food co-op, an organic farm and meetings with local governments, the network is using Detroit as the launching point. Its goal is to spread the mission to other cities.
According to the Detroit Food Policy Council, 69% of Detroit households experience food insecurity.
Urban farming is one solution for food insecurity, but Ellis also said the organization works on policy - meaning access to food is also on the ballot Tuesday.

title: President Trump reshuffles schedule, adds back Iowa and Kansas rallies ahead of midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — As early voting surges across the country, President Donald Trump is reshuffling his weekend schedule to rally Republicans in two states with critical Senate races, underscoring his party’s push to drive turnout ahead of Election Day.
The Republican president will now visit Iowa and Kansas for back-to-back campaign rallies on Sunday, according to a person familiar with his plans who insisted on anonymity to discuss his schedule. Both rallies had previously been canceled.
The last-minute reversal comes amid a nationwide surge in early voting. Nearly 10 million more Americans had cast ballots five days before Election Day than at the same point in 2022, according to an Associated Press analysis of voting data. The increases have been particularly pronounced in states with competitive Senate races, including Iowa and Kansas, where early voting is up roughly 30%.
Democrats and Republicans each hope that rise favors them as they fight for control of Congress in an election that has turned largely on affordability issues and the president’s unpopularity. At the start of the month, Trump promised a marathon sprint of his signature rallies to shore up Republican candidates, and he has headlined 25 of them so far in October.
Weekend rallies back on after Trump says, ‘I don’t feel I have to go’
The president on Thursday furiously pushed back at the notion that the initial cancellation of his Kansas rally, which became public as he was returning to Washington from another campaign event in South Carolina, was tied to fatigue or his health. He lashed out at a reporter who asked about the change in his plans for Kansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is seeking reelection.
“I’m not going to Kansas because he’s doing very well,” Trump said, seeming to refer to Marshall. The president added that “I feel perfect” and that “I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas.”
The Republican National Committee initially said in canceling the rallies that Trump would do telerallies instead to reach more voters. But the person familiar with the latest plans said the Iowa and Kansas rallies have been rearranged to accommodate the new telerallies added to Trump’s schedule.
Trump’s original plans had him in Salina, Kansas, on Saturday and in Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday. Then the plans shifted so he would instead do a “72-hour sprint” of phone rallies, meant so the president could reach more voters nationwide, according to the RNC.
Sunday’s rally in Iowa will now be held in Cedar Rapids instead of Dubuque, according to another person familiar with the plans who spoke on the condition of anonymity to share information that was not yet public.
Both Kansas and Iowa are home to battleground Senate races that will help determine whether Republicans hold onto their narrow majority in the chamber in the midterm elections.
Trump has already traveled to both states this month to boost Marshall in Kansas and Republican Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, who currently serves in the House.
In an interview with a Kansas City radio station on Friday, Trump called Marshall “fantastic” and credited the senator for pushing his administration on policies benefiting Kansas farmers such as expanding tax-free use of red-dyed diesel.
Trump criticized Marshall’s Democratic challenger, Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton, as a “radical” who has “caused turmoil with the church because he’s so liberal.” Hamilton has said that if Jesus were standing before them now, “Roger Marshall would call him ‘woke.’”
Both parties hope a surge in voting favors them
Early voting is significantly outpacing the last midterm election, with millions more Americans casting ballots in advance.
In Texas, where voters are deciding closely watched Senate, House and governor’s races, more than 6.3 million Texans had voted early as of Wednesday, compared with 4.2 million at the same point four years ago, a 50% increase.
Advance voting has also increased more than 30% from the same point four years ago in Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Kansas, states with competitive Senate races. In South Carolina, where voters are choosing a successor to the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, early voting is up 83%.
Historic amounts of money have flowed into this year’s midterm elections. Republicans have expressed concerns about their voters not turning out amid voter dissatisfaction with Trump and high costs, issues Democrats have focused on in their campaigns.
In Michigan’s Senate race, the wrong Democrat remains in the headlines
Michigan Democrats hoped to put a bruising Senate primary behind them after progressive Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in August.
They’ve had no such luck as Election Day approaches.
Stevens reemerged in the final week before the general election, appearing on CNN to reaffirm that she would vote for El-Sayed while calling on him to repair relations with Jewish and Black voters. Her appearance came hours after her fiance said he would vote for El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.
Then on Friday, after agreeing to campaign alongside El-Sayed and Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina in Detroit on Sunday, Stevens released a lengthy statement on social media criticizing her former rival once again. She called on him to condemn an advertisement linking U.S. support for Israel to rising grocery prices and address concerns about his past rhetoric.
“Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens wrote. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”
El-Sayed has apologized for some of his past comments while attempting to unify Democrats.
