title: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
text:
(Aging Untold) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body.
‘Intense amount of burning’
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning.
“It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said.
She compared it to a toothache.
“You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said.
Her pain was on her back and flank.
“Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said.
Following the nerve pathway
The pain does not show up in random spots, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
“That’s the clue to people. It’s not like you’re going to get a spot over here that hurts, and then the spot on the right side hurts. It’s following what we call the dermatome of the nerve. So you can map out the nerve to see what’s happening,” Rogers said.
She said shingles is the same virus that causes chickenpox, but it is a reactivation.
What the rash looks like
The rash is distinctive, Cradduck said.
“Mine was very red, almost fiery red, but very close rash,” Cradduck said.
When she had shingles the second time it came back on the same nerve pathway and was not as bad.
“It is a crazy amount of pain,” Cradduck said.
The shingles vaccine
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said she is an advocate for the vaccine.
“The shingles vaccine, which I’m a real advocate for, is two shots. Some people forget to do the second shot,” O’Rourke said.
Rogers said the shingles vaccine does not take the condition away, but it may help if you get it.
“It may make your symptoms much milder,” Rogers said.
She said age and health play a role.
“As you get older, your immune system is not as effective. So you can’t fight things as well as you did, or if you’re under stress or have autoimmune disease or anything that compromised immune system,” Rogers said.
When the pain doesn’t go away
O’Rourke said a friend who had shingles ended up with eye nerve pain.
“It didn’t go away completely. Now he’s on medicine to treat the eye nerve pain, and that has its own side effects,” she said. “So it’s really a potentially long-term damaging disease.”
Like ‘a houseguest in the attic’
Cradduck explains shingles to people with an analogy.
“It’s kind of like having a bad houseguest that lives in the attic. And then every once in a while, it comes out and decides to wreak havoc, but only in one hallway. And then it goes back to the attic,” Cradduck said. “It can choose a different hallway. It can choose a different nerve path.”
Keeping the immune system strong
Rogers said a great immune system suppresses it.
“It doesn’t allow it to come out,” Rogers said.
Rogers said to minimize inflammation.
“That comes back down to the basics. It’s sleep, nutrition, all those different things help keep your immune system strong,” Rogers said.

title: North Korea linked to $6.3 billion hack on Binance, blockchain intelligence firms say
text:
(AP) - A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm says a North Korean unit was likely behind the hack that impacted more than $6 billion on Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets.
The cryptocurrency exchange said Friday that deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. It said it will cover all losses.
The company said on X Friday that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional “points of breach.”
TRM, in a post on its website Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea’s elite hacking unit. “We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said.
“An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes,” TRM said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.
In February last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.
“Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack,” TRM said.
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was “likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor,” its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. DPRK stands for the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name.
Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
In December 2022, South Korea’s spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea’s capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.
Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform, and stepped down as the company’s CEO. U.S. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.
Zhao posted Thursday on X that “User funds are safe!” but added that the theft “does look like a hack on Binance.” He added that while he doesn’t manage Binance anymore, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”
The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.
“This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet,” he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users’ “private keys,” or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Binance said on X it had “found no evidence of any wallet private key leak” and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

title: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
text:
SHELBURNE, Vt. (Aging Untold) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump.
Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver.
How she started
Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked.
Jordan died a decade ago.
“I miss her so much,” Meiler said.
Still competing at 91
Meiler continues to compete.
“I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said.
Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them.
“I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.”
Inspiring others
One of the people Meiler has inspired is University of Vermont freshman Jason Lei.
“I want to be moving like you when I’m older as well,” he told Meiler.
“It makes me feel like 60 again,” she said with a smile.
Meiler has also inspired Gene Meiler, her husband of 65 years.
“She’s impressed me, that’s for sure,” Gene Meiler said. “That’s why I married her. She impressed me.”
Flo Meiler said she is happy to continue running the track. When she feels like she is slowing down, she adds a few more exercises.
“I’m very happy,” Flo Meiler said. “The good Lord has given me my health and my talent.”

title: Trump says Iran war goal met as gas prices rise
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The U.S.-led war against Iran, which began February 28, has affected every part of America. Now it may play a critical role in the upcoming midterm elections.
President Donald Trump launched the war with one major objective: preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Earlier in the war, the president gave additional reasons for military action against Iran. At a recent campaign rally, Trump said that goal has already been met.
“We obliterated Iran’s nuclear enrichment capacity with Operation Midnight Hammer, Operation Epic Fury,” Trump said. “We defeated them militarily, financially and otherwise. And now we are ensuring just one thing: we have to make sure that they never, ever have a nuclear weapon, and we will do that very easily.”
Trump has made that declaration numerous times. On October 10, White House correspondent Jon Decker asked the president, “Why not just declare victory and be done with it?”
“Because I have to keep it that way,” Trump said. “I don’t want to do it in two years. We have to have a guarantee that they won’t do it in the future. It’s actually a very good question.”
Gas prices have risen 40% since the war began, while fighting between the U.S. and Iran continues. The average price of a gallon of regular gas is $4.20, according to AAA.
Diesel, which is primarily used by truckers and farmers, sells for an average of more than $6 per gallon.
Gas and diesel prices remain elevated because of continuous threats from Iran in the Strait of Hormuz.
Likely voters in key Senate races told pollsters that high prices for food and energy are their top concerns.
Trump has told reporters and supporters that gas prices will fall once the war with Iran ends. There is no sign the war, now entering its ninth month, will end soon.

title: Roof of a water tower in NYC where a rare family of barn owls nested has been removed
text:
Roof of a water tower in Manhattan where a rare family of barn owls nested has been removed
The roof of a water tower where a family of celebrity barn owls had been nesting in Manhattan’s Upper West Side has been removed, sparking outrage among New Yorkers who have been captivated by the elusive birds.
Related video above: Annual loon count finds the population in Maine is down, but not concerning
The barn owl family was discovered weeks ago, drawing crowds of people in the street eager to get a glimpse of the birds, including nature photographers. It is believed to be the first documented instance of barn owls nesting in Manhattan in modern history.
Jessica Wilson, the executive director of NYC Bird Alliance, said that she saw one barn owl fledgling Thursday on the roof of a nearby building after the roof of the water tower, which is located atop a building, was removed. Barn owl fledglings “should not be out in the middle of the day” because barn owls are nocturnal, she said.
“It had been disturbed from the nest,” Wilson added. “We didn’t see any more fledglings.”
NYC Bird Alliance received reports Thursday morning from residents and birders of work happening at the top of the tower, Wilson said. When Wilson got to the building, no workers were present. Enforcement police with the state Department of Environmental Conservation also arrived, Wilson said, and they all were able to access the building's roof with the permission of the building's superintendent. Wilson saw that the top of the water tower where the barn owls had been nesting was gone.
The New York Department of Environmental Conservation said in a statement that its police officers “investigated the area and found that the roof of the water tower on the building was removed, exposing the barn owl nest.”
The officers told the building owner to “halt demolition of the water tower until further notice” while the department investigates any potential violations, the department added.
Reached by phone, the building's superintendent declined to comment. It's not immediately clear who owns the building or ordered the removal of the water tower's roof.
Thomas Obersteiner, an Upper West Side resident, said he saw a man with an extension cord climbing down from the water tower around noon on Thursday.
The news of the water tower roof removal prompted criticism.
“I am outraged by reports that construction work on an Upper West Side water tower destroyed part of the structure that was home to Manhattan’s first Barn Owl nest, potentially endangering a pair of owls and their several fledglings," New York State Sen. Erik Bottcher said in a social media post, adding that “active migratory bird nests” are protected by state and federal law.
“Our city’s wildlife deserves protection, and there must be accountability when these protections are violated," Bottcher said.
“That nest was well-known, incredibly well-known, written about widely,” said David Barrett, a Manhattan-based birder who runs the popular social media account, Manhattan Bird Alert. "It should never have happened.”
Barrett said he observed the water tower Thursday and saw that the roof had been removed.
Birds have captivated New Yorkers in the past. Residents have fallen in love with American woodcocks, who are known to stop in Midtown Manhattan’s Bryant Park every year as they migrate north in early spring. After Flaco the Eurasian eagle-owl died in 2024, dozens of mournful fans gathered to say goodbye to the beloved creature who flew around Manhattan and became a joy to many after someone let him out of his zoo enclosure the previous year. Then there was Pale Male, a red-tailed hawk who nested above Fifth Avenue for three decades before dying in 2023.
Barn owl sightings in New York City parks are very rare, according to the New York City Department of Parks & Recreation. New York is at the northern fringe of the barn owl’s range and the barn owl population has declined “at an alarming rate” over time, according to the state Department of Environmental Conservation.
Barn owl fledglings depend on their parents to hunt for them because they don't know how to hunt yet, Wilson said. The fledglings' parents bring them food at their nest. Without the nest, Wilson added, "we’re worried that these barn owl fledglings might not survive.”

title: Dismayed by the relationship between Susan Collins and our military
text:
Casey Carbonneau was born, raised and lives in Maine. He has spent his career in technology, including a background in operational security and cybersecurity.
My background is in operational security and cybersecurity. I love what I do.
I worked at the Air Force as a civilian IT specialist. The program executive office I fell under was responsible for Air Force modernization. At the basic level, that meant making airmen’s jobs easier, better and safer. We were also unique because we saved money for the American taxpayer. What would normally take multiple aircraft and aircrews could, due to our work, be accomplished with one.
In early 2025, after Donald Trump took office and named Pete Hegseth his secretary of defense, we began seeing a disturbing level of operations security violations. Protocols were being ignored so unvetted individuals could access secure systems to harvest sensitive information at an astounding scale.
These problems were run up the chain of command. The response was that this is just what we are doing now, despite everyone in that chain of command being fully aware that ignoring the protocols and procedures unnecessarily put American lives at risk.
In my 20 years working in private and public organizations, I had never seen anything like it. We were being told to actively ignore our operations security training, even simple things like being ordered to respond to unknown emails lacking a cryptographic signature. This is training you would receive at any workplace in America that uses computers. And we were ordered to ignore it.
Knowing lives were at risk, I reached out to Sen. Susan Collins’ office. Not only was she representing me and my state as a senator, her positions on the Senate Appropriations Committee and the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence made her the most appropriate and best person to contact.
Despite repeated attempts of calling, emailing, sending letters and leaving voicemails requesting to speak with her, no one from her office followed up with me about these concerns. I requested a phone call from Sen. Collins or, preferably, a face-to-face meeting with her in a secure room. I provided my USAF position and explained that I could not share specifics due to national security concerns. What I was witnessing warranted such follow-up directly from her. I did not receive the requested follow-up, which I still deem to be necessary.
I left the Air Force in mid-2025 due to my conscience. I couldn’t be complicit in the death of my fellow Americans. The thought of a child losing a parent for completely preventable reasons was something I couldn’t be a part of.
After the war in Iran began, I had to read news reports of people I had worked with being killed in the Middle East, despite no declaration of war ever having been made. Susan Collins knows the war is unconstitutional, she knows America is being made less safe and she continues to do nothing.
So when the reports came out of her pay-to-play schemes with private defense contractors, it all made sense. The reason she never got back to me was she already knew what was happening. The current Trump administration has given her the green light to sell our military off to the highest bidder, foreign or domestic. Collins is pivotal in handing the keys to the United States military to private, for-profit companies. She is allowing them to put American lives at risk in return for money and power.
Some of our finest and bravest Americans have died while Collins looks the other way. American children go without parents because of her complicity and corruption.
Sen. Collins doesn’t just need to be voted out, she should be investigated for her actions.
Editor’s note: Asked about the author’s communication with Sen. Collins’ office, a spokesperson replied: “Mr. Carbonneau wrote or called us 10 times between 2013 and 2024. He received a response either in writing or through a call back from our staff to address his concerns, unless he indicated that he did not wish to receive a response.”

title: Netanyahu claims that Arab-led parties ‘stole’ the election as his bloc loses majority in Israel
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — Israel’s final election results confirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority and that weeks of difficult negotiations among very different parties, from ultra-Orthodox Jewish to secular to Arab-led, lie ahead.
The results released early Friday showed Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday’s election. The main opposition bloc won 48. Arab-led parties secured the other 19, a historic showing. Now parties must meet, bargain and seek a way to team up for at least 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, remains in charge.
“Now comes the truly hard part,” centrist politician Yair Lapid said on X, urging patience and adding: “If you want to know if something’s happening behind the silence you’re hearing now, the answer is yes.”
The president will task someone with forming a government
Difficult decisions lie ahead. Will the main opposition parties that campaigned hard to unseat the divisive Netanyahu make the politically sensitive choice to partner with Arab-led ones? Or will they toss their vows aside to team up with Netanyahu in a potentially fractious unity government?
Friday is when much of Israel starts winding down for Shabbat, and it was not clear who might be meeting with whom. Israelis debated possible coalitions and challenges, as some expressed traditional wariness around Arab parties and others insisted it was time for Israel to take a deep breath and embrace them.
“There are options for all of this, not like in the United States, where there are only two parties,” said Beny Engalrd, a resident of Tel Aviv.
The election results still need to be certified and submitted to the president next Wednesday. Then President Isaac Herzog will task someone with forming the new government. That could be the leader of the party that received the most votes — Netanyahu — or whoever leaders of the various parties believe is best suited.
If multiple attempts to form a government fail, Israel faces a new election early next year. Herzog this week said he will do everything in his power to avoid that scenario.
Netanyahu and Likud target Arab parties without evidence
In the hours before final results were announced, Netanyahu and his Likud party amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance.
The opposition quickly accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population, which makes up 20% of the population and showed up at the polls like never before in outrage over Netanyahu’s far-right allies like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. His party lost seats.
In Netanyahu’s first public comment Friday, he posted on X asserting it is forbidden to form a coalition with Arab parties.
The head of Israel’s election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, had said “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him. In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims but asked the agency to investigate.
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu’s party were accusing Qatar of involvement — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group. Qatar issued a denial, calling the allegations “ridiculous and dangerous.”
As it announced results, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. Acting Director General Dean Livne did not elaborate but warned that reports about the investigation had been “entirely unfounded.”
“It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population,” he said.
By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be trying to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab-led parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for chief rival Gadi Eisenkot or others to join with them.
The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to “cast aspersions” on an entire section of the population that “exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner.”
The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament, saying that “allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless.”
The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week.
Opposition could assert control in the upcoming Knesset
Even as coalition negotiations begin, the new Knesset is expected to be sworn in Nov. 10. Once it convenes, Eisenkot’s bloc could join forces with the Arab parties to elect a new Knesset speaker, giving them control over the parliamentary agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.
Already, hundreds of Israelis have been holding rallies urging Eisenkot and others to join forces with the Arab-led parties, a step that has happened only once before, briefly, in 2021.
“I believe we should join forces and cooperate with the Arab parties, a legitimate population in the state of Israel,” said Miri Sklair, a resident of Jaffa.
If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over yearslong corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into security failures before the devastating Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

title: Early voting jumps across Senate battlegrounds as millions more Americans vote ahead of Election Day
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Early voting is continuing to significantly outpace the last midterm election, with millions more Americans casting ballots in advance and particularly sharp increases in states hosting competitive Senate races, according to an Associated Press analysis of voting data five days before Election Day.
The surge is especially pronounced in Texas, where voters are deciding closely watched Senate, House and governor’s races. More than 6.3 million Texans had voted early as of Wednesday, compared with 4.2 million at the same point four years ago, a 50% increase.
Advance voting has also increased more than 30% from the same point four years ago in Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Kansas, states with competitive Senate races. In South Carolina, where voters are choosing a successor to the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, early voting is up 83%.
The data, compiled by the AP, offers a glimpse of early voter participation five days before an election that will determine control of Congress and other key contests.
Across the country, more than 43 million Americans had voted early in person or returned mail ballots, nearly 10 million more than in 2022. The figures cover 47 states and Washington, D.C., compared with 48 states and the nation’s capital four years ago.
In states that provide information on voters’ party affiliation, about 6.8 million Democrats and 5.2 million Republicans have cast ballots early. Those figures do not account for all early voters nationwide or indicate which candidates received their votes.
The increase comes as voters prepare to decide control of Congress two years into President Donald Trump’s second term, with Republicans holding the House and the Senate.

title: Brewers revel in their first World Series win with Milwaukee parade
text:
Brewers revel in their first World Series win with Milwaukee parade
Tens of thousands of exuberant Brewers fans flooded the streets, watched from parking garages, and cheered from office-building windows in downtown Milwaukee on Friday to celebrate the franchise's first World Series title.
The small-market Brewers gave their long-suffering fans the championship they had been waiting for with a 4-1 win over the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday, clinching the Series in five games. It was their first Fall Classic appearance in 44 years.
The team got off the bus and started walking the route on Friday while high-fiving the crowd. Later, the Brewers brought the trophy past the Bob Uecker mural along the parade route.
"Unbelievable," said parade attendee Mark Diedrich, a 76-year-old who has been an on-and-off partial season ticket holder since the 1980s. "You just never thought it would happen. But it did."
Players on buses chugged cans of Miller Lite beer, walked the parade route high-fiving fans and hoisted the Commissioner's Trophy as the cheers echoed through the streets. Every level of the Brewers franchise was represented in the parade, from owner Mark Attanasio to manager Pat Murphy, grounds crew members and behind-the-scenes staff.
The Johnsonville sausages, fan favorites that race during every home game, were also walking the parade route.
Brewers players, coaches and staffers waved to fans from the top of buses, some of them bearing the message, "Won. Our Way," to update their postseason slogan of “Win Our Way.” Several players, such as outfielder Sal Frelick and second baseman Brice Turang, removed their shirts in a nod to this season’s MLB-wide "Tarps Off" craze as they exhorted the crowd.
Sister station WISN's News Chopper 12 got an exclusive look at the Wisconsin National Guard flyover during the 2026 Brewers World Series Championship Parade.
The Wisconsin National Guard said it was a four-ship formation of UH-60 helicopters.
"We are proud to join the city of Milwaukee and citizens of Wisconsin in celebrating the Milwaukee Brewers' World Series victory!" the Wisconsin National Guard posted.

title: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
text:
(Aging Untold) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body.
‘Intense amount of burning’
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning.
“It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said.
She compared it to a toothache.
“You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said.
Her pain was on her back and flank.
“Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said.
Following the nerve pathway
The pain does not show up in random spots, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
“That’s the clue to people. It’s not like you’re going to get a spot over here that hurts, and then the spot on the right side hurts. It’s following what we call the dermatome of the nerve. So you can map out the nerve to see what’s happening,” Rogers said.
She said shingles is the same virus that causes chickenpox, but it is a reactivation.
What the rash looks like
The rash is distinctive, Cradduck said.
“Mine was very red, almost fiery red, but very close rash,” Cradduck said.
When she had shingles the second time it came back on the same nerve pathway and was not as bad.
“It is a crazy amount of pain,” Cradduck said.
The shingles vaccine
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said she is an advocate for the vaccine.
“The shingles vaccine, which I’m a real advocate for, is two shots. Some people forget to do the second shot,” O’Rourke said.
Rogers said the shingles vaccine does not take the condition away, but it may help if you get it.
“It may make your symptoms much milder,” Rogers said.
She said age and health play a role.
“As you get older, your immune system is not as effective. So you can’t fight things as well as you did, or if you’re under stress or have autoimmune disease or anything that compromised immune system,” Rogers said.
When the pain doesn’t go away
O’Rourke said a friend who had shingles ended up with eye nerve pain.
“It didn’t go away completely. Now he’s on medicine to treat the eye nerve pain, and that has its own side effects,” she said. “So it’s really a potentially long-term damaging disease.”
Like ‘a houseguest in the attic’
Cradduck explains shingles to people with an analogy.
“It’s kind of like having a bad houseguest that lives in the attic. And then every once in a while, it comes out and decides to wreak havoc, but only in one hallway. And then it goes back to the attic,” Cradduck said. “It can choose a different hallway. It can choose a different nerve path.”
Keeping the immune system strong
Rogers said a great immune system suppresses it.
“It doesn’t allow it to come out,” Rogers said.
Rogers said to minimize inflammation.
“That comes back down to the basics. It’s sleep, nutrition, all those different things help keep your immune system strong,” Rogers said.

title: Investigators are trying to figure out why 2 helicopters collided in Oregon, killing 3 people
text:
Federal investigators in Oregon will work to determine why a helicopter on a test flight collided with another chopper flown by a young instructor and her student, killing all three people aboard both aircraft.
The National Transportation Safety Board said Friday morning that its team was on its way to examine the wreckage near the airport in McMinnville, about an hour’s drive southwest of Portland. The town lies in the broad, flat Willamette Valley near the foothills of the Coast Range, in the heart of Oregon’s wine country.
The crash happened around 2 p.m. Thursday on a cloudy day. Law enforcement photos showed a crumpled red helicopter laying in a farm field, while a green helicopter came to rest upside down.
Leo Rodriguez was working on a nearby barn roof at his family’s winery when the helicopters collided.
“There was an explosion mid-air,” he told KPTV. “I bent over to do something and then, boom, and I look up and the planes were already going down.”
Rodriguez said the tail end of the larger helicopter was struck, then it turned and began going toward the ground. He said the other helicopter fell straight down.
“It just happened so fast,” he said.
Few details are immediately available about why the smaller Robinson R22 helicopter collided with the Airbus AS350B3 helicopter that the NTSB said was on a maintenance flight that is typically done after maintenance or repair. The Robinson was on an instructional flight.
The victims included 38-year-old Tyler Sturdevant, a pilot from Oregon, 22-year-old Maddie Aasbo, a flight instructor from Texas, and a 31-year-old student pilot from the United Kingdom, whose name has not been released, Yamhill County Sheriff Sam Elliott said during a news conference. Aasbo and the British student pilot were on the Robinson helicopter, while Sturdevant was on the Airbus.
The owners of the two helicopters — Jerry Trimble Helicopters and Precision — both said they are cooperating with authorities on the investigation while trying to help the grieving families of the victims.
Precision, a helicopter charter and maintenance company that also helps fly drone missions for the military, said in a post on Instagram that Sturdevant was their “beloved” senior pilot.
“Tyler has touched countless lives, not only through his love of flying, but through the many pilots he mentored, encouraged, and helped along the way,” Precision posted. “His legacy lives on in every pilot he helped bring up and every life he made a difference in.”
His LinkedIn page says he worked as a pilot examiner for the Federal Aviation Administration for the past four years while continuing to work at Precision for more than 20 years.
The Jerry Trimble school offers everything from demo flights for first-time flyers to advanced training.
___
Associated Press writers Jamie Stengle in Dallas and Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut, contributed.

Boston Celtics and Owners Give More Than $200 Million to Boston Children’s Hospital
New England’s basketball team and its ownership group have made a sizable donation to Boston Children’s Hospital.

Boston Children’s Hospital announced Oct. 29 that the Boston Celtics and their ownership group, in association with the Boston Celtics Shamrock Foundation, donated more than $200 million.
The gift is the largest in the hospital’s history. The announced total includes a $100 million gift from Celtics co-owner Rob Hale and his wife, Karen, first announced in December 2025. Their contribution supports the hospital’s new pediatric behavioral health campus.
Part of the funding will help build a children’s mental health facility on the Franciscan Children’s campus in Boston’s Brighton neighborhood.
A groundbreaking ceremony was held Oct. 8th for the project, whose first phase includes a planned 116-bed psychiatric hospital. The expansion is expected to nearly double Boston Children’s inpatient psychiatric capacity.
The donation will also support research into new treatments for childhood diseases and help establish an innovation fund for new approaches to children’s health care.
Additional funding will go toward advanced training for pediatric nurses and family programs that promote healthy lifestyles.
Founded in 1869 as a 20-bed hospital, Boston Children’s has grown into a 491-bed medical center serving children and adolescents.
It is also a pediatric teaching affiliate of Harvard Medical School.
And there you have it! The Boston Celtics and their ownership group have donated more than $200 million to Boston Children’s Hospital.

title: More than 42 million Americans have cast early midterm ballots
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting.
According to the University of Florida Election Lab, early midterm turnout is similar to the 2018 “blue wave.” The lab said enthusiasm appears to be on the Democrats’ side.
Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political scientist, said the U.S. could be headed toward record turnout.
“It’s possible that we will beat the 2018 turnout rate. That was the highest turnout rate for midterm elections since 1914. But there are uneven patterns of turnout,” McDonald said.
McDonald said the uneven turnout levels come from a partisan divide.
“Registered Democrats, unaffiliated, those people who don’t have a party registration, are engaged at the moment. But registered Republicans are not as much,” McDonald said.
Democrats account for 44% of early votes, compared with about 31% for Republicans.
McDonald said the early voting rate has increased this cycle for young voters and minorities.
“Makes me believe that this electorate is going to be the most diverse electorate for a midterm election in U.S. history. We can see high levels of engagement among AfricanAmericans, Hispanics, Asian Americans, but we don’t see as much among whites,” McDonald said.
There are limits to McDonald’s model. Not all states require party registration, and some states do not place much emphasis on early voting.
“So places like Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, they’re going to have maybe a third of their votes cast early. So they’re going to be very much unlike the vote by mail states or other states that have large volume of in-person early voting,” McDonald said.
McDonald said Democrats are building an early lead in early voting, but Republicans will make up some amount of ground on Election Day. Results won’t be announced until after the polls close Tuesday, November 3.

title: Bringing cancer screening conversations to the salon chair
text:
ANDRESON, S.C. (InvestigateTV) - Do you only go to the doctor when you have an ache or feel sick? For many women that answer can be “yes.”
A 2025 survey said that every one in six women say they missed or may have missed a routine cancer screening within the past year.
A South Carolina salon is partnering with a statewide health initiative to have important conversations about cancer screening with clients.
Kimberly Cheatham, owner of Kreative Kimistry in Anderson, has joined the Pink Palmetto Project, an effort by the South Carolina Cancer Alliance focusing on breast and cervical cancer education.
Cheatham said her clients often get personal with her.
“They confide in me when they don’t even feel comfortable telling their families things and their friends, because they know that I have a connection to them,” Cheatham said.
Personal loss drives mission
Cheatham’s mother died from colon cancer at age 62.
“I’m still dealing with the effects of it now because I have really bad PTSD about going to the doctor for, you know, getting my exams and stuff,” she said.
That loss motivates her to reach out to clients, particularly younger women.
“And that’s why I want to talk to women and just, especially like even younger women like the one that I have here, because the earlier you get this taken care of, the better,” Cheatham said.
Addressing disparities
Brenda Thorpe, senior community engagement director for the South Carolina Cancer Alliance, said data shows significant disparities in breast cancer outcomes.
“When I looked at the data, we see a huge disparity with women when it comes to breast cancer, right? That’s the most common cancer that women are impacted by. But the data also shows a disparity for African-American women. And so African-American women are diagnosed at a later stage for breast cancer,” Thorpe said.
When diagnosed in later stages, treatment is often harsher, and the chance of survival can go down. According to Breast Cancer Prevention Partners, black women have a 40% higher death rate from breast cancer compared to white women.
Nicole Echols, CEO of the South Carolina Cancer Alliance, said salons provide a comfortable setting to reach women.
“We know that we can get into the spaces and have conversations and talk to women about how important it is for their breast health and how important screening is and how important early detection is and how it really can save your life,” Echols said.
The project aims to ensure women know the signs of cancer and keep up with their screenings.
“The grief and the emotions that I went through, I wouldn’t want anybody to have to go through that,” Cheatham said. “So, if you can go and prevent that from happening, then I really feel like if I can help you do that.”
Kreative Kimistry is the only salon in the Upstate participating in the Pink Palmetto Project. The South Carolina Cancer Alliance hopes to expand the program with additional funding.
Skin cancer screening
Hair stylists are playing another vital role in cancer screening.
Stylists Against Skin Cancer is a dermatologist-led educational campaign for hair professionals that focuses on the detection and prevention of skin cancer in the scalp.
Because hair professionals see the entire scalp, they can find suspicious skin growth that clients might not see or feel. Then they can encourage the customer to visit a dermatologist for further investigation.

title: Family says animal hospital worker took pug home after they paid for euthanasia
text:
COWETA COUNTY, Ga. (WSB) — A Georgia family said they paid hundreds of dollars for an animal hospital to euthanize their 4-year-old pug, then learned months later the dog was still alive.
The family said they were shocked by the discovery. They believe a worker at the hospital took the dog home.
Dog became sick
Rebecca Belote said her 17-year-old son and the pug, named Cha Cha, wore matching hoodies.
“She hardly walked anywhere because he carried her everywhere,” Belote said.
Belote said Cha Cha then became sick. She said the family was told the dog was in organ failure and had diabetic ketoacidosis.
Belote said Senoia Animal Hospital recommended the dog be euthanized. She said the decision affected her son and her husband.
“They both took it kind of hard. My son was really attached to the dog,” Belote said.
Photo on Facebook
The family said Cha Cha was not euthanized in March as they believed and that a hospital worker took the dog home, keeping her for months.
Belote said she was on Facebook when she saw a picture of Cha Cha.
“I knew scrolling like, ‘That’s my dog,’” Belote said.
Belote said a former hospital worker confirmed a hospital employee took Cha Cha.
Hospital denies claim
Belote said the hospital denied the claim.
“They have a lawyer and they won’t talk about it. They just say it didn’t happen,” Belote said.
Belote said she spoke with the worker’s husband, who confirmed his wife had Cha Cha. She said he told her the pug was in good health.
Belote said the hospital eventually put Cha Cha down. She said she thinks the hospital did so to hide what happened.
“The fact that they put a healthy dog down. That’s just sick,” Belote said.
The animal hospital did not respond with a statement.

title: Searsmont welcomes home Robbins family member months after deadly lumber mill explosion
text:
As she prepared to come home from Massachusetts General Hospital after five and a half months there, Lily Robbins asked if she could drive the ambulance herself. Her supervisor at Searsmont EMS, where Robbins is a volunteer, laughed.
“I told her it was too soon!” recalled Amy Drinkwater, the interim EMS chief.
Robbins and several others were seriously injured in a fire and explosion at Robbins Lumber mill on May 15. They were all either first responders or members of the Robbins family, and Lily Robbins is both. Three people have died, including Lily’s father, Alden Robbins.
On Friday, though, Drinkwater’s recollection reflected the celebratory mood: Lily Robbins was finally coming home to Searsmont. Drinkwater, who has visited her at the hospital recently, said Robbins has been eager to get back and to do medical work again.
She left Mass General on Friday midday. A caravan of seven trucks from the Searsmont Fire station went to pick her up, joined along the way by first responder vehicles from dozens of agencies, including many that had been in Searsmont on May 15.
Arriving back on Friday for a reception, trucks rang their bells and honked horns, and a crowd of locals, friends and extended family members cheered and waved.
Robbins walked slowly into the fire station, greeting people. One hand was wrapped in a bandage; burn marks showed on the other and on her face. Robbins looked at the little kids holding up “welcome home” signs.
“Thank you all so much,” she said. Later, she added thanks for everyone who has sent cards, letters or gifts.
“I’ve read every single word of every single card I got, and it made me smile,” she said.
She went into a deep embrace with three of her closest friends from college who are all paramedics — Taylor Church, Blake Tripp and Lila Bell. With tears streaming down their faces, they said it doesn’t feel real to have Robbins home at last.
Church said she’s been texting nonstop with Robbins, and they already have plans to get together at Church’s house.
The day was meant to feel like a big hug for Robbins and her family, said Jodi Staples, a fellow EMS volunteer who was driving one of the ambulances in the procession on Friday. Supporters started bringing homemade cookies and signs to the fire station earlier in the morning. Deb Pickering came from Belfast wearing a Searsmont Strong T-shirt.
“We want to let her know we’ve been thinking about her all this time,” Pickering said.
Members of the Robbins extended family came with signs, too.
“We have prayed so hard for her,” Lily’s great aunt Suzanne Philbrook said with tears in her eyes. “We’re so grateful God spared her life.”
On May 15, a silo full of wood shavings at Robbins Lumber caught fire, exploded and rocketed off the ground about an hour after the initial fire. Dozens of volunteer firefighters and EMS personnel had arrived at the mill. Morrill volunteer firefighter Andrew Cross died the same day, and Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury died in June, shortly before Alden Robbins.
Other people injured in the explosion were on hand Friday to help welcome Lily Robbins home, including Thomas Wolf, a Searsmont Fire volunteer and an employee of Robbins Lumber. He walked into the fire station on Friday morning to take his place in the procession.
“Hospitals are great but there’s nothing more satisfying than being at home,” he said. “I can’t wait for Lily to get home and be in that environment.”
Wolf’s most severe injuries were to his head; he also has visible scarring from burns on his hands, though he said he can now hold a pencil to write. He has returned to work at Robbins and intends to volunteer with the fire service again.
The explosion has motivated more people in town to volunteer, as well. Searsmont Selectman Chris Staples said he thinks eight people have joined the fire and EMS, doubling the roster.
He decided to volunteer himself and plans to take his fire truck driving test on Sunday.
Robbins’ homecoming reception is healing for the town, said Clerk Angela Cilley. When Cilley posted about it on Facebook hundreds of people cheered the news and Lily Robbins responded, saying, “I’m so grateful for this community.”
“It’s something joyful for the town after so much uncertainty and loss,” Cilley said on Friday. “I think people want to see her face to make sure it’s real.”
The family founded Robbins Lumber in 1881 and still operates it, which is a point of pride in the community. The town and the company are closely intertwined. Searsmont is raising relief funds by selling stickers, hats and shirts with an image of Robbins Lumber alongside fire department and EMS logos. Kids from the area often take field trips and tours of the lumberyard.
Lily Robbins, 23, graduated from the University of Maine a week before the explosion and plans to apply to medical school, her great aunt Jane Newcomb said Friday.
The Midcoast Villager reported Robbins needed several blood transfusions during her treatment at Mass General. A GoFundMe organized by the restaurant where she worked in Camden to support her recovery has raised more than $81,000.
Investigations into the fire and explosion are ongoing. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration has a mid-November deadline to release its findings. In August, a separate agency, the National Institute of Occupational Safety and Health, called for better labeling and identification of hazards at silos and more training to deal with them.

title: Customers suffer chemical burns after drinking margaritas at a NC Chili’s, officials say
text:
FOREST CITY, N.C. (WHNS/Gray News) – A round of drinks turned into a medical nightmare when three customers ordered margaritas and immediately suffered chemical burns inside and around their mouths.
Health officials investigating the incident at a Chili’s Grill & Bar in Forest City, North Carolina, said the drinks were contaminated after a powerful industrial degreaser was mistaken for sugar.
The dangerous mix-up began when a restaurant worker obtained granulated degreasing agent from an outside contractor power-washing the building’s exterior, according to the Foothills Health District.
The employee poured the chemical into an unlabeled container, brought it inside and left it in the bar area. The next day, another employee assumed the white granular substance was sugar and used it to prep the bar’s margarita station.
Shortly after the three customers took their first sips and suffered burns, employees who tasted the mixture reported identical burning symptoms.
County health inspectors immediately suspended the restaurant’s food service permit and mandated a full sanitation of the facility.
The permit was reinstated Thursday after Environmental Health Specialists verified all corrective actions were completed, according to Health Director Jason Masters, who emphasized that state food codes strictly require proper labeling, storage and handling to prevent chemical contamination.

title: Scottish police conduct inquiries into ex-Prince Andrew and Epstein's visit to king's estate
text:
Scottish police conduct inquiries into ex-Prince Andrew and Epstein's visit to king's estate
Police in Scotland are conducting inquiries into the time former Prince Andrew spent at the king’s private estate at Balmoral with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, authorities said Friday.
Police Scotland said the inquiries were at a "very early stage."
"All inquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries," police said in a statement. "We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further."
Images released earlier this year by the U.S. Department of Justice appeared to show the former prince, now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, on a shooting trip at the estate with Epstein.
Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested and held for hours by British police in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office related to his links to Epstein.
It was the first time in nearly four centuries that a senior British royal had been arrested.

title: Experts eye key voting blocs ahead of Midterms
text:
NEW YORK CITY (Gray Media) - With millions of ballots already cast ahead of Election Day, conversations surrounding voter turnout are intensifying. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress.
Lincoln Mitchell, a political analyst and professor at Columbia University, says the first group feeling pressure is rural voters. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. While Mitchell does not expect these voters to dramatically flip parties, financial strain could depress turnout or weaken enthusiasm for Republicans and President Donald Trump.
The second crucial bloc is Latino voters. Mitchell notes that while the demographic is far from monolithic, its influence will be decisive in battleground states—particularly Texas, home to one of the cycle’s most competitive Senate races. Despite recent gains made by the GOP among Hispanic voters in states like Texas, Arizona, and Florida, Mitchell questions whether those inroads will hold over the long run.
Finally, experts are watching young white men, a demographic that turned out heavily for Trump in 2024. Mitchell points to foreign policy and affordability as two major factors driving potential shifts. If even a fraction of these voters stay home or shift away from the GOP, the ripple effect could be devastating for Republican candidates on the ballot.
Midterm elections historically cut against the party occupying the White House. Looking to buck that precedent, President Trump has urged supporters to vote as if his name were directly on the ballot. Tuesday night will reveal whether that mobilization strategy succeeded, or if shifting voter dynamics hand Democrats a major breakthrough.

title: Boothbay Region Surveyors Relocates to Former Midcoast Conservancy Building
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After sitting vacant for almost a year, the former Route 1 headquarters of Midcoast Conservancy now has new inhabitants.
Boothbay Region Surveyors moved into the space at 290 Route 1 in Edgecomb in early October purchasing the building in March. Midcoast Conservancy moved out of the building in October 2025 and moved all services to its office in Waldoboro.
Owner Nicholas Plummer said his goal with the new space is to consolidate all of his files in one location and also bring the company more visibility.
“My first criteria was to have all of my files in one location,” Plummer said. “It gives us a little more room to spread out. We were kind of all crammed into one floor.”
Plummer has been a professional land surveyor since 2017 and created Boothbay Region Surveyors the same year, buying the records of other surveyors. Over the years, he continued to buy out other surveyors, and he is now the steward of over 20,000 records and files from different land surveys completed by almost 10 other surveyors.
Before moving into the new space on Route 1, Plummer was storing two-thirds of his files at the company’s original office at the Old Town Garage in Boothbay. When landlord died last year, Plummer said the family decided to sell the building so he began searching for a place to move his business. The rest of his files were stored in Bristol in an outbuilding near his home.
The renovation included making one room a “dry plan room,” Plummer said, designed to keep moisture out to preserve the documents within. The room contains 42 filing cabinets full of records.
“I have the records of a lot of people,” Plummer said.
Plummer said he worked out a deal with Midcoast Conservancy. To get a better price, he offered some of his services with the purchase. He referenced the organization’s mission statement and its goal to expand its 16,000 acres of conserved land to 30,000 by 2030.
“So I thought, hey, they might need a surveyor,” Plummer said.
Midcoast Conservancy co-Executive Director of Engagement Stephanie Hanner said the organization is “very pleased” with the arrangement with Plummer and his business. The sale included a combination of cash and surveying services, which Hanner said will allow Midcoast Conservancy to meet some of its surveying needs while also allowing their former building to continue to be “purposeful” to the community.
“It’s a good example of how creative, mutually beneficial arrangements can work well for local organizations and businesses,” Hanner said. “We look forward to continuing to work with our existing surveying partners as well.”
Surveyors are responsible for looking for the boundaries of a property, whether that is a stone wall, stream, or roadway. Plummer said the secondary job within his profession is to help with site development.
While some of the tools are advanced and designed with modern day technology, Plummer said the surveyor’s metal detector has not changed in 40 years.
“The technology that we use is growing a little bit,” Plummer said.
Boothbay Region Surveyors serves customers from the Boothbay region to Rockland to Bangor.
The new location is also next to a substation and Plummer said he hopes the building will not lose power in a storm or outage so he and his team can work consistently throughout the year. He also said the more central location on the main road helps with the commute for his employees.
“Someone’s dreams of moving to the Midcoast of Maine is not going to stop because there’s an ice storm,” Plummer said. “They still have to meet whatever deadline for spring start of construction and they need their survey done in January.”
For more information, call 633-4445 or go to brsmaine.org.

title: 4 more activists charged in intimidation campaign against University of Michigan over Israel ties
text:
DETROIT (AP) — Four more people have been charged with participating in a criminal intimidation campaign against University of Michigan officials to try to force the school to cut financial ties to Israel, federal authorities said Friday.
The new indictment comes nearly five months after eight pro-Palestinian activists were charged with conspiracy.
The indictment describes threats and vandalism at officials’ homes, some businesses and the Jewish Federation of Detroit.
Investigators have highlighted several incidents over the past few years, including fake bloody corpses that were placed in a university board member’s yard and the 2024 spray-painting of anti-Israel messages at the home of Santa Ono, who was school president at the time.
Two of the four new defendants were arrested and will make their first court appearance Friday while the other two people were not in custody, the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Detroit said.
The eight people charged in June have pleaded not guilty.
“From Pharaoh to Hitler to Hamas, those who terrorize Jews have been the bad guys. As Americans, our job is to fight the bad guys,” U.S. Attorney Jerome Gorgon Jr. said.
Since the Israel-Hamas war began, pro-Palestinian protesters have demanded that the University of Michigan’s endowment stop investing in companies with ties to Israel. But the university has said it has less than 0.1% of its total endowment placed with funds that might include companies in Israel.
In 2024, a pro-Palestinian camp on campus was cleared by police after a month. The university said it was a threat to public safety.

title: Three Bob Fergusons and two JFKs: A brief history of same-name ballot confusion
text:
Three Bob Fergusons and two JFKs: A brief history of same-name ballot confusion
Before there were two Dan Sullivans, there were three Bob Fergusons.
In 2024, Washington’s Democratic state Attorney General Bob Ferguson was joined in the gubernatorial primary race by two other Democratic hopefuls with the same name.
Was it a coincidence? More like an age-old election trick that’s come up again in this year’s tightly contested Alaska U.S. Senate race.
In Washington two years ago, a Republican activist had paid the other two Bob Fergusons to run in the hopes that their names on the ballot would confuse voters — an effort to weaken the attorney general’s candidacy. But the decoys ultimately dropped out after just a few days when the first Bob Ferguson, who went on to be elected governor, threatened legal action and publicly derided their candidacy as an “attack on our democracy.”
Now, the tables have turned with Republicans accusing Democrats of a similar ploy in Alaska. A New York Times story Wednesday revealed that Democrats appeared to be behind having a potential Republican spoiler candidate, retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan, siphon votes from incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. The Justice Department has preemptively sued to block the results if the incumbent loses. Both Alaska and DOJ are investigating, and President Donald Trump has called for the criminal prosecution of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, writing in a Truth Social post that she should “suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done.”
“So should the FAKE Dan Sullivan,” Trump wrote. “Nothing else will do!”
But there’s a long history of political operatives from both parties deploying the tactic — and largely getting away with it.
“It’s a time-honored tradition,” said Thomas Kahn, director of the Center for Congressional and Presidential Studies at American University.
“It’s not a good practice,” Kahn added, but “if trying to confuse voters was a crime, then every politician would be in jail.”
The case of the spoiler grocery clerk
One century-old example of same-name ballot stacking came in the 1930 Nebraska Republican U.S. Senate primary, when incumbent George W. Norris was dismayed to suddenly see another George W. Norris, a grocery clerk, running. “I’m finished unless the other George W. Norris is kept off the ballot,” the incumbent senator said at the time.
It was ultimately a technicality that spoiled the candidacy for the spoiler grocer. Just as Sen. Norris prepared to withdraw from the Republican primary and run as an independent, the chief justice of the Nebraska Supreme Court ruled that the other Norris was ineligible because his petition had not been legally filed in time.
Perhaps no other same-name candidate was more opportunistic than the “other JFK.” Rather than a decoy deployed by the opposite party, John Francis Kennedy, a Gillette razor factory stockroom supervisor, was a private citizen who merely capitalized on the Massachusetts name recognition of then-Sen. John Fitzgerald Kennedy. John Francis filed for state treasurer in 1954 and won without any party endorsement or public campaigning.
The high school dropout from South Boston went on to win three terms. During his 1956 reelection bid, he was challenged by another political newcomer who entered the race because he was outraged that someone would pirate the good name of the Massachusetts senator. That candidate’s name was John M. Kennedy.
Simply possessing the same name as a candidate is constitutionally protected under ballot access rules. Criminality occurs when operatives cross into falsifying residency documents, laundering campaign funds or offering direct payments in exchange for filing.
That was the case in Florida in 2020. Authorities claimed that Republican state Sen. Frank Artiles recruited “ghost candidate” Alex Rodriguez with a $50,000 payment to run for office in the Florida legislature and to cause the Democratic incumbent with the same surname, Jose Javier Rodriguez, to lose the election by taking votes away in the razor-thin race. Alex Rodriguez received over 6,000 votes in the election, and Republican candidate Ileana Garcia beat the incumbent by just 32 votes.
Artiles was ultimately convicted of excessive campaign contributions and procuring the falsification of a candidate oath form. Alex Rodriguez had sworn that he lived in the district’s limits when he actually resided in another county.
While Florida law permits ghost candidates but prohibits people making excessive amounts of campaign contributions over $1,000, Bob Ferguson leaned on an 81-year-old Washington state law that makes it a felony to challenge someone with the same name “and whose political reputation is widely known, with intent to confuse and mislead the electors” to get the other two Bob Fergusons to drop their candidacies after just 72 hours when he threatened legal action.
Jockeying on the Alaska ballot
In Alaska, Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy said in a post on X that he would investigate if the “scheme” of recruiting a second Dan Sullivan to run “violated Alaska’s laws.” The Department of Justice last week preemptively filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate election if the incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, asking the court to potentially delay the certification of the election if the incumbent is defeated but would have won if “all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan” had “been cast instead for Senator Sullivan.”
Legal experts have said the suit is unlikely to succeed. The state’s Supreme Court already ruled to keep the retired teacher on the ballot and Alaska’s Division of Elections sought to differentiate between the two Sullivans by listing the senator as the incumbent Republican and the other without a party affiliation.
Alaska’s top-four primary election process — where the top four vote-getters advance to the general election regardless of their partisan affiliations — and ranked-choice voting system make the state particularly susceptible to same-name and spoiler candidate hijinks. The ranked-choice system, however, allows voters to show a preference for more than one candidate, so even if voters were hypothetically confused about which Dan Sullivan to vote for, they could select both, which would still favor the incumbent senator over Peltola.
The August primary for Alaska’s Senate seat saw multiple efforts to boost minor candidates to hurt Peltola or the incumbent Sullivan. One group, Fair Deal Alaska, spent more than $800,000 attacking Peltola while promoting a lesser-known Democratic candidate and a Green Party candidate. A post-primary campaign finance filing revealed the group was mostly funded by the Senate Leadership Fund, the top GOP super PAC in Senate races.
And in 2024, Alaska’s Democratic Party sued to keep someone off the U.S. House ballot: Eric Hafner, who has no apparent ties to the state and is serving time in a federal prison in New York. The Democratic Party argued that it and its preferred candidate — ironically, Peltola — would be harmed because having an unaffiliated Democrat on the ballot “would confuse voters.”
A divided state Supreme Court allowed Hafner to remain on the ballot. He is running again this year, also in the House race, and is on the November 3 ranked vote general election ballot.

title: Ted Cruz takes up Maine lobstering bill pushed by Susan Collins
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON — Senate Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz said his panel will take up legislation next month to extend a moratorium on new North Atlantic right whale protections, a move the Texas Republican credited to Maine GOP Sen. Susan Collins five days out from one of the most pivotal elections of her career.
Collins, who is in a competitive reelection campaign against Democratic nominee Troy Jackson, requested the committee take up the lobster industry-backed bill in a September letter with Sen. Angus King, I-Maine.
Cruz wrote Thursday on X that Collins’ “leadership has been instrumental in advancing this bill to protect Maine’s lobstermen from burdensome regulations. I hope we can move this bill without changes or further delay to put on President Trump’s desk ASAP.”
The House-passed bill is a priority for the state’s lobster industry, which argues an extension of the moratorium, set to expire Dec. 31, 2028, for another seven years would provide greater certainty — particularly with the presidency up in the air in 2028.
Congress first imposed the moratorium in late 2022 at the behest of the Maine delegation on both sides of the aisle, inserting it into a year-end spending package.
The move came in response to a Biden administration “biological opinion” issued in 2021 recommending tougher restrictions to try to keep the endangered right whales from getting tangled up in commercial fishing lines — a major contributor to the population’s decline.
But the potential for major changes such as a mandate to use “ropeless” gear and fishery closures was too much for the Maine lobster industry, which fears a future administration could revive similar efforts.
To try to balance the concerns of environmentalists, the 2022 law appropriated $20 million to “support the adoption of innovative fishing gear deployment and fishing techniques to reduce entanglement risk to North Atlantic right whales,” part of an overall $280 million appropriated in recent years for right whale recovery efforts.
The Maine Department of Marine Resources has been using the congressionally appropriated funds to collect data for the past few years. Collins and King wrote last month that extending the regulatory pause would allow such efforts to continue and better inform future decisions.
According to the Maine Lobstermen’s Association, the industry supports about $2 billion in annual economic activity and 17,500 jobs.
“It is critical that any future regulatory actions appropriately balance protecting North Atlantic right whales with the economic and practical realities facing Maine’s lobster industry,” Collins and King wrote.
Tight margins
Compounding matters for the industry has been tariff-driven uncertainty and higher inflation.
In response to Trump administration tariffs, the Canadian government initially retaliated against a range of U.S. exports, including seafood; after Collins and others intervened, Canada walked those levies back.
Still, other tariffs and cost increases have hit the industry hard, said Curt Brown, president of Bold Coast Seafood in Prospect Harbor, Maine. “Our traps are built of vinyl-coated steel. Trap prices have gone up, bait prices have gone up, fuel prices have gone up. So margins are tight,” he said.
Brown and other industry representatives say implementing greater protections for right whales would make matters worse, increasing costs and potentially forcing some lobstermen out of business.
“I don’t think you will find any fisherman that says they want to harm a whale; we all support very healthy oceans,” said Virginia Olsen, executive liaison and political director for Maine Lobstering Union Local 207.
But Olsen, whose family has worked in the lobster business for five generations, said more time is needed to study the new data coming in through the Maine Department of Marine Resources’ research.
Hence the Trump administration-backed legislation introduced by Reps. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y. — another top midterm target of Democrats — and Jared Golden, D-Maine, who is retiring, to extend the moratorium through 2035.
It passed the House on Sept. 1, but not without opposition from most Democrats and even a couple Republicans sympathetic to the whales’ plight. The vote was 219-196, with 10 Democrats in favor and two Republicans opposed — Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Aaron Bean of Florida.
While Fitzpatrick has previously voted against his party on matters concerning endangered species, Bean represents Amelia Island, the winter calving and nursery ground for the whales. Amelia Island has its own cottage industry to protect, with the annual Right Whale Festival scheduled for next month.
Aside from Golden and fellow Maine Rep. Chellie Pingree, other House Democrats who supported the measure include those in tough races in swing districts, such as Washington’s Marie Gluesenkamp Perez and Texas’ Vicente Gonzalez.
Maggie Goodlander and Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, next door to Maine, also supported the bill. Pappas is running for Senate to replace the retiring Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, against former GOP Sen. John Sununu; Inside Elections rates the race Tilt Democratic.
Lame-duck opportunity
With Democrats expected to make big gains next Tuesday, the lame-duck session may be the best chance for the bill’s supporters to get the bill enacted.
While Pingree is herself a senior Appropriations Committee member, the potential losses of Collins and Lawler, combined with Golden’s scheduled departure, could make it an uphill climb in the 120th Congress.
Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales rates Collins’ and Lawler’s races each a Toss-up.
The bill has already been an assist to Lawler, who has pointed to it as evidence of his ability to work across the aisle. His race is in a district former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024.
Golden originally introduced his own bill that would implement an identical extension. Lawler, who represents a landlocked district in New York’s Hudson Valley, said he joined the effort through a desire to “fight for small business.”
Golden returned the favor last month by endorsing Lawler in his hometown paper The Journal News, highlighting their cooperation on the bill.
The reasons for House GOP leaders taking up Lawler’s identical, separate bill have never been made clear; some speculate it simply has to do with ensuring the credit goes to a vulnerable Republican.
While a Senate Commerce markup could give the measure some momentum, the battle for floor time in November and December will be intense. Collins, the Senate Appropriations chair, could try to insert the bill into another year-end spending package, though her staff wouldn’t comment on legislative strategy.
‘False dichotomy’
The North Atlantic right whale, with a remaining population of roughly 380, has been experiencing what’s known as an “unusual mortality event” under the Marine Mammal Protection Act for the last decade. Over 20% of the whales have either been either killed or injured, largely due to entanglements in fishing gear and collisions with ships.
Still, supporters of the bill point to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data showing an increase in the number of individual whales since 2020, and 2026 was the largest calving season since the beginning of the unusual mortality event.
Jason Joyce, a lobsterman and director of advocacy for the New England Fishermen’s Stewardship Association, said the numbers demonstrate the need for more data before new regulations are imposed.
“What has happened since the current pause was put into place is births are up and deaths are down, so we’re in a better position now than we were when they were going to overregulate us,” Joyce said.
But Katherine Sayler, southeast representative for Defenders of Wildlife, said even with the recent growth the population is still down significantly compared to historical population levels.
“We’re not even close to the 500 North Atlantic right whales that we estimated in the population approximately 20 years ago,” said Sayler.
Dan Moss, senior government relations representative for Defenders of Wildlife, added that the bill would sideline the work of a team established by NOAA nearly three decades ago to address risk to whales, and that it effectively ignores a court ruling that found current regulations for right whales in lobster fisheries are insufficient under federal law.
Backers and opponents of the bill have focused on the potential for regulations requiring the use of ropeless gear to reduce whale entanglements.
In this system, there’s still rope to connect individual traps, however it lacks the vertical line that leads to a buoy. Instead it relies upon systems that remain submerged until the trap owner triggers them just prior to retrieval.
During House floor debate, Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman, D-Calif., argued that the federal government was “dragging its feet” on right whale regulations, including by de-prioritizing ropeless gear.
Both Olsen and Joyce said there are significant safety concerns related to the design of ropeless gear, since crew could become entangled without a simple method to retrieve them as with conventional gear.
“If my crew is wrapped and entangled in that rope and goes overboard, in my panic, I have to stop, grab a tablet, log in, open the app, deploy the buoy, wait for the buoy to get to the surface, and then put it in my hauler,” Olsen said. “There’s no way that my crew is going to come up alive.”
But Sayler argued the bill creates “the false dichotomy that there cannot be coexistence between fisheries and whales at a time when they face so many threats.”
She said that right whales play an important role in the ocean ecosystem through the nutrients they create and “that they are worth having on the planet for their incredible intrinsic value.”
Story by David Jordan, CQ-Roll Call, Inc. Distributed by Tribune Content Agency, LLC.

title: Aging Untold: When health changes your sex life, intimacy doesn’t have to disappear
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we address how aging and illness can impact intimacy, sharing practical ways for couples to talk openly and safely navigate sex after a diagnosis.
Then, we discuss clinical trials, why older adults are frequently underrepresented and what questions to ask before participating in a study.
Plus, we meet a 91-year-old world record holder in track and field proving that staying active has no age limit.
Health can affect intimacy as we age and the Aging Untold experts are addressing questions many couples are afraid to ask out loud: When is it safe to resume sex? What if it isn’t? And what should you ask your doctor?
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first step is figuring out what’s behind the change. Competence and consent are the first things to consider, she said.
For physical issues, like erectile dysfunction, a doctor can often help.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said one of the biggest misconceptions couples carry is treating intimacy and sexuality as interchangeable — and they’re not.
Older adults are often left out of clinical trials, but they can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, according to the Aging Untold experts.
When considering a clinical trial, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the first step is to think about what the clinical trial is trying to answer.
Many people see clinical trials as a last resort, but one of the biggest benefits is access, Rogers said.
“You get great access to tomorrow’s medicines today — devices, therapies and other things that will not be available to everybody else for years.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said participants should know going into a trial that they might receive a placebo.
Read the full article for more on clinical trials, how to find them and which ones compensate participants.
The long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach, according to new research.
There are new studies indicating that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy.
According to a study released in October 2025, peanut allergy rates in children under 3 have dropped by roughly 43% over the last decade.
Flo Meiler’s home is filled with medals, and she holds two world records.
The Vermont woman started competing in track and field at 60, and she was hooked. She is now 91 and still competes.
“I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said.
