title: 4 hospitalized after lightning strike at elementary school
text:
EL MIRAGE, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — Authorities in Arizona say several adults were injured by a lightning strike at an elementary school bus drop-off Friday morning.
First responders said they were called just after 8:30 a.m. for reports of a lightning strike at El Mirage Elementary School.
Four people, all identified as adults, were conscious and taken to a nearby hospital for treatment, according to the El Mirage Police Department.
El Mirage Fire Captain Joseph Rivera said one woman was holding an umbrella when lightning struck in the vicinity. The woman reported feeling pain in both of her arms.
Capt. Rivera said none of the people were directly struck by the lightning.
Carrie, a librarian at the El Mirage Library across the street, said she was doing her morning duties before the strike.
“The lightning and the thunder were right on top of each other, so loud that it made me jump,” she said. “It felt like the building almost shook.”
Carrie said the strike was followed by a wave of “at least a dozen” car alarms going off across the street.
“It’s wild,” she added. “Then the rain just came down in buckets.”
The strike happened during the first round of storms that began passing through the Phoenix area Friday morning.
Around 8 a.m., fast-moving storms began passing through the area, with viewers reporting hail and heavy rain in Peoria, Sun City and Buckeye.

title: Dom Burgess, Dani Pelletier Win Week Eight Athlete Honors

The votes are in, and two postseason performances have earned the Fall Week Eight Athlete of the Week honors.
Dom Burgess of Van Buren is the boys winner, while Dani Pelletier of Madawaska takes the girls honor.
Both came through with important tournament goals during a Week Eight ballot that featured 14 Aroostook County athletes from soccer and cross country.
Boys Athlete of the Week: Dom Burgess, Van Buren
Burgess stepped up when Van Buren entered tournament play.

Congratulations to Dom Burgess of Van Buren, your Fall Week Eight Boys Athlete of the Week.

Pelletier delivered one of the biggest moments of Week Eight.

title: 2 Trump attempts to change the DC landscape play out in the courts as midterms near
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Hearings in lawsuits against two separate administration-backed projects were unfolding in a single federal court building Friday, revealing the breadth of President Donald Trump’s attempts to mold parts of the District of Columbia as he wishes — and the underlying executive authority claims that lie beneath them.
The cases involved are an impending shutdown and reconfiguration of a historic public golf course and the construction of the monumental arch that, at 250 feet (75 meters), would be 100 feet taller than the Statue of Liberty is from its base to the top of the torch. The two projects are barely three miles or five kilometers apart.
The hearing on the proposed golf course change began as other recent ones have: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes grilled Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. over how Trump’s desires to turn the golf course, near the National Mall, into a world-class facility have become urgent plans that match his public pronouncements.
At one point, Reyes read the code of conduct to government attorneys on presenting erroneous or false information during a hearing.
Reyes ordered Friday’s hearing after multiple Truth Social posts by Trump indicated that there were plans for the golf course and construction was expected to begin Nov. 15. Trump said the park would be closed 15 months while work goes on.
A flurry of Trump posts sets off chaos
The presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic in multiple court hearings afterward when officials from the Interior Department, Justice and National Park Service could not confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually asked whom she should trust. The Justice Department filed notice Wednesday night that the plans were real.
“On Friday, October 30, 2026, the National Park Service will submit to the National Capital Planning Commission for review a rendering designed by Tom Fazio for a World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events,” the notice said.
Reyes locked in on the filing and Trump’s multiple Truth Social announcements as she questioned Woodward.
At one point, as they talked about plans that Woodward said only came about this week, he slipped and included tree cutting as part of the preparation for the closure.
Reyes responded immediately: “News flash.” She allowed him to correct himself that the tree cutting, which occurred earlier this month, was not part of the plan to close the East Potomac Golf Links.
She said she intended to appoint a special master to investigate the administration’s statements to the court.
Another case is also a referendum on executive authority
The golf course lawsuit was one of two cases in court Friday dealing with the Trump administration’s push to expand its executive authority as the president remakes the federal areas of the capital near the National Mall and along the Potomac River.
Three courtrooms away, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan was to hold a hearing on a motion asking that she call a temporary halt to plans to begin construction as early as Nov. 5 on the memorial arch. The arch is opposed by a small group of veterans and an architectural historian who sued in federal court in Washington, saying Congress must endorse the project.
“The public interest leans heavily against allowing defendants to blaze ahead,” the plaintiffs said in seeking the injunction. “This court should enter a preliminary injunction blocking defendants from beginning construction on Memorial Circle in the hope that they can render the arch a fait accompli before this Court has made a final determination.”
Legal experts who have been watching the numerous cases underway say that what might appear at first glance to be vanity projects are in truth cases that test the limits of presidential power.
Past administrations pursued legal theories that were sometimes legally sound, sometimes not, said David Super, law professor at the Georgetown University Law Center.
“But there was always the assumption that you would try to do things that were legal,” he said. “What we’re seeing here now is that if you think the federal courts can’t stop you, you can do things there indisputably illegal. He said that’s ”going to do long-term damage to the country.”

title: Sabattus police charge Auburn 16-year-old with kidnapping after driving into Sabattus pond
text:
Sabattus police charged an Auburn 16-year-old with kidnapping, driving to endanger and two other charges after a stolen vehicle was driven into Sabattus Pond earlier this month.
Police received calls early on the morning of Oct. 18 about a car operating without its lights and being driven recklessly that crashed into the pond.
Investigating officers determined the car was being operated by the 16-year-old and was carrying six other juveniles as young as 13.
Sabattus police Chief Wayne Drake told media four of the car’s occupants were girls and that several told investigators the driver refused to let them out of the car.
“The reason we charged the driver of the car with kidnapping is because multiple juvenile females that were in the car stated that they were begging the driver to stop and let them out once they realized the situation they were in,” Drake told News Center Maine. “Then he locked the doors and would not stop.”
In a Facebook post Friday, Drake said the youth was charged with kidnapping, reckless conduct, driving to endanger and operating without a license. Because he is a minor, his name was not being release.

title: Maine coalition honors domestic violence advocates as governor announces $25,000 contribution
text:
HALLOWELL, Maine (WABI) - The Maine Coalition to End Domestic Violence presented its 2026 Champions of Change Awards on Friday to Mainers working to protect victims of domestic violence.
At the event, Gov. Janet Mills announced a $25,000 contribution from her state contingent account to the coalition’s Liberation Fund.
The fund helps survivors leaving abusive homes with expenses including children’s clothing, gas and security cameras.
“Domestic violence affects everyone. Every age, every gender, every socioeconomic status,” Mills said. “Many of us know someone who has experienced abuse. Champions like the people you’re honoring here tonight do ensure the victims find safety, justice and peace,”
The Champions of Change Award was presented to Taylor Kilgore, an attorney and owner of Kilgore Law, where she works to protect children and families in the foster care system. The award also went to Celia Demos and Jessica Duma, both nurses with Maine CDC Public Health Nursing, for their efforts to support survivors of domestic violence.
The coalition also presented the Deb Chapman Legacy Award to Johnnie Walker, director of housing and shelter services at Partners for Peace.
If you or a loved one are experiencing domestic violence, help is available. Contact Partners for Peace’s 24-hour hotline at 1-800-863-9909. You can find other organizations near you here.

title: Maine heating oil prices have set yet another record high
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s heating oil prices have risen to yet another high.
The average price for a gallon of heating oil is now $6.05, up from last week’s high of $6.04, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources.
In eastern and Down East Maine, prices range from a low of $5.71 to a high of $6.40.
That statewide average is 82% higher than this time last year, when heating oil went for $3.32 a gallon.
Mainers will now have to spend an additional $750 to fill a standard 275-gallon tank.
“Heating oil prices in Maine are now breaking records week after week, putting growing pressure on Maine families as temperatures continue to drop,” said Celina Cunningham, acting energy commissioner. “I encourage Maine people to stay informed of current prices, review incentive options through Efficiency Maine, and to contact their Community Action Agency if they need immediate relief.”
Energy prices have been climbing globally since February when President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched a surprise war against Iran. Although Trump said that the war would last only weeks, it entered its eighth month this week.
That war effectively halted fuel shipments out of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s natural gas and oil passes. The ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine also has strained global fuel supplies as both sides have traded blows on each other’s energy infrastructure as Trump moves ahead with plans to import Russian diesel. A first shipment departed for the U.S. last week.
Earlier this month, the Trump administration released about $37 million in low-income heating assistance for Maine. An additional $1.4 million was awarded to the state’s four federally recognized tribes. The administration also is tapping the Northeast heating oil reserves for the first time since 2012 when Hurricane Sandy devastated the northeastern U.S.
About half of Maine households (more than 300,000) rely on heating oil to stay warm during the winter, and consumption can average 2 to 7 gallons a day, depending on how cold it is outside. That means the 13.2 million gallons flowing from the Northeast stockpile would amount to approximately nine days of consumption at a rate of five gallons a day.
Correction: An earlier version of this report understated the additional cost to fill a standard heating oil tank.

title: Man accused of sending attacker to sexually assault fiancée at home with children, police say
text:
BUCKEYE, AZ. (AZFamily/Gray News) - An Arizona man is accused of sending another man to sexually assault his fiancée while she was home with her children, according to police.
Zarian Dyer, 23, was arrested at his job Thursday morning and charged with aggravated assault, sexual abuse, attempted sexual assault, kidnapping and conspiracy.
Buckeye police initially responded to a home the evening of Oct. 16 after Bella Torres reported that an unknown man entered her house and attacked her. Torres fought off the intruder, identified as 20-year-old Adrian Ayala, who fled the scene and was arrested the following day at his Goodyear home.
In home security video, Ayala can be heard telling Torres her partner sent him to assault her through an arrangement made on Reddit — a claim Ayala’s attorney later reiterated in court.
Detectives searched phones and devices belonging to both men, discovering communications outlining the planned attack, Buckeye Police spokesperson Carissa Planalp said. Prosecutors alleged Dyer instructed Ayala to assault Torres while she was home alone and FaceTime him during the attack.
A motive remains under investigation, police said.

title: Ex-band director facing molestation charges critically injured after shooting self during arrest
text:
BOSSIER PARISH, La. (KSLA/Gray News) - A former high school band director facing dozens of sex offense charges is in critical condition after shooting himself during an arrest Thursday, authorities said.
Bossier Parish Sheriff’s deputies were serving an arrest warrant for 56-year-old Kevin Williams at his Bossier City home when he resisted, according to officials. During a physical struggle, Williams pulled a handgun from his waistband and shot himself.
Deputies immediately administered first aid until emergency medical personnel arrived. Williams was transported to an area hospital, where he remains in critical condition.
Williams, a now-former band director at Haughton High School, was previously arrested Sept. 22 on 50 counts of molestation of a juvenile and 50 counts of felony carnal knowledge of a juvenile.

title: Midterms 2026: The data center debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Midterms 2026: The data center debate
On Election Day, thousands of Americans will vote on data center-related ballot measures — an issue that has become a political flashpoint ahead of the 2026 midterms
Midterms 2026: The data center debate
On Election Day, thousands of Americans will vote on data center-related ballot measures — an issue that has become a political flashpoint ahead of the 2026 midterms
The explosive growth of data centers across the U.S. has become a new political flashpoint ahead of the 2026 midterms.
The rapid build-out across the country has left frustrated neighbors pleading for a pause, while forcing elected officials to weigh the economic gains against the potential political fallout.
The 'Data Center Capital of the World'
In Loudoun County, Virginia, known as the "Data Center Capital of the World," the topic has become the center of heated debate among neighbors and officials.
Greg Pirio has lived in Loudoun County for the last 14 years. He says a lot has changed in that time, including the most notable: the data center next door.
The massive building stands just 150-200 yards away from his front door, taking a short walk to reach it.
"We got to stop it. We can't continue to do this, and the grid can't continue to support more data centers," Pirio said.
The impacts, Pirio claims, are real. He says the facility operates diesel generators and natural gas turbines 24/7, creating constant humming, air and light pollution that have disrupted his sleep, scared the local wildlife, and impacted neighbors' health.
The data center boom, by the numbers
Data centers like the one near Pirio have spread quickly across Loudoun County, with over 200 facilities now in operation.
Nationwide, the number of data centers has surged to more than 4,000, with Virginia leading the way at over 720 planned or operational centers, according to April statistics from Baxtel.
The political consequences
President Donald Trump has long supported the growth of data centers, emphasizing their economic benefits and the growing need to beat China in the AI race.
But political analysts warn the messaging misaligns with growing voter sentiment.
"That's not what people believe, and it's not what they want to hear," political analyst Larry Sabato said. "Donald Trump seems determined to make the Republican Party bear the whiplash, because he's essentially saying over and over again, 'These are wonderful things. You ought to have them. This can make you rich.'"
The debate has left many officials stuck with a risky balancing act: embrace data center gains or bow to voters' concerns and political backlash.
The data center 'pros' vs. 'cons'
Many officials argue the added revenue generated by data centers has balanced local government budgets, helped lower property tax rates and injected direct investments into local communities.
Last year, for example, Loudoun County gained $1.3 billion in tax revenue, which helped fund and build its new recreation center.
Some state lawmakers are also advocating for a portion of that revenue to be used to mitigate the negative impacts of data centers.
"It could be used to build additional sound barriers. It could be putting up more aesthetically pleasing trees around the area," said state Del. David Reid, representing District 28 of Loudoun County. "They have the money to be able to do it."
For Pirio, however, the cons of living near a data center far outweigh the benefits, and he warns other communities facing similar:
"Slow things down. Make sure communities are protected," Pirio said. "Make sure that you understand how they are going to be powered, what kind of noise they're going to be making, how are they going to impact the quality of your life? Because it can be horrific, and that has been our experience."

title: Packers’ Jacobs says TD celebration was modeled after gospel song. Here’s why it drew attention
text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. (AP) — Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs says he was paying homage to a gospel song rather than making light of his recent arrest when he briefly had his hands behind his back while celebrating a touchdown Thursday night.
This was Jacobs’ second game of the season after coming off the commissioner’s exempt list. He was placed on that list after charges were filed against him in August stemming from a May altercation with his then-girlfriend during which she said he threw her to the ground.
Jacobs pleaded no contest last month to misdemeanor charges of battery and criminal destruction of property.
Jacobs had just scored on a 1-yard run in the second quarter of the Packers’ 27-19 victory over the Carolina Panthers when he put his hands behind his back for a moment while accepting congratulations from teammates. The video garnered plenty of attention on social media as some who watched on television believed Jacobs was simulating getting handcuffed.
Jacobs said he instead was modeling his celebration after a gospel song called “Break Every Chain.”
“The guys did it with me,” Jacobs said. “I didn’t think it was going to be a thing that can be perceived a certain type of way. But it’s 2026, and it is what it is.”
Jacobs said he had spoken with Savion Williams and other receivers before making his season debut, and they came up with the idea that he would do a celebration thanking God after his first touchdown of the season. That celebration happened Sunday, as he went to his knees and raised his arms aloft after scoring in a 20-17 loss at Detroit.
They also had planned this “Break Every Chain” celebration after his second touchdown of the season. When Jacobs was asked about putting his hands behind his back as part of the celebration, he noted that the telecast only showed a brief portion of what he did.
“It was more to it than that,” Jacobs said. “They stopped showing the celebration after that. Like I said, it is what it is.”
Jacobs hadn’t been able to play or practice while he was on the commissioner’s exempt list. He was removed from that list last week, enabling him to play again even though the NFLs investigation of him remains ongoing.

title: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (InvestigateTV) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.”
When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death.
Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock.
How the discovery happened
Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins, founder of Vivacelle Bio, said he was running an experiment he thought would fail. “But it didn’t fail.”
For years, Simpkins, who is now a surgery professor at the UKMC School of Medicine, had been trying to find an answer for septic shock and focused his research on blood experiments.
He drained mice of their blood until they were clinically dead, then injected them with a substance called VBI-1.
“The mice woke up. They woke up from being dead,” Simpkins said. “They were walking around. I called my wife, excited. I said, this is working. This is what’s going on here. This isn’t supposed to work.”
Simpkins said the survival rate is nearly 100% when the product is injected into the arteries of mice experiencing hemorrhagic shock. He is waiting to test it on humans. He said a person could receive about 2 liters.
Simpkins said VBI-1 would end blood shortages with the hope they never happen again.
He said the substance could also be safer than blood alone for people in hemorrhagic shock. He and his team named the product “better than blood” because of ischemia reperfusion injury, which he said is caused by a person’s own blood being reinfused.
Ischemia reperfusion injury happens when blood is reintroduced to the body after blood loss. The oxygen in the new blood can create toxins in the body, which damage tissue, including the brain.
“When we infused our product, we don’t get that,” Simpkins said.
The substance uses nanoparticle technology. It is derived from another of Simpkins’ discoveries, VBI-S, which is awaiting FDA approval to help treat septic shock.
“If you look at the damage caused by blood to the brain when you infuse it, the animal’s own blood, and you compare that to our fluid, and you see no damage,” Simpkins said.
Simpkins said the components of VBI-1 are soybean oil, egg lecithin and egg yolk.
It sounds like simple ingredients, but he says combined they could fix complicated problems facing our country. Since 2020, U.S. blood supplies have reached “critically low levels” multiple times.
And in 2026, the American Red Cross announced a national blood supply crisis, only the second time it’s ever released that warning. Dr. Simpkins says his product would mean an end to these blood shortages.
Transfusion specialist cites limits
Dr. Richard Galbraith, a University Health KC pathologist and director of transfusion medicine, said the potential is there.
“If it works and if it’s safe, then it could be a boon for sure,” he said.
Galbraith said he was “extremely interested” and “hopeful” when he first saw Simpkins’ study on VBI-1. But he sees limitations.
“Having a completely synthetic replacement for blood that’s, I think, is extremely unlikely,” Galbraith said.
Galbraith said blood will still be needed and blood drives will continue to matter.
“It’s still critically important. There are many uses for blood beyond shock,” he said.
Galbraith said University Health goes through at least 500 units of blood a day. He said chronic blood shortages have affected the entire country for several years. He said patients with chronic blood disease and those with certain cancers would still depend on blood transfusions.
Galbraith said VBI-1 could help people in hemorrhagic shock and during blood shortages.
“This hopefully can be a means of saving those people,” Galbraith said. When asked whether it could help during blood shortages, he said, “Oh, I think, definitely.”
He said the product must go through appropriate clinical trials.
“We need to ensure it goes to the appropriate clinical trials to make sure it’s going to work and it’s going to help and that it’s safe,” Galbraith said. “And if those concerns are addressed and met, then I’m happy to use it in our patients too.”
Other possible uses
Members of Simpkins’ lab team said they are ready to prove the discovery.
“I don’t think transfusion’s necessarily something we ever thought we would optimize any better,” said UMKC scientist Nathan Carpenter.
The team said they have only begun to explore the product’s potential.
UMKC scientist Danielle Kinsey said the team hopes the product can be used to prevent organ rejection after transplants.
“We have this hope that it can be used in the process of transplantation, so specifically given to patients before they receive their transplanted organ with hopes of decreasing the immune response,” Kinsey said.
Asked how to categorize VBI-1, Simpkins said, “There’s no category. There’s no other. It’s a different new category, actually, of therapeutics.”
Simpkins said he does not know the limits of the substance, but remains confident it will save lives.
“We’ll be sending more people back to their families, back to their loved ones, and that’s really what it’s all about,” Simpkins said.
Clinical human trials for VBI-1 could take one to two years. Simpkins hopes the product receives FDA approval and is on the market by 2031.

title: Actually, ‘Rocky’ Deserved to Win Best Picture
text:
Actually, ‘Rocky’ Deserved to Win Best Picture
Rocky is the only movie I can think of whose title appears onscreen twice in the opening credits.
The very first image of the movie is its title — ROCKY — in huge block letters scrolling from right to left across the screen as Bill Conti’s triumphant fanfare plays.
After the title passes off the screen, the scene shifts to a boxing match that appears to be taking place inside an old church. Club fighter Rocky Balboa dukes it out with another pugilist, Spider Rico. Rocky wins the fight, but he gets headbutted above his left eye. Rocky’s prize for this glorious victory: Forty bucks and a scar on his forehead that will never heal.
The whole scene, from opening bell to the final emotional gut-punch of learning the pathetic amount of money he’s earned for a night’s work, takes about five minutes. Then the opening credits resume and once again the word “Rocky” flashes on the screen. This time the name’s tiny, and appear over a wide shot of a dingy, dirty Philadelphia street. Now Rocky’s name is almost literally in the gutter; he nearly steps on it as he stumbles home.
The dual titles, one big and one small, introduces one of Rocky’s most important and prevalent themes: The gulf between people’s big dreams and their hopeless realities, and the struggle to press onward when that gulf seems insurmountable and everyone around you makes you feel small. When Rocky begins, the “Italian Stallion” has already been a boxer for years; later we learn he’s already 30 and mostly earns a living serving as muscle for a loan shark.
Through sheer luck, he receives a title shot against the heavyweight champion of the world, Apollo Creed. The night before the fight, Rocky can’t sleep. He goes to the Philadelphia Spectrum and wanders around the empty arena. From the ring, he gazes at an image of himself on an enormous banner — the big “ROCKY” of his imagination and the little Rocky of the streets juxtaposed in a single image.
At that moment, Rocky doesn’t believe in himself, partly because nobody has ever believed in him before. Even some of Rocky’s friends underestimate his spirit and his intelligence because he looks like a palooka. That’s how it’s been for the last half century for Rocky as well. A lot of cinephiles underestimate it because it looks like a simplistic sports film about a palooka. They fixate on its bombastic moments and don’t catch its subtleties, like its recurrent use of big and small Rockys to symbolize his insecurities.
They laugh at Rocky punching sides of beef as part of his eclectic training regimen without observing how that act parallels the insult that stings Rocky a few scenes prior. When he refuses to break the thumbs of a man who owes Rocky’s boss some money, the loan shark’s driver yells, “So long meat bag!” For Rocky, smashing his fists into a cow carcass is as much a way to strengthen his muscles as it is a rejection of the image forced upon him by society.
Above all, the film’s critics complain that while Rocky may be an effective formula boxing picture, it’s unworthy of the prize of Best Picture, which it won at the Academy Awards in 1977 against some extremely tough competition. The Daily Beast put Rocky in the headline of their “Worst Oscar Winners” piece along with 2004’s Crash. The Christian Science Monitor once chose Rocky as one of the Best Picture winners that “weren’t supposed to win.” The expansive Filmsite.org lists the film on its Oscar winners page next to the word “WORST!” highlighted in red.
The argument against Rocky winning Best Picture is typified by this 2025 piece listing the “worst” Best Picture winners in Oscar history:
This was also the year of Bound for Glory (which was never going to win), Network, Taxi Driver, and the best, most prescient, and most sophisticated of the year, which has since become a classic: All the President’s Men.
Whether All the President’s Men is the best film of 1976, or the most sophisticated, is debatable. (I’m not sure how it was more prescient than Network, which was practically clairvoyant about mass media’s dark future.) Regardless, All the President’s Men is an outstanding journalistic thriller; and Taxi Driver and Network are both exceptional films as well.
But you know what else is an exceptional film? Rocky.
Awards experts often discuss “narratives” and their impact on the Oscar race; the uplifting (or disturbing) behind-the-scenes stories that shape the winners of these prizes as much (or more) than the actual onscreen performances. Sylvester Stallone arguably had the greatest Oscar narrative of all-time: An out-of-work actor, Stallone wrote Rocky’s screenplay in three days and then — despite his financial desperation — refused to let anyone else play the title role, even though his obstinance imperiled the massive paycheck he could have received had he allowed producers to cast an established leading man as Rocky Balboa.
Stallone bet on himself, convinced the powers that be to give him the role, and then delivered a terrific performance. Then Rocky became the single biggest box-office hit of 1976, turning Stallone from a nobody to a massive movie star almost overnight. It’s a great Oscar narrative, even if Stallone ultimately lost the year’s Best Actor prize to the late Peter Finch from Network, and the Best Original Screenplay award to that film’s writer, Paddy Chayefsky.
But Stallone’s real-life story means more to Rocky than some feel-good vibes. Part of the reason Stallone was the only person to play Rocky Balboa is because Stallone suffused all of his own feelings about himself and his own career — his frustrations, his anxieties, his desires — into the character. Stallone may not have directed Rocky — John G. Avildsen did — but many sequences verge on pure autobiography.
Consider the scene early in the film where Rocky goes to visit his buddy Paulie (Burt Young) at a bar. He winds up catching a news report about heavyweight boxing champ Apollo Creed (Carl Weathers), whose next fight will celebrate America’s upcoming bicentennial. The bartender is dismissive (and more than a little racist).
“Will you take a look a that guy?” he gripes. “I mean, where are the real fighters gonna come from?”
READ MORE: Sylvester Stallone Blames Himself For Bad Rambo Sequels
After the bartender drops a racial epithet and calls Apollo a clown, Rocky replies “You’re calling Apollo Creed a clown?” then adds “This man is champion of the world. He took his best shot and become champ. What shot did you ever take?”
There Rocky clearly voices Stallone’s own philosophy — as evidenced by Rocky itself. His admiration for those who take their shot dovetails with Rocky’s later confession (not long after he wanders the empty Philadelphia Spectrum) that he cannot defeat Apollo, so he only wishes to survive the fight and “go the distance” — something none of Creed’s prior opponents had ever done.
In other words: Despite the fact that he has has no shot at victory, he’s going to take one anyway. And those words mirror Rocky’s most famous image: Stallone ascending the steps to the entrance of the Philadelphia Museum of Art, where he raises his arms in victory to celebrate the conclusion of his training for his underdog bout with Apollo.
The image of Stallone atop the steps remains one of the most iconic shots in 1970s cinema. But while everyone remembers Rocky’s big celebration, and the sound of Bill Conti’s rousing score, they often forget that Stallone’s sprint up the steps is actually the second scene set at the Art Museum.
Rocky first climbs the museum’s steps on the first day of his training. That time, he wheezes and struggles as he limps to the top of the plaza, clutching his side with a nasty cramp. The Conti music in this run is wistful and melancholic.
But faced with adversity, Rocky (and Stallone) continued; kept working and pushing. Eventually, he willed himself to the top of the proverbial mountain. He took his shot. His triumph is not in necessarily beating Apollo Creed (Spoiler alert: he doesn’t beat him) but in seeing a difficult task through to the end.
That is why Rocky endures 50 years later, and why so many generations of audiences have fallen in love with the character and related to his journey. It’s also why, 50 years later, Rocky remains an outstanding piece of 1970s cinema; gritty, tough, funny, sad, and filled with terrific, quotable dialogue — like when Rocky defends his work for the loan shark (“It’s a living!”) and his grizzled trainer Mickey spits back “It’s a waste of life!”
When people dismiss Rocky’s Oscar win, I usually assume what they are actually dismissing are its sequels, which did grow more formulaic and increasingly outlandish over time until, in 2006’s Rocky Balboa, Stallone was literally 60 years old fighting the heavyweight champ of the world. (Then again, no matter what else each Rocky sequel is about, they are all about Stallone’s life at the time he wrote them. Rocky II is about a man dealing with sudden celebrity; Rocky III is about a massive star struggling with career complacency; even Rocky Balboa is about a man who feels he still has more to say and do pushing back against an industry that’s deemed him over the hill. Plus, in a world where a nearly 60-year-old Mike Tyson headlines the most-streamed sporting event ever, is Rocky Balboa in an exhibition match against the champ really that absurd?)
Either way: A movie is not its sequels. And the original Rocky is a masterpiece. That doesn’t mean Taxi Driver and Network aren’t masterpieces as well. They are; if either had won Best Picture, they would have been worthy winners as well. But it’s not Rocky’s fault that a lot of great movies came out in 1976. The film took its shot, and it went the distance.

title: In-N-Out Burger CEO floats 3 additional states for possible expansion
text:
In-N-Out Burger CEO floats 3 additional states for possible expansion
In-N-Out Burger could expand to three additional states, the fast-food chain's CEO Lynsi Snyder said in a recent interview.
Video above: In-N-Out Burger announced two changes to ingredients in September
The beloved California-based fast-food chain is considering expanding to Oklahoma, Arkansas and Mississippi, Snyder said in an interview with Terry Crews posted to In-N-Out's website.
A timeline on the expansion was not given.
The chain currently has more than 400 locations in 10 states across the U.S.: California, Texas, Arizona, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Tennessee, Oregon, Idaho and Washington.
Snyder said In-N-Out's supply truck travels from Texas to Tennessee, and there are states along that route that would make sense when the time comes to expand.
"If you look at the map, you've got Texas. There's Arkansas, Mississippi, Oklahoma. There are some states that are possibilities," Snyder said. "New Mexico has been waiting for us, and that will be soon."
The first New Mexico location is expected to open in 2027.
The CEO is celebrating 78 years of In-N-Out Burger, which was founded on Oct. 22, 1948, in Baldwin Park, California.

title: 21-year-old woman arrested for social media post threatening to assassinate Trump
text:
VOLUSIA COUNTY, Fla. (Gray News) - A 21-year-old woman was arrested after allegedly posting a photo of herself with a caption that she was going to shoot President Trump.
“We are not going to tolerate threats to assassinate the president,” the Volusia County Sheriff Mike Chitwood wrote in a social media post on Oct. 30.
Allison Albro was charged with written threats to kill and unlawful use of a communications device after allegedly writing, “Going to the trump rally in my city so I can shoot him with my Glock! Wish me luck guys!!” the night before.
President Trump was scheduled to hold a campaign rally on Oct. 30.
According to Chitwood, the department’s Domestic Security Unit and U.S. Secret Service went to Albro’s home. She reportedly told officers she did not have access to weapons.
“I would strongly advise anyone else thinking of posting a “joke” along these lines to think twice,” Chitwood wrote.

title: Voting in Maine | Voting Information
text:
To be eligible to vote in Maine, you must meet the following requirements:
- At least 18 years old by the General Election
- A United States citizen
- A resident of the municipality in which you want to vote
If you feel you have been denied the opportunity to vote, discuss the situation with the local clerk or warden. If you cannot resolve the issue, contact the state Elections Division at 207-624-7650.
Voter rights
Registered voters do not need to show ID to get a ballot.
Mainers may vote by absentee ballot instead of voting in person at the polling place and do not need a reason to vote by absentee ballot.
Unregistered voters can register on Election Day and vote. You must register in person and show ID and proof of where you live. If you don’t have ID or proof of residence, you can cast a challenged ballot.
If a voter is in line at the voting place at 8 p.m. on Election Day, he/she still may register and vote.
Voters may see a sample ballot and get help on how to mark the ballot before voting. They also may ask for help to read or mark the ballot.
If a voter makes a mistake, they can get a new ballot.
Voters have the right to use Maine’s Accessible Voting System at their voting place. For those voters with disabilities who prefer to vote absentee, an accessible electronic ballot is available for voters to complete independently at home using screenreader technology.
Voters may not be harassed when voting or be pressured about how to vote.
Registering to vote
You can register to vote online through the Maine Secretary of State’s website, by filling out a voter registration card at your town office or city hall, through any Motor Vehicle branch office, in most state and federal social service agencies, or at voter registration drives.
You can also download and print a Maine voter registration application on the Secretary of State’s website.
If you cannot print the voter registration application, contact your town clerk to have a voter registration card mailed to you. A printed version of the voter registration card, with your original signature, must be kept on file by your town clerk, so the card cannot be transmitted electronically.
Completed voter registration cards may be hand delivered or mailed to your town office or city hall.
When you register for the first time in Maine, you’ll need to provide identity documents that show you have established your voting residence in the state of Maine.
The following documents are acceptable proof of identification for the purposes of registering to vote:
Government document or credential with photo ID (i.e. driver’s license, state ID, valid U.S. passport, military ID, ID card issued by a federally recognized tribe)
Government ID document/credential without photo (i.e. certified birth certificate or signed Social Security card)
An official document that shows name and address of voter (i.e. eligibility for public benefits, utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck)
Student photo ID from a state-approved public or private school or institute of higher education in Maine
Verified unique identifier (Maine driver’s license number or last four numbers of Social Security number)
The deadline for registering in person is the close of polls on Election Day. If registering by mail or third person, registration must be received by the voter’s town or city by close of business 21 days before Election Day. (For the Nov. 3 General Election the deadline was Oct. 13.) Registering online must be done by 5 p.m. on the 21st day before Election Day. Voter can register through the BMV up to the seventh day before Election Day. (For the Nov. 3 General Election, that deadline is Oct. 27.)
Absentee voting
Any registered voter may cast an absentee ballot instead of voting in person at a voting place on Election Day. You don’t need to have a specific reason or be unable to vote at the voting place on Election Day to receive an absentee ballot.
To vote absentee, complete an absentee ballot application to get a ballot. Then, fill out and deliver the ballot back to the municipal clerk.
Absentee ballots may be requested beginning two months before Election Day. The deadline to request an absentee ballot or vote in the presence of the clerk is by close of business on the Thursday prior to the election.
To be counted, absentee ballots must be received by the municipal clerk by 8 p.m. on Election Day.
If you plan to use the U.S. mail to receive or return your absentee ballot, the U.S. Postal Service advises requesting your ballot no later than 15 days prior to Election Day and returning your ballot no later than seven days prior to Election Day.
Ballots can also be dropped off in person or via an absentee ballot drop box at your municipal office (if available) no later than 8 p.m. on Election Day.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Sunshine returns for Halloween weekend, but chilly temperatures stick around Saturday
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Friday. We’ve had another somewhat unsettled day across the region today, with a cold front bringing scattered rain showers to Aroostook County. The good news is that we’re finally going to see a return to some nicer weather heading into the upcoming Halloween weekend. High pressure is expected to take control of our weather once again, bringing plenty of sunshine for both Saturday and Sunday. Temperatures won’t be quite as warm as what we experienced Thursday, with a pretty chilly Halloween expected across the region. The other unfortunate part of the forecast is that the rainfall we’ve seen today isn’t expected to make much of a difference in our ongoing drought conditions.
Scattered rain showers are expected to continue across portions of the region through the evening hours tonight. With colder air working its way into the region behind the departing cold front, I wouldn’t be surprised to see some of those lingering rain showers briefly mix with or change over to snow showers, especially across northern portions of Aroostook County. I’m not expecting any sort of substantial snowfall accumulation from these showers though. Skies should gradually begin to clear as we work our way through the overnight hours, allowing temperatures to fall back into the 20s by tomorrow morning. Most locations will see low temperatures in the mid to upper 20s, with some of our colder towns in the North Woods falling into the lower 20s. Northwesterly winds around 5 to 10 MPH, with some gusts approaching 25 MPH, will also make for a chilly evening.
The good news is that we’re looking at a pretty nice day across the region tomorrow, especially for anyone with outdoor Halloween plans. With high pressure building back into the region, we’ll see plenty of sunshine throughout the day Saturday. Unfortunately, temperatures will be noticeably cooler compared to what we’ve experienced over the last couple of days. High temperatures for most locations will only reach the lower 40s, with a few of our warmer towns in southern Aroostook County potentially reaching the mid 40s. For some perspective, Caribou’s average high temperature for tomorrow is 47 degrees, meaning we’re looking at temperatures running a few degrees below average. Northwesterly winds around 5 to 10 MPH will also add a bit of a chill to the air, but I don’t expect the winds to be particularly strong throughout the day.
For those of you planning on heading out trick-or-treating tomorrow evening, I think we’re looking at a pretty decent forecast overall. The biggest thing you’ll want to prepare for will be the chilly temperatures, especially once the sun begins to set. Looking at our Halloween planner for Caribou, temperatures will only reach around 41 degrees during the afternoon hours, before beginning to fall back through the 30s during the evening. By 7 PM, we’re looking at temperatures around 36 degrees, with readings falling to around 31 degrees by 9 PM. The good news is that rain chances remain at zero throughout the entire day, so there’s no need to worry about any rain or snow ruining those Halloween plans. I’d certainly recommend making sure the kids have an extra layer underneath their costumes though, especially if they’re planning on spending a good amount of time outside. Temperatures will continue falling overnight Saturday, with lows returning to the lower to mid 20s by Sunday morning.
Heading into Sunday, we’re looking at another pretty nice day across the region, with plenty of sunshine expected once again. The primary difference between Saturday and Sunday will be the temperatures, with warmer air beginning to work its way back into the region. High temperatures Sunday are expected to climb into the upper 40s to lower 50s across most of Aroostook County. Caribou and Fort Kent should reach around 50 degrees, while Presque Isle and Houlton could see temperatures climbing into the lower 50s. Winds will be coming from a westerly direction, generally around 5 to 10 MPH. Overall, I think Sunday is shaping up to be a pretty decent day, especially considering we’re officially heading into November.
Looking a little further ahead into the beginning of the new work week, our stretch of relatively quiet weather looks to continue. High pressure is expected to remain the dominant influence over our weather through at least the first half of next week, keeping precipitation chances fairly minimal. Temperatures will also continue to moderate, with highs Monday potentially climbing into the mid to upper 50s across much of the region. That’s several degrees above average for the beginning of November. Some additional cloud coverage is possible heading into Tuesday, with temperatures potentially cooling off a bit compared to Monday.
There is some uncertainty developing in the forecast heading into the middle of next week. A weak disturbance passing to our north could bring another opportunity for rain showers to portions of Aroostook County, particularly Tuesday night into Wednesday. Unfortunately, I don’t expect this to be the sort of substantial rainfall we desperately need to help improve our ongoing drought conditions. The latest forecast guidance continues to suggest that any rainfall associated with this system would likely remain fairly light, potentially less than a quarter of an inch. The National Weather Service in Caribou continues to highlight the ongoing drought as a major concern, with streamflow and groundwater levels remaining below to well below normal across much of the region. Our next opportunity for a more organized storm system may arrive toward the end of next week or even into the following weekend, but there’s still quite a bit of uncertainty surrounding the timing of that system. For more details on what to expect heading into the Halloween weekend and the beginning of November, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening, and happy Halloween!

title: ‘She’s a miracle’: Family says 2-year-old is healing after crash that killed her parents
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) — A fatal head-on collision on an Alaska highway last week killed a Fairbanks couple.
According to Alaska State Troopers, 38-year-old Sasha Hart and her husband, 41-year-old David Hart, were killed in the Oct. 19 crash on the Parks Highway near Trapper Creek.
According to troopers, Sasha Hart was driving a Subaru Forester south on the Parks Highway when she crossed the center line and collided head-on with a northbound Ford F-250.
Their 2-year-old daughter, Paige, was also in the Subaru and survived.
“She’s a miracle. Aren’t you?” Shery Elterman-Hart, David Hart’s sister, said as she held her niece during an interview.
A life built in Fairbanks
According to the Hart family, the couple just celebrated their 10-year anniversary. They built a life together in Fairbanks, where they blended Sasha’s Jamaican and David’s Alaskan lifestyles.
“She just became one of us. We were really close with David before they met, but then when she came, she just sort of lumped right in,” Elterman-Hart said.
The family said the two enjoyed traveling and watching hockey. They also shared a love for food, the family said.
Above all, they loved being parents to their daughter.
“She was their entire world,” Katie Ragsdale, David Hart’s sister, said. “I don’t know if it’s Paige’s house or their house.”
Paige’s recovery
The family said certain traits of David and Sasha are seen in Paige, including the same “stink” face as her mother and her father’s sweet tooth.
“You still have a piece of them, a living piece of them still on Earth,” Ragsdale said.
According to the family, Paige is healing fast after suffering six broken bones from the crash.

title: Be sure your voice is heard, go vote
text:
The BDN Editorial Board operates independently from the newsroom, and does not set policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com.
You’ve endured months of increasingly nasty campaign ads. Your mailbox has been crammed full of mailers, mostly trashing political opponents. Your phone has been inundated with calls and texts from candidates.
Now, it is time for you to vote on Tuesday, Nov. 3.
The too-close-to-call U.S. Senate race between Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson has gotten the most attention, and campaign cash, this year. The race is one of the few that will help determine which political party will control the U.S. Senate for the remainder of Donald Trump’s presidency. The choice is between Collins and her long record, which includes chairing the Senate Appropriations Committee and securing money for needed projects in Maine communities, and Jackson, the long-time president of the Maine Senate, who could help Democrats work to hold Trump more accountable and halt, and perhaps reverse, some of his most damaging actions.
Polling shows the race to be exceedingly close, so every ballot matters.
In Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, former Republican Gov. Paul LePage is running against State Auditor Matt Dunlap, a Democrat. The seat is open because Rep. Jared Golden unexpectedly announced a year ago that he would not seek reelection. He cited the increasing nastiness of politics for one reason for his departure from Congress. That race is also close as national pundits predict Democrats will gain control of the U.S. House of Representatives.
In the 1st Congressional District, Rep. Chellie Pingree is expected to cruise to victory of Republican challenger Ron Russell, who also ran against her two years ago. Pingree won that contest by more than 20 percentage points.
Maine’s governorship is open with Gov. Janet Mills ending her tenure at the end of year due to term limits. Most polls show Democrat Hannah Pingree with a comfortable lead against Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett. This important contest has been largely overshadowed by the turbulent — and costly — Senate race.
The Bangor Daily News opinion page sought subscriber questions for the candidates for governor, House and Senate. The detailed Q&As, which covered health care, Social Security, climate change, accountability, and other issues, can be found at www.bangordailynews.com/candidates-questions/.
Every seat in the Maine Legislature is up for election this fall. Many communities also have municipal races and school board seats up for election on Tuesday. In Bangor, a record 12 candidates are seeking three seats on the city council. The slate of candidates is as varied as it is deep, offering voters needed choices as the city faces vexing challenges, especially homelessness, substance use and high housing costs.
Voters in Penobscot County will see a question asking whether county commissioners should be authorized to move the overcrowded county jail to a location outside of Bangor. The commissioners have already spent $100,000 to hold a parcel of land in Hampden for a proposed new jail. This question does not authorize or raise the funds for a new jail. That will be put to county voters in the future, likely next year.
The BDN’s news and politics teams provide extensive coverage of these, and other, campaigns. They also have answers to questions about how and where to vote.
You can find your polling place and even see a sample ballot using the secretary of state’s voter information lookup service.
If you’re not registered to vote yet, Maine allows you to register up to and on Election Day. You’ll need to provide proof of residency, so bring identification — a photo ID works but so does an official piece of mail like a utility bill that proves you live where you say you live — when you go to the polls.
Even if there is a problem with your registration, you still can vote under Maine’s challenged ballot law, so there’s no reason to leave a polling place without having your say. If you make a mistake on a ballot, you can take it to a volunteer at the polling place and ask for another.
Maine’s elections are safe, secure and fair, thanks to the hard work of municipal clerks and town office staff, state officials, and legions of volunteers. They deserve our thanks.
Make sure your voice is heard, by turning in your absentee ballot or heading to the polls on Tuesday.

title: For the first time in years, Maine homes are selling for under their asking prices
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing
This section of the BDN aims to help readers understand Maine’s housing crisis, the volatile real estate market and the public policy behind them. Read more Housing coverage here.
More home sellers across Maine are accepting offers that are less than what their property is listed for, presenting a new opportunity for hopeful buyers who have been scared off by high prices since the pandemic.
Last month, only a quarter of Maine homes sold for more than their asking price, according to data from Redfin. That dropped from five years ago when roughly half of Maine’s single family homes sold for more than they were listed for.
Local real estate professionals believe several factors are contributing to this trend, though all agreed it’s a sign of how the market has corrected from the frenzy that erupted during the pandemic. It could be the first glimpse of hope for many families who were boxed out of the market for years by fierce competition and record-high home values.
At the height of the pandemic, demand for Maine homes skyrocketed but there weren’t enough properties to go around, leading to bidding wars over homes that stayed on the market for only a few days before closing.
“Two years ago, you listed, got half a dozen showings and were under contract in four or five days,” said Karen Burns, a Bangor-based broker for Century 21 Real Estate.
Mainers continuing to overprice their homes is perhaps the foremost factor of more of them selling under asking. This is fueled by sellers believing they can rake in pandemic-era profits when, in reality, the market has softened and slowed considerably in the last few years, Burns said.
“I list homes every day and some people are thinking about what their neighbor sold their house for two years ago,” Burns said. “It’s a different market now.”
While prices haven’t reverted to what they were before 2020, inventory has remained healthy and properties are staying on the market longer, said Laurie Smallidge, a realtor at Better Homes and Gardens Real Estate The Masiello Group. This allows buyers to be selective and negotiate favorable terms and fair prices.
“It’s not like COVID where there were multiple offers on a property and you had to do whatever it takes — no contingencies, cash, close in 30 days,” Smallidge said.
Homes with more reasonable prices usually get more attention from buyers rather than sitting on the market, growing stale and needing price cuts to regenerate interest.
In Bangor, nearly half of single-family homes on the market had at least one price reduction, according to Redfin data.
Some single-family homes in desirable areas of southern and coastal Maine are the exception to this trend, as they’ll likely still sell for more than asking. This is especially true if the home is updated or unique in some way, said Tom Landry, Broker at the Landry Team at Benchmark Real Estate.
Additionally, mortgage interest rates have risen to 7% or more at a time when families are already grappling with high prices and additional economic uncertainty. This means more buyers aren’t willing to make hefty economic investments — such as sinking their savings in a pricey home — and are looking for a fair price, Smallidge said.
On the seller’s side, most homeowners want to get their properties off their hands before winter and the holiday season when Maine’s real estate market quiets, Burns said. For sellers who have already moved into a new home, they usually don’t want to pay to heat and maintain two homes through the winter.
This urgency to sell before the snow falls will make sellers more likely to accept an offer below asking.
For prospective buyers yearning to own a home but waiting for interest rates to decline, Landry urged them to act now while the market is leaning in their favor, as mortgages can always be refinanced if and when interest rates decline.
“This is a unique opportunity for buyers and they shouldn’t squander it,” he said. “Rates might go down in a year or two, but you’ll already have the house and you didn’t deal with a bidding war.”

title: This family runs a distillery in an old fire station
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
DALE, Wis. (InvestigateTV) — A Wisconsin family runs a distillery in an old fire station along Highway 96 in Dale, with a business designed to support the fire departments that keep them safe.
Volunteer firefighter Alex Hopfensperger works at the family business, Old Station 31 Spirits.
“Right now we’re distilling in-house vodka and gin, so we have the four vodkas and two gins,” Alex Hopfensperger said.
“We wanted to become a part of the community, and 20-plus years ago, part of becoming part of the community was joining the volunteer fire department,” Rob Hopfensperger said.
Alex’s father, Rob, is also a volunteer firefighter. He and his wife, Tavia, decided to honor the fire service when they created Old Station 31 Spirits.
“You start to do it and, you know, I’m on it, then your sons get on it, your daughter-in-law gets on it, and it’s just, and we have that,” Rob said.
“Living in a small town, people just pop in and you get to meet so many different people and people that have memories of this place,” Tavia said. “We’ve heard hundreds of fire station stories. That fire service connection, when they come in the building, it’s a brotherhood.”
The tasting room and museum feature artifacts and memorabilia honoring local departments and those who gave their lives.
“We have a memorial for the 9/11. We do the stair climb every year at Lambeau Field and then they give you badges with the firefighters that perished there, and we are starting our collection of those badges,” Tavia said.
Old Station 31 Spirits makes its products grain to glass.
“We take a department every month and sell a particular drink for that department, and then those proceeds we donate back to that department,” Rob said.
The family business plans to expand its reach when the time is right.
“We’re going to be filling up our own barrels with whiskey and then in five-ish years with the barrel age process we’ll be able to enjoy that ourselves,” Alex said.
The business has stayed in the small town where it started.
“There’s a lot of our fellow distillers or distilleries in Wisconsin that is either in a bigger city or they’re in a tourist area. And as you probably know, Dale is neither,” Rob said.

The show will track every major race on Maine’s ballot, from the seismic Senate contest to the open 2nd Congressional District seat and the race for governor. We will closely follow U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Democrat Troy Jackson in a race that could decide control of the Senate. Decision Desk HQ, the BDN’s election results partner, gives Jackson a 60% chance of winning. As of Friday, it gives Democrats a 62% chance of taking the Senate.
The show will feature live views of the races. Maps will show results town by town as they arrive. Other screens will show where votes are still out, which towns could still swing a race, how places are tracking against past campaigns, how the parties’ seat counts stand in the Legislature and how Maine fits into the national fight for the Senate.
Two strategists — Republican Joe Turcotte and Democrat Rachel Irwin — will help me analyze results as they come in. Both are veterans of these kinds of campaigns and intersected with each other while working for their state parties more than a decade ago.

Irwin, a Brewer native, founded Double Tap Democracy, which works with social media creators and runs digital ads for campaigns and causes. She is working on this year’s U.S. Senate race and previously worked for Senate Democrats’ campaign arm.

A close Senate race may not end Tuesday night. If blank ballots and write-ins keep both candidates under a majority, Maine would hold its first statewide ranked-choice count in a general election, and that could take a week or more.

title: Pope Leo XIV becomes the first pope to vote in a US election
text:
Pope Leo XIV becomes the first pope in history to vote in a US election
Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election.
Video above: Pope Leo XIV blasts 'delusion of omnipotence' fueling U.S.-Israeli war in Iran
The Vatican confirmed Friday that the Chicago-born pontiff had submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago ahead of November’s midterm elections, citing his long-standing belief in civic participation.
Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen” and has done so “whenever he was eligible to do so,” the Holy See press office said.
The statement said he had also voted while living in Peru whenever he was eligible.
“The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” it added.
Leo’s vote was first reported by the Chicago Sun-Times, which quoted the chief of staff at the Will County clerk’s office as saying the pope, registered at a New Lenox address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3.
Video below: Trump in April says, "I'm not a fan of Pope Leo"
It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. His brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St. Jude’s, an Augustinian-run parish in New Lenox, Illinois. The elder Prevost attends Mass there, and Leo gave a talk at the parish in 2024 while still a cardinal.
Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections.
The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a ballot in a primary, when parties choose their nominees for the general election. No such declaration is required in general elections.
While registered in heavily Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative suburban Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.
The records also show that he submitted ballots in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022.

title: Ex-Husson professor accused of possessing child sex abuse material
text:
An ex-Husson University assistant professor allegedly possessed child sexual abuse material.
Jonathan Houck, 33, of Bangor has been charged with six counts of possession of child sexual abuse material and four counts of violations of privacy, according to Katy England, a spokesperson for the Bangor Police Department.
Husson learned about the investigation early on Sept. 21, spokesperson Sarah Walker Caron said. He was escorted from campus and fired within an hour.
News of the arrest came after a series of social media posts detailed allegations against Houck and a cryptic release by Husson said that an unnamed employee had been fired amid a police investigation. The posts accused Houck of filming women he was teaching.
Bangor police searched the home and office of Houck, a professor of exercise science and assistant cross country coach, on Sept. 18, according to a search warrant affidavit filed in Penobscot County Superior Court.
Dropbox, an online file sharing service, flagged with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children on June 29 that Houck allegedly uploaded sexually explicit images of children younger than 16, the affidavit said. Four images were uploaded to Dropbox between November 2020 and June 30, 2026, the affidavit said. Videos were also uploaded.
The tip ultimately was directed to Bangor police on Aug. 31, once it was determined where the conduct originated.
“Husson University is deeply disturbed by Jonathan Houck’s alleged conduct,” Walker Caron said. “Husson cannot comment on personnel matters or ongoing legal matters, but the university has and will continue to comply with all law enforcement requests in a prompt manner.”
Houck was arrested and booked into the Penobscot County Jail at 1 p.m. Friday, records show.
While investigating the alleged child sexual abuse material, Bangor police discovered evidence of other crimes, England said.
A Husson student accused Houck of filming partially dressed students with hidden cameras in a TikTok video posted hours before the school issued its initial statement.
In the video, she describes a fall 2025 exercise science class where the students’ body weights were needed. In a lab for the class, they were supposed to undress and weigh themselves, she said. She undressed to her bra and underwear, weighed herself, got dressed and went back to class.
She said she learned this week that there were hidden cameras near the scale taking footage of the weigh-ins. Police showed her three pictures of herself that were on the professor’s devices but they were blurry, so she said it could have been screenshots from a video.
She said she is “one of God knows how many victims.” The Bangor Daily News does not name victims of crimes without their permission. The student did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“I’m disgusted, I don’t really have words,” the student said in the video.
She said Houck was her adviser and had classes and conversations with him in the year since that class.
Houck is not included on the school’s online staff directory, and a page about him as an assistant coach for the university no longer exists.

title: Judge orders 3 taxpayer-funded Trump administration ads to be pulled from TV and social media
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — The federal government must pull three taxpayer-funded Trump administration ads that appear to have been made for political or propaganda purposes, including one touting the president’s claim that every American will get $5,000 if Republicans keep control of Congress in the upcoming election, a judge ruled Friday.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, in ordering the government to take down the advertisements entitled “$5,000 to Americans,” “Every Democrat Voted Against No Tax on Tips,” and “Cost of Socialism.”
She said they must be taken off official government websites, including social media sites such as YouTube, Instagram and the like. She also ordered the cancellation of any slots, placements, reservations, or arrangements for the airing or distribution of the ads through authorized third parties, including by Trump’s flagship super PAC, MAGA Inc.
Responding to the ruling, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: “This Biden-appointed activist judge issued a lawless order to stop the administration from sharing patriotic videos.”
Rochon ruled during a hearing in which she considered expanding a temporary restraining order she issued two weeks ago, when she banned a series of ads that glorify President Donald Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms.
The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have made to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they aren’t aimed at helping members of the public benefit from specific government programs, according to the plaintiffs.
After Rochon issued the order, she noted that she was doing so on a Friday afternoon and that the government would have no excuse to delay taking them down immediately. Rochon was nominated to the court by then-President Joe Biden, a Democrat.
A government lawyer acknowledged that he would be able to immediately notify relevant individuals responsible for taking down the ads.
“Everyone is here. Everyone can hear my order. No one is at the theater,” the judge quipped in a reference to excuses offered by government lawyers when her recent order, which was issued during a weekend, wasn’t immediately obeyed.
The plaintiffs sought the removal of at least 13 ads, but Rochon only ordered that the three be pulled, at least for now. She said there are instances in which the president’s office is entitled to inform the public of its policies, justify its policies and respond to attacks on its policies.
Rochon said the plaintiffs were seeking to restrict the office in ways that were “broad and far reaching” and she found herself siding with the government on many of the ads.
But she added that irreparable harm could result to the plaintiffs if she didn’t ban the ads while the court case proceeds, though she noted that she could reverse herself and restore the ads or ban additional ads after hearing more evidence in the coming weeks.
“This court can neither postpone an election nor turn back the clock,” Rochon said after concluding that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claims regarding the ads and would suffer harm if they were not taken down.
“This temporary restraining order will stop the administration’s wanton disregard for the law while the court hears the full case,” said Bradley Girard, a lawyer with Democracy Forward. “Congress has made clear that partisan ads cannot be funded with taxpayer dollars, and we are proud to work with this coalition to earn today’s result.”

title: More than 42 million Americans have cast early midterm ballots
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting.
According to the University of Florida Election Lab, early midterm turnout is similar to the 2018 “blue wave.” The lab said enthusiasm appears to be on the Democrats’ side.
Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political scientist, said the U.S. could be headed toward record turnout.
“It’s possible that we will beat the 2018 turnout rate. That was the highest turnout rate for midterm elections since 1914. But there are uneven patterns of turnout,” McDonald said.
McDonald said the uneven turnout levels come from a partisan divide.
“Registered Democrats, unaffiliated, those people who don’t have a party registration, are engaged at the moment. But registered Republicans are not as much,” McDonald said.
Democrats account for 44% of early votes, compared with about 31% for Republicans.
McDonald said the early voting rate has increased this cycle for young voters and minorities.
“Makes me believe that this electorate is going to be the most diverse electorate for a midterm election in U.S. history. We can see high levels of engagement among AfricanAmericans, Hispanics, Asian Americans, but we don’t see as much among whites,” McDonald said.
There are limits to McDonald’s model. Not all states require party registration, and some states do not place much emphasis on early voting.
“So places like Maine, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, they’re going to have maybe a third of their votes cast early. So they’re going to be very much unlike the vote by mail states or other states that have large volume of in-person early voting,” McDonald said.
McDonald said Democrats are building an early lead in early voting, but Republicans will make up some amount of ground on Election Day. Results won’t be announced until after the polls close Tuesday, November 3.

title: Child dressed as Grim Reaper startles Florida neighbors
text:
Child dressed as Grim Reaper startles Florida neighbors
Residents in San Carlos Park, Florida, were startled Wednesday evening when a child dressed as the Grim Reaper roamed the neighborhood, ringing doorbells and peering through windows.
Resident Haley Harris described her encounter with the cloaked figure.
"I heard this, like, shriek. I thought it was a little kid that got hurt or something like that, so I turned," Harris said. "I look at the Grim Reaper standing in the street with his, you know, his stick."
"I know it's Halloween season, but I was like, maybe this isn't a joke. Should I run?" Harris said, recounting the moment. "I sort of start to jog inside, and then he started to chase after me. But then, he ended up walking off. So after that, I figured, you know, it's probably just some kid trying to be funny."
Harris shared a video of the encounter online, which showed the figure ringing doorbells and peeping through a door.
"You always have to have your head on a swivel, and someone just doing this [in] like broad daylight — that's terrifying," said Ava Camputaro, who reacted to the video.
Two neighbors who had the cloaked character on their doorsteps called the non-emergency line. The Lee County Sheriff’s Office later revealed that the Grim Reaper was a child with no criminal intent.
Harris said she ultimately believed it was a spooky prank but expressed concern for the child’s safety.
"I was worried more about his safety, especially, you know, a young kid who probably doesn't know better going up to strangers' homes looking strange," Harris said. "It's not Halloween yet, so some people might not be appreciative of that."
The sheriff’s office confirmed the child was returned to their parents and advised residents to avoid confronting individuals in similar situations. Instead, they recommended using security cameras and contacting law enforcement.

title: InvestigateTV+ Weekend: Plane crashes near airports
text:
(InvestigateTV) — For millions living in the shadow of an airport, the danger isn’t hypothetical. For one mother, it cost her everything.
Plus, not every danger comes from above, sometimes it’s sitting right outside your window.
Danger Zone
When a UPS plane crashed just seconds after taking off in Louisville, Kentucky last year, the incident killed not just the three crew onboard but a dozen people on the ground in an industrial area near the runway. That crash is now shining a light on millions of Americans who live or work in “Danger Zones” in close proximity to airports. Although the FAA has established minimum buffers designed to avoid worst-case scenarios when aviation disasters occur, experts say more needs to be done to protect homes and businesses.
Our national investigative team examined federal crash data to see where these accidents are happening and how often, and found examples from across the country of plane crashes into homes and neighborhood streets — often injuring and killing not just those onboard the aircraft, but people on the ground.
Senior National Investigative Reporter Joce Sterman sat down with some of those pushing for change industry wide — including a Florida mayor whose city has seen a series of close-proximity crashes - and the grieving mother of a 4-year-old boy killed in one of those crashes when a plane hit the family’s car just feet from the airport. We also hear from a retired airline pilot and safety advocate about potential solutions on both sides of the runway fence.
Generator carbon monoxide dangers
When the power goes out during a hurricane or storm, many families turn to generators to stay safe. But a new federal report finds that same backup power can create a hidden danger of its own.
Investigators spent four years studying carbon monoxide poisonings in southeast Louisiana — and now they’re calling for a major change in how close generators can be to your home.
Electric aircraft & EMS response times
When seconds matter in a medical emergency, getting help there fast can mean the difference between life and death.
Now, some rural communities are testing a new way to close that gap — a one-person aircraft that can carry a paramedic and full life-saving gear straight to a patient, skipping the roads altogether.
Photojournalist Greg Simpson in Charlotte introduces us to the woman flying it.
Tips to tackle credit card debt
Many of you are focused on credit card bills right now as rates stay high and prices keep climbing. In this Watching Your Wallet, Consumer Investigator Rachel DePompa lays out a plan to tackle your credit card debt between now and the end of the year.
