title: Sanford mayoral, City Council candidates discuss solutions for public safety concerns
text:
Sanford’s mayoral and City Council candidates have been speaking up about their concerns over public safety, highlighted by the recent closure of Heritage Crossing, ahead of Tuesday’s election.
The area near the old Woolen Mill has become an “attractive nuisance and extraordinary public safety hazard,” the city has said, and the City Council voted this month to extend the road closure until public safety officials determine it’s safe.
With the city already facing uncertainty over how plans for a potential data center and biosolid processing plant fit into its future, the topic of chronic homelessness has become the latest big issue looming over the local election.
We asked the four mayoral candidates and seven council candidates how they would tackle the topic. For the few who didn’t meet our Wednesday deadline, we’ve included parts of their responses to a similar question during a recent Meet the Candidates event.
Here’s what you need to know about where the candidates stand.
MAYORAL CANDIDATES
Two of the candidates running to succeed Mayor Becky Brink emphasized cooperation between local and state authorities as key to addressing public safety.
Deputy Mayor Maura Herlihy said the Sanford police and fire departments do an exceptional job addressing safety, and more support is coming in the form of plans for a supportive housing project and a recovery home project in Alfred. She believes areas like Heritage Crossing need more investments in security — like cameras — to deter illegal activity.
If elected, she plans on strengthening relationships with county and state officials “to secure immediate winter sheltering options and push for judicial reforms that holds individuals accountable in their rehabilitation.”
Pete Tranchemontagne, a current member of the City Council, said his safety concerns with Heritage Crossing begin with preventing major fires at the mill. He also said one of his biggest priorities would be working with state and local officials to acquire necessary funding and keep the cost off Sanford’s taxpayers.
“This would be one of my biggest priorities because public safety is the number one job of local government, followed by reducing the community’s tax burden through economic development,” he said.
Tranchemontagne has largely been campaigning on the issue of public safety, citing dozens of letters he’s sent to lawmakers and other state officials requesting additional assistance from local agencies to combat safety issues.
Daniel White said he has developed a strategy to address the environmental hazards at Heritage Crossing, in the event the city is able to acquire the property.
“By initiating a feasibility study and securing federal, state, and historic preservation grants, we can revitalize this site into a textile heritage museum,” he said in an email. “Regarding pressing safety concerns, I maintain full confidence in the capabilities of our public safety officials.”
Matthew Dupuis did not respond to a request for comment, but at the city’s Meet the Candidates night, he voiced his concerns with how much the city would legally be able to do. He said that as much of a problem as chronic homelessness is, the city’s options for those who do not want assistance are limited.
CITY COUNCIL HOPEFULS
Among the seven City Council candidates for two open seats, Alex Clary, Michael Perry and Meagan Crawford all agreed that transparency and education are a priority to ensure residents are able to stay informed about local issues.
Crawford also said she would work towards establishing a warming center, while Shawn Goowdin said that while the idea of a warming shelter is heartfelt, he would have concerns regarding funding and building maintenance.
“The best thing we can do for the people of Sanford, both housed and unhoused, is to keep the mill building closed,” Goodwin said.
Council member Jonathan Martell, who is running for reelection, said during the Meet the Candidates night that the city’s choice to pause its syringe service program late last year was a step in the right direction, but that police also need to be provided with enough support and resources to allow them to keep the city safe.
Victoria Pariyar said chronic homelessness is an issue that also goes hand in hand with mental health, and that respect towards those suffering from it was important in solutions considered by municipalities.
“People are nervous,” she said. “I think more businesses would help.”
Bryce Lambert said the city would need to find a way to help the police department with enforcement without violating any laws.
“It’s gonna take some creative measures to get there,” he said.

title: Bringing cancer screening conversations to the salon chair
text:
ANDRESON, S.C. (InvestigateTV) - Do you only go to the doctor when you have an ache or feel sick? For many women that answer can be “yes.”
A 2025 survey said that every one in six women say they missed or may have missed a routine cancer screening within the past year.
A South Carolina salon is partnering with a statewide health initiative to have important conversations about cancer screening with clients.
Kimberly Cheatham, owner of Kreative Kimistry in Anderson, has joined the Pink Palmetto Project, an effort by the South Carolina Cancer Alliance focusing on breast and cervical cancer education.
Cheatham said her clients often get personal with her.
“They confide in me when they don’t even feel comfortable telling their families things and their friends, because they know that I have a connection to them,” Cheatham said.
Personal loss drives mission
Cheatham’s mother died from colon cancer at age 62.
“I’m still dealing with the effects of it now because I have really bad PTSD about going to the doctor for, you know, getting my exams and stuff,” she said.
That loss motivates her to reach out to clients, particularly younger women.
“And that’s why I want to talk to women and just, especially like even younger women like the one that I have here, because the earlier you get this taken care of, the better,” Cheatham said.
Addressing disparities
Brenda Thorpe, senior community engagement director for the South Carolina Cancer Alliance, said data shows significant disparities in breast cancer outcomes.
“When I looked at the data, we see a huge disparity with women when it comes to breast cancer, right? That’s the most common cancer that women are impacted by. But the data also shows a disparity for African-American women. And so African-American women are diagnosed at a later stage for breast cancer,” Thorpe said.
When diagnosed in later stages, treatment is often harsher, and the chance of survival can go down. According to Breast Cancer Prevention Partners, black women have a 40% higher death rate from breast cancer compared to white women.
Nicole Echols, CEO of the South Carolina Cancer Alliance, said salons provide a comfortable setting to reach women.
“We know that we can get into the spaces and have conversations and talk to women about how important it is for their breast health and how important screening is and how important early detection is and how it really can save your life,” Echols said.
The project aims to ensure women know the signs of cancer and keep up with their screenings.
“The grief and the emotions that I went through, I wouldn’t want anybody to have to go through that,” Cheatham said. “So, if you can go and prevent that from happening, then I really feel like if I can help you do that.”
Kreative Kimistry is the only salon in the Upstate participating in the Pink Palmetto Project. The South Carolina Cancer Alliance hopes to expand the program with additional funding.
Skin cancer screening
Hair stylists are playing another vital role in cancer screening.
Stylists Against Skin Cancer is a dermatologist-led educational campaign for hair professionals that focuses on the detection and prevention of skin cancer in the scalp.
Because hair professionals see the entire scalp, they can find suspicious skin growth that clients might not see or feel. Then they can encourage the customer to visit a dermatologist for further investigation.

title: North Korea's Kim calls for rapid expansion of drone technology and observes weapons tests
text:
North Korea's Kim calls for rapid expansion of drone technology and observes weapons tests
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for rapidly expanding the country's drone technology and observed tests of various weapons, state media reported Friday, as his nation remains embroiled in a standoff with rival South Korea along their heavily fortified border.
The report came a day after South Korea's military said North Korea launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea in what were its first ballistic weapons firings in 17 days.
The North's official Korean Central News Agency said that Kim on Thursday visited an exhibition of a variety of attack and other drones that show recent achievements in the field of unmanned aeronautical technology.
In a speech at the exhibition, Kim stressed the need to seize “the absolute superiority in the drone technology” and announced unspecified steps needed to “rapidly expand and strengthen the unmanned aeronautical technology,” KCNA said.
To mark the event, KCNA said that North Korea later conducted test-launches of various drones, missiles and weapons from the 600 mm-calibre ultra-precision multiple rocket launchers. KCNA photos showed Kim watching soaring weapons or him clenching his fist while his teenage daughter was clapping her hands beside him. South Korea's spy agency assesses that the girl, reportedly about 13, is likely Kim's heir.
Tensions between the two Koreas have been running high since last month's land mine blasts at their border that wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded an apology. But Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.
Last week, North Korea threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border.
North Korea has pulled out of talks with the U.S. and South Korea after Kim's high-stakes diplomacy with President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019. In recent weeks, North Korea has dialed up weapons testing activities in a likely attempt to boost its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore talks with Kim.
On Saturday, Kim made a surprise visit to a Chinese border town via a newly opened bridge and vowed to develop bilateral ties. Kim has recently taken steps to cement ties with China, North Korea's economic pipeline, after years of prioritizing ties with Russia, including by sending troops and ammunition to support its war against Ukraine.

ACLU releases video of ICE agent slashing tires of a legal observer in Oregon
text:
ACLU releases video of ICE agent slashing tires of a legal observer in Oregon
The incident comes amid a surge of ICE activity in the state
ACLU releases video of ICE agent slashing tires of a legal observer in Oregon
The incident comes amid a surge of ICE activity in the state
The ACLU has released video of an ICE agent slashing the tires of a legal observer's vehicle in Portland, Oregon.
Two people being represented by the American Civil Liberties Union filed an administrative complaint this week with the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The incident occurred on Oct. 7 amid an ICE surge in the state of Oregon.
See the incident in the video above
The video shows the side view of the legal observer's car. A nondescript vehicle with flashing lights drives alongside them and rolls down its driver's side window to reveal the driver in a black mask and baseball cap. The pursuing vehicle even cuts in toward them, forcing the observers to stop their vehicle. When stopped, the driver and passenger get out of the pursuing vehicle, revealing ICE agents wearing masks and "Police ICE" tactical vests. The ICE driver, wearing gloves, produces a knife and stabs once into the legal observer's car before it can drive off. The car drives forward about 20 feet, stopping again.
A second ICE vehicle can then be seen behind the legal observer's car. The first ICE driver hops out of his car again to run toward the legal observer's car and stab at the same tire two more times, then runs back behind the two ICE vehicles.
"What happened to us is not unique, and that is what is so terrifying," said the Portland-area residents in a statement, identified by the ACLU as A.P. and M.P. "We observe and record public ICE activity in order to shine a light on their abusive behavior and to create a record of what our government is up to. Because of that, they are terrorizing us and anyone else who dares to exercise their First Amendment right to hold our government accountable. We hope that sharing our story will bring attention to their reckless and unconstitutional attacks on our communities."
Legal observers are neutral parties, usually providing assistance to people exercising their 1st Amendment rights, especially in incidents that involve law enforcement. With the second Trump administration's immigration crackdown, it's become more common for legal observers to act as witnesses to and provide video documentation of possible ICE misconduct.
"The right to record publicly visible law enforcement activity is fundamental to our democracy," said Scarlet Kim, a senior staff attorney with the ACLU.
The ACLU complaint demands that DHS "investigate the incident, preserve all relevant evidence, and discipline the responsible agents" and that DHS conduct "a comprehensive investigation of the nationwide pattern of ICE agents retaliating against individuals observing and recording their activities," according to a statement.
This news comes amid two other recent stories of ICE misconduct. In Houston, an ICE agent accused of ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. In Ohio, a former ICE agent was sentenced after pleading guilty to a federal charge of lying to an agent with the Dept. of Homeland Security during a domestic violence investigation involving him and his significant other.

title: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
text:
(Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War.
The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment.
“This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release.
Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies.
During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains.
The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

title: That Creepy Castle Across From Portsmouth? It Was a Prison.
text:
The Creepy Castle Across From Portsmouth Has a Dark History
We continue with Garret's Creepy Fact Storytime... Back to Portsmouth we go.
If you've ever spent any time along the Portsmouth waterfront, there's a good chance you've looked across the river and noticed that enormous castle-looking building sitting over at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard.
You know the one I'm talking about.
Huge walls. Tall towers. Arched windows. It looks like something you'd expect to see in an old horror movie.
And I've always wondered about that place.
Turns out, it wasn't built for royalty. It wasn't some wealthy family's waterfront mansion.
It was a prison. And its history is a lot more interesting than I ever imagined.
New England Had Its Own Alcatraz
The building is the former Portsmouth Naval Prison, located on Seavey's Island in Kittery, Maine.
Yes, Maine. Even though it's called the Portsmouth Naval Prison, it's actually across the Piscataqua River from Portsmouth, New Hampshire.
The prison opened in 1908 and eventually earned the nickname "Alcatraz of the East."
When it was constructed, the building was considered the largest poured-concrete structure in the world.
And you can understand why it earned that intimidating nickname.
Between the island location, the powerful currents of the Piscataqua River, and those castle-like towers, it wasn't exactly the kind of place you'd want to find yourself checking into.
The Island Was Holding Prisoners Before the Castle Even Existed
Here's something that surprised me.
According to the Naval Sea Systems Command, the site was originally home to Camp Long, a prisoner-of-war camp established during the Spanish-American War in 1898.
More than 1,600 Spanish prisoners of war were held there.
About a decade later, the naval prison opened on the same site.
READ MORE: The Strange History Behind Portsmouth's Oldest Cemetery
And over the next 66 years, an extraordinary number of men would pass through those walls.
According to research highlighted by the Portsmouth Public Library, more than 86,000 men passed through the prison between 1908 and 1974.
During World War II, the prison held more than 3,000 sailors and Marines at one time.
And there's another piece of World War II history connected to the building.
After Germany surrendered in 1945, German submarine crews were questioned at the prison by U.S. naval intelligence.
Think about that for a second.
A place we drive past today was once part of the military history of two world wars.
What Happened When the Prison Closed?
In 1974, the Navy officially closed the Portsmouth Naval Prison.
And what happened next is part of what makes this place so fascinating.
The enormous building remained standing.
For more than 50 years, the old castle has watched over Portsmouth Harbor, while life has continued on both sides of the river.
There have been multiple attempts over the years to find a new use for the building, but none has resulted in a completed redevelopment.
And it isn't just the history that's difficult to ignore.
It's the appearance.
Those towering walls. The rows of windows. The old fortress architecture.
Knowing that thousands of men once lived behind those walls gives the place a completely different feeling.
You can see over 300 pictures of the prison from the Naval History and Heritage Command website.
Could the Castle Finally Get a New Life?
There's actually been a recent development involving the old prison.
In August 2026, New Hampshire Public Radio reported that Senator Jeanne Shaheen had requested $5 million in federal funding for a feasibility study examining whether the former prison could become a "sailor campus."
The idea would be to explore recreational programs and support services for sailors stationed at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard while their submarines undergo repairs.
It's an interesting possibility for a building that has sat unused as a prison for more than half a century.
But the proposal was still in the planning stage when it was reported.
The Castle Is Still There, Watching Over the Harbor
One thing worth mentioning: the old prison isn't open for regular public tours. It's located within an active naval shipyard with restricted access.
But you don't have to go inside to appreciate just how unusual this piece of Seacoast history really is.
The next time you're walking along the Portsmouth waterfront, take a look across the river.
That enormous castle isn't just another historic building.
It was once one of the most recognizable military prisons in the country.
And more than a century after it opened, it still has a way of making you wonder what life was like behind those walls.
Personally, I think it looks creepy enough from the outside. I don't need to find out what those empty hallways sound like at night.

title: Ground cinnamon recalled ahead of holiday season due to elevated lead risk, FDA says

text:
(Gray News) - Ground cinnamon is being recalled in 14 states ahead of the holiday season.
SLR Food Distribution Inc said it’s voluntarily recalling Wise Wife Brand Ground Cinnamon because it could be contaminated with elevated levels of lead, according to a recall alert.
The affected cinnamon was sold in retail and grocery stores between Sept. 8, 2025, and June 28, 2026, in Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Nebraska, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin.
According to the recall notice, lead exposure can impact nearly every bodily system, with effects depending on dosage, duration, and an individual’s age and weight. Low-level, short-term exposure may not produce immediate symptoms, and no illnesses have been reported to date.
Here’s what to check for:
- Description: 110 grams (3.88 ounces) clear plastic container with a black screw-top cap.
- Best-before date: April 25, 2027.
- UPC: 0688474302754 (printed on the back label)
Short-term exposure to very low levels of lead may not cause any symptoms, and so far, no illnesses have been reported as a result of the potentially contaminated cinnamon, according to the recall alert.
Consumers are advised not to consume the recalled product and to throw it away or return it to the place of purchase for a full refund.

title: Experts eye key voting blocs ahead of Midterms
text:
NEW YORK CITY (Gray Media) - With millions of ballots already cast ahead of Election Day, conversations surrounding voter turnout are intensifying. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress.
Lincoln Mitchell, a political analyst and professor at Columbia University, says the first group feeling pressure is rural voters. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. While Mitchell does not expect these voters to dramatically flip parties, financial strain could depress turnout or weaken enthusiasm for Republicans and President Donald Trump.
The second crucial bloc is Latino voters. Mitchell notes that while the demographic is far from monolithic, its influence will be decisive in battleground states—particularly Texas, home to one of the cycle’s most competitive Senate races. Despite recent gains made by the GOP among Hispanic voters in states like Texas, Arizona, and Florida, Mitchell questions whether those inroads will hold over the long run.
Finally, experts are watching young white men, a demographic that turned out heavily for Trump in 2024. Mitchell points to foreign policy and affordability as two major factors driving potential shifts. If even a fraction of these voters stay home or shift away from the GOP, the ripple effect could be devastating for Republican candidates on the ballot.
Midterm elections historically cut against the party occupying the White House. Looking to buck that precedent, President Trump has urged supporters to vote as if his name were directly on the ballot. Tuesday night will reveal whether that mobilization strategy succeeded, or if shifting voter dynamics hand Democrats a major breakthrough.

title: Big 12 fines UCF $100K after 'discriminatory chants'
text:
Big 12 fines UCF $100K after 'discriminatory chants directed at BYU'
The Big 12 Conference has issued a $100,000 fine to the University of Central Florida after what it described as "discriminatory chants" directed at Brigham Young University while the Cougars played the Knights on Saturday.
Video above: Big 12 investigates reports of 'inappropriate chants' from OSU student section during BYU game
In a statement released Wednesday, the conference said it had completed its review of the discriminatory chants, issued the fine, and was implementing the following new conference-wide policy measures — effective immediately — to establish escalating consequences for discriminatory conduct at its athletic events:
- A confirmed first incident during a game will result in an automatic minimum $100,000 fine.
- A formal warning will follow the first incident, providing the institution an opportunity to immediately address the behavior and prevent further incidents.
- A second confirmed incident during the same game will result in an in-game competitive penalty, e.g., a 15-yard unsportsmanlike penalty in football or an unsportsmanlike two-shot technical foul in basketball, and may result in an additional $500,000 fine.
- Individuals ejected for discriminatory conduct will be prohibited from attending all athletic events for the remainder of the academic year and are subject to applicable University fan/student conduct policies.
Once paid, the fine will be directed toward student education initiatives, according to the conference.
Though the conference acknowledged that UCF followed pregame protocols and took immediate actions during the game "including removal of some individuals responsible for the conduct," it added that discriminatory behavior "has no place in the Big 12."
"The Big 12 remains committed to providing a respectful environment for student-athletes, coaches and fans," the statement reads. "Discriminatory conduct will not be tolerated, and the Conference will continue working with its member institutions to prevent such behavior and ensure meaningful consequences when incidents occur."
Saturday's game resulted in a 39-31 double-overtime victory for UCF over previously undefeated No. 2 BYU, the highest-ranked opponent to visit the Knights in program history.
Hearst sister station WESH was at the game and can report that some UCF fans could be heard chanting, "(expletive) the Mormons."
We are otherwise working to verify with either school what chant, or chants, prompted the fine.
"After becoming aware of the conference's decision, we will be reviewing our options," a UCF spokesperson said in a statement. 
WESH spoke with several students on the UCF campus Thursday. They say they don't want a few bad apples to define their fan base.
"I think it's a bit unfair," UCF student Alberto Socias said of the BIG 12's fine, "but I also understand the need for keeping these comments outside of sports."
From afar, Socias said he saw some fans removed by security from the Acrisure Bounce House for yelling the anti-Mormon slurs. 
"I feel like it was a loud minority," he said, "because they were screaming it super loud, so it seemed like a lot of people were saying it. But in reality, it was just a loud few people."
Brock Sly from Utah said he's still a Cougars fan after transferring from BYU to UCF. He's also a member of  The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.
"I'm kind of conflicted," Sly said. "I appreciate UCF's response, but at the same time, I feel like it's never something that should be chanted out in public. Bigotry is never OK. It wouldn't be OK against any other religion."
Sly said he supports the Big 12's updated policy to crack down on fan misconduct.   
"I think a fine, students don't really recognize that," Sly said, "but if they see the team getting penalized, they're going to realize like, hey, that's probably not something we can be doing. We're actively hurting our teams, so let's stop."
WESH emailed UCF on Thursday asking if it will appeal the fine, how many fans were kicked out of the game, and whether any students could face discipline.
The university responded that it has nothing additional to share at this time.

title: Christa Pike gives first public comments since her failed execution
text:
Christa Pike gives first public comments since her failed execution
Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection a month ago, is speaking out for the first time, saying she is recovering, "but healing is not the same as being okay."
Video above: Media witnesses recall what happened during Christa Pike’s failed execution
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak," Pike said in a written statement her attorneys say was dictated to them. "And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."
Pike, 50, was hospitalized after she survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike soon after the failed procedure was on a ventilator, and her attorneys did not expect her to survive. But she woke up and began talking and walking with assistance.
Pike said she was "prepared to die" by execution, but instead "woke up alone in a hospital confused and in pain," according to the statement.
It's the first public comment attributed to Pike since the botched execution. She is the only person to ever survive being injected with lethal chemicals in an execution, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.
Pike has launched what will likely be a protracted legal battle to prevent a second attempt to put her to death. She was returned to prison earlier this month after a 10-day hospitalization and has continued receiving medical care, according to her lawyers.
"Since that night, I have been largely isolated in the prison's medical ward, away from other people and the human connections that mean so much to me," Pike said in the statement. "That isolation brings its own kind of pain. I spent 28 years in solitary confinement and much of what I am experiencing today is a repeat of that condition."
State is investigating what went wrong
In the immediate aftermath of the botched execution, Tennessee’s Republican Gov. Bill Lee ordered an investigation into what went wrong in the death chamber and indefinitely postponed another execution scheduled this year.
The failure to execute Pike also upset Slemmer's family, who said the attention on Pike's condition has taken attention away from the victim.
"I think the state owes me a big apology," May Martinez, Slemmer's mother, told CNN affiliate WTLV this month.
Lee is not inclined to commute Pike’s sentence, he told reporters this week in Nashville.
"She's still incarcerated under the laws of the State of Tennessee," Lee said, according to CNN affiliate WSMV. "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts."
CNN’s Avni Trivedi contributed to this report.

title: Husson University employee under investigation
text:
A now-former assistant professor at Husson University was arrested Friday and accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, authorities said.
A student at the university in Bangor also accused Jonathan Houck of secretly filming her and other students undressing during a school assignment. University officials say they are “deeply disturbed” by the allegations against Houck and that he was terminated in mid-September.
Houck, 33, of Bangor, was arrested after a tip from the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, Bangor police said in a news release. He was taken into custody Friday afternoon, and staff at the Penobscot County Jail confirmed he was being held on $50,000 cash bail.
On Friday morning, Houck did not respond to requests for comment at a phone number and email listed for him. It wasn’t clear whether he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf.
Houck faces six counts of Class C possession of child sexual abuse material and four counts of violation of privacy, a Class D crime, police say.
Penobscot County Deputy District Attorney Chelsea Lynds said in a phone call that the six felony-level charges are related to material depicting children under 12, while the allegations of privacy violations stem from “different conduct.”
The file hosting service Dropbox alerted the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children on June 29 that a user named Jonathan Houck had uploaded files depicting a child being sexually assaulted, according to a search warrant affidavit by the Bangor Police Department.
Detectives found that, between 2020 and 2026, Houck uploaded at least two video files of sexually explicit material involving “a prepubescent minor,” according to the affidavit. During execution of the warrant at Houck’s Pearl Street home last month, Bangor police seized numerous electronic devices, including six cellphones, eight computers and four storage drives.
ALLEGED UNIVERSITY MISCONDUCT
The university learned about the investigation on Sept. 21, and within an hour, Houck was “escorted from the campus and relieved of his duties,” Sarah Walker Caron, the university’s director of communication, said in a written statement Friday.
“Husson cannot comment on personnel matters or ongoing legal matters, but the university has and will continue to comply with all law enforcement requests in a prompt manner,” the statement read. “As always, our primary concern is that the needs of our students are met and that the continuity of the education is maintained.”
Houck was listed on the university’s website as an assistant professor in the College of Science and Humanities. Several documents online, including from Husson University ceremony programs and the Maine Science Festival, indicate that he was part of the exercise science program.
He also participated in research on body composition at the university that was published in April 2025, according to a page on the Husson University Repository that has since been removed.
On Thursday, a student at the university in Bangor posted a video to social media alleging that Houck filmed her and other students undressing without their knowledge.
The student, Abigail Dudley, said she recently met with Bangor detectives who showed her images taken during an exercise science class in the fall of 2025.
She said the students were told to record their body weight during class. Houck instructed the students to step between a set of dividers, take off their clothes and step on the scale, she said. Somewhere near the scale was a hidden camera, Dudley said, and that footage was allegedly found on Houck’s electronic devices.
“I feel disgusted every time I wake up in the morning,” Dudley said in the video. “I’m terrified to walk into school. I look everywhere for cameras. I can’t even use the bathroom here.”
Dudley is now working with attorneys, who said in a written statement Friday that she is “horrified to learn about the shocking conduct” of her former instructor.
“Husson caused an unfathomable breach of trust against Abigail Dudley, other Husson students, and the broader community,” attorney Star Wagner said. “Students place their trust in educational institutions to provide a safe learning environment, and that trust was violated here.
“Serious questions must be answered regarding Husson’s role in allowing this abuse to occur.”
Staff Writer Drew Johnson contributed to this report.
HOW TO GET HELP
IF YOU or someone you know has experienced sexual harassment or assault, you can call the statewide Sexual Assault Crisis and Support Line at 800-871-7741 for free and confidential help 24 hours a day.
TO LEARN more about prevention and response in Maine, visit the Maine Coalition Against Sexual Assault website at mecasa.org.
FOR OTHER support or referrals, call the NAMI Maine Help Line at 800-464-5767 or email [email protected].

title: Hall-Dale boys soccer beats NYA to reach C South final
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
FARMINGDALE — The Hall-Dale boys soccer team is still trying to play a perfect 80 minutes in the Class C South playoffs. They’ll have at least one more opportunity.
The top-seeded Bulldogs took a two-goal lead in the first half and held on to beat fifth-seeded North Yarmouth Academy 2-1 in a Class C South semifinal Friday afternoon.
“It’s an amazing thing,” said Hall-Dale senior Karter Eldridge. “For 10 of us seniors, this is our last game on this field, and to walk away with a win is really special for us.”
Hall-Dale (15-1), the two-time defending state champion, will meet No. 2 Mt. Abram in the regional final on Tuesday.
NYA finished 9-7.
Eldridge and junior Korigan Greenhalgh scored to give Hall-Dale its two-goal lead.
“So far, through two games (in the playoffs), we’ve certainly been battle-tested,” said Hall-Dale coach Jesse Rowe.
Highlight on the road back for Greenhalgh
Greenhalgh scored with 4:37 remaining in the first half, taking a nice pass from Collin McArthur and nailing a shot into the net for the first goal of his varsity career.
“He loves the ball on that right foot,” Eldridge said. “I knew he was going to score that one.”
It was a big moment for Greenhalgh, who missed the Bulldogs’ title run last season because of a torn ACL.
“The fact he could go in and score that goal was huge,” Rowe said. “You could tell the team was excited, not just for him, but for that battle back (from injury).”
Rough and tumble
In a physical matchup, five yellow cards were handed out.
Playing keep away
Rowe was happy with the play of his backs, including Reid Parlin and Jack Chapin, for keeping the Panthers from getting clean shots on Hall-Dale goalie Landon Gilbert.
“It was definitely one of those games where everybody had to play together and stay together,” Rowe said. “Defensively, I thought that was a huge part (of the win).”
Statistical leaders
Hall-Dale: Karter Eldridge (goal), Korigan Greenhalgh (goal), Collin McArthur (assist), Kris McGrath (assist)
NYA: Read Weiss (goal), Gage Kloza (9 saves)

title: Market Basket to open next week in Scarborough
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new Market Basket supermarket will open Nov. 6 in Scarborough in the The Downs development off Haigis Parkway.
“We’re excited to be here and to become a part of the community,” store director Eric Beaulieu said Thursday as employees and contractors put finishing touches on the building, landscaping and product displays.
Beaulieu said he has already hired 300 people — including Scarborough High School students and other Greater Portland residents — and there are many other full- and part-time positions available.
This will be the fourth Market Basket in Maine, after stores in Biddeford, Westbrook and Topsham. The Massachusetts-based company operates more than 90 stores across New England.
It will be the second supermarket to open in The Downs, a 577-acre mixed-use development of a former horse-racing facility that stretches from Route 1 to Payne Road.
Maine’s first Costco opened there in 2023 and is driving nearly 2 million shoppers annually to nearby businesses, a study found.

title: President Trump reshuffles schedule, adds back Iowa and Kansas rallies ahead of midterms
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — As early voting surges across the country, President Donald Trump is reshuffling his weekend schedule to rally Republicans in two states with critical Senate races, underscoring his party’s push to drive turnout ahead of Election Day.
The Republican president will now visit Iowa and Kansas for back-to-back campaign rallies on Sunday, according to a person familiar with his plans who insisted on anonymity to discuss his schedule. Both rallies had previously been canceled.
The last-minute reversal comes amid a nationwide surge in early voting. Nearly 10 million more Americans had cast ballots five days before Election Day than at the same point in 2022, according to an Associated Press analysis of voting data. The increases have been particularly pronounced in states with competitive Senate races, including Iowa and Kansas, where early voting is up roughly 30%.
Democrats and Republicans each hope that rise favors them as they fight for control of Congress in an election that has turned largely on affordability issues and the president’s unpopularity. At the start of the month, Trump promised a marathon sprint of his signature rallies to shore up Republican candidates, and he has headlined 25 of them so far in October.
Weekend rallies back on after Trump says, ‘I don’t feel I have to go’
The president on Thursday furiously pushed back at the notion that the initial cancellation of his Kansas rally, which became public as he was returning to Washington from another campaign event in South Carolina, was tied to fatigue or his health. He lashed out at a reporter who asked about the change in his plans for Kansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is seeking reelection.
“I’m not going to Kansas because he’s doing very well,” Trump said, seeming to refer to Marshall. The president added that “I feel perfect” and that “I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas.”
The Republican National Committee initially said in canceling the rallies that Trump would do telerallies instead to reach more voters. But the person familiar with the latest plans said the Iowa and Kansas rallies have been rearranged to accommodate the new telerallies added to Trump’s schedule.
Trump’s original plans had him in Salina, Kansas, on Saturday and in Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday. Then the plans shifted so he would instead do a “72-hour sprint” of phone rallies, meant so the president could reach more voters nationwide, according to the RNC.
Sunday’s rally in Iowa will now be held in Cedar Rapids instead of Dubuque, according to another person familiar with the plans who spoke on the condition of anonymity to share information that was not yet public.
Both Kansas and Iowa are home to battleground Senate races that will help determine whether Republicans hold onto their narrow majority in the chamber in the midterm elections.
Trump has already traveled to both states this month to boost Marshall in Kansas and Republican Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, who currently serves in the House.
In an interview with a Kansas City radio station on Friday, Trump called Marshall “fantastic” and credited the senator for pushing his administration on policies benefiting Kansas farmers such as expanding tax-free use of red-dyed diesel.
Trump criticized Marshall’s Democratic challenger, Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton, as a “radical” who has “caused turmoil with the church because he’s so liberal.” Hamilton has said that if Jesus were standing before them now, “Roger Marshall would call him ‘woke.’”
Both parties hope a surge in voting favors them
Early voting is significantly outpacing the last midterm election, with millions more Americans casting ballots in advance.
In Texas, where voters are deciding closely watched Senate, House and governor’s races, more than 6.3 million Texans had voted early as of Wednesday, compared with 4.2 million at the same point four years ago, a 50% increase.
Advance voting has also increased more than 30% from the same point four years ago in Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Kansas, states with competitive Senate races. In South Carolina, where voters are choosing a successor to the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, early voting is up 83%.
Historic amounts of money have flowed into this year’s midterm elections. Republicans have expressed concerns about their voters not turning out amid voter dissatisfaction with Trump and high costs, issues Democrats have focused on in their campaigns.
In Michigan’s Senate race, the wrong Democrat remains in the headlines
Michigan Democrats hoped to put a bruising Senate primary behind them after progressive Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in August.
They’ve had no such luck as Election Day approaches.
Stevens reemerged in the final week before the general election, appearing on CNN to reaffirm that she would vote for El-Sayed while calling on him to repair relations with Jewish and Black voters. Her appearance came hours after her fiance said he would vote for El-Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.
Then on Friday, after agreeing to campaign alongside El-Sayed and Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina in Detroit on Sunday, Stevens released a lengthy statement on social media criticizing her former rival once again. She called on him to condemn an advertisement linking U.S. support for Israel to rising grocery prices and address concerns about his past rhetoric.
“Abdul promises to get money out of politics,” Stevens wrote. “He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”
El-Sayed has apologized for some of his past comments while attempting to unify Democrats.

title: Family says animal hospital worker took pug home after they paid for euthanasia
text:
COWETA COUNTY, Ga. (WSB) — A Georgia family said they paid hundreds of dollars for an animal hospital to euthanize their 4-year-old pug, then learned months later the dog was still alive.
The family said they were shocked by the discovery. They believe a worker at the hospital took the dog home.
Dog became sick
Rebecca Belote said her 17-year-old son and the pug, named Cha Cha, wore matching hoodies.
“She hardly walked anywhere because he carried her everywhere,” Belote said.
Belote said Cha Cha then became sick. She said the family was told the dog was in organ failure and had diabetic ketoacidosis.
Belote said Senoia Animal Hospital recommended the dog be euthanized. She said the decision affected her son and her husband.
“They both took it kind of hard. My son was really attached to the dog,” Belote said.
Photo on Facebook
The family said Cha Cha was not euthanized in March as they believed and that a hospital worker took the dog home, keeping her for months.
Belote said she was on Facebook when she saw a picture of Cha Cha.
“I knew scrolling like, ‘That’s my dog,’” Belote said.
Belote said a former hospital worker confirmed a hospital employee took Cha Cha.
Hospital denies claim
Belote said the hospital denied the claim.
“They have a lawyer and they won’t talk about it. They just say it didn’t happen,” Belote said.
Belote said she spoke with the worker’s husband, who confirmed his wife had Cha Cha. She said he told her the pug was in good health.
Belote said the hospital eventually put Cha Cha down. She said she thinks the hospital did so to hide what happened.
“The fact that they put a healthy dog down. That’s just sick,” Belote said.
The animal hospital did not respond with a statement.

title: County Soccer Teams and Cross Country Runners Chase Championships This Weekend
text:
County Teams Chase Soccer Finals and Cross Country State Titles in Huge Weekend of High School Sports
If you're following Aroostook County high school sports this weekend, there's going to be plenty to keep up with.
We've reached the regional semifinals in soccer, with County teams looking to earn their way into next week's championship games. At the same time, some of the area's best distance runners are headed to Augusta for the Maine State Cross Country Championships.
There are some terrific stories heading into the weekend, too.
Houlton's boys are trying to keep their remarkable soccer tournament run going after knocking off the top seed. Both Presque Isle soccer teams are still alive in Class B. Several County rivals will meet in Class D, and Houlton/GHCA's boys cross country team will be looking to defend its state championship.
It's shaping up to be one of the biggest weekends of the fall season.
Here's what to watch Friday and Saturday.
Girls Soccer Semifinals
Class B North: Presque Isle Gets Another Home Game
Saturday, October 31 | 1 p.m.
(7) Cony at (3) Presque Isle
Presque Isle's girls are one win away from the Class B North championship game, but they'll be facing a team that has already pulled off a major upset.
The third-seeded Lady Wildcats advanced with a 3-1 win over Skowhegan on Wednesday. Peyton Boinske scored twice, and Carrlyn Buck added another goal.
Now Presque Isle welcomes seventh-seeded Cony, which knocked off second-seeded Gardiner 2-1 in the quarterfinals.
Cony has already shown it can beat one of the higher seeds. Presque Isle will be looking to make sure that run ends Saturday afternoon.
Class C North: Fort Kent and Houlton Meet With a Trip to the Final on the Line
Friday, October 30 | 4:30 p.m.
(4) Houlton at (1) Fort Kent
We're guaranteed to have a County team playing for the Class C North girls championship.
Top-seeded Fort Kent hosts fourth-seeded Houlton on Friday afternoon, and both teams are coming off impressive quarterfinal performances.
Fort Kent shut out Maine Central Institute 3-0 to advance, while Houlton rolled past Central 7-2.
Ava Ezell and Raina Ezell each scored three goals for the Shires in that win.
Now Houlton takes its offense on the road against the top-seeded Warriors, with a regional championship berth going to the winner.
Class D North: Fort Fairfield and Central Aroostook Renew Their Rivalry
Saturday, October 31 | Noon
(3) Central Aroostook at (2) Fort Fairfield
There's another all-County semifinal Saturday when Fort Fairfield welcomes Central Aroostook.
The second-seeded Tigers advanced with a 4-0 shutout of Washburn. Chloe White scored twice, while Kendall Ainsworth and Madison Parks also found the back of the net. Addison Cole recorded the shutout.
Central Aroostook had to hold off Van Buren in a 3-2 quarterfinal.
Lilly Burtt scored twice for the Lady Panthers, with Stevi Pierce adding the third goal.
Both teams have earned their way into the final four, and now one of them will move on to play for the Class D North championship.
Class D North: Madawaska Heads to the Top Seed
Saturday, October 31 | 1 p.m.
(5) Madawaska at (1) Penobscot Valley
Madawaska has already won one close game on the road this postseason.
The fifth-seeded Owls defeated Ashland 2-1 in overtime Wednesday to earn a trip to the Class D North semifinals.
Now they'll travel to face top-seeded Penobscot Valley.
It'll be another tough test away from home, but Madawaska has already shown it can find a way through a tight tournament game.
Eight-Person Girls: Wisdom Welcomes Undefeated Sumner
Friday, October 30 | 3 p.m.
(3) Sumner at (2) Wisdom
Wisdom's girls are back home Friday, with an opportunity to reach the regional championship.
The Lady Pioneers advanced with a 6-1 win over George Stevens Academy.
Ellie Cyr scored three goals and added an assist, while Blake Pelletier and Peyton Roy each contributed a goal and an assist. Madisyn Cyr also scored.
Now Wisdom faces third-seeded Sumner, which comes into the game unbeaten.
It's a big matchup for the Pioneers and another opportunity to continue what has already been a strong postseason.
Boys Soccer Semifinals
Class B North: Presque Isle Heads to John Bapst
Saturday, October 31 | Noon
(4) Presque Isle at (1) John Bapst
Presque Isle's boys are headed to the Class B North semifinals after defeating Erskine Academy 4-1 on Wednesday.
Now the fourth-seeded Wildcats travel to face top-seeded John Bapst.
The Crusaders survived a close quarterfinal against Caribou, winning 2-1 after the eighth-seeded Vikings gave them a serious challenge.
Presque Isle will be looking to take advantage of its opportunity Saturday and earn a place in the regional championship.
Saturday, October 31 | 2 p.m.
(3) Fort Kent at (2) George Stevens Academy
Fort Kent’s boys are hitting the road Saturday afternoon with a trip to the Class C North championship on the line.
The third-seeded Warriors are coming off a 2-0 quarterfinal victory over Washington Academy, with Dom Cyr and Finn Marquis each finding the back of the net.
Now Fort Kent heads to Blue Hill to take on second-seeded George Stevens Academy in what should be a good semifinal matchup.
The Warriors have already shown they can get the job done defensively, and they’ll need another strong performance against a higher-seeded opponent.
Kickoff is set for 2 p.m. Saturday, with the winner advancing to the Class C North regional championship.
Class D North: Madawaska Hosts Hodgdon
Friday, October 30 | 6 p.m.
(4) Hodgdon at (1) Madawaska
Madawaska's boys have been one of the top teams in Class D North, and they'll have another home game Saturday evening.
The top-seeded Owls are coming off a 5-0 victory over MSSM, a game that also marked head coach Ben Gagnon's 100th career coaching win.
Josh Querze and Aiden Gagnon each scored twice in the victory, while Quinn Pelletier added another.
Hodgdon's path to the semifinals was a little more dramatic.
The fourth-seeded Hawks defeated Easton 3-2 in a game that saw Hodgdon build a two-goal lead before the Bears battled back.
Wyatt Oliver scored twice, Finn Gardiner added another, and goalkeeper Aiden Ciarleglio made several important saves to help Hodgdon advance.
Now the two County teams meet with a trip to the Class D North championship on the line.
Class D North: Central Aroostook and Fort Fairfield Meet Again
Friday, October 30 | 3 p.m.
(3) Fort Fairfield at (2) Central Aroostook
It's another all-County semifinal in Class D, this time in Mars Hill.
Central Aroostook survived a penalty-kick finish against Penobscot Valley to advance, while Fort Fairfield shut out Washburn 3-0.
Asher Winters scored twice for the Tigers, Dax Milton added the other goal, and Levi Cole recorded the shutout.
The Panthers will have home-field advantage Saturday, but Fort Fairfield comes in after a strong quarterfinal performance.
One of these teams will be moving on to the Class D North championship.
Eight-Person Boys: Wisdom Travels to Calais
Friday, October 30 | 2:30 p.m.
(3) Wisdom at (2) Calais
Wisdom's boys are one win away from a regional championship appearance after shutting out Lee Academy 5-0.
Cayden Hartgrove led the Pioneers with two goals and two assists. Zeek Cyr added a goal and an assist, while Preston Lavoie and Sam Paradis each scored.
Bentley Nadeau recorded the shutout in goal.
Now the third-seeded Pioneers head to second-seeded Calais, which advanced with a 3-0 win over Van Buren.
Eight-Person Boys: Houlton Looks to Keep Its Upset Run Going
Friday, October 30 | 6:30 p.m.
(9) Houlton at (4) Penobscot Christian
Houlton's boys delivered one of the most memorable moments of the tournament Wednesday.
The ninth-seeded Shires knocked off top-seeded Mattanawcook 2-1 in overtime, with James Baillargeon scoring the winning goal with just four seconds remaining.
His brother Will scored Houlton's first goal.
Now Houlton heads to undefeated Penobscot Christian for another big challenge.
The Shires have already shown that seeding doesn't decide the outcome. Friday they'll try to keep their remarkable run going and earn a place in the regional championship.
State Cross Country Championships: County Runners Head to Augusta
And while the soccer semifinals are taking place across Northern Maine, some of the County's top runners will be competing for state championships Saturday.
The Maine State Cross Country Championships are scheduled for Cony High School in Augusta, bringing together the top qualifying teams and individuals from around the state.
Aroostook County will have runners competing in both Class B and Class C.
Class B: Presque Isle and Caribou Look to Build on Strong Regional Performances
The Class B races will feature several County athletes who have already turned in impressive performances this fall.
On the girls' side, Presque Isle finished second at the Northern Maine regional championships, while Caribou placed third.
Caribou's Emma Graves enters the state meet after winning the Northern Maine Class B individual championship.
Presque Isle's Lillian Johnson and Aleah Rideout have also been among the area's strong performers.
Now they'll have the opportunity to test themselves against the best runners from Southern Maine as well.
For both programs, Saturday represents the culmination of a fall season filled with competitive meets and strong performances.
Class C: Houlton/GHCA Boys Looking to Defend Their State Championship
One of the biggest County storylines in Augusta will be the Houlton/GHCA boys cross country team.
The Shires are the defending Class C state champions, and they're coming into Saturday's meet with plenty of momentum.
Houlton/GHCA won its second consecutive Northern Maine regional title last weekend, scoring just 30 points and placing four runners among the top five finishers.
Malachi Witmer, Brayden Drake, Wyatt Quint and Logan Witmer helped lead that performance, giving the Shires another opportunity to compete for a state title.
The challenge now is to put together one more strong team race against the best Class C competition in Maine.
Class C Girls: Individual Qualifiers Ready for Their State Meet
The County will also have several individual runners competing in the Class C girls championship.
Houlton's Charlotte Estabrook and Isabella McCarthy earned their places at the state meet with strong regional performances.
Eleanora Streeter of Washburn and Sadie Wigmore of MSSM also qualified individually.
For these runners, Saturday is an opportunity to finish their seasons competing against the top Class C athletes in the state.
And with the team and individual championships all being decided on the same day, there will be plenty to follow in Augusta.
One of the Biggest Weekends of the Fall
By the time Saturday evening rolls around, we'll know which County soccer teams are headed to the regional championships and how our local runners finished at the state cross country meet.
There are rivalry games, championship opportunities, undefeated opponents and underdog stories all packed into two days.
Whether you're following the action from a soccer sideline or keeping an eye on the results from Augusta, there's plenty to be excited about.
We'll continue following the County teams and athletes throughout the weekend, with results, photos and updates as they become available.

title: UMaine scientists analyze 4-billion-year-old Martian meteorite
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) — Scientists at the University of Maine have identified one of the oldest known Martian meteorites on Earth while analyzing rock samples.
The meteorite, named Teghaza 001, is more than 4 billion years old. Only two other known Martian meteorites are older.
The specimen was originally recovered in the Sahara Desert in 2022. Professor Alicia Cruz-Uribe and her colleagues later analyzed the rock as part of a collection of Martian samples.
According to a study published in the journal Science, the rock dates back to the early formation of Mars, offering researchers a rare look into the planet’s early geologic history.

title: Falmouth football ousts defending champion Westbrook in B South quarterfinal
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
FALMOUTH — It was Harper Drosdik’s first start at quarterback. And it was in the opening round of the Class B South playoffs.
The Falmouth junior was confident, however, and proved it.
Drosdik threw and ran for nearly 200 yards, Falmouth’s defense made a clutch fourth-quarter stop, and the fourth-seeded Navigators ousted defending champion Westbrook, 20-14, in a regional quarterfinal Friday night.
“Before the game, there was nerves. As soon as you step on the field, it just kind of goes away,” Drosdik said. “I knew I was ready, I was prepared. All the coaches helped me, and I was just trying to stay calm back there and just do my job.”
Drosdik was starting in place of Micah Derrig, who broke his collarbone in the Navigators’ regular-season finale.
Westbrook, the No. 5 seed, finished 3-6.
“I’m proud of our kids, proud of our coaches. Give Falmouth credit, they’re a well-coached team,” coach Sam Johnson said. “I thought we had a chance there at the end, we just kind of came up short. That’s football, that’s life.”
SHAKE IT OFF
• Falmouth (4-5) began the game in a hole. Lucas Roberson retrieved the opening kickoff on a hop, cut to his right and raced 72 yards through an opening for a 7-0 Westbrook lead 12 seconds into the game.
On the Falmouth sideline, coach Brandon Dorsett told his team to “flush it out.”
“We got kicked in the face,” he said. “But we responded. … You trust the kids, and they did a great job.”
• On their first drive of the second quarter, the Navigators went 77 yards in 11 plays, capped by a 4-yard run by Owen Ross. Falmouth also got points on its next two drives, with Drosdik scoring on a 1-yard run, and then Theo Roediger connecting on a 23-yard field goal 20 seconds before halftime after the Navigators recovered the kickoff.
Westbrook’s Thomas Coleman ran 31 yards for a touchdown to make it 17-14 with 5:32 left in the third quarter, but another Roediger field goal, this time from 35 yards, made it 20-14 with 9:17 to play.
KEY STOPS
Westbrook drove from its 27 to the Falmouth 41 in pursuit of the go-ahead score, but the Navigators’ Louis Sustersic, Wes Howard and Brendon Welch teamed up to stop Coleman on fourth-and-1 from the 32 with 4:10 to go.
A sack by Riser Backman on the next drive helped lead to another turnover on downs that sealed the victory.
“They played lights out,” said Dorsett, who said the game plan was to lock in on Westbrook running back and receiver Andre Hicks III, who finished with 20 yards on two carries. “One of the best defensive performances we’ve had all year, which is what we need in the playoffs when the stakes are high.”
FINDING A RHYTHM
• Falmouth didn’t treat its new starting quarterback gently. Drosdik completed 12 of 23 passes for 143 yards, and also ran 12 times for 48 yards. As the game went on, the junior seemed to grow more comfortable with leading the offense.
“It makes me feel very confident in myself,” Drosdik said about getting the trust from his coaches. “I trust my teammates out there. They’re playmakers, and they’re great.”
• Those playmakers stepped up at key moments. His top target was Howard, who had a 29-yard catch on Falmouth’s first touchdown drive and back-to-back 17-yard grabs before the final field goal.
“I need to step up, but we also have three other great receivers that I’m able to rely on,” Howard said. “(And Drosdik) is definitely a great quarterback, his natural ability’s right there.”
UNSUNG HERO
Wherever the ball seemed to go with Westbrook on offense, Dane Langelier followed. The nose tackle made plays sideline to sideline, got great push up front, and was selected as the defensive player of the game.
STAT LEADERS
• Falmouth: Harper Drosdik (12 of 23, 143 yards; 12 carries, 48 yards, touchdown); Wes Howard (five catches, 75 yards), Brendon Welch (13 carries, 31 yards), Owen Ross (seven carries, 17 yards, touchdown)
• Westbrook: Thomas Coleman (five carries, 59 yards, touchdown), Lucas Roberson (72-yard kickoff return for touchdown), Cole Tanner (six carries, 23 yards)

title: New study reveals 43% drop in childhood peanut allergies over last decade
text:
(Aging Untold) — Recent research suggests that the long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach. New studies indicate that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy.
Dr. David Hill, lead author of the study, believes the reversal in guidance is a major factor in this decline.
“It’s safe to say in all likelihood, there are tens of thousands of kids today that don’t have food allergy that may have if we hadn’t made these recommendations about early allergen introduction,” Dr. Hill said.
For many families, the change in medical guidance has been transformative.
Kristie Herring, whose son Parker suffered from a severe peanut allergy, said the diagnosis was a “total surprise” given their family history.
Parker has been undergoing oral immunotherapy, a treatment involving slowly increasing doses of peanut protein, which has allowed him to safely consume peanut butter again.
However, experts caution that oral immunotherapy is not without risks and that early introduction is not a guaranteed cure for everyone. Food allergy remains a complex condition with multiple causes.
The American Academy of Pediatrics now recommends early introduction of peanut products for all infants without a history of prior reaction, provided they are already eating other solid foods. Pediatricians advise starting small and feeding peanut foods regularly—at least twice a week—through the first year and beyond. Importantly, whole peanuts should never be given to infants due to the significant risk of choking.
For those whose children have already developed a peanut allergy, specialists recommend consulting an allergist about available treatment options and maintaining vigilance in managing the condition.

title: Outreach coordinator says about 7 people in Aroostook County are living in tents
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Outreach coordinator Lori-Ann Chandler said about seven people she is working with in Aroostook County are living outside in tents as nights get colder.
“I’ve got maybe 7 that’s out, like completely out, which isn’t bad compared to what it could be,” Chandler said. “But yeah, there’s about 7 people right now that I’m currently working with that are literally in a tent.”
Room available at Homeless Services of Aroostook
Homeless Services of Aroostook sees an increase in people looking for a place to stay every year during this time. Executive Director Kari Bradstreet said there is still room available, but people have to be willing to come inside.
Bradstreet said outreach coordinators work to build relationships and help people make that transition.
“Lori just connecting with them is able to bridge between the tent to services with us,” Bradstreet said.
Concern about winter
Bradstreet said the number of families looking for housing has gone down over the past year. She said she is concerned that could change as winter approaches and the cost of heating oil rises.
“I think it ebbs and flows. I am concerned of what the winter is going to bring for families with, you know, the cost of heating oil and everything, the economy, just the way that it is. I am concerned that we’re going to see more families,” Bradstreet said.
How to contact Homeless Services of Aroostook
Bradstreet said the priority for now is getting people somewhere safe and connecting them with services.
Anyone who needs a place to stay, or knows someone who does, can call Homeless Services of Aroostook at 764-4125.

title: Packers’ Jacobs says TD celebration was modeled after gospel song. Here’s why it drew attention
text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. (AP) — Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs says he was paying homage to a gospel song rather than making light of his recent arrest when he briefly had his hands behind his back while celebrating a touchdown Thursday night.
This was Jacobs’ second game of the season after coming off the commissioner’s exempt list. He was placed on that list after charges were filed against him in August stemming from a May altercation with his then-girlfriend during which she said he threw her to the ground.
Jacobs pleaded no contest last month to misdemeanor charges of battery and criminal destruction of property.
Jacobs had just scored on a 1-yard run in the second quarter of the Packers’ 27-19 victory over the Carolina Panthers when he put his hands behind his back for a moment while accepting congratulations from teammates. The video garnered plenty of attention on social media as some who watched on television believed Jacobs was simulating getting handcuffed.
Jacobs said he instead was modeling his celebration after a gospel song called “Break Every Chain.”
“The guys did it with me,” Jacobs said. “I didn’t think it was going to be a thing that can be perceived a certain type of way. But it’s 2026, and it is what it is.”
Jacobs said he had spoken with Savion Williams and other receivers before making his season debut, and they came up with the idea that he would do a celebration thanking God after his first touchdown of the season. That celebration happened Sunday, as he went to his knees and raised his arms aloft after scoring in a 20-17 loss at Detroit.
They also had planned this “Break Every Chain” celebration after his second touchdown of the season. When Jacobs was asked about putting his hands behind his back as part of the celebration, he noted that the telecast only showed a brief portion of what he did.
“It was more to it than that,” Jacobs said. “They stopped showing the celebration after that. Like I said, it is what it is.”
Jacobs hadn’t been able to play or practice while he was on the commissioner’s exempt list. He was removed from that list last week, enabling him to play again even though the NFLs investigation of him remains ongoing.

title: Payton Pritchard scores 30 points, Celtics win NBA Cup opener
text:
BOSTON — Payton Pritchard scored 30 points, and the Boston Celtics raced past the Chicago Bulls 125-111 on Friday night in the NBA Cup opener for both teams.
Jayson Tatum added 26 points in 34 minutes. Paul George finished with 18 points and eight assists for Boston, which has won its last four games.
The Celtics got the lead up to 32 with 1:52 left in the first half. Chicago didn’t cut into the lead until the fourth quarter after Boston’s starters had already been pulled.
Pritchard paced the Celtics’ attack early, scoring 20 points in the first half in another big night against the Bulls after scoring 28 points in 22 minutes in a Boston win over Chicago on Oct. 26. He knocked down 9 of 17 shots Friday.
Boston also dominated the game inside, scoring 56 points in the paint.
Caleb Wilson had 23 points for the Bulls, who have lost four straight games. Norman Powell finished with 16 points and Matas Buzelis added 14.
Chicago shot just 38% (35 of 92) from the field and 30% (15 of 50) from the 3-point line
Boston beat Chicago by 35 points on Monday, converting 25 Bulls turnovers into 39 points.
After turning the ball over 25 times in a 35-point loss to Boston on Monday, Chicago had trouble taking care of the ball again on Friday, turning it over 16 times leading to 21 Celtics points.
Up next
Bulls: Visit Philadelphia on Monday.
Celtics: Visit Orlando on Sunday.

title: UMaine football seeking to snap 7-game losing streak
text:
Two longtime football rivals who have had disappointing seasons will try to gain some satisfaction when the University of Maine and the University of Rhode Island square off at Centreville Bank Stadium in Pawtucket, Rhode Island, at noon Saturday.
URI’s Meade Stadium is undergoing a $42 million renovation prompting the move to Pawtucket.
It will be the 94th meeting between the two dating back to 1911. UMaine holds a 62-28-3 advantage, but URI has won the last four meetings.
UMaine is 1-7 overall, 1-4 in the Coastal Athletic Association, and has lost seven in a row. URI, the preseason coaches’ poll’s favorite to defend its CAA title, is 4-4 and 1-3.
“We play them every year and I know what to expect,” said URI head coach Jim Fleming. “It is going to be a typical Maine-Rhode Island game. There is no love lost. It becomes very, very physical. It becomes very emotional, and we’re both going to have to be at that edge to be able to play our best.”
“I have a ton of respect for URI, a team that has had our number the past four years,” said UMaine fifth-year head coach Jordan Stevens, who has never beaten URI. “Seeing them on tape, seeing their culture, seeing their energy, their enthusiasm to play. That is evident on film.”
He said they are explosive on offense led by wide receiver Marquis Buchanan and his 49 receptions for 763 yards and six touchdowns.
“They find a way to maximize their personnel and get the ball down the field. They chip away at the defense and also hit explosive (plays). Their defense swarms to the football,” Stevens said.
UMaine will try to get its offense untracked. It has been a year-long struggle as the Black Bears enter the game ranked 121st among 124 Football Championship Subdivision teams in points scored per game (13.4) and total yards per game (281).
Caden Drezek has started the last two games at quarterback and, on the year, has completed 49.1% of his passes for 647 yards and three touchdowns with two interceptions. Nick Laughlin (34 catches, 327 yards, 3 TDs) and Evan Wallace (27-for-280) have been the top receivers and Rashawn Marshall is the leading rusher with 442 yards on 108 carries and three TDs.
Defensively, UMaine continues to be led by linebacker Sam Oppenheimer, whose 82 tackles, including 43 solo tackles, are 10th most in the country. He also has two interceptions. Linebacker Noah Carpenter has 62 tackles, safety Jeremiah McGill has 61 tackles and an interception and defensive end Chris Bacon has a team-high 3 ½ sacks among his 24 tackles. He also leads the team with eight quarterback hurries.
The Rams have been without 2025 All-CAA first team quarterback Devin Farrell, chosen the CAA’s preseason Offensive Player of the Year. He hasn’t recovered from off-season surgery.
Alex McClelland has recently won the starting QB job from Tyler Budge and has completed 57.9% of his passes for 672 yards and five TDs with two interceptions. He has also run the ball 49 times for 218 yards and four touchdowns.
R.J. Barrow is the leading rusher with 262 yards on 70 carries.
The defense has been led by linebacker Rohan Davy (57 tackles, interception), safety Andre DePina-Gray (50 tackles, 2 interceptions) and defensive linemen Dave Picariello (46 tackles) and Case Mankins (30 tackles, team-high 5 ½ sacks).
The state’s six Division III football schools will also be in action on Saturday.
Husson University, 2-5 overall and 2-2 in the Conference of New England, will travel to Milton, Massachusetts, to take on Curry College (4-3, 3-1) at noon. The University of New England from Biddeford (2-5, 2-2) will look to build on its 46-35 win over Husson with a road game at Nichols, also at noon. Nichols is also 2-5 and 2-2.
UNE has won all five meetings with Nichols.
Curry beat Husson, 40-21, a year ago to snap a five-game losing streak at the hands of the Eagles.
The third noon start will involve Maine Maritime Academy (0-7, 0-4) entertaining seventh-ranked Endicott. Endicott is 7-0 and 4-0.
The three CBB schools in NESCAC — Colby, Bates and Bowdoin — are all 0-6, but one of them will enter the win column because Colby will host Bates at 7 p.m. Saturday. Bowdoin will await 5-1 Wesleyan for a 1 p.m. kickoff.

title: Man accused of sending attacker to sexually assault fiancée at home with children, police say
text:
BUCKEYE, AZ. (AZFamily/Gray News) - An Arizona man is accused of sending another man to sexually assault his fiancée while she was home with her children, according to police.
Zarian Dyer, 23, was arrested at his job Thursday morning and charged with aggravated assault, sexual abuse, attempted sexual assault, kidnapping and conspiracy.
Buckeye police initially responded to a home the evening of Oct. 16 after Bella Torres reported that an unknown man entered her house and attacked her. Torres fought off the intruder, identified as 20-year-old Adrian Ayala, who fled the scene and was arrested the following day at his Goodyear home.
In home security video, Ayala can be heard telling Torres her partner sent him to assault her through an arrangement made on Reddit — a claim Ayala’s attorney later reiterated in court.
Detectives searched phones and devices belonging to both men, discovering communications outlining the planned attack, Buckeye Police spokesperson Carissa Planalp said. Prosecutors alleged Dyer instructed Ayala to assault Torres while she was home alone and FaceTime him during the attack.
A motive remains under investigation, police said.
