title: Where the candidates in Maine stand on partisanship
text:
Your Choice, Your Voice: Where the candidates for office in Maine stand on partisanship
Maine's Total Coverage asked viewers what issues they are most interested in learning more about heading into the midterm election.
After hundreds of submissions, the No. 1 issue on voters' minds is partisanship. Maine's Total Coverage asked all the candidates for governor and congressional office about their stance on the issue.
Gubernatorial candidates
The race for the Blaine House began with two crowded primaries. Republican Bobby Charles was the winner of a seven-way ranked-choice voting primary and Democrat Hannah Pingree won in a five-way race. Independent Rick Bennett, who left the Republican Party last year, was the only independent who got the required number of signatures to get on the November ballot.
The next governor will have to work with the legislature and face a variety of challenges, including a $1.3 billion budget shortfall.
That means the governor will have to work with both parties of the legislature to pass a bipartisan budget.
Bennett left the Republican Party last year to run this race as an independent, and has been vocal on the campaign trail that partisanship should not have a place in our politics.
"This is why I'm running as an independent. Because we don't have a lot of choices. Voters end up usually getting a Republican and a Democrat," he said. "I'm running as an independent to be an alternative choice for people so that they can have agency to throw off the partisanship and do things differently."
Charles said he plans to work with all lawmakers as governor, regardless of their party affiliation.
"Tell me where we can work together, tell me what's missing," he said. "Can we work on addiction services? Can we work on property taxes? Can we work on some of the mandates that, you know, we don't need anymore?"
Pingree said it's up to governors across the country to stand up to Pres. Donald Trump.
"I'm ready to stand up to this president. At the same time, I actually do think Maine people, we work together in our communities. They want people in Augusta to actually get along and find solutions to problems like education and health care," she said.
The last six years, state budgets have only passed with one party's support. All three candidates said they hope to get the budgets back to bipartisan pieces of legislation.
Senate candidates
The midterms are high stakes for both parties. Democrats are hoping to take the majority in Congress, heading into President Trump's final two years in office. Republicans, who hold the majority in both chambers, want to keep it.
The highly-anticipated Senate race has been closely watched for months. Senator Susan Collins is seeking a historic sixth term in Washington. Democrat Troy Jackson replaced Graham Platner as the party's nominee in late July after Platner dropped out following a sexual assault allegation he denies. Jackson, who finished third in the Democratic primary for Maine governor, now seeks to help Democrats flip the U.S. Senate.
Working with President Trump has been a major conversation between the two candidates in this race. Jackson has criticized Collins for her voting record, claiming the senator votes with Trump 96% of the time.
Collins questions that statistic.
"If you look at another study that looks at something like 90% of the votes, that number goes way down," Collins said. "And the fact is, if you use the 30% study, I had a very similar percentage with the Biden administration, which shows what a bogus study it is."
Collins said she's worked with five presidents during her nearly 30 years in the Senate. She says she always puts Maine first, pointing to her vote against Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill.
Jackson has been critical of the President through his Senate campaign, but says he will try and work with him. He also says voters have already seen him work across the aisle, pointing to his time working with Republican Gov. Paul LePage.
"I'm not going to let personal animosity get in the way of doing whatever I can to help move this state forward," Jackson said.
Candidates for Maine's 1st Congressional District
The race for Maine's 1st Congressional District is a rematch. Army veteran Ron Russell is challenging Congresswoman Chellie Pingree for her seat in Washington.
Pingree has held the congressional seat for nearly two decades. Russell ran against her back in 2024, but lost.
Russell secured the Republican nomination back in June, defeating newcomer Joshua James Pietrowicz.
The Republican challenger says he agrees with many of President Trump's decisions during his second term, but he wants to make it clear that doesn't mean he will always vote in the president's favor.
The congressional hopeful also says he wants to build relationships across the aisle.
"I'm not beholden to President Trump, nor Mike Johnson, nor the Republican Party, candidly," Russell said. "I'm beholden to the 547,000 people who will vote in November, the registered voters in Congressional District Number One."
Congresswoman Pingree says 2026 is not the year to be supporting the President, but she says she works with Republicans any time she can. Pingree also says it's harder to work with the administration this time around than it was in Trump's first term.
"I believe that the Republicans should be standing up much more and fighting back, and that has been left to us," Pingree said. "In the first term, we could often work with them, we could find ways to cooperate or come to an agreement. Now they don't negotiate, they don't reveal information. It's just a completely different world."
Candidates for Maine's 2nd Congressional District
The race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District began when Congressman Jared Golden still planned to run for his seat.
Former two-time Republican Governor Paul LePage got in the race to take on Golden. LePage was uncontested in the primary. Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap filed paperwork to primary Golden.
Golden eventually left the race, and three other candidates got in to primary Dunlap.
Dunlap said he thinks it's exciting that people care so much about democracy and says he's concerned about Pres. Trump.
"[Democracy has] been under assault under this administration, you know, with all the gerrymandering of the legislative districts around the country to advantage the Republicans, and the assault on mail voting — which we don't have, mail voting — we have absentee balloting. But there's a lot of concern about that, and people feel this is something that we really need to address," Dunlap said. "In terms of the partisanship, I mean, that's been really directed almost exclusively by the president."
LePage called the partisanship we've been seeing "insane" and said he'll work with anyone as long as it's good for Maine.
"We have to start talking to each other," he said. "Just recently, Jared Golden called me and said, you know, I got a bill that's really important for Maine. Can you help by getting Republicans in Washington to join? And I got on the phone, spoke to leadership, and the Republicans are the ones that voted for it. Democrats didn't. So it can be done."
If Democrats take control of either chamber of Congress, they will have to work with President Trump for his last two years in office.

title: More about the services offered at Sweetser's Hope and Healing centers
text:
More about the services offered at Sweetser's Hope and Healing centers in Maine
An estimated 3.4 million people nationwide received mental health and substance use treatment at a certified community behavioral health clinic (CCBHC) last year. That marks a nearly 13% jump, according to the 2026 CCBHC Impact Report from the National Council for Mental Wellbeing.
Sweetser's senior director of community-based services, Joey Rossignol, joined Maine's Total Coverage on Friday to discuss what Sweetser's clinics have to offer.
Sweetser's Hope and Healing centers are located in Brunswick, Lewiston and Sanford, and they are a one-stop shop for mental health and substance use treatment. Rossignol said the centers serve anyone who needs help, regardless of insurance or ability to pay.
The Hope and Healing centers' model of care includes walk-in access; a single team working to deliver therapy, medication management and medication-assisted treatment; 24/7 mobile crisis response; and support services such as care coordination, peer support and primary care screening.
The Hope and Healing Center in Brunswick also features a full-service pharmacy and a free peer resource center.
Rossignol said the new report from the National Council for Mental Wellbeing verifies everything that Sweetser sees on the ground, namely that CCBHCs are not only effective but also reduce barriers to accessing treatment.
The report states that clinics served about 42% more people after transitioning to a certified community behavioral health model, particularly in rural areas, and that nearly a quarter of those clinics offer same-day access to care. According to the report, half of CCBHC clients with opioid use disorder receive medication treatment, which is nearly three times the national rate.
Rossignol said that more than three quarters of CCBHCs report better outcomes with law enforcement, such as diverting people from arrest into treatment. He also said that many clinics are seeing fewer emergency room and hospital visits among their clients, and that a majority of CCBHC clients report better employment outcomes.
If you or someone you love is struggling, stop by a Sweetser Hope and Healing Center location during walk-in hours from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., call 1-800-434-3000 or send an email to info@sweetser.org. Rossignol said reaching out is a sign of strength, and that help is closer and more available than many people realize.

title: The relationship between Christian nationalism and Americans’ views of democracy
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The number of Americans who identify with Christian nationalism is slightly declining, but religion remains a large part of politics for both candidates and voters ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
“We see where Americans fall on this spectrum of Christian nationalism, which really tells us a lot about what they think democracy is and how it’s functioning,” said Andrew Whitehead, a professor of sociology at Indiana University Indianapolis and a research fellow for the Charles F. Kettering Foundation.
Whitehead cited data from the Kettering Foundation and Gallup’s annual national survey of more than 23,000 adults. He said around 14% of the U.S. population strongly embraces Christian nationalism, with just over 16% at least sympathetic to it.
Christian nationalism is the belief that Christianity defines the nation and the government should take active steps to keep it that way.
“Even though there are fewer Americans who embrace Christian nationalism, there are Americans in positions of power in federal government and media who will take that rhetoric of Christian nationalism and really make it part of the national discourse,” Whitehead said. “So fewer Americans embrace it strongly, but it is much more a part of our national political discussions than it ever used to be.”
Among white Americans, 31% are at least sympathetic to Christian nationalism. A third of men are at least sympathetic, while 28% of women responded similarly.
Christian nationalism is also strongly associated with political party. More than half of Republicans, 55%, strongly embrace or sympathize with it.
Whitehead said Americans who embrace Christian nationalism and those who reject it view democracy differently.
“They’re more worried about certain threats, quote unquote, to democracy than are Americans who reject Christian nationalism,” he explained. “When we asked them about how democracy is functioning, Americans who strongly embrace Christian nationalism right now say democracy is doing great; for those that reject it, very few think democracy is doing well or even okay.”
Whitehead said the nearly 70% of respondents who resist or reject Christian nationalism are being driven to the polls this midterm cycle.
“Right now, they’re very motivated for Congress to check the power of the executive branch,” he added, “something that hasn’t been happening in these first two years of the Trump administration.”
It is far more common for Republicans to combine religion and politics, but this election cycle, five Democrats are on the ballot in Congressional races who are clergy or in training to become clergy.

title: Customers suffer chemical burns after drinking margaritas at a NC Chili’s, officials say
text:
FOREST CITY, N.C. (WHNS/Gray News) – A round of drinks turned into a medical nightmare when three customers ordered margaritas and immediately suffered chemical burns inside and around their mouths.
Health officials investigating the incident at a Chili’s Grill & Bar in Forest City, North Carolina, said the drinks were contaminated after a powerful industrial degreaser was mistaken for sugar.
The dangerous mix-up began when a restaurant worker obtained granulated degreasing agent from an outside contractor power-washing the building’s exterior, according to the Foothills Health District.
The employee poured the chemical into an unlabeled container, brought it inside and left it in the bar area. The next day, another employee assumed the white granular substance was sugar and used it to prep the bar’s margarita station.
Shortly after the three customers took their first sips and suffered burns, employees who tasted the mixture reported identical burning symptoms.
County health inspectors immediately suspended the restaurant’s food service permit and mandated a full sanitation of the facility.
The permit was reinstated Thursday after Environmental Health Specialists verified all corrective actions were completed, according to Health Director Jason Masters, who emphasized that state food codes strictly require proper labeling, storage and handling to prevent chemical contamination.

title: Christa Pike says she feels constant pain in her first statement since failed execution
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/AP) - Christa Pike said she is in constant pain since surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee last month but thankful for the love and support she has received.
Pike issued her first public statement through her attorneys on Friday. She said she went into the execution chamber prepared to die in peace and woke up alone and confused in a hospital bed.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” Pike said.
Pike said she had not contemplated a life beyond her execution date.
“I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position. I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured,” Pike said.
She said she is thankful for the medical workers who saved her life and the people who showed her kindness.
“I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone,” she said.
Pike was convicted in 1996 in the “Jobs Corps Murder,” a name that came about because both Pike and the victim — 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer — were members of the Jobs Corps at the time of the girl’s 1995 killing.
Prosecutors and testimony have said Pike conspired with two others, 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson, to kill Slemmer over relationship issues.
It was discovered throughout the case that the offenders had carved a pentacle into Slemmer’s chest and taken a piece of her skull as a souvenir of the grisly murder.

title: Trump says Iran war goal met as gas prices rise
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The U.S.-led war against Iran, which began February 28, has affected every part of America. Now it may play a critical role in the upcoming midterm elections.
President Donald Trump launched the war with one major objective: preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Earlier in the war, the president gave additional reasons for military action against Iran. At a recent campaign rally, Trump said that goal has already been met.
“We obliterated Iran’s nuclear enrichment capacity with Operation Midnight Hammer, Operation Epic Fury,” Trump said. “We defeated them militarily, financially and otherwise. And now we are ensuring just one thing: we have to make sure that they never, ever have a nuclear weapon, and we will do that very easily.”
Trump has made that declaration numerous times. On October 10, White House correspondent Jon Decker asked the president, “Why not just declare victory and be done with it?”
“Because I have to keep it that way,” Trump said. “I don’t want to do it in two years. We have to have a guarantee that they won’t do it in the future. It’s actually a very good question.”
Gas prices have risen 40% since the war began, while fighting between the U.S. and Iran continues. The average price of a gallon of regular gas is $4.20, according to AAA.
Diesel, which is primarily used by truckers and farmers, sells for an average of more than $6 per gallon.
Gas and diesel prices remain elevated because of continuous threats from Iran in the Strait of Hormuz.
Likely voters in key Senate races told pollsters that high prices for food and energy are their top concerns.
Trump has told reporters and supporters that gas prices will fall once the war with Iran ends. There is no sign the war, now entering its ninth month, will end soon.

title: Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a US general election
text:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV has become the first pontiff to vote in a U.S. general election, casting a mail-in ballot in a contest that will decide America’s political future as the Trump era slowly comes to an end.
The Vatican confirmed Friday that the Chicago-born pontiff had submitted a mail-in ballot in the city ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, citing his long-standing belief in civic participation.
Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen” as he has done “whenever he was eligible to do so,” the Holy See press office said.
The statement said he had also voted while living in Peru, where he lived as a missionary priest and bishop for over 20 years.
“The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” it added.
Leo holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship, and is also the head of state of a foreign country, the Holy See. The city-state is an absolute monarchy with no political elections.
U.S. federal law allows citizens living abroad, even those working for foreign governments, to vote via absentee ballot. Americans working for foreign governments aren’t automatically at risk of forfeiting their U.S. citizenship, though the U.S. State Department says on its website that it may “actively review” the citizenship status of Americans who “serve as a foreign head of state, foreign head of government, or foreign minister.”
This election, Illinois voters are deciding whether to elect Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to his third term, and they’re also filling an open U.S. Senate seat after longtime Catholic Democrat Dick Durbin’s retirement. There are no statewide issues on the Illinois ballot. President Donald Trump is not on the ballot, but he has campaigned hard to try to preserve Republican control of the U.S. House and Senate for the final two years of his second term.
The pope, registered at a New Lenox, Illinois, address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3, said Kim Fladhammer, chief of staff to the Will County clerk, on Friday. The Chicago Sun-Times first reported the request.
The request was made just 10 days before Leo underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Leo has been slowly resuming his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital Oct. 17.
It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. The pope’s older brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St. Jude’s, an Augustinian-run parish in New Lenox, Illinois. The elder Prevost attends Mass there, and Leo gave a talk at the parish in 2024 while still a cardinal.
Prevost’s past votes have gone Democratic and Republican
Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections.
The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a primary ballot. No such declaration is required in general elections.
While registered in heavily Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative suburban Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.
The records also show that he submitted ballots in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022.
Clashes with Trump
Since becoming pope, Leo has drawn criticism from Trump for repeatedly condemning the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran and calling for dignified treatment of immigrants, following the Trump administration’s crackdown and mass deportation program.
Earlier this year, Trump called Leo “weak” and captive to the “radical left,” kicking off a remarkable back-and-forth public argument that dominated Leo’s April trip to Africa.
Responding to Trump, Leo told reporters en route to Algeria: “I’m not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the church works for.”
The public dispute has subsided in recent months.
“We try to let things pass if there are misunderstandings,” the Vatican foreign minister, Archbishop Richard Paul Gallagher, told reporters this week. “With anybody, we would be looking to approach it and say, ‘OK, there may be a misunderstanding, let’s move on and try to rebuild trust and confidence.’”
Leo and Trump have not spoken by phone since the pope’s May 2025 election. Last week, however, Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the humanitarian crisis in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
Asked why Trump and Leo haven’t spoken, Gallagher said the Holy See has found a capable conduit in the U.S. ambassador to the Holy See, Brian Burch, and hadn’t needed to elevate any issue higher.
A pope who follows US politics closely
Leo has made clear on several occasions that he follows local and national U.S. politics closely and is not afraid to intervene.
Recently, Leo reiterated official church teaching declaring the death penalty “inadmissible.” He made the pronouncement in a social media post on the World Day Against the Death Penalty, which came as the U.S. announced plans to livestream an execution by firing squad. The plans were later scrapped.
In 2025, Leo intervened in a debate over abortion, after Chicago Cardinal Blase Cupich announced plans to give a lifetime achievement award to Sen. Durbin. The plans drew objection from some conservative U.S. bishops given the powerful Democratic senator’s support for abortion rights. Leo called for respect for both sides, but he also pointed out the contradiction between people who call themselves “pro-life” but also support the death penalty.
Also in 2025, Leo said he was “very disappointed” that his home state of Illinois approved a law allowing medically assisted dying, which is condemned by the Catholic Church.
The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, in a note commenting on the confirmation of Leo’s midterm vote, urged Catholics to put “our faith before our politics” and uphold human dignity and the common good.
“As Catholics and Americans, we are blessed to be able to participate in our nation’s political and public life,” said the conference’s director of public affairs, Chieko Noguchi. “In voting, our Holy Father sets the example that encourages each citizen to exercise their civic responsibility.”
___
Associated Press writers Holly Meyer in Nashville, Tennessee, and Scott Bauer in Madison, Wisconsin, contributed to this report.

title: Are Mainers ready to return to life without the U.S. Senate race?
text:
August 2025. The Lewiston-Auburn Balloon Festival was deemed a success, and the last of season’s lobster boat races had just wrapped in Portland Harbor.
Taylor and Travis were engaged, but they hadn’t told us yet, and Jimothy was but a nameless baby raccoon trying to get by.
We had never Googled “Totenkopf” and hadn’t thought about our second cousins in years. Text messages from unknown numbers were primarily sent by scammers posing as the DMV.
The most overplayed commercial on TV belonged to Skyrizi.
Gov. Janet Mills was still being coy about whether she’d run for U.S. Senate when a video dropped of a burly blond man in a hooded sweatshirt, fired up about access to healthcare and the futility of foreign wars.
At that moment, life as we knew it changed for the next 14 months and counting — a roller coaster that, in a few days, will come crashing to a halt.
Remember, it was exciting at first. People packed town halls, and pundits analyzed Reddit posts. Pleas for $5 popped up in our algorithms, and we stuck signs in our yards to show passing cars where we stood.
National commentators couldn’t stop talking about our state, prompting questions from friends and relatives around the country. People wanted to know what we thought about political leadership, a welcome change from being asked where to get the best lobster rolls.
Strangers knocked on our doors seeking our support, glossy flyers filled our mailboxes aiming to grab our attention. Our phones lit up with calls and texts asking for our opinions.
After a while, though, the barrage began to take its toll.
We started posting “no trespassing” signs and cursing the constant stream of card stock as we hauled it from the mailbox to the recycling bin.
We’ve silenced countless calls from “potential spam” and stopped looking at our text messages, knowing chances aren’t good that it’s going to be a funny meme from a friend.
Our downtime in front of reality shows and football games has been marred by accusations of corruption set to ominous orchestral music.
It’s enough to make you want to throw a water bottle — or, worse, to wish away Maine’s precious fall in favor of it all being over.
Next Wednesday, though, how will we really feel? Can Role Model and Cooper Flagg keep Maine relevant enough for our liking? Are we ready for our political influence to revert to the rare scenarios in which it matters if we split our four measly electoral votes?
If only our representatives could convince us they cared all along and spare us the whiplash from what campaigning has become.
Think of the money and trees that regular check-ins could save, and of the votes that might actually be swayed by sustained communication with the citizenry.
Imagine choosing between candidates based on their accomplishments and not which fact-adjacent attacks seem the least concerning.
Maybe Skyrizi is right, that “nothing is everything,” and not just in terms of moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis.

title: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (InvestigateTV) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.”
When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death.
Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock.
How the discovery happened
Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins, founder of Vivacelle Bio, said he was running an experiment he thought would fail. “But it didn’t fail.”
For years, Simpkins, who is now a surgery professor at the UKMC School of Medicine, had been trying to find an answer for septic shock and focused his research on blood experiments.
He drained mice of their blood until they were clinically dead, then injected them with a substance called VBI-1.
“The mice woke up. They woke up from being dead,” Simpkins said. “They were walking around. I called my wife, excited. I said, this is working. This is what’s going on here. This isn’t supposed to work.”
Simpkins said the survival rate is nearly 100% when the product is injected into the arteries of mice experiencing hemorrhagic shock. He is waiting to test it on humans. He said a person could receive about 2 liters.
Simpkins said VBI-1 would end blood shortages with the hope they never happen again.
He said the substance could also be safer than blood alone for people in hemorrhagic shock. He and his team named the product “better than blood” because of ischemia reperfusion injury, which he said is caused by a person’s own blood being reinfused.
Ischemia reperfusion injury happens when blood is reintroduced to the body after blood loss. The oxygen in the new blood can create toxins in the body, which damage tissue, including the brain.
“When we infused our product, we don’t get that,” Simpkins said.
The substance uses nanoparticle technology. It is derived from another of Simpkins’ discoveries, VBI-S, which is awaiting FDA approval to help treat septic shock.
“If you look at the damage caused by blood to the brain when you infuse it, the animal’s own blood, and you compare that to our fluid, and you see no damage,” Simpkins said.
Simpkins said the components of VBI-1 are soybean oil, egg lecithin and egg yolk.
It sounds like simple ingredients, but he says combined they could fix complicated problems facing our country. Since 2020, U.S. blood supplies have reached “critically low levels” multiple times.
And in 2026, the American Red Cross announced a national blood supply crisis, only the second time it’s ever released that warning. Dr. Simpkins says his product would mean an end to these blood shortages.
Transfusion specialist cites limits
Dr. Richard Galbraith, a University Health KC pathologist and director of transfusion medicine, said the potential is there.
“If it works and if it’s safe, then it could be a boon for sure,” he said.
Galbraith said he was “extremely interested” and “hopeful” when he first saw Simpkins’ study on VBI-1. But he sees limitations.
“Having a completely synthetic replacement for blood that’s, I think, is extremely unlikely,” Galbraith said.
Galbraith said blood will still be needed and blood drives will continue to matter.
“It’s still critically important. There are many uses for blood beyond shock,” he said.
Galbraith said University Health goes through at least 500 units of blood a day. He said chronic blood shortages have affected the entire country for several years. He said patients with chronic blood disease and those with certain cancers would still depend on blood transfusions.
Galbraith said VBI-1 could help people in hemorrhagic shock and during blood shortages.
“This hopefully can be a means of saving those people,” Galbraith said. When asked whether it could help during blood shortages, he said, “Oh, I think, definitely.”
He said the product must go through appropriate clinical trials.
“We need to ensure it goes to the appropriate clinical trials to make sure it’s going to work and it’s going to help and that it’s safe,” Galbraith said. “And if those concerns are addressed and met, then I’m happy to use it in our patients too.”
Other possible uses
Members of Simpkins’ lab team said they are ready to prove the discovery.
“I don’t think transfusion’s necessarily something we ever thought we would optimize any better,” said UMKC scientist Nathan Carpenter.
The team said they have only begun to explore the product’s potential.
UMKC scientist Danielle Kinsey said the team hopes the product can be used to prevent organ rejection after transplants.
“We have this hope that it can be used in the process of transplantation, so specifically given to patients before they receive their transplanted organ with hopes of decreasing the immune response,” Kinsey said.
Asked how to categorize VBI-1, Simpkins said, “There’s no category. There’s no other. It’s a different new category, actually, of therapeutics.”
Simpkins said he does not know the limits of the substance, but remains confident it will save lives.
“We’ll be sending more people back to their families, back to their loved ones, and that’s really what it’s all about,” Simpkins said.
Clinical human trials for VBI-1 could take one to two years. Simpkins hopes the product receives FDA approval and is on the market by 2031.

title: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
text:
(Aging Untold) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often.
The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part.
Start with the question the trial is trying to answer
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the first step is to change the question you ask.
“I think the first thing we have to do is not think about, ‘Can this clinical trial help me?’ but ‘What is this clinical trial trying to answer?’” Rogers said. “That’s what most of these trials are about.”
A trial is not a last resort
Rogers said many people see clinical trials as a last resort.
“I think a lot of people think that it’s a last resort option, that you don’t have anything else, when in fact one of the biggest benefits is it gives you access,” Rogers said. “You get great access to tomorrow’s medicines today — devices, therapies and other things that will not be available to everybody else for years.”
Where to find a study
Rogers said people can search at ClinicalTrials.gov , check with their physician or look at academic centers and other organizations specific to a disease or condition that have their own studies.
What participants may get
Rogers said participants can receive close monitoring and access to specialists.
“Many of them will pay for gas, and everything like that,” Rogers said. “Some of them even pay you for the study.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said that the National Institutes of Health (NIH) keeps a list of clinical trials and which compensate participants.
Know what to expect going in
What participants should know is that they might receive a placebo, she said.
“You might be the one getting the placebo, you might get the drug itself,” O’Rourke said. “So knowing that going in, the expectation wouldn’t be that I’m going to get the drug or that I’m going to see if I’m going to get better.”
She said she has seen people often come away from trials feeling hopeful and feeling they are giving back to their community.
Clients who joined a local clinical trial group also found support, O’Rourke said.
“The social workers there were amazing,” she said. “They had support groups, and it gave them access to resources in the community that they didn’t know about, in addition to all the medical specialists. So I saw that being a huge value for people, especially when you’re older.”
Why older adults are needed in trials
O’Rourke said older adults are often left out of research.
“I’ve heard older people called ‘evidence free’ because nobody really studies them,” O’Rourke said. “They’re not included in the studies.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said older adults should be included because medication does not affect all age groups in the same way.
“Medication metabolizes so differently in our older community than it does in our younger community, so without having them as participants, they’re often walking blind,” Cradduck said.
Cradduck added that new medicines cannot be approved without clinical trials.
“You can’t have a new medicine come out without a clinical trial. It’s not going to be approved,” Cradduck said. “If we want new medications, if we want new hope, we have to have these clinical trials.”
Addressing the “guinea pig” concern
Many people tell themselves they don’t want to be a guinea pig, Cradduck said.
“You’re not a guinea pig,” she said. “By the time it’s reached this point, it has been thoroughly tested repeatedly.”
Cradduck said there are adverse effects with everything that gets prescribed.
Resources
Key takeaways
- Tomorrow’s medicine today. Clinical trials are not a last resort. They are a way to access cutting-edge treatments early.
- Older adults are essential. Drugs affect older bodies differently, and participation builds safer future treatments.
- Ask the right questions. Find out what scientific question the trial is trying to answer to make sure it aligns with your goals.
- Know where to look. Start at clinicaltrials.gov , and check with your physician, academic centers or other organizations that run their own studies.
- Know what to expect. Participants may get a placebo or the drug itself, and the NIH lists which trials compensate participants.

title: How to check water safety before a lake or river outing
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A new report from Environment America found bacteria levels were potentially unsafe on at least one day at 69% of more than 4,500 river and lake testing locations in 17 states.
John Rumpler, clean water director and senior attorney at Environment America, said the group’s “Safe for Swimming” report matters as a consumer issue as well as an environmental one.
“I can only imagine that if a family drove two or three hours to go to lakeside cabin, and they were planning to spend the entire week at the lake, and then suddenly there was E. coli in the water,” Rumpler said. “I don’t know that I could put that to dollars and cents, but I think we might agree that’s a ruined vacation right there.”
Rumpler said E. coli turned up in every state in the analysis.
“All across the country in all of these 17 states, we found E. coli, which people may be familiar with E. coli as a nasty bacteria. It’s an indicator of fecal matter, in other words, poop,” Rumpler said. “And so to be clear, we’re not saying all of these waters are contaminated all the time. But about half of these 4,000-plus monitoring sites had elevated E. coli levels on 25% or more of the days that they were tested. So it’s a pretty widespread problem.”
Rumpler said the contamination comes from sewage overflows, stormwater runoff and leaking septic tanks.
Environment America’s online dashboard breaks down the results state by state.
Rumpler said he believes federal and state governments could do more, and that the cost does not have to fall on taxpayers.
“If the federal government does step up and provide more resources to address this problem, then less of that financial burden is going to be on the backs of ratepayers and local citizens of any community,” Rumpler said. “But let me say this, I wouldn’t want any local or state official to use a lack of federal funding as an excuse. Everyone needs to do their part.”
Contamination levels can change daily. Before swimming, check state or county health advisories and the EPA’s water quality portal.
Additional steps include avoiding rivers and lakes for 48 to 72 hours after heavy rain, when sewage overflows and runoff tend to peak. Water that is discolored, smelly, foamy or near a discharge pipe should also be avoided.

title: Wabanaki Public Health cuts nearly 20% of workforce amid multi-million-dollar detox deficit
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness has eliminated nearly 20% of its workforce after grappling with multi-million-dollar funding deficits tied to its residential withdrawal and detox services.
The organization eliminated 24 positions Friday, following an earlier round of 20 layoffs. Leadership attributes the cuts to severe structural shortfalls at the Cedar Road Detox and Medication-Assisted Withdrawal facility, which has run a $2 million annual deficit since opening in 2023.
Structural shortfall leaves $2M annual gap
The 10-bed Cedar Road program costs roughly $3 million each year to operate, but generates only about $1 million in reimbursement revenue—even under maximum capacity.
“We know we are underfunded in that program, and we also know even best-case scenario, when we have all those beds full and we’re getting those reimbursements, we will still be short on our budget for those services,” said Lisa Sockabasin, Co-CEO of Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness. “So for a service that costs this organization $3 million , we’re only getting $1 million in reimbursement.”
Co-CEO Rebecca Petrie noted that MaineCare and private insurance reimbursements cover only about one-third of the facility’s operating costs. While federal grants have assisted other agency initiatives, strict guidelines bar those funds from being used to support detox services.
“You hear a lot where an organization is receiving this money from a grant program like the Rural Health Transformation Grant program,” Petrie said. “Those funds were not able to be used for detox because they’re restricted.”
‘Heartbreaking’ toll on frontline workers
Leadership described the staff reductions as an agonizing necessity for an organization dedicated to treating substance use disorders across Maine communities.
“They’re all brokenhearted,” Petrie said. “These are dedicated professionals that truly and deeply believe in the people and the services that we provide, and to have to make this decision due to finances has been incredibly heartbreaking.”
A call for regional collaboration
Despite the staffing blow, Sockabasin and Petrie said they hope the crisis spurs immediate action among state lawmakers, healthcare partners, and community leaders to reform behavioral health reimbursement rates.
“In order to do that, we need to be around the same table,” Sockabasin said. “On the same team, tackling the same complications together so we can see healing that will be magnified in community, and we know we can do that. We just need to do that pretty quickly.”
The date for the closure has not yet been set.

title: A few showers around today... Then a stellar Halloween weekend
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) -A few showers around for some areas today that won’t amount to much accumulation. Once they move out this afternoon it will set up yet another fantastic fall weekend with plenty of sunshine. Halloween Saturday will be a great day for outdoor events and trick-or-treating even though it will be on the cooler side and Sunday will be yet another very pleasant fall day with highs near or into the 50s for most. It will get chilly overnight but overall about as good a weekend as you could ask for this time of year.
Today: Some showers north, otherwise mainly sunny and breezy
A few showers will work their way through the region into the early morning hours but should clear by midday at the latest. Highs top out in the 50s and 60s with some breeziness out of the west with gusts perhaps as high as 30 mph for some.
Tonight: A mostly clear night with seasonable lows
Clouds will clear mostly and it will cool off into the 30s for most across the state in line with seasonal averages. It will stay somewhat breezy overnight with winds out of the west still around 10-15 mph.
Saturday: Clear skies but cooler, overall a pleasant Halloween
It will be a cooler day Saturday with highs only reaching near or just above 50. But will be filled with sunshine. Winds will be light and it should be generally a very nice day to be outside and taking in the fall weather and doing some trick-or-treating.
Saturday night: A cold and clear night
Temps will drop off quickly on Saturday night with clear skies so if you’ve got any late night Halloween events make sure to grab your jacket because it’ll get chilly fast. Temps will drop into the mid to low 20s for a large portion of the state and winds will be light. Don’t forget to reset your clocks!
Sunday: A slightly warmer day with clear skies
It will be a few degrees warmer than Saturday and clear skies. Most places get to the middle 50s with some colder areas still stuck in the 40s. It will feel comfortable though with full sun for most. Winds will be light.
Sunday night: Near freezing for most
It will be chilly once again but probably not as cold as the previous night. Most places will be clear and drop to only the middle 30s or so with some spots into the 20s.
Today: A few showers early especially north, otherwise sunny with highs in the 50s and 60s. Winds W at 10-20 mph
Tonight: Clear. Lows in the 20s and 30s. Winds NW at 5-10 mph.
Saturday: Cooler but sunny. Highs near 50. Winds NW at 10-15 mph
Saturday night: Cold with lows in the middle 20s. Winds light.
Sunday: Warmer with highs in the 50s. Winds light.
Sunday night: Clear with lows in the middle 30s. Winds light.

title: No serious injuries after car hits Maine DOT work zone in Standish
text:
STANDISH, Maine (WABI) - No one was seriously hurt after a car crashed into a Maine DOT work zone Thursday afternoon in Standish.
State police said 32-year-old Merlin Maston fell asleep at the wheel on Chadbourne Road and rear-ended a state DOT trailer.
A road worker standing outside the truck was struck by the car but reported no injuries and declined a trip to the hospital.
Maston and another worker also were not hurt. The crash remains under investigation.

title: Furrow, Gallagher and Maskala could bring needed change to Bangor
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Michael Capeci is the former chair of the Bangor Republican Committee. He is a Bangor resident who cares deeply about the future of his community and its local government.
Bangor voters are preparing to elect three members to the City Council in what appears to be one of the largest fields of candidates in the city’s history. Each winner will serve a three-year term, and voters have an opportunity to help shape Bangor’s future.
Bangor has been an amazing place for me to live, and I care deeply about the direction of our city. From spending and taxation to crime and public health, Bangor faces significant challenges. Addressing them requires leaders who offer practical solutions, take fiscal responsibility seriously and can work with others to get things done.
That is why I support Michael Furrow, James Gallagher and Jennifer McGinley Maskala.
Michael Furrow is a 30-year Bangor resident, veteran, husband and father of two. He has regularly attended council meetings for five years, taking the time to understand the issues facing our community.
As a young person, I appreciate Mike’s focus on economic development and retaining young people in Bangor. Our city needs to create opportunities for the next generation to build their lives here rather than leave in search of better prospects.
Mike also recognizes that Bangor cannot shoulder the entire burden of providing services for eastern Maine. The state and surrounding communities must share responsibility for addressing regional challenges such as homelessness, substance use and crime.
Equally important, Mike says he is committed to collaboration. Progress requires councilors who can work with colleagues and public officials, even when they disagree. His willingness to find common ground is one reason he has my vote.
James Gallagher is a lifelong Bangor resident who has owned multiple businesses downtown. His experience gives him firsthand knowledge of the challenges facing local businesses and the downtown community.
I first met James in 2023, when I chaired the Bangor Republican Committee. What impressed me most was his willingness to speak with anyone willing to listen. By the end of our conversations, I realized we agreed on more than we disagreed on.
I share James’ view that Bangor needs to take more decisive action on homelessness. His proposal to declare a state of emergency and establish an emergency shelter deserves serious consideration.
As a business owner, James also understands the importance of sound fiscal management. His ideas for exploring new funding sources and providing property tax relief merit consideration as the city balances its budget and meets residents’ needs.
Above all, James seems to value transparency and listens to people regardless of their background or political views. He understands that effective local government requires accountability and public engagement. He has earned my vote.
Jennifer McGinley Maskala is the third candidate I support. I first heard Jennifer speak at the Bangor High School candidate forum. Although I have not met her personally, I was impressed by her emphasis on government efficiency and responsible use of taxpayer dollars.
As program director for the Wild Blueberry Commission, Jennifer brings professional experience that could be valuable as Bangor confronts its budget challenges. Her call to return to basics by prioritizing infrastructure repairs while pursuing spending reductions and property tax relief is an approach worth considering.
Fiscal responsibility is not simply about cutting spending. It means directing limited resources toward essential services and maintaining the infrastructure residents depend on. Taxpayers deserve a city government that uses their money effectively and delivers results.
When choosing whom to support, I consider more than policy proposals. I also look for candidates who listen, collaborate and can turn ideas into results.
Furrow, Gallagher and Maskala each bring different experiences and ideas to Bangor’s challenges. I believe their approaches to economic development, homelessness and fiscal responsibility deserve serious consideration.
Our city needs leaders who take taxpayers’ concerns seriously and remember that people can disagree on policy while remaining neighbors, not enemies. I encourage Bangor voters to learn more about these three candidates and consider supporting them in this year’s election.

title: Decades-old Blue Hill dental practice will close in mid-December amid legal dispute
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A Blue Hill dental practice that’s served area residents for three decades is set to close in mid-December amid legal troubles.
Blue Hill Peninsula Dental will close permanently on Dec. 17 due to circumstances beyond the practice’s control, according to owner Dr. Mike Gillins.
The closure comes as many regions throughout Maine, particularly in rural areas, battle varying levels of dentist shortages, though Hancock County overall is relatively well served by dental practices. In some pockets of the state, the gap in dental coverage has left many residents struggling with long wait times for emergency care.
Maine has seen an influx of dental providers obtaining licenses in the past 18 months, Therese Cahill, CEO of the Maine Dental Association, said last month.
The office’s roughly 2,000 patients will be referred to area providers, Gillins said, adding that the practice is following closure guidelines stipulated by the Maine Board of Dental Practice.
The practice has no pending disciplinary cases with the board, but there is an ongoing court case related to the practice, according to board records and court documents. Gillins declined to comment on the nature of the court case.
“It’s just financial considerations and a bunch of things beyond our control that made a perfect storm,” Gillins said Thursday.
Gillins is named as one of three defendants in a Cumberland County equitable relief civil case filed by TD Bank in late June, according to court records.
Gillins is aware of one Ellsworth practice that is currently taking new patients, noting the “severe shortage in the state of Maine of dental and hygiene providers.”
The office will remain open until mid-December for emergency treatment and to help transfer patient records to new providers, Gillins said.
The practice notified patients of the closure earlier this week, the prosthodontics specialist said.
Gillins, the office’s only dentist on staff, took over the practice in November 2020 from Dr. Juan Aponte, but the dental office has been open for roughly three decades, he said.
Gillins said he will not be opening another practice but will tend to some personal matters once the office is shuttered.

title: Federal election monitors will observe polling in South Portland next week
text:
The U.S. Department of Justice will send federal monitors to observe polling in South Portland during Tuesday’s midterm election, in addition to Portland and Lewiston.
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said a total of three municipalities have been notified by the Justice Department about its plans to send federal election observers next week.
The monitors are expected to rotate at each of the municipality’s polling places throughout the day.
Bellows said the department has been sending election monitors for decades, and federal observers were in Maine for the 2024 congressional races.
“Any monitors are subject to the same laws and rules as any other observer at the poll, they can observe what’s taking place, but they may not interact with voters, handle ballots or equipment or disrupt voting in any way,” Bellows said in a statement. “We will monitor their activities to ensure that they follow state and federal law and that every voter is able to cast their ballot free from interference or intimidation.”
Thursday was the last day for early voting in Maine.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Former Husson University professor under investigation for alleged child porn
text:
Former Husson University professor arrested for possession of child sexual abuse material
A now-former assistant professor at Husson University in Bangor has been arrested and taken to the Penobscot County Jail.
The Bangor Police Department says Jonathan Houck, 33 of Bangor, is facing six counts of possession of sexual abuse material and four counts of violation of privacy. He was taken into custody on Friday after a warrant was issued for his arrest.
Houck was an assistant professor of exercise science and assistant cross country coach. Court records say he is being investigated for possession and dissemination of child sexual abuse material.
Court documents say detectives searched Houck's Pearl Street home and his campus office in mid-September, seizing dozens of items.
According to investigators, the case began in June when Dropbox alerted the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children that an account with Houck's username uploaded four sexually exploitative images involving children under 16.
Husson says it is complying with all police requests and that the school is in "close contact with impacted students to ensure their needs are met."
"Husson University is deeply disturbed by Jonathan Houck’s alleged conduct. The university learned of the investigation early on September 21, and this individual was escorted from campus and relieved of his duties within an hour. He is no longer employed by Husson University," the school said in a statement.
Maine's Total Coverage is aware of claims made by a student on social media who says law enforcement spoke with them about pictures recovered during their investigation.
This is a developing story that will be updated as Maine's Total Coverage is able to confirm additional information.

title: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls.
It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores.
Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option.
Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access.
In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. The network encourages locals to eat healthy produce grown by themselves or their neighbors.
Aisha Ellis, farm manager for the network, said she has seen a difference in the 20 years the network has been in operation.
“You would start seeing people more regulated health wise. You’ll see people come back to life, participating. And you start creating different food traditions in your home,” Ellis said.
Through a local food co-op, an organic farm and meetings with local governments, the network is using Detroit as the launching point. Its goal is to spread the mission to other cities.
According to the Detroit Food Policy Council, 69% of Detroit households experience food insecurity.
Urban farming is one solution for food insecurity, but Ellis also said the organization works on policy - meaning access to food is also on the ballot Tuesday.

title: Maine to get $2.8M in GM data privacy settlement
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine will receive more than $2.8 million from General Motors for selling drivers’ private location and behavior data.
Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey joined a coalition of 36 attorneys general in the case against GM.
The settlement, announced by the AG’s office on Thursday, required GM to pay the states a total of $220 million. Additionally, GM must limit the driving data it collects and protect drivers’ personal information going forward and delete that data upon the consumer’s request.
The lawsuit alleged that GM sold drivers’ data to third parties, including data brokers who then sold the data to insurance companies. The data was used by insurance companies as a factor in setting rates.
From 2016 to 2024, GM enrolled millions of drivers in its Smart Driver program, which tracked their driving habits. The company pitched the tool as a way for drivers to improve their own driving safety but sold the data to insurance companies after telling drivers that would not happen without their express consent, according to the AG’s office.
GM bundled the Smart Driver program with OnStar services. Sales employees received bonuses and were ranked based in part on how many customers they signed up for the services. In many cases, dealership employees accepted terms and conditions on behalf of customers without their consent, the AG’s office said.
Data received by insurers included how many times a person drove their vehicle, the start and end times of each drive, how many times they braked or accelerated quickly, and whether they went faster than the speed limit, according to the AG’s office.
A 2024 New York Times investigation found that the insurance companies used the information provided by GM to change rates, sometimes increasing drivers’ premiums. GM discontinued the Smart Driver program after the Times’ report.
In a statement on Friday, GM highlighted that the program was discontinued and said the settlement agreement “reinforces steps we’ve taken to strengthen our privacy practices. Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share.”
According to the settlement, the money Maine receives from GM “may be used for purposes that may include, but are not limited to, attorneys’ fees, and other costs of investigation and litigation, or be placed in, or applied to, any consumer protection law enforcement fund, including future consumer protection or privacy enforcement, consumer education, litigation or local consumer aid fund or revolving fund, used to defray the costs of the inquiry leading hereto, or for other uses permitted by state law, at the sole discretion of the Attorney General of Maine, or any purpose allowable under state law.”
A spokesperson from the AG’s office on Friday described it as a law enforcement case as opposed to a restitution case, such as a class action lawsuit that would compensate victims. Such settlements in Maine and other states typically support consumer protection operations, the spokesperson said.
The case was co-led by Washington and Oregon, assisted by the Executive Committee of Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Kentucky, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, Utah, and Vermont, and also joined by the attorneys general of Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, the District Of Columbia, Florida, Hawai’i, Idaho, Kansas, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Virginia, and Wisconsin.

title: Maine ranks among top states to find a job, report says
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine may be known as Vacationland, but it’s also one of the best states in the country to find a job, a report from WalletHub shows.
In its 2026 ranking of the best and worst states for jobs, the personal finance website placed Maine at No. 7, between Washington at No. 6 and Texas at No. 8.
Nebraska claimed the top spot, while West Virginia ranked last at No. 50.
Maine’s peer New England states also ranked among the top 20, with New Hampshire at No. 5, followed by Connecticut (No. 8), Rhode Island (13), Massachusetts (18) and Vermont (20).
Grading system
To determine the rankings, WalletHub evaluated all 50 states across two categories: job market and economic environment.
Maine performed significantly better in the job market category than in the economic environment category.
The job market category carried greater weight because WalletHub considered its factors more influential in a job seeker’s decision to relocate for work.
Researchers assessed each state using 34 metrics across the two categories, assigning weights based on each metric’s relative importance. Each metric was scored on a 100-point scale, with 100 representing the most favorable conditions for job seekers. WalletHub then calculated a weighted average across all metrics to determine each state’s overall score and ranking.
Hospitality job gains
Maine’s latest employment figures offer additional insight into the state’s labor market.
The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate stood at 3.3% in September, up slightly from 3.2% in August, according to the latest report from the Maine Department of Labor released earlier this month.
Unemployment rates have remained within a narrow range between 3.1% and 3.3% for 25 consecutive months.
The state also added 1,700 nonfarm wage and salary jobs in September, with leisure and hospitality accounting for most of the increase.
The Department of Labor is due to release its next monthly report on Friday, Nov. 20.

title: The Latest: Peltola denies knowing of effort to put another Sullivan on Senate ballot
text:
Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has denied knowing anything about an effort to put another candidate on the Alaska ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent, as the Justice Department escalated a criminal investigation with new grand jury subpoenas.
President Donald Trump on Thursday canceled weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas, opting instead to support Republican candidates with telerallies that his party said could reach more voters in nearly two dozen states in the final days of a midterm election that could cost the GOP control of Congress.
Ohio governor candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton, is off the air after the Republican spent about a quarter of what his campaign initially said it would invest to run it.
The Latest:
Former US diplomats, national security officials urge Trump to enforce Russian sanctions law
Nearly 20 experts said recent U.S. policy decisions risk putting the goal of ending Russia’s war on Ukraine further out of reach, according to a letter to the president obtained by AP.
“To restore American leverage, we urge you to enforce the sanctions law you signed,” they said, referring to the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia Act.
They also called on Trump to reverse his Russian diesel deal, release Patriot interceptors that Ukraine is counting on for its defense and ensure Ukraine is part of any negotiations over a peace deal.
The letter was signed by retired Gen. Wesley K. Clark, retired Gen. Philip Breedlove and former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine William Taylor, among others.
Pentagon accuses newly fired general of leaking sensitive information
The Pentagon has accused a newly ousted three-star general of leaking sensitive information to the media just hours after officials confirmed his removal from a top military planning post.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia as head of strategy, plans and policy for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, a defense official said late Wednesday. Typically, the general in the position and their staff are responsible for generating and coordinating military plans for both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the president.
No reason was given for the firing, the latest in a series of ousters or departures of military leaders under Hegseth. However, a Pentagon official, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, later said in a statement that Sylvia was under investigation over allegations of sharing classified information about the Iran war, the Russia-Ukraine conflict and other topics with journalists.
DOJ escalates its elections scrutiny with day-after subpoenas of California officials
The U.S. Justice Department has issued subpoenas to California officials in an escalation of its scrutiny of local election administration.
The Associated Press obtained copies of three subpoenas sent Oct. 21 and Oct. 24 to employees of the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder, ordering them to appear in court on Nov. 4, the day after the election.
The subpoenas request any documents and communications related to letters sent in July and October by federal officials to state election officials outlining allegations of noncitizens on the state’s voter rolls.
They also seek any information about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted. All four U.S. attorneys in California were issuing subpoenas, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.
The subpoenas represent the latest salvo in a fight between the Trump administration and California over the eligibility of voters in the heavily Democratic state, amplifying pressure on local election officials to comply with exhaustive government demands and setting the stage for legal challenges.
El-Sayed and Stevens appear together as Democrats seek unity in Michigan Senate race
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed will campaign Sunday in Detroit alongside former primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens, marking their first public appearance together in months after a week in which lingering divisions spilled into public view.
The two will be joined by South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn, one of the country’s most prominent Black politicians, at a get-out-the-vote event at a Detroit church, according to two people familiar with the plans who were not authorized to discuss them publicly. The event was first reported by The Associated Press.
The joint appearance — their first since a Democratic unity breakfast days after the Aug. 4 primary — follows weeks of Democrats struggling to unite behind El-Sayed following his razor-thin victory over Stevens. She received significant support from the Jewish and Black communities, leading to concerns about turnout in the general election.
Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad featuring Amy Acton’s estranged mother is off the air in Ohio
Ohio governor candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton, is off the air after the Republican spent about a quarter of what his campaign initially said it would invest to run it.
Ramaswamy said during a campaign appearance in Vandalia, Ohio, on Thursday that the ad’s planned run was over. His campaign originally said it would spend $4 million to air the ad, but data from the ad-tracking firm AdImpact showed it spent roughly $1 million.
The divisive spot had provoked backlash in Ohio and among politicians of both parties across the nation. It featured Donna Arthur calling her daughter a lifelong liar. That was despite the two having not seen each other for nearly 50 years. Arthur lost custody of her children in 1978 after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12.
Trump cancels rallies in Kansas and Iowa, opting for telerallies to reach more voters, RNC says
President Donald Trump lambasted a reporter who asked about his health and whether travel fatigue prompted him to cancel a Kansas rally over the weekend. Trump called him “disgusting,” and told him to get “in shape,” and said he’d hold a tele-rally for Sen. Roger Marshall instead.
President Donald Trump on Thursday canceled weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas, opting instead to support Republican candidates with telerallies that his party said could reach more voters in nearly two dozen states in the final days of a midterm election that could cost the GOP control of Congress.
The president traveled to South Carolina Thursday for the second time in a month, a sign of Republican anxiety about Darline Graham’s ability to fend off a robust challenge from Democrat Annie Andrews for a critical U.S. Senate seat.
Voters in South Carolina have not sent a Democrat to the Senate in nearly three decades. But Andrews, a pediatrician who previously ran unsuccessfully for Congress, is urging voters seeking change to “try something new for once.”
That message could resonate in an election year defined by voter frustration with the economy, gas prices and the war in Iran, putting Trump’s Republican Party on defense in territory where they have rarely had to compete in recent years.
Peltola denies she knew of effort to stack Alaska ballot with same-name candidate
Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about an effort to put another candidate on the Alaska ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent as the Justice Department escalated a criminal investigation with new grand jury subpoenas.
“I just want to clear the air,” she said at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”
Peltola is running against Sen. Dan Sullivan. A person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press that subpoenas seeking grand jury testimony or documents, along with records preservation demands, were issued after The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan Jr. as part of an alleged effort to confuse voters.

title: North Korea linked to $6.3 billion hack on Binance, blockchain intelligence firms say
text:
(AP) - A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm says a North Korean unit was likely behind the hack that impacted more than $6 billion on Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets.
The cryptocurrency exchange said Friday that deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. It said it will cover all losses.
The company said on X Friday that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional “points of breach.”
TRM, in a post on its website Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea’s elite hacking unit. “We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said.
“An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes,” TRM said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.
In February last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.
“Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack,” TRM said.
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was “likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor,” its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. DPRK stands for the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name.
Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is “working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice.”
Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
In December 2022, South Korea’s spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea’s capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.
Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform, and stepped down as the company’s CEO. U.S. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.
Zhao posted Thursday on X that “User funds are safe!” but added that the theft “does look like a hack on Binance.” He added that while he doesn’t manage Binance anymore, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”
The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.
“This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet,” he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users’ “private keys,” or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Binance said on X it had “found no evidence of any wallet private key leak” and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

title: Midterm candidates say they are winning voters across party lines
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Some midterm election candidates have recently been promoting their ability to win over voters from across party lines but experts say it may not be enough to change outcomes in November.
In recent weeks, Democratic candidates in several states have promoted endorsements from Republican officials and voters.
In Alaska, Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski endorsed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins on Tuesday.
In Kansas, two former Republican governors, Bill Graves and Mike Hayden, announced in September and October that they are backing Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Adam Hamilton.
In Texas, the campaign for Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico said that over two dozen former GOP officials have endorsed Talarico.
Kel Seliger, a former GOP state senator, joined the list of officials who endorsed Talarico this week, instead of the Republican candidate in the race, Attorney General Ken Paxton.
“I’ve served with both people,” he said. “James Talarico is not some wild-eyed socialist and and he may believe in a lot of things that Democratic Party believes in that I don’t. But I think he’s going to be honest. And I think he’s going to be frank and direct. I think that the things that he does are going to be what is best for Texas. Not what’s best for Elon Musk.”
Republicans expect crossover support
Republican Party officials say they also expect cross-party voting for their candidates.
“I do think you’re seeing that this cycle, especially in races like in Michigan with Mike Rogers against Abdul El-Sayed, and in Texas with Ken Paxton against James Talarico,” said Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee.
Baldassarre also cited the campaign coalition, “Democrats for Mike Rogers.”
Political scientist: Effect tends to be small
While candidates have continued to promote the bipartisan support in the final days of the election season, Texas Politics Project Research Director Joshua Blank said cross-party voting tends not to make a large difference in elections.
“We’re not talking about a large group of Republicans crossing party lines to vote for Democrats, or a large group of Democrats possibly crossing party lines to vote for Republicans,” he said. “We’re ultimately talking about what are kind of idiosyncratic behaviors they’re going to take place among a small, small share of the electorate,” Blank said. “Now, if the elections close, this could really matter.”
Recent polling has found that some of the midterm races have become increasingly close and, in some cases, statistically tied.
