title: Still need an idea for carving your pumpkin? NPS has free national park-inspired stencils
text:
Looking for Halloween ideas? NPS offers free national park pumpkin stencils online
Still have pumpkins to carve ahead of Halloween?
If you're struggling to come up with a design, the National Park Service has you covered.
NPS is having a non-competitive "Park Pumpkin Carvings Challenge" and is offering free, park-inspired, printer-friendly pumpkin stencils for Halloween.
You can take a look at some of them in the player above, and you can download stencils by clicking HERE.
While some of the designs simply play on the natural beauty of America's parks, others are inspired by beloved traditions, such as Fat Bear Week and camping in a national park. And one of the designs serves as a fun, yet important reminder to keep a safe distance from animals at the parks. 
"Looking for something a little out of the box, or maybe a design that really flies off the pumpkin this spooky season? Nothing says “scary” quite like a 2,000-pound furry mammal you’ve annoyed, launching you into another dimension. Or the tree above. Either way, it comes with a thud. Talk about a smashing Halloween. Which is why we always recommend admiring bison from a safe distance. They’re magnificent, unpredictable, and not particularly interested in your Halloween costume," NPS said in a social media post.
How to carve the pumpkin designs
On its website, NPS released these simple instructions to download and carve the Park Service-inspired designs:
- Step 1: Pick your favorite template below and print it to match the size of your pumpkin’s surface area. Or create your own pumpkin park artwork!
- Step 2: Cut out the dark area of the template.
- Step 3: Use the template to trace the image on your pumpkin.
- Step 4: Carefully carve out the design (or close enough) with a knife. Kids — grab an adult to help with this step.
Once carved, NPS is encouraging folks to add their pumpkins to the "growing parks pumpkin patch" by posting their "pumpkin park art" on social media with the hashtags #FindYourPark or #EncuentraTuParque.

title: Maine lawmaker’s son was arrested by ICE 10 miles from a new life in Canada
text:
Federal immigration agents detained the adopted son of a Maine lawmaker for two days this week after New Hampshire police stopped him just 10 miles short of Canada, which had just granted him citizenship.
Jessie Laurel Tepler-Mujambere, 28, set out on Wednesday, shortly after his citizenship paperwork arrived in the mail, according to his adoptive mother, Sen. Denise Tepler, D-Topsham, who took him in as a teenager when his biological father brought him to Maine from Burundi and abandoned him at a shelter. She and her husband, Sheldon Tepler, a lawyer in Lewiston, later adopted him.
Police in Colebrook, New Hampshire, stopped him that afternoon and turned him over to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Teplers said. He spent the next two days in custody in different locations across New Hampshire. An agent drove him to a Vermont border station on Friday afternoon.
The case comes as immigration advocates criticize President Donald Trump’s crackdown for sweeping up nonviolent immigrants who are following legal paths to status. In Maine, that has included working asylum seekers who entered the country on visas. The Teplers said their son’s detention accomplished nothing except costing taxpayers money.
“This is ridiculous. The taxpayers paid for his last two nights in a county jail in New Hampshire,” Denise Tepler said in a Friday interview. “They are paying for this transfer to Vermont.”
The family will cover the rest, she said, including hundreds of dollars in fees after his car was towed.
An ICE spokesperson said in a statement Friday that Tepler-Mujambere had overstayed the visa he used to enter the country in 2014 and had detained him “pending his removal to Canada.” It referred to federal incentives offered to immigrants like Tepler-Mujambere’s who were willing to “self-deport now,” including a free airline ticket and $3,000.
The Colebrook Police Department did not respond to a message seeking comment.
When Tepler-Mujambere first arrived in the U.S., he unsuccessfully sought legal status through a program for abused and neglected immigrant children, his family said. He then applied for asylum, which allowed him to get a work permit. He earned an associate degree and worked in health care.
Sheldon Tepler was born in a refugee camp in Montreal after his parents fled the Holocaust. When he obtained Canadian citizenship a few years ago, he realized his adopted son could also get it through him.
“The lights went on: This kid can live in Canada,” he said.
Canada approved Tepler-Mujambere’s citizenship on July 22, according to a photo of the certificate his adoptive sister, Maya Tepler, shared with the Bangor Daily News. The official document did not arrive until Wednesday.
By then, his work permit had expired and the federal government had not renewed it. He spent the months of waiting mostly exercising and reading the Bible, Denise Tepler said.
“I gave him a hug and kiss goodbye and he was excited,” she said.
She thought he planned to cross in Jackman. But at 4:37 p.m., he texted her that Colebrook police had arrested him.
Colebrook is about 10 miles south of the U.S. Customs and Border Protection port of entry in Canaan, Vermont, which is typically used by Mainers traveling toward Montreal. Its police department takes part in a federal program that gives local officers some immigration enforcement powers. (Maine lawmakers banned such partnerships last year.)
“I told them I’m waiting on my asylum but I wa[s] heading to Canada and I have documents to show,” he texted his family, according to a screenshot.
He spent the next two days moving between the Strafford County Jail in Dover, New Hampshire, and an ICE field office in Manchester. Staff for U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat from Maine’s 1st District, helped the family keep track of his case, a Pingree spokesperson confirmed.
ICE accused him of overstaying the visa he used to enter the country as a teenager, the Teplers learned. The agency offered him voluntary departure, which is sometimes called “self-deporting,” according to Pingree’s office.
“What, exactly, did this accomplish? New Hampshire police and ICE put him through this ordeal, tied up personnel, and spent taxpayer dollars to accomplish absolutely nothing. This was nothing more than a colossal waste of resources, manpower, and taxpayer dollars,” Pingree said in a statement.
By Thursday evening, officials seemed likely to simply release him. On Friday, an agent drove him to the Highgate Springs border crossing in Vermont’s northwest corner.
He arrived in Canada around 4 p.m. Friday, Maya Tepler said. His car was still sitting in a Colebrook lot more than 100 miles away, packed with his belongings.

title: Students learn the power of giving through painting pet portraits
text:
WINNECONNE, Wis. (InvestigateTV) — Seventh graders at Winneconne Middle School are painting pet portraits for a community project.
Students in Susan Meunier’s new leadership class are tracing and painting portraits of pets. Vaughn Wurtz and her classmates are working on the project at the school.
“We had to do a project for something to do with the community that benefits the community,” Wurtz said.
Aubrey Salm and Paul Reinke helped come up with the idea.
“We’re doing pet portraits for Go Fetch and we’re going to donate all of the money to the humane society,” Salm said.
Meunier said the students are working hard on the portraits.
“They are putting so much effort into it,” Meunier said.
She said the students told Go Fetch in an interview, “It might not be the best painting but we’ll try our hardest.” Meunier said they are trying hard on everything.
Meunier said the value of the project is in the lesson.
“I’m glad they’re seeing the work it does, but really the reward for that work, it’s definitely worth it to go out and be the positive light to see that carry on to other people,” Meunier said.
Meunier said she teaches math by trait.
“Even when I’m teaching math, we just want to teach good humans,” Meunier said. “I always tell them, our goal for you is to go out in the world and do good and be on your own, and in math, sometimes that’s hard to connect those, but this is really showing them we want them to be the positive.”
Reinke said he plans to continue the work.
“I’m going to keep doing this all the way through high school, maybe college,” Reinke said. “It feels amazing, helping people in general.”
Salm said the project has an effect on her classmates.
“Seeing how everyone, even in my class, it makes everyone so happy, knowing that it will make other people happy, it’s just amazing to know,” Salm said.
Wurtz said the school has a set of guidelines called the Winneconne Way.
“We have this thing called the Winneconne Way, it’s PAW: Practice Kindness, Always Show Respect and Work to do your Best,” Wurtz said. “I feel like this class really tries to follow those rules.”

title: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
text:
(Aging Untold) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love.
The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates.
Step away before things escalate
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room.
“You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.”
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help.
“If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said.
Treat communication as behavior
Caregivers should consider what the person they care for is going through, Cradduck said.
“Their communication is really behavior,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to figure out what’s going on that’s causing the frustration.”
She said unspoken expectations can also cause conflict.
“You expecting something from somebody oftentimes turns into spoken resentment,” Cradduck said. “So then, you’re frustrated and you’re yelling and they have no idea.”
A person may be cognitively whole and still not know what a caregiver wants if the caregiver has not said it, she said.
Choose words and tone with care
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke listed words that can escalate a conversation:
- No
- You
- Always
- Never
- Don’t
- You can’t
In addition to the words, tone affects how a caregiver is perceived, Cradduck added.
“It’s not just what you say, it’s how you say it,” Cradduck said.
“If you want to have a better day, have a better tone,” Ambrose said.
She said miscommunication is often the source of conflict.
“All drama and conflict comes from one thing, and that’s miscommunication,” Ambrose said.
She said the way a person communicates is a cue to how that person is feeling, and caregivers should have the emotional maturity to manage themselves.
Meet people where they are
O’Rourke described a visit to her father in a nursing home. He was upset about a missing key for his wheelchair, and staff members were upset with him for being upset. She said she took out a key, turned it on the arm of the chair and got it to work.
Her heart rate went up in that moment, despite her training.
“But then I realized, I don’t have to be right,” O’Rourke said. “I can let go and be with him where he is.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said that when communication is off and there’s a misunderstanding, people begin to second-guess themselves and things can spiral toward anger.
A caregiver can be as distraught as the person receiving care, she said.
Check negative self-talk and name the fear
The Aging Untold experts also addressed negative thoughts and venting to others.
Ambrose said she sees “low-level energy” in Facebook groups where people complain about the person they care for or about others involved — and that kind of drama will make the caregiver more miserable.
But Cradduck said she likes that such groups exist because caregivers can vent in a safe place before they walk into the room.
Negative thoughts, such as “she just never listens to me,” lead to negative and hurtful words, she said.
O’Rourke said venting about fears, frustrations and stress to someone else helps a caregiver feel more balanced going into another conversation.
Rogers addressed underlying fear and said it is something caregivers do not talk about enough.
Go in without a set outcome, and treat adults as adults
How a caregiver goes into the conversation matters too.
O’Rourke said that a caregiver who goes into one with a specific outcome in mind “will lose.” BUt a caregiver who goes in with no outcome, aiming for a successful connection, can build on that.
Cradduck cautioned that caregivers should not treat an adult like a child.
“When you’re trying to parent or you’re trying to correct them like you would a child, then you’re creating a conflict because they’re not going to be happy,” Cradduck said.
The caregiver has to be “the peaceful adult” and keep the calm, but that it is not always easy, she said.
Key takeaways
- Step away to calm down. Remove yourself or get help when you notice signs such as feeling hot, shaky or tense in the jaw.
- See communication as behavior. Consider what the person you care for is going through and what is causing the frustration.
- Say what you expect. Unspoken expectations can turn into spoken resentment.
- Watch your tone and your self-talk. Tone affects how you are perceived, and negative thoughts can lead to hurtful words.
- Ditch the “dance of normalcy” and reclaim your agency. Let go of old relationship dynamics and choose who you want to be now, even when the past is complicated.
- De-escalate to prevent burnout.

title: How to check water safety before a lake or river outing
text:
(InvestigateTV) — A new report from Environment America found bacteria levels were potentially unsafe on at least one day at 69% of more than 4,500 river and lake testing locations in 17 states.
John Rumpler, clean water director and senior attorney at Environment America, said the group’s “Safe for Swimming” report matters as a consumer issue as well as an environmental one.
“I can only imagine that if a family drove two or three hours to go to lakeside cabin, and they were planning to spend the entire week at the lake, and then suddenly there was E. coli in the water,” Rumpler said. “I don’t know that I could put that to dollars and cents, but I think we might agree that’s a ruined vacation right there.”
Rumpler said E. coli turned up in every state in the analysis.
“All across the country in all of these 17 states, we found E. coli, which people may be familiar with E. coli as a nasty bacteria. It’s an indicator of fecal matter, in other words, poop,” Rumpler said. “And so to be clear, we’re not saying all of these waters are contaminated all the time. But about half of these 4,000-plus monitoring sites had elevated E. coli levels on 25% or more of the days that they were tested. So it’s a pretty widespread problem.”
Rumpler said the contamination comes from sewage overflows, stormwater runoff and leaking septic tanks.
Environment America’s online dashboard breaks down the results state by state.
Rumpler said he believes federal and state governments could do more, and that the cost does not have to fall on taxpayers.
“If the federal government does step up and provide more resources to address this problem, then less of that financial burden is going to be on the backs of ratepayers and local citizens of any community,” Rumpler said. “But let me say this, I wouldn’t want any local or state official to use a lack of federal funding as an excuse. Everyone needs to do their part.”
Contamination levels can change daily. Before swimming, check state or county health advisories and the EPA’s water quality portal.
Additional steps include avoiding rivers and lakes for 48 to 72 hours after heavy rain, when sewage overflows and runoff tend to peak. Water that is discolored, smelly, foamy or near a discharge pipe should also be avoided.

title: Suspect caught on video confessing to killing family, college professor, prosecutor says
text:
LORAIN COUNTY, Ohio (WOIO/Gray News) - Moments after a celebrated college professor and his wife were shot to death inside their Ohio home, prosecutors say the suspect knocked on a stranger’s door and asked to be recorded on video confessing to the killings.
Asia Nguyen-Duy, 31, of Ashland, Oregon, appeared in court Thursday, being carried in by several police officers, placed in a chair and rolled to the defense table.
Nguyen-Duy previously went by Daniel Jones. Court records show they legally changed their name in 2025. During Thursday’s hearing, Nguyen-Duy said they are gender-neutral and prefer to be called Asia Nguyen-Duy.
They are facing six counts of murder, four counts of felonious assault and one count of tampering with evidence in the deaths of 64-year-old Pipo Nguyen-Duy and 56-year-old Thi Tran Phong.
During the hearing, prosecutors revealed that Nguyen-Duy, covered in scratches and blood, approached a nearby resident. They asked them to record a video, and admitted to killing their family, claiming they were “escaping a cult” and taking full responsibility for the acts.
Police were first alerted Wednesday morning after finding a smoldering, modified vehicle registered to Nguyen-Duy in an Oberlin College parking lot containing loose ammunition and magazine packaging.
Officers found Nguyen-Duy nearby and conducted a welfare check at the victims’ home, discovering both dead from multiple gunshot wounds.
Pipo Nguyen-Duy was an internationally exhibited photographer and longtime studio art professor at Oberlin College.
A judge set bond at $3 million, and the case has been bound over to county common pleas court.

title: Ask 8 Investigates: What is and isn't allowed at the polls on Election Day
text:
Ask 8 Investigates: What is and isn't allowed at the polls on Election Day
Anyone who encounters an issue at the polls can contact the Secretary of State’s Office
Ask 8 Investigates: What is and isn't allowed at the polls on Election Day
Anyone who encounters an issue at the polls can contact the Secretary of State’s Office
Voters reached out to 8 Investigates with questions about what sort of behavior is allowed at the polls on election day.
In Maine, voters who need assistance may bring a friend or relative into the booth to help them read or fill out their ballot. The helper does not have to be a Maine voter and doesn't have to be old enough to vote, but cannot be the voter’s employer or union official. Maine law prohibits helpers from telling voters how to vote or helping them make decisions. They are solely there to help fill out the ballot according to the voter’s wishes.
Voters who don’t have someone to help can ask a clerk for assistance from an election official. Children younger than 18 may also accompany a voter into the booth to observe the process.
Maine law prohibits making audible phone calls from inside a voting place, but it doesn't bar voters from using phones to search for information about the candidates from inside the voting booth. Voters may also review a sample ballot beforehand and bring notes into the booth.
Campaign materials, political advertising and signature collection are prohibited within 250 feet of the polls, but voters are allowed to wear campaign buttons as long as they're no larger than 3 inches across.
Early voting has ended, and the deadline to request an absentee ballot has passed. As of Friday, voters will need to vote in person on Election Day. Anyone who encounters an issue at the polls can contact the Secretary of State’s Office.

title: Letter to the Editor: Choosing Our Treasurer
Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
text:
What to know about the $6.3B hack on Binance, likely the biggest-ever crypto theft
Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. Blockchain firms have pointed to the attack coming from a North Korean hacking unit.
The company said it has reserved more than $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the stolen assets and was beginning to recover assets for users. Binance worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets.
Related video above: Trump meets cryptocurrency leaders in August
The cryptocurrency exchange has promised to cover all losses, and it has been sharing regular updates on its social media channels as it uncovers more information about the hack.
“We are working nonstop to resolve this,” Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said Friday in a video posted to X.
In an exchange Friday with reporters at the White House, President Donald Trump said U.S. officials were investigating the Binance hack. Asked whether North Korea was involved, Trump said: “We’re looking at that.”
Here's what we know about the hack, possible North Korean involvement and Binance's investigation.
North Korean hackers are suspected in the attack
Binance said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional “points of breach.”
U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM, in a post on its website late Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea’s elite hacking unit. “We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said.
“An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes,” TRM said. “Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists."
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X.
Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is “working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice.”
Experts have said that North Korea turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities in recent years as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
In December 2022, South Korea’s spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets over the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea’s capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the world's best.
Many are calling this the biggest crypto theft on record
While about half of the stolen assets were frozen, there is evidence that the hackers already are transferring and converting some of what wasn’t recovered, said Garrick Hileman, an independent cryptocurrency analyst.
“Like in money laundering, you bring in the stolen goods and launder those through a mixer or tumbler,” he said. “You mix it in with other cryptos, and it’s harder to track.”
How long it will take the hackers to turn that into something usable isn’t clear, he said. “The bottom line is there are places in the world where you can take your bitcoin and get that converted,” Hileman said.
TRM and several other crypto firms and experts have said the hack represents the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.
In February of last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack. TRM listed the Bybit hack when it referenced similarities between the Binance hack and previous attacks linked to TraderTraitor.
Binance's founder, Changpeng Zhao, wrote on X that while Binance's hack might be the largest in terms of its dollar value, previous attacks on other companies like the crypto exchange Mt. Gox have had a more substantial impact in terms of the bitcoin amount affected, he said.
Experts warn this scale of hacking could become more commonplace.
“A cyber attack of this level is a matter of when, not if, particularly alongside the rise of AI,” said Andy Ward, a senior vice president at Absolute Security. “Cyber threats are becoming more sophisticated and widespread as ever, and it is likely only a matter of time before an even larger hack, with even greater financial fallout, makes headlines.”
Where experts — and Binance — say things went wrong
The hack has raised questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, co-founder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.
“This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet,” he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' “private keys,” or unique authorizations, digitally and that are connected to the internet.
Teng, Binance’s co-CEO, confirmed in a nearly five-minute video posted on X Friday that Binance's own hot wallet was affected. “User assets are held under Binance's established security architecture," he said. "The vast majority sits in cold wallets” — which are offline and used for secure storage — “and are only moved into a hot wallet when a user makes withdrawal.”
Teng said Binance's tech and security teams are “still deep” in investigating the hack. He said it was not carried out by one person and that the attackers used complex tactics, including a "self-destruct mechanism" that is making the incident more difficult to investigate.
“We are working with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence firms, token issuers and other exchanges to trace and recover stolen funds," Teng said. "We will do everything within our power to make sure that these bad actors will be held accountable.”
Binance has said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two.
Associated Press journalists John Seewer, Aamer Madhani, Hyung-jin Kim and Kim Tong-hyung contributed to this report.

title: Prosecutors drop felony charge against rapper Rick Ross in domestic violence case
text:
MIAMI BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her, court records said.
The Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office filed paperwork Thursday to drop a felony charge of battery by strangulation because of “insufficient evidence.” Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, still faces a misdemeanor charge of battery domestic violence.
Ross, 50, has pleaded not guilty to all charges, and his attorney said Friday that his client would continue to defend himself against the allegations. Ross surrendered at the Miami Beach police station on Oct. 1, two days after the woman filed a report with police, officials said. He was freed on bail several hours later.
According to an arrest report, a woman told Miami Beach detectives that she had been living with Ross when he accused her of cheating on him and struck her multiple times on Aug. 28. She said Ross also choked her with the collar of her shirt and slammed her into a wall. The woman said she was eventually able to leave the home and returned later — after Ross left — to collect her belongings.
Ross previously pleaded no contest to aggravated assault in 2017 after he was accused of forcing a man into a guesthouse at his suburban Atlanta mansion in 2015 and beating him with a handgun, according to Georgia court records. Under a Georgia first-time offender program, the court issued an order exonerating Ross of guilt on that felony count.
Ross is a longtime South Florida resident who gained prominence in 2006 with his debut single “Hustlin’.”
The rapper and entrepreneur helped put Miami on the musical map in the early 2000s, when most hip-hop fans looked to Atlanta and Houston as Southern rap headquarters. “Hustlin’” was certified platinum twice by the Recording Industry Association of America and sparked a bidding war for Ross. He eventually signed with Def Jam Records, headed by Jay-Z.
Ross’ debut album, “Port of Miami,” also went platinum, debuting at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart. It was the first in a series of chart-toppers, including 2008’s “Trilla” and 2009’s “Deeper Than Rap.” He has been nominated for nine Grammy Awards.
In 2008, he founded the influential label Maybach Music Group, boosting the careers of signees like Wale, Meek Mill and French Montana.
His most recent album, “Set In Stone,” was released in July.

title: Obituary: June Frances Meserve
text:
BIDDEFORD – June Frances Meserve, 98, died on Oct. 27, 2026. She was born on Feb. 28, 1928, in Chicopee, Mass., to the Reverend William and Mrs. Ada Gunter.
After graduating from Watertown High School, June attended the University of New Hampshire for a year before transferring to Bryant and Stratton Business School. She then became a secretary in the athletic department at Northeastern University, where she worked for several years. She would remain a loyal fan of NU teams for the rest of her life.
June met Robert Meserve in the summer of ’45 in Ocean Park, Maine. In 1951, they were wed and went on to spend 71 years together. Their marriage was anchored by steadfast devotion to their family, church and community.
June moved to Reading when her father became minister of the Old South Methodist Church in 1946. For over seven decades she was an active member of the church. She served as president of the United Methodist Women, was leader of the Dorcas Circle for many years, and often played the piano for chapel worship services. She also played regularly for worship services at the Daniels Nursing Home, declaring jauntily that she was going to play for the “old folks” when she herself was an octogenarian.
For 20 years June worked as a teacher aide in Reading, first at Prospect Street School and then at Barrows, becoming an invaluable resource to teachers in both schools. She was an excellent cook whose Sunday dinners in particular were epic. She loved picking berries and made pies, cakes, and jams. Her family learned to expect deliciousness and was never disappointed! In summertime June taught craft classes in Ocean Park. An artistic and creative person, she excelled at wood painting, calligraphy, knitting, and other crafts. Using an antique sewing machine and steely determination, she made everything from dresses to hats to Halloween costumes. She also enjoyed gardening, reading, visiting the seashore (especially Ocean Park), and most importantly spending time with family and friends. Her joyful spirit and ready laugh endeared her to all.
June was predeceased by her husband, Robert, and her son-in-law, Oscar Demiranda. She is survived by her son David and his wife Maria of Scottsdale, Ariz., son Mark and his wife Linda of Merrimac, Mass., daughter Loretta and her husband Jon of Kennebunk, Maine, daughter Nancy of Biddeford, Maine; and several grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
The family is grateful to the staff members of Atria Senior Living in Kennebunk and St. Andre Health Care in Biddeford for their kindness and compassion.
A private burial service will be held at Forest Glen Cemetery in Reading.
Arrangements are made by Dennett, Craig & Pate Funeral Home, 365 Main St., Saco.

title: That Creepy Castle Across From Portsmouth? It Was a Prison.
text:
The Creepy Castle Across From Portsmouth Has a Dark History
We continue with Garret's Creepy Fact Storytime... Back to Portsmouth we go.
If you've ever spent any time along the Portsmouth waterfront, there's a good chance you've looked across the river and noticed that enormous castle-looking building sitting over at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard.
You know the one I'm talking about.
Huge walls. Tall towers. Arched windows. It looks like something you'd expect to see in an old horror movie.
And I've always wondered about that place.
Turns out, it wasn't built for royalty. It wasn't some wealthy family's waterfront mansion.
It was a prison. And its history is a lot more interesting than I ever imagined.
New England Had Its Own Alcatraz
The building is the former Portsmouth Naval Prison, located on Seavey's Island in Kittery, Maine.
Yes, Maine. Even though it's called the Portsmouth Naval Prison, it's actually across the Piscataqua River from Portsmouth, New Hampshire.
The prison opened in 1908 and eventually earned the nickname "Alcatraz of the East."
When it was constructed, the building was considered the largest poured-concrete structure in the world.
And you can understand why it earned that intimidating nickname.
Between the island location, the powerful currents of the Piscataqua River, and those castle-like towers, it wasn't exactly the kind of place you'd want to find yourself checking into.
The Island Was Holding Prisoners Before the Castle Even Existed
Here's something that surprised me.
According to the Naval Sea Systems Command, the site was originally home to Camp Long, a prisoner-of-war camp established during the Spanish-American War in 1898.
More than 1,600 Spanish prisoners of war were held there.
About a decade later, the naval prison opened on the same site.
READ MORE: The Strange History Behind Portsmouth's Oldest Cemetery
And over the next 66 years, an extraordinary number of men would pass through those walls.
According to research highlighted by the Portsmouth Public Library, more than 86,000 men passed through the prison between 1908 and 1974.
During World War II, the prison held more than 3,000 sailors and Marines at one time.
And there's another piece of World War II history connected to the building.
After Germany surrendered in 1945, German submarine crews were questioned at the prison by U.S. naval intelligence.
Think about that for a second.
A place we drive past today was once part of the military history of two world wars.
What Happened When the Prison Closed?
In 1974, the Navy officially closed the Portsmouth Naval Prison.
And what happened next is part of what makes this place so fascinating.
The enormous building remained standing.
For more than 50 years, the old castle has watched over Portsmouth Harbor, while life has continued on both sides of the river.
There have been multiple attempts over the years to find a new use for the building, but none has resulted in a completed redevelopment.
And it isn't just the history that's difficult to ignore.
It's the appearance.
Those towering walls. The rows of windows. The old fortress architecture.
Knowing that thousands of men once lived behind those walls gives the place a completely different feeling.
You can see over 300 pictures of the prison from the Naval History and Heritage Command website.
Could the Castle Finally Get a New Life?
There's actually been a recent development involving the old prison.
In August 2026, New Hampshire Public Radio reported that Senator Jeanne Shaheen had requested $5 million in federal funding for a feasibility study examining whether the former prison could become a "sailor campus."
The idea would be to explore recreational programs and support services for sailors stationed at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard while their submarines undergo repairs.
It's an interesting possibility for a building that has sat unused as a prison for more than half a century.
But the proposal was still in the planning stage when it was reported.
The Castle Is Still There, Watching Over the Harbor
One thing worth mentioning: the old prison isn't open for regular public tours. It's located within an active naval shipyard with restricted access.
But you don't have to go inside to appreciate just how unusual this piece of Seacoast history really is.
The next time you're walking along the Portsmouth waterfront, take a look across the river.
That enormous castle isn't just another historic building.
It was once one of the most recognizable military prisons in the country.
And more than a century after it opened, it still has a way of making you wonder what life was like behind those walls.
Personally, I think it looks creepy enough from the outside. I don't need to find out what those empty hallways sound like at night.

title: Lewiston is among the Maine schools that are adding more recess breaks. Here’s why.
text:
Recess. It’s most young students’ favorite time of day.
For 25 minutes, they can get outside and socialize with their friends, climb on the playground, or participate in activities that help them get their energy out.
Experts say it’s one of the most important parts of a young student’s day. It’s proven to not only increase a student’s level of physical activity, but also helps them in the classroom by improving their memory and attention, helping them stay on-task and avoid disruptive behavior, according to studies from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
That’s exactly why some schools in Maine have added additional recess time for students, and teachers and administrators are reporting notable improvements.
Roxanne Lenhert and Melissa Hunt with Lewiston Public Schools emphasize the importance of getting kids outside to play, especially in a world where screens seem to rule. Lenhert is an occupational therapist and Hunt is a physical therapist.
“They’re getting those social skills as well, so they’re learning how to interact with each other and how to help their peers. We have some students with delayed motor skills and I’ve seen some take their hands and say, ‘Let me help you.’ They’re learning those skills,” Hunt said.
In Farmington-area Regional School Unit 9, adding additional time outside has improved attendance, reduced tardiness and smoothed out classroom routines. If students arrive early enough, they can have an additional 15 minutes of recess before school starts.
“Teachers report that students are arriving calmer and more prepared, and making much smoother morning adjustments,” said Stacey Gilbert, principal at a Farmington elementary school.
“Parents are equally excited about the initiative, noting that morning battles to get ready have turned into students rushing them out the door so they can get to school on time for recess,” she said.
In Lewiston, Montello Elementary School added an additional 20 minutes of play per day for kindergarten through third grade. Principal Tiffany Sax said the decision improved physical stamina, classroom focus, and supports healthy child development.
“During these play breaks, we encourage staff to join in the play with students to model positive social behaviors, and support students with learning appropriate conflict resolution skills.
“While we are still evaluating the long-term impact of this addition, the immediate response is clear: Students love the extra time to play, and overall office referrals are down compared to previous school years,” Sax said.
RECESS STRUCTURE
In Lewiston, students in kindergarten through sixth grade have 25 minutes of recess a day, said Lenhert, who rotates around the district’s schools with Hunt.
The amount of time a school has for recess is up to the administrators at each building.
Maine law requires kindergarten through fifth grade to have at least 30 minutes of recess a day, which can include transition time from classes or to lunch or recess. Classrooms incorporate a “brain break” through instructional periods and encourage the use of outdoor space, Sax said.
Some schools in Lewiston, like Farwell Elementary School, offer an additional 20 minutes for kindergarten only. Raymond A. Geiger Elementary School has a 15-minute team-building block for structured play for first and second grade students. Structured play can mean that a teacher decides how to spend the time, rather than having students decide.
Where recess takes place is less important than the ability for students to have a break, educators said.
However, if it’s too cold or raining, and students stay inside for recess, teachers said the difference in behavior is noticeable. Lenhert said when students do not have outdoor recess, it can impact their ability to participate and focus.
“As adults, when we are expected to sit for long periods of time, how much better do you feel when you can go outside, move your body for a little bit. Your heart rate is increased and you come back to the table and can feel the benefits. It’s evident in little bodies as well,” said Lenhert.
A newly formed group in Maine would like to see recess increased across the state.
The Maine chapter of Say YES to RECESS is calling for two 30-minute recess periods, creating protected time for children to move, play, connect and learn through play.
“This isn’t about choosing recess over academics,” chapter leader Danielle Dalton, of Scarborough, said in a recent op-ed. “It is about recognizing that play is part of learning, and that some of the most important skills children develop cannot be taught solely through instruction.”
BENEFITS OF PLAY
When students are outside, they can choose to play on the playground, organize a sports game, or use the equipment the schools have, like jump ropes.
Climbing on the structures helps build their muscles, specifically their hand muscles, which can then help young children with writing. Running around helps reset the student’s nervous system, which helps them perform better in class, educators said.
Hunt also emphasized the importance of children watching each other play. It helps strengthen their motor skills if can they imitate a friend’s motions.
“The motor imitation is really good. I don’t think we can always get the same type of motor imitation when watching a movement video. It’s beneficial to see another human being in your space do the activity, then think, ‘I’m going to do that,'” Hunt said.
The pair said students’ strength to climb on the monkey bars or to hold their heads up when they lay on their stomachs has gone down from a lack of play and more screen time. Lenhert said that beyond the screens, sometimes families in the area do not feel safe sending their children outside to play where they live.
In addition to recess, teachers are encouraged to incorporate physical activity through the day, even if it’s just standing up and walking around the classroom. Some of the elementary schools have hopscotch painted on the walkway, or signs that encourage students to stretch as they walk along the pathway as a way to stimulate movement.
“It’s just really important,” said Hunt. “I really hope to see all schools take a step more in the direction of integrating more movement through the day and not just on the screen.”

title: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
text:
(Aging Untold) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often.
The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part.
Start with the question the trial is trying to answer
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the first step is to change the question you ask.
“I think the first thing we have to do is not think about, ‘Can this clinical trial help me?’ but ‘What is this clinical trial trying to answer?’” Rogers said. “That’s what most of these trials are about.”
A trial is not a last resort
Rogers said many people see clinical trials as a last resort.
“I think a lot of people think that it’s a last resort option, that you don’t have anything else, when in fact one of the biggest benefits is it gives you access,” Rogers said. “You get great access to tomorrow’s medicines today — devices, therapies and other things that will not be available to everybody else for years.”
Where to find a study
Rogers said people can search at ClinicalTrials.gov , check with their physician or look at academic centers and other organizations specific to a disease or condition that have their own studies.
What participants may get
Rogers said participants can receive close monitoring and access to specialists.
“Many of them will pay for gas, and everything like that,” Rogers said. “Some of them even pay you for the study.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said that the National Institutes of Health (NIH) keeps a list of clinical trials and which compensate participants.
Know what to expect going in
What participants should know is that they might receive a placebo, she said.
“You might be the one getting the placebo, you might get the drug itself,” O’Rourke said. “So knowing that going in, the expectation wouldn’t be that I’m going to get the drug or that I’m going to see if I’m going to get better.”
She said she has seen people often come away from trials feeling hopeful and feeling they are giving back to their community.
Clients who joined a local clinical trial group also found support, O’Rourke said.
“The social workers there were amazing,” she said. “They had support groups, and it gave them access to resources in the community that they didn’t know about, in addition to all the medical specialists. So I saw that being a huge value for people, especially when you’re older.”
Why older adults are needed in trials
O’Rourke said older adults are often left out of research.
“I’ve heard older people called ‘evidence free’ because nobody really studies them,” O’Rourke said. “They’re not included in the studies.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said older adults should be included because medication does not affect all age groups in the same way.
“Medication metabolizes so differently in our older community than it does in our younger community, so without having them as participants, they’re often walking blind,” Cradduck said.
Cradduck added that new medicines cannot be approved without clinical trials.
“You can’t have a new medicine come out without a clinical trial. It’s not going to be approved,” Cradduck said. “If we want new medications, if we want new hope, we have to have these clinical trials.”
Addressing the “guinea pig” concern
Many people tell themselves they don’t want to be a guinea pig, Cradduck said.
“You’re not a guinea pig,” she said. “By the time it’s reached this point, it has been thoroughly tested repeatedly.”
Cradduck said there are adverse effects with everything that gets prescribed.
Resources
Key takeaways
- Tomorrow’s medicine today. Clinical trials are not a last resort. They are a way to access cutting-edge treatments early.
- Older adults are essential. Drugs affect older bodies differently, and participation builds safer future treatments.
- Ask the right questions. Find out what scientific question the trial is trying to answer to make sure it aligns with your goals.
- Know where to look. Start at clinicaltrials.gov , and check with your physician, academic centers or other organizations that run their own studies.
- Know what to expect. Participants may get a placebo or the drug itself, and the NIH lists which trials compensate participants.

title: 3 dead in Oregon helicopter collision, including flight instructor and student pilot
text:
MCMINNVILLE, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) — Three people are dead after two helicopters crashed into each other Thursday afternoon near an Oregon airport, officials said.
Crash location and road closure
The Yamhill County Sheriff’s Office said the crash was reported around 2:15 p.m. near Lafayette Highway and Southeast Stringtown Road.
The crash scene is near McMinnville Municipal Airport, southeast of McMinnville.
Aircraft involved
The two helicopters were identified as an Airbus Helicopters AS350B2 and a Robinson R22, according to the NTSB.
Jerry Trimble Helicopters, a flight training company, posted on social media that one of its aircraft was involved in the crash.
Victims identified
Yamhill County Sheriff Sam Elliott said at a news conference Thursday night that a flight instructor from Texas and a student pilot from the U.K. were inside the Robinson helicopter. He identified the instructor as 22-year-old Maddie Aasbo.
The student pilot’s name has not been released because officials are still working to notify the family.
The third victim, 38-year-old Tyler Sturdevant of Newberg, was in the Airbus at the time of the crash, according to the sheriff.
Witness account
A witness said he was standing on the roof of a nearby barn when he saw the two helicopters crash into each other and then hit the ground just outside the perimeter of the airport. He said he immediately called 911.
The crash is under investigation.

title: Rick Bennett denounces GOP campaign promoting him as ‘progressive choice’ for governor
text:
Independent gubernatorial candidate Rick Bennett is disavowing the support of a Republican-backed political action committee spending hundreds of thousands of dollars promoting him as the “progressive choice” for Maine governor, calling it a cynical attempt by wealthy out-of-state donors to manipulate the election.
Bennett, a former chair of the Maine Republican Party who broke with the GOP over President Donald Trump to run as an independent, has supported LGBTQ+ rights and other policies associated with Democrats but is hardly campaigning as a progressive.
Reached by phone Thursday evening, Bennett told the Midcoast Villager the supposed support for his campaign is a “cynical” and “offensive” attempt to siphon progressive votes from Democrat Hannah Pingree to benefit Republican Bobby Charles, who trails Pingree in the polls.
“This sort of intervention is unwanted. I would love to see it curtailed,” Bennett said. “These guys that are backing this PAC are out-of-state centimillionaires if not billionaires trying to manipulate Maine elections.”
Bennett said the effort illustrates the need to overhaul the campaign finance system. Noting more than $400 million is projected to be spent on political advertising in Maine this year, he said donors should instead give their money to charities to help people afford heating oil this winter.
“I call it the political-industrial class. There’s so much money flowing through that people are putting their kids through college by putting these mailers out. They don’t give a damn about the Maine people and the Maine elections,” Bennett said.
The group behind the advertising, No Nonsense PAC, officially registered itself with the Maine Ethics Commission as supporting Charles and opposing Pingree.
But it has also spent at least $169,000 promoting Bennett, the long-shot third candidate in the race, including sending at least three mailers to voters portraying the former Republican as the progressive alternative to both major-party candidates.
Polls show Pingree with a substantial lead over Charles, while Bennett has struggled to gain traction. A new CNN poll released Thursday showed Pingree at 53%, Charles at 39% and “other” at 4%, suggesting Bennett does not have much of a chance.
The apparent strategy behind the No Nonsense PAC effort is to persuade voters who might otherwise support Pingree to vote for Bennett instead, potentially improving Charles’ chances of winning. Unlike in Maine’s congressional elections, ranked-choice voting is not used in general elections for governor. That means the candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority. Votes for Bennett cannot be transferred to Pingree or Charles if he finishes last.
The No Nonsense PAC mailers call Bennett “the progressive choice” and highlight his positions on issues that appeal to liberal voters, including support for LGBTQ+ rights and universal healthcare.
“Don’t settle for establishment politics. Vote your values,” one mailer readers. Another says Bennett “voted to protect gender-affirming care” and “championed LGBTQ non-discrimination protections.”
On the reverse, the mailers attack Pingree as corrupt and blame her for driving up taxes and prices on household goods.
But rather than an earnest effort to support the independent, the No Nonsense PAC’s own financial disclosures show it is funded and run by prominent Republicans. Its money comes overwhelmingly from major Republican donors, including some of the country’s wealthiest conservative political financiers.
The group has reported raising more than $1.2 million and spending more than $818,000 on independent expenditures in the governor’s race through Oct. 29. Its reported spending includes roughly $332,000 opposing Pingree, $169,000 supporting Bennett and $265,000 supporting Charles directly.
Among No Nonsense PAC’s contributors is Thomas Klingenstein, a New York investor and chair of the conservative Claremont Institute, who gave $100,000. Klingenstein has been a major financial supporter of Republican candidates in Maine and beyond, including putting $3 million this year behind an effort to boost Garrett Mason, who lost the Republican gubernatorial primary to Charles.
Other contributors include Roger Penske, the billionaire automotive and racing executive, who gave at least $200,000; David DeLorme, a Freeport businessman who contributed at least $200,000; and Contract Farming of Maine LLC, a company historically associated with egg producer Jack DeCoster. Steven Ritzi, a former high school classmate of Charles who has also contributed to his campaign, gave $20,000.
The PAC has also hired Republican political consultants to carry out its advertising campaign.
Its largest expenditures have gone to Red Maverick Media, whose co-founder Mike Leavitt previously served as executive director of the Maine Republican Party. On its website, the firm lists Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins among its clients. In September, the PAC also reported paying $20,000 to Percipient Strategies, a political research firm that says on its website it served as a lead research contractor for Make America Great Again Inc., a super PAC supporting Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.
Under campaign finance laws, independent expenditure groups like No Nonsense PAC can raise and spend unlimited amounts of money as long as they do not coordinate directly with campaigns or candidates.
The No Nonsense PAC and Charles campaign did not respond to requests for comment from the Midcoast Villager. But Charles’ campaign previously said in a statement to WGME: “No Nonsense PAC is an independent committee. The Bobby Charles campaign doesn’t control it, doesn’t coordinate with it and isn’t going to direct its spending from a podium either.”
Pingree’s campaign dismissed the impact of the spending, with spokesperson Mary-Erin Casale saying “late outside spending and misleading tactics” won’t change the candidate’s emphasis on working to win every vote.
But the Maine Democratic Party was not willing to give Bennett a pass.
At an Oct. 13 press conference in Portland, before the “progressive choice” mailer reached voters, Democratic officials accused the No Nonsense PAC of trying to undermine Pingree and called on Bennett to denounce its support.
“It’s awfully convenient that Rick Bennett has chosen to say something now, just five days before Election Day and after over $150,000 has already been spent on his behalf,” Maine Democrats spokesperson Lauryn Fanguen told the Villager. “He’s had weeks to speak up while the Maine Democratic Party repeatedly called him out and multiple news outlets asked him to respond. He chose silence.”
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Air defense systems deployed at Mar-a-Lago and Palm Beach airport
text:
Air defense systems deployed at Mar-a-Lago and Palm Beach airport
Surface-to-air missile systems have been deployed at Mar-a-Lago and Donald J. Trump International Airport at the request of the U.S. Secret Service, according to federal officials.
The systems are designed to defend against aerial threats, including aircraft and drones.
Officials have not disclosed a specific reason for the deployment.
In a statement, a U.S. Secret Service spokesperson said the agency is operating in a heightened threat environment.
"The U.S. Secret Service is operating in a heightened threat environment, and we continuously adapt our protective operations to incorporate cutting-edge tools, technology, and methods to safeguard our protectees. At the request of the U.S. Secret Service, NORAD and U.S. Northern Command are providing Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System capabilities in support of our protective operations," the statement said.
NORAD and U.S. Northern Command also confirmed the deployment in a statement, saying the systems were placed in and around Mar-a-Lago at the Secret Service’s request.
"At the request of the U.S. Secret Service (USSS) and under NORAD and USNORTHCOM authorities, NORAD and USNORTHCOM deployed ground-based air defense assets in and around Mar-a-Lago, Florida. Due to security considerations, we cannot provide tactics, techniques and procedural specifics. For further detail, we refer you to the USSS."
Aviation expert weighs in on deployment
Michael Leighton, an aviation expert and pilot, said he believes the deployment signals concern about a potential confirmed threat, although federal officials have not confirmed that is the reason.
"The only reason that they would do that is that they had a credible threat," Leighton said.
Leighton said the growing use of drones in warfare has increased concerns about how adversaries could use the technology to target protected locations.
"Drone warfare has become a big thing and for the Department of Defense, their biggest concern is that an enemy, domestic or foreign, would use a drone guided by our GPS signals, the same GPS signals that you have in your car and on your cell phone, which are extremely accurate," Leighton told sister station WPBF.
Why surface-to-air defense systems are used
The systems are designed to detect and counter aerial threats. Leighton said ground-based missile systems can provide a faster response than scrambling a fighter jet to intercept a potential threat.
"They’re concerned about if we don’t have enough time to scramble an F-16 to intercept, because it takes a few minutes for that F-16 to get there, whereas if a target was identified and there was a problem, a ground-based surface-to-air anti-aircraft missile could be launched in seconds," Leighton said.
Leighton said he feels the deployment of the systems is likely also a deterrent. 
"These missiles were put in place in public where people could see them for a reason, and I wouldn't be alarmed. I would be relieved," he said.
He said it's a sign that federal officials are taking every step possible to prevent something from happening.
"Those missiles are manned the whole time, and so if they identify a threat that the missile is designed to deter, they're going to use it, and as an American citizen, I would be happy for that to happen. I don't want anybody to get hurt," he said.
Federal officials have not publicly identified a specific threat connected to the deployment at Mar-a-Lago or Donald J. Trump International Airport.

title: 'Days of our Lives' star Robert Kelker-Kelly's cause of death revealed
text:
'Days of our Lives' star Robert Kelker-Kelly's cause of death revealed
Robert Kelker-Kelly's cause of death has been revealed.
The actor, best known for playing Bo Brady on "Days of Our Lives," died from arteriosclerotic heart disease, numerous reports claim, citing the St. Charles County medical examiner.
His death was ruled natural.
Kelker-Kelly died Oct. 3 after police were called to his home in St. Charles County, Missouri, for reports of an unconscious man. Authorities say Kelker-Kelly experienced chest pains shortly before becoming unresponsive.
Arteriosclerotic heart disease is heart disease linked to arteriosclerosis, or “hardening of the arteries.”
When it affects the arteries supplying the heart, plaque buildup can narrow them and reduce blood flow. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute says atherosclerosis is a common type of arteriosclerosis and describes coronary heart disease as occurring when “plaque builds up in the coronary arteries.”
Kelker-Kelly got his start in soap opera acting when he played Sam Fowler on “Another World” in 1987. He would also later go on to play Stavros Cassadine on “General Hospital."
Kelker-Kelly was one of the actors to star as Bo Brady on “Days of Our Lives,” and his character was known for his steamy and dramatic relationships with Hope Williams Brady, played by Kristian Alfonso, and Billie Reed, played by Lisa Rinna. Kelker-Kelly took on the role of Bo in 1992 after Peter Reckell. Reckell originated the role in the early 1980s and then later returned as Bo Brady in 1995.
Kelker-Kelly was also a professional pilot.
He was married to actress Linda Rattner from 1988 to 1992. Then, from 1997 to 2013, he was married to “Days of Our Lives” costar Miriam Parrish, who played Jamie Caldwell. Both of the marriages ended in divorce, People reports.

title: An ICE officer has been charged after striking a man with a car in Houston
text:
HOUSTON (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston was charged Friday with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, prosecutors said.
The Harris County District Attorney’s office says Mario Alberto Morales was behind the wheel of an unmarked black vehicle on Oct. 10 when it struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, who was running away. Parra Hernandez was later placed in custody with a broken leg.
Few federal officers during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown have faced criminal charges for their actions in the field, although some encounters have come under investigation.
The case in Houston was brought by District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, who is also investigating the fatal shooting of a Mexican homebuilder in July that set off protests in the nation’s fourth-largest city.
ICE did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment about the indictment charging Morales.
ICE has said Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the car and called accusations that the officer intentionally struck him false and “reckless.” Teare has said the surveillance footage clearly contradicts the ICE account.
In the video, a Jeep Cherokee speeds over a median and drives toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away. The video does not show the car hitting him — that view is blocked by another vehicle — but it shows the SUV inches away from him. The footage then shows Parra Hernandez on the ground.
Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation
Other aspects of ICE’s account have also been called into question.
ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day and was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him. FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston, said Mendoza-Cervantes’ daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017. She also said his real name is Jose Hector Jimenez.
Teare’s office has also said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE’s statement.
ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for nearly a decade.
Parra Hernandez has been in the country for more than 30 years. He was living in the U.S. without authorization, according to FIEL, which has been working with his family.
Fatal summer Houston shooting also under investigation
Teare said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence “either intentionally or through gross negligence.” He said the ICE officer who drove the SUV that struck Parra Hernandez fled the scene before the vehicle could be impounded.
In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his requests for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his van. DHS has said Salgado Araujo had “weaponized his vehicle” before the shooting and that an officer fired in self-defense. Other passengers in the van have disputed that account.
Teare has not given a timetable for when his office’s investigation into the shooting will be complete. In September, a witness to the shooting was seen entering a courthouse area reserved for grand jury proceedings.
___
Wilder reported from Austin.
___
Wilder is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.

title: Bill Green’s endorsement ad shows he’s out of touch
text:
In his latest ad for Susan Collins, Bill Green’s attempt at characterizing Troy Jackson as unqualified to represent Maine in Congress is laughable. He insinuates that Troy is “just a logger” who can supply people with a cord of wood.
Jackson spent more than 20 years in the Maine Legislature, often in leadership roles. Our current legislature is comprised of many who are “just a logger,” “just a fisherman,” “just a housewife,” “just a tradesperson,” “just an educator,” etc. Would Mr. Green also imply that none of them would be qualified to serve Maine in a higher office?
It is obvious that after more than 40 years as a media journalist, Bill Green is still “just a hack.” He is oblivious to the shameful way Susan Collins and her Republican colleagues sit back and watch Trump and his co-conspirators move this country away from democracy and down the path of authoritarianism.

title: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
text:
(Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War.
The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment.
“This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release.
Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies.
During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains.
The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

title: Top federal prosecutor in Alaska says criminal probe underway over would-be spoiler Senate candidate
text:
Justice Department seeks to isolate Alaska ballots as criminal probe underway over Senate candidate
A federal judge has barred the Justice Department from threatening or coercing election workers to stop processing ballots.
The order issued late Friday also bars the Justice Department from demanding local election officials segregate or not count ballots that the federal government deems may have been cast by ineligible voters.
It marks another blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to assert control over local elections.
It comes just hours after the U.S. Department of Justice pushed for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion, while federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.
This is a breaking news story. Check back for updates.
The U.S. Department of Justice pushed Friday for a court order to isolate certain Alaska ballots to investigate potential voter confusion, while federal officials confirmed the existence of a criminal probe over a Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent.
The dueling developments came days before Tuesday's ranked choice general election, in a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. The race is among a handful nationwide expected to determine control of the Senate.
Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage that the investigation has been ongoing for several months, but recent revelations from The New York Times that Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a "significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska."
Separately, the Justice Department — as part of a lawsuit it filed last week — asked a judge to order that state elections officials isolate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan to investigate potential voter "confusion" with the senator.
Alaska Assistant U.S. Attorney E. Bryan Wilson, in a filing, said the government "seeks to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary."
The Department of Justice also filed with the court a list of proposed questions it seeks to compel the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to answer as part of the civil case seeking to block certification of the Senate race if the incumbent loses. President Donald Trump has said he told the department to file the case.
State election officials made efforts to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot
Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot. Democrats, including the DSCC, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats' behest.
The request to segregate the ballots in Alaska comes after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Justice Department's request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election sent to some 20,000 people the administration contends may not be U.S. citizens. California officials argued the list is highly unreliable and most likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
Justice Department attorneys in the Alaska case said there is a "substantial risk" that Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy "will mislead voters and ultimately result in an electoral process that lacks integrity."
"To guard against this danger, the United States seeks an order directing Defendants to preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary," the filing states. It requests a decision by Monday.
Attorneys for the state in response questioned how segregation was possible, writing that voters' ballots are comingled in the ballot box on Election Day and that election workers couldn't segregate ballots ranking Dan J. Sullivan without violating ballot secrecy protections. Ballots segregated or not wouldn't reveal any voter's reason for voting for Dan J. Sullivan, they said.
They have asked a judge to dismiss the case and said Alaska elections officials already took steps to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. The senator is listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent, while the challenger is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. That's also how they appeared on the August open primary ballot.
Attorneys for the state also have argued that Alaska's ranked voting system further addresses concerns about potential confusion by allowing voters to rank both Sullivans.
Timing of Justice Department announcements unusual
Heyman on Friday would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into or the targets of the probe, but asked members of the public to come forward with tips that could help investigators.
It's highly unusual for Justice Department officials to publicly discuss a criminal investigation or even confirm its existence. The timing of the press conference is particularly notable given the Justice Department has had a longstanding practice of avoiding taking public steps in the weeks leading up to an election that could be perceived as attempting to influence a political outcome.
At a campaign event in Juneau late Thursday, Peltola began her speech by saying she wanted to "clear the air."
"I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about," Peltola said. "I am not interested in tricking voters."
Federal prosecutors this week issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas and requests to preserve records, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy said, following The New York Times' reporting, that he'd ordered an investigation into whether any violations took place.
Meanwhile, the Alaska Democratic Party has sued state elections officials, alleging absentee in-person voting sites did not open as advertised in some rural communities. The director of the Division of Elections in a letter dated Monday said the agency signs agreements with local or tribal offices to operate the sites and that most of the 18 highlighted had opened. A message seeking comment from the state Department of Law was not immediately returned.
___
Durkin Richer reported from Washington. Bohrer reported from Juneau, Alaska.

title: Letter to the Editor: Support for Trevor Doiron
Midterm candidates say they are winning voters across party lines
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Some midterm election candidates have recently been promoting their ability to win over voters from across party lines but experts say it may not be enough to change outcomes in November.
In recent weeks, Democratic candidates in several states have promoted endorsements from Republican officials and voters.
In Alaska, Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski endorsed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins on Tuesday.
In Kansas, two former Republican governors, Bill Graves and Mike Hayden, announced in September and October that they are backing Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Adam Hamilton.
In Texas, the campaign for Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico said that over two dozen former GOP officials have endorsed Talarico.
Kel Seliger, a former GOP state senator, joined the list of officials who endorsed Talarico this week, instead of the Republican candidate in the race, Attorney General Ken Paxton.
“I’ve served with both people,” he said. “James Talarico is not some wild-eyed socialist and and he may believe in a lot of things that Democratic Party believes in that I don’t. But I think he’s going to be honest. And I think he’s going to be frank and direct. I think that the things that he does are going to be what is best for Texas. Not what’s best for Elon Musk.”
Republicans expect crossover support
Republican Party officials say they also expect cross-party voting for their candidates.
“I do think you’re seeing that this cycle, especially in races like in Michigan with Mike Rogers against Abdul El-Sayed, and in Texas with Ken Paxton against James Talarico,” said Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee.
Baldassarre also cited the campaign coalition, “Democrats for Mike Rogers.”
Political scientist: Effect tends to be small
While candidates have continued to promote the bipartisan support in the final days of the election season, Texas Politics Project Research Director Joshua Blank said cross-party voting tends not to make a large difference in elections.
“We’re not talking about a large group of Republicans crossing party lines to vote for Democrats, or a large group of Democrats possibly crossing party lines to vote for Republicans,” he said. “We’re ultimately talking about what are kind of idiosyncratic behaviors they’re going to take place among a small, small share of the electorate,” Blank said. “Now, if the elections close, this could really matter.”
Recent polling has found that some of the midterm races have become increasingly close and, in some cases, statistically tied.

title: Presque Isle police urge Halloween safety for drivers, trick-or-treaters
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Trick-or-treaters will go door to door this weekend, and the Presque Isle Police Department is reminding residents to stay safe and save the scares for Halloween costumes and decorations.
Tips for drivers and trick-or-treaters
Police said drivers should slow down and watch for children and families on foot. They also recommended that trick-or-treaters carry flashlights or glow sticks to help drivers see them.
“It’s very important to remain vigilant of all of the pedestrian traffic and even the ones in other vehicles,” Officer Darcie Fonzie said. “There’s children of all ages that will be out. Lots of little kids, just lots of foot traffic.”
Officer Sean Farrell said flashlights, glow sticks, and similar gear are helpful. “We get out of our cars, we put high-visibility gear on for a long period of time,” Farrell said.
Extra patrols planned
Police also said there will be extra patrols on foot and in cruisers to encourage safety this Halloween.
