title: Man pleads guilty to federal hate crimes in deadly firebomb attack on demonstrators
text:
DENVER (AP) — An Egyptian man faces an additional life sentence after pleading guilty Thursday to federal hate crime and other charges for a deadly firebombing attack on demonstrators in Boulder, Colorado, last year.
Mohamed Soliman is already serving life in prison plus hundreds of years of additional time after pleading guilty to state charges last spring. Federal prosecutors, who previously said they would not seek the death penalty against Soliman, said at his change-of-plea hearing they would seek a life term plus 50 years in prison for the dozen counts.
Soliman spoke through an interpreter at the hearing and said little besides “yes” and “no” responses to the judge’s questioning, such as whether he understood the consequences of pleading guilty. That was in contrast to his change-of-plea hearing and sentencing in state court in May, when Soliman apologized to the victims and expressed regret for the attack but also defended his basic view motivating it.
Prosecutors accused Soliman of attacking the demonstrators because they were Jewish
Wearing a brown shirt and khaki-colored pants, Soliman was led out of court in handcuffs and shackles without looking at the victims in the courtroom.
Yelling “Free Palestine,” Soliman lit and threw two Molotov cocktails at the demonstrators who were marching in support of hostages taken in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel.
Federal prosecutors accused Soliman of attacking in June 2025 because the demonstrators were Jewish. The flames badly burned Karen Diamond, 82, and injured a dozen others.
Diamond died three weeks later. Her family says she suffered “indescribable pain.”
In all, Soliman pleaded guilty to nine federal counts of hate crimes, including one resulting in Diamond’s death and eight for attempting to kill other demonstrators. Three additional counts were federal explosives charges.
US attorney says plea agreement was ‘victim-driven’
The plea agreement, including Soliman’s proposed sentence, was “victim-driven” and gave them all they sought, Colorado U.S. Attorney Peter McNeilly said in a news conference after the hearing.
Not pursuing the death penalty allows victims to get closure more quickly, Ed Victor, a Boulder demonstrator who was unhurt but close enough to feel heat from the flames.
“He’s not getting out. It moves him, I believe, off of the public stage much quicker,” Victor said.
A group of victims sat stoically in the courtroom, some taking notes as the judge asked Soliman if he understood the proceedings. Several victims intended to make statements at Soliman’s sentencing but declined to do so in court Thursday, Assistant U.S. Attorney Melissa Hindman told the court.
Soliman is to be sentenced in January
Colorado U.S. District Judge John Kane said he would review sentencing guidelines before deciding whether to accept or reject prosecutors’ sentencing recommendation. He noted the guidelines are not binding.
“Sometimes I follow that advice and sometimes I don’t,” Kane said.
Soliman’s federal sentencing was set for Jan. 7.
Boulder residents, particularly the Jewish community, have described being unnerved by the attack in their city northwest of Denver that’s home to the University of Colorado.
The group “Run for Their Lives” had been demonstrating weekly downtown. Soliman got near the demonstration on the Pearl Street pedestrian mall of shops and restaurants by posing as a gardener.
Federal authorities alleged Soliman planned the attack for a year. After his arrest, Soliman told police he sought “to kill all Zionist people,” a reference to the movement to establish and protect a Jewish state in Israel, according to an FBI affidavit.
Federal officials said he was in the U.S. illegally. He entered in 2022 on a tourist visa that expired the following year, then filed for asylum.
He was granted work authorization, but it too expired, federal officials said.
Soliman worked a series of low-paying jobs and was living with his wife and their five children in a Colorado Springs apartment at the time of the attack.
The couple divorced in April. Soliman recently dropped his opposition to removing his family from the U.S.
Prosecutors say Soliman planned even more harm
Prosecutors in Soliman’s state case argued he planned for even more harm. He tried twice to buy a gun and was denied, they said.
He threw two Molotov cocktails — bottles filled with flammable liquid that are lit, thrown and burst into flames when they shatter — but brought 18 to the demonstration in a box.
Of the 29 attack victims identified by state prosecutors, 13 were physically injured. Prosecutors considered the rest victims because they could have been hurt.
An injured dog led to a state animal cruelty charge.
While in court to plead guilty to the state charges in May, Soliman said he has known and respected Jewish people but questioned the deaths of innocent people in Israeli attacks on Gaza.
“Yes, I am against Israel and I can’t deny that. And that is my right,” Soliman said.

title: 3 dead in Oregon helicopter collision, including flight instructor and student pilot
text:
MCMINNVILLE, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) — Three people are dead after two helicopters crashed into each other Thursday afternoon near an Oregon airport, officials said.
Crash location and road closure
The Yamhill County Sheriff’s Office said the crash was reported around 2:15 p.m. near Lafayette Highway and Southeast Stringtown Road.
The crash scene is near McMinnville Municipal Airport, southeast of McMinnville.
Aircraft involved
The two helicopters were identified as an Airbus Helicopters AS350B2 and a Robinson R22, according to the NTSB.
Jerry Trimble Helicopters, a flight training company, posted on social media that one of its aircraft was involved in the crash.
Victims identified
Yamhill County Sheriff Sam Elliott said at a news conference Thursday night that a flight instructor from Texas and a student pilot from the U.K. were inside the Robinson helicopter. He identified the instructor as 22-year-old Maddie Aasbo.
The student pilot’s name has not been released because officials are still working to notify the family.
The third victim, 38-year-old Tyler Sturdevant of Newberg, was in the Airbus at the time of the crash, according to the sheriff.
Witness account
A witness said he was standing on the roof of a nearby barn when he saw the two helicopters crash into each other and then hit the ground just outside the perimeter of the airport. He said he immediately called 911.
The crash is under investigation.

title: Dating again? What older adults should know about sexual health and protection
text:
(Aging Untold) — Dating, intimacy and connection can be an important part of emotional and physical well-being for older adults. That includes people who are divorced, widowed, remarried or dating again for the first time in decades.
The Aging Untold experts are addressing the topics of sexual health, how it has changed over the years and how to stay protected.
You can’t tell by looking
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said appearances do not show whether someone has a sexually transmitted disease.
“You can’t tell by looking at someone if they have a sexually transmitted disease,” Rogers said. “You say, ‘Oh, they look healthy.’ You can’t tell by that.”
She said age does not change that risk.
“Getting older does not make you immune to getting a sexually transmitted disease,” Rogers said. “Just because you retired, your sexual health didn’t.”
Rogers said older adults have to take precautions to protect themselves against several diseases.
Condoms are about more than preventing pregnancy.
Over the decades, prevention options have changed, including for HIV.
And human papillomavirus, or HPV, is the most common sexually transmitted disease, Rogers said. The virus can cause cancer later in life, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Menopause is not protection
Having gone through menopause does not mean you do not need protection, the Aging Untold experts said.
“A lot of people think, ‘Well, I’ve been through menopause, I can’t get pregnant. I don’t need to protect myself,’” gerontologist Sam Cradduck said. “Menopause doesn’t protect you from gonorrhea or syphilis or HIV or HPV.”
Cradduck also said syphilis contracted at a younger age can show up later in life, and it shows up in communities where older adults live.
“That lives forever in you,” Cradduck said. “We’ve seen neurosyphilis in communities.”
Start the conversation
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said prevention starts with getting tested and having a conversation with your partner.
It can be awkward to ask a new partner whether they have been tested, especially for people who were married for many years before dating again, but the conversation still matters, she said.
One approach is to start by saying that an active sex life is important to you, then ask how the other person feels about getting tested and what the two of you will do to prevent infection, O’Rourke said.
Talk to your doctor as well, get tested and know what your risk factors are because you might have some and not know it, Rogers added. And protect yourself.
“That test might have been one month ago and things have changed,” Rogers said.
One of the risk factors that Rogers noted is a weakened immune system.
“If your immune system is not strong, you can’t fight off what you get exposed to,” Rogers said.
Protection details that matter
Cradduck added that people should check to see if the products they plan to use can be used together.
“Wearing a condom is important, but a lot of condoms and a lot of lubricants don’t go well together, and so you will impair the integrity of the condom with certain lubricants,” she said.
She also said people with a latex allergy should not use a latex condom.
Rogers said that it is easy for someone who has one disease to get another.
“When we treat people for chlamydia or gonorrhea, we treat for the other one as well,” Rogers said.
She added that PrEP, pre-exposure prophylaxis, a medication taken to prevent HIV infection, does not provide protection against other sexually transmitted diseases.
Couples who are dating after being widowed, each with one sexual partner, should still use protection, Rogers said.
“They only had one sexual partner that they know about,” Rogers said. “I used to get this all the time. ... You only know what the person told you. You don’t really know, so still protect yourself.”
Rogers said people should talk to their health care provider, talk to their partner and know whether they have risk factors that put them at risk for other things.
Name the diseases
To address the topic of sexually transmitted diseases, O’Rourke said she thinks it helps to name specific diseases instead of using the term “STDs.”
“STD seems like a distancer, like you don’t really hear syphilis. When I hear syphilis, my ears perk up. I think it’s important to really say what those diseases are, and then what do we get if we have it and it progresses and you’re older? I want to say the word cancer,” O’Rourke said.
Key takeaways
Be mindful of diseases, including gonorrhea and syphilis
Close the education gap: The three Ps are partners, practices and protection
Use today’s prevention tools, such as advanced screenings, immune supports and daily PrEP

title: To preserve the economies, culture and traditions of Maine, it’s time for Troy
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ken Elowe of Bristol is the retired director of the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife’s Bureau of Fish and Wildlife Resource Management.
As a registered independent with a long history in Maine government, I had many chances to work with Maine’s delegation, including Sen. Susan Collins. I voted for her over several election cycles. But things have changed, and the challenges faced by people and businesses in Maine have changed.
Sen. Collins has changed also.
Maine’s economy, culture, traditions and recreation have their foundation in natural resources. From commercial fishing, farming, timber management, sawmills, paper mills, recreational fishing, hunting and guiding and historic sporting lodges, our coastal, inland and rural businesses statewide are rooted in the amazing natural resources that we have and share.
These natural resource businesses are solid ways to make a living, but at times they operate on narrow economic margins. Changes to markets or operating costs can quickly shrink those margins and cause different business decisions. We saw this when changes happened to Maine’s paper industries, with mills separating from their traditional timberlands. We are on the threshold of major changes again for our foundational industries.
The high cost of diesel fuel is a major challenge for those heating their homes with oil. It is likewise a major economic challenge for the timber industries, which rely on diesel fuel for logging operations, trucking and sawmills.
Likewise, farm and commercial fishing vessels also depend on diesel fuel. High fuel costs are reducing operating margins. With tariffs affecting equipment, parts and product markets, operating margins are reduced even more.
These industries provide jobs all across the rural landscapes of the state. Hard economic decisions made necessary by high fuel costs and tariffs will cause loss of jobs in areas that have few alternatives. But the present challenges of high diesel fuel costs and tariffs are not due to global shifts in manufacturing or competitive economics. They are caused by national policies that created antagonistic tariff and trade relations with longtime allies and a war with Iran that created the present high oil prices and does not seem to have an easy or smooth way out.
Our forests are the foundation of our wood economies and also our recreational economies, culture and traditions. Across the country, people who hunt, fish, camp and recreate on private lands commonly do so while paying large lease sums for the privilege. Maine, and much of the New England, has a culture and tradition of respectful use of private lands
These privileges are not guaranteed, and a large-scale change to landowners that do not have a history of Maine’s traditions may not only shift available jobs in logging and sawmills, but also access to forest lands that support jobs and traditions in the hunting, fishing and recreational sectors.
Sen. Collins may be successful in bringing some project dollars to Maine. But we are breaking new ground with the current administration. Collins has enabled and is complicit in the one-sided decisions affecting our foundational economies and traditions. Her position as chair of the Appropriations Committee should afford her the ability to leverage other Republicans to stand up against unilateral decisions being made by this administration. She is, as a senior senator and chair of a powerful committee, more than only one vote.
If she truly is as effective as she claims, she should be able to leverage pressure to rein in this administration. She has chosen not to, and continually falls back on the excuse of being only one vote, meaning that she will never help take back the role of Congress as a co-equal branch of government.
Our citizens, economy, jobs and the future of our culture and traditions are being stressed. We need someone who will help shift the balance and give Congress back to us as a functional and equal branch of government. It is time to elect Troy Jackson, for the sake of Maine and the nation.

title: Netanyahu’s party claims election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority
text:
Netanyahu’s party claims election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party on Thursday amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance, as final results showed his bloc had lost its majority in parliament.
The opposition accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population after a historic showing by Arab-led parties in an attempt to delegitimize the election. If the rest of the opposition teams up with Arab parties, a rare and politically risky move, they could potentially form a majority government in parliament, the Knesset.
Results released by election officials early Friday showed Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member assembly, well below the 68 seats it had controlled at its peak in the previous parliament. His main opposition won 48 seats and Arab-led parties secured the other 19.
The count is complete, but the results still need to be certified and submitted to the country's president next Wednesday.
Commission to look into possible foreign interference
Netanyahu's party, Likud, has been spreading claims of malfeasance by Arab-led parties since exit polls indicated the prime minister had suffered a setback in Tuesday's vote. But it ramped up the rhetoric after the head of Israel's election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him.
In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims. But given their serious nature, he asked the agency to investigate.
Netanyahu's party responded with an inflammatory statement: "The elections in Israel have been stolen!” it said, claiming — without evidence — that the alleged election interference was “aimed at facilitating a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and toppling of the right wing government.”
Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu’s party were accusing Qatar — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group.
Qatar issued a quick denial, calling the allegations “ridiculous and dangerous.”
As it announced its results early Friday, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. In a video statement, the commission's acting director general, Dean Livne, did not elaborate, but warned that reports about the probe had been “entirely unfounded.”
“It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population,” he said.
Netanyahu's opponents accuse him of undermining vote
Netanyahu's main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, said Likud was trying to delegitimize the results. “They are doing this because they lost,” he said.
Eisenkot ridiculed the accusation of foreign interference with a tongue-in-cheek statement, saying: “I welcome the fact that Netanyahu is finally condemning Qatari involvement in the State of Israel.”
Netanyahu has long faced accusations that former top aides of his accepted money from Qatar.
By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be positioning himself to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties, who could potentially give Eisenkot the backing he needs to oust Netanyahu.
The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to “cast aspersions” on an entire section of the population that "exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner.”
The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament. It said that even though an investigation was taking place, “allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless.”
The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week.
Netanyahu campaigned on anti-Arab sentiment
Even ahead of the vote, Netanyahu and Likud painted the Arab-led parties as a danger to Israel, which critics called an attempt to further marginalize Arab citizens. Arab citizens of Palestinian descent make up 20% of the population but are often viewed with suspicion because of their sympathies with other Palestinians.
Those campaign attacks, along with anger over the divisive Netanyahu and his far-right government, brought outraged Arabs to the polls like never before.
On Thursday, Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, accused Netanyahu of “attempting to undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimization campaign directed against the will of the public — and against the Arab public in particular.”
“Netanyahu is working to steal the election,” the Arab-led Joint List party asserted Thursday.
The head of the Arab-led Ra’am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed the investigation into election interference and said his party had nothing to do with the case, while accusing Netanyahu of a campaign of incitement.
President Isaac Herzog called it a “sensitive moment” and called for a full investigation. He warned that “we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy.”
Difficult decisions are ahead as parties seek coalitions
The developments amplified the difficult decisions for the weeks ahead. Those include whether some Jewish and Arab parties would team up in a historic alliance, or whether some parties that campaigned on ousting Netanyahu would toss that aside and join forces with him.
While the race for a 61-seat majority needed to control the 120-seat Knesset plays out, Netanyahu remains in charge.
If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over yearslong corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into the security failures that led to the devastating Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
Eisenkot has left door open to cooperation with Arab-led parties
Even without a role in a coalition, Arab-led parties could assert their growing power by supporting other Netanyahu opponents in the next parliament. That could include electing a new speaker, giving them control of the agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.
Eisenkot has indicated he is open, with conditions, to joining forces with the Arab-led parties. Ahmad Tibi, second on the Arab-led Joint List, told Army Radio the opposition bloc reached out to him to discuss replacing the Knesset speaker, and he told them the party would support the bloc’s candidate.
There were small rallies overnight in Tel Aviv, and in far more conservative Jerusalem, in support of a coalition that includes Arab-led parties. Until 2021, no Arab party had joined a coalition government, and that was brief.
If a new government cannot be formed after multiple attempts, Israel would face a new election early next year. On Wednesday, Herzog signaled he wanted to avoid that step – something Eisenkot has said as well.
New elections bring new questions, including whether Arab citizens would again go to the polls in large numbers and whether the tens of thousands of Israelis who flew home to vote would do it again. Many had said they took that step to save the country from Netanyahu.

title: Skowhegan football shuts out Brunswick for B North quarterfinal win
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SKOWHEGAN — The Skowhegan football team’s dominant defense and another big game from quarterback Austin Lancaster helped the River Hawks earn a long-awaited victory.
Skowhegan rolled to a 35-0 win over Brunswick in a Class B North quarterfinal Friday at Reginald Clark Memorial Field. It was the River Hawks’ first playoff victory since they won the 2022 Class B state title.
“It’s kind of like getting the monkey off our back here,” said Skowhegan coach Brad Cyr. “My message all week was that we want winning to be normal, and we can’t do that unless we get some of these wins in the playoffs. It’s a huge win for the boys and a huge win for the program.”
Third-seeded Skowhegan (6-3) advances to face No. 2 Cony (7-1) at 7 p.m. next Friday in Augusta. Cony, which beat the River Hawks 42-35 in Week 2, had a bye to the semifinals.
HOW THEY DID IT
• Skowhegan junior Austin Lancaster again ran wild, going for 201 yards in the first half. He converted in some tight spots early, rushing 47 yards for a touchdown on third-and-24 to put Skowhegan up 7-0, and throwing a 28-yard scoring pass to Christian Ouellette on fourth-and-6 to make it 14-0.
• Controlling the line of scrimmage, Skowhegan held sixth-seeded Brunswick (2-7) to just 102 yards. The River Hawks also forced three turnovers recovered — two fumbles and an interception by Matthew Keister.
“I had great blocking up front, and it was great all around,” said Lancaster, who has rushed for 892 yards this season. “(Our defense) is a great group of guys up front. They can play with anyone; size, strength, it doesn’t matter — they’ll get it done.”
WHAT IT MEANS
• After some rebuilding years following its state title run four years ago, a Skowhegan group that had never won a playoff game now has done so. The River Hawks’ sixth win of 2026 is one shy of their combined total from 2023-25.
• Skowhegan gets a shot at revenge against Cony. The River Hawks had a remarkable battle with the Rams early in the season, coming back from a 20-point deficit to take the lead late in the game before the Rams ultimately pulled out the victory.
“(It’s going to take) some great defense all around — great offense and great defense,” said Lancaster, who passed for 194 yards and rushed for 113 in that Week 2 matchup. “Just don’t let them score, I guess.”
UNSUNG HERO
Skowhegan’s defense stuffed Brunswick in the run game and put pressure on sophomore quarterback Max Caouette. Asher Ouellette helped lead that effort, sacking Caouette early in the third quarter and working his way into the backfield on seemingly every play.
“He’s not a huge defensive end type, but he gets after it,” Cyr said. “He wants to be physical, and he quite frankly doesn’t want to play anything on offense — he just wants to go at it on defense. This was was the first night since the first game he hasn’t had a cast on, so having two hands helped him out, too.”
NOTABLE QUOTABLE

title: InvestigateTV+: Prison program helping veterans
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ takes you inside a peer-led prison program helping incarcerated veterans rebuild purpose through discipline and mentorship and talk to the supporters who say it’s breaking the cycle.
Plus, how art is helping dementia patients reconnect and communicate.
Then, an unlikely dog-and-cat friendship brings comfort to one family.
Helping veterans rebuild
American Legion Veterans Memorial Post 432 at Elayn Hunt Correctional Center was the first prison-based American Legion post in Louisiana, helping incarcerated veterans heal and rebuild their lives.
The program is recognized for a zero percent recidivism rate. No one from the post comes back to prison.
The benefits of art therapy
Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected.
Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases.
Cancer conversations
Do you only go to the doctor when you have an ache or feel sick? For many women that answer can be “yes.”
Three-legged besties
A 1-year-old dog named Blueberry and a 10-month-old cat named Meadow were adopted together after they met at the veterinary hospital run by Last Chance Animal Rescue in Waldorf, Maryland.
Rachel Clarke, who adopted both animals, said Blueberry “loves to play, and she loves to snuggle.” She said Meadow is “a little more independent, but Blueberry goes where Meadow goes.”

title: Benefit supper scheduled for family of Hancock County father who died of cancer
text:
MARIAVILLE, Maine (WABI) - Communities in Hancock County are gathering this weekend to support the family of a local father who recently died following a battle with cancer.
Danny Dunn passed away after fighting a rare form of lymphoma for more than a decade. He is survived by his wife, Hannah, and their two young children.
Neighbors are hosting a benefit supper on Sunday, Nov. 1, at 5:30 p.m. at the Mariaville Grange Hall. All proceeds from the event will go directly toward supporting Dunn’s family. Organizers said attendees can arrive Sunday evening to share stories and offer their support.
An online fundraiser launched on GiveSendGo has already raised more than $162,000 to assist the family with expenses.
Dunn’s brother, Dustin Dunn, expressed gratitude for the outpouring of support from the surrounding community.
“First of all, I’d like to thank everyone,” Dustin Dunn said. “It’s been a huge weight off our shoulders, knowing that his wife and kids have all this love and support and help... just taking the stress off of his wife and kids basically, at least for a while.”
More information and access to the online campaign can be found on the GiveSendGo fundraiser page.

title: MaineHealth Brings in Third Party to Reassess Labor and Delivery Closure
text:
MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital will host a public forum via Zoom on Wednesday, Nov. 4 to introduce independent experts reviewing the data and process behind the decision to close the labor and delivery unit at the hospital.
In a Monday, Oct. 26 press release, MaineHealth Vice President of Communications and Public Affairs Kathleen Taggersell said the review team will assess whether alternatives considered by the hospital’s management were “reasonable, feasible, and sustainable.”
On Aug. 6, MaineHealth voted to close the labor and delivery unit at Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta on Friday, Dec. 18. The decision came after two other votes from the MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital Local Board and the Coastal Region Board.
In the announcement of the closure, MaineHealth said the decision the system will not close any additional labor and delivery programs anywhere in the health system during the next two years.
Under the new regional model, the Damariscotta and Brunswick-based hospitals would operate as “one coordinated regional OB-GYN and certified nurse midwife team,” hospital officials said in the announcement. Patients will be transitioned to MaineHealth Mid Coast Hospital in Brunswick.
Lincoln Hospital President Cindy Wade said in a Tuesday, Oct. 27 interview that the creation of the review team and forum is for transparency, as well as more input on the assessment and to see if there are any alternatives that can be approached. The research will consider if the decision to close the labor and delivery unit is reasonable and appropriate, she said.
“It’s really transparency, but also, because they have in-depth experience in rural maternity care, workforce sustainability, community engagement, and other things,” Wade said.
According to the press release, the five-member review team brings in knowledge from areas such as maternal-fetal medicine, family medicine, nurse midwifery, public health, and healthcare operations.
Wade said the idea for the review came after the Legislature’s Health Coverage, Insurance, and Financial Services Committee held a hearing on Aug. 27, at which committee members suggested a third-party review of the assessment that led to the decision to close the unit.
She said after conversation at the senior team level of MaineHealth, the organization decided to move forward with creating a review team to see if all possibilities were looked at and considered.
At the Nov. 4 forum, community members will be able to meet who is on the team and can send in questions beforehand to a designated email.
Taggersell said reviewers are free to reach conclusions that differ from those of MaineHealth or other stakeholders. If the review team comes up with opposing information assessment leading to the decision to close, Wade said it would remain in the hands of MaineHealth’s three boards – local, regional, and system – if there will be reconsideration.
“I’m appreciative of the fact that we’ve been able to have independent experts come in and take a look at this,” Wade said. “I think that is certainly, you know, something we welcome. So, we look forward to hearing what their feedback is.”
The review team is expected to have a full report by Friday, Dec. 11 and Wade said it will then be up to the MaineHealth system to make a consideration based on the results.
Conversation surrounding the closure started before the decision was made. For months, community members, including the grassroots Miles Delivers Action Coalition, pushed back against the closure, bringing in attention for local and state politicians. The coalition has since transitioned its work to focusing on reversing the decision and finding alternatives to the closure.
In a Sunday, Oct. 25 email from the coalition, members urging the community to submit public comment by Friday, Oct. 30 to support the state’s proposed maternity care closure rules and asking the Maine Department of Health and Human Services to “strengthen them further.”
The email references that Maine recently enacted a law that requires hospitals 120 days notice before closing labor and delivery services, pushing for the citizen-led petition to use the legislation in favor of reversing the decision.
On April 3, Gov. Janet Mills signed L.D. 2189, “An Act to require Prior Notification of Closures of Labor and Delivery Units and Changes in Maternity or Newborn Care Services by Hospitals as Recommended by the Commission to Evaluation the Scope of Regulatory Review and Oversight over Health Care Transactions That Impact the Delivery of Health Care Services in the State.”
“But advance alone isn’t enough,” the email said. “Patients need clear communication, continuity of care, and assurance that hospitals are prepared for obstetric.”
The independent review public forum is from 6-7 p.m. on Nov. 4. Questions for the review team can be sent in advanced to [email protected].

title: Man pleads guilty to federal hate crimes in deadly firebomb attack on demonstrators
text:
DENVER (AP) — An Egyptian man faces an additional life sentence after pleading guilty Thursday to federal hate crime and other charges for a deadly firebombing attack on demonstrators in Boulder, Colorado, last year.
Mohamed Soliman is already serving life in prison plus hundreds of years of additional time after pleading guilty to state charges last spring. Federal prosecutors, who previously said they would not seek the death penalty against Soliman, said at his change-of-plea hearing they would seek a life term plus 50 years in prison for the dozen counts.
Soliman spoke through an interpreter at the hearing and said little besides “yes” and “no” responses to the judge’s questioning, such as whether he understood the consequences of pleading guilty. That was in contrast to his change-of-plea hearing and sentencing in state court in May, when Soliman apologized to the victims and expressed regret for the attack but also defended his basic view motivating it.
Prosecutors accused Soliman of attacking the demonstrators because they were Jewish
Wearing a brown shirt and khaki-colored pants, Soliman was led out of court in handcuffs and shackles without looking at the victims in the courtroom.
Yelling “Free Palestine,” Soliman lit and threw two Molotov cocktails at the demonstrators who were marching in support of hostages taken in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel.
Federal prosecutors accused Soliman of attacking in June 2025 because the demonstrators were Jewish. The flames badly burned Karen Diamond, 82, and injured a dozen others.
Diamond died three weeks later. Her family says she suffered “indescribable pain.”
In all, Soliman pleaded guilty to nine federal counts of hate crimes, including one resulting in Diamond’s death and eight for attempting to kill other demonstrators. Three additional counts were federal explosives charges.
US attorney says plea agreement was ‘victim-driven’
The plea agreement, including Soliman’s proposed sentence, was “victim-driven” and gave them all they sought, Colorado U.S. Attorney Peter McNeilly said in a news conference after the hearing.
Not pursuing the death penalty allows victims to get closure more quickly, Ed Victor, a Boulder demonstrator who was unhurt but close enough to feel heat from the flames.
“He’s not getting out. It moves him, I believe, off of the public stage much quicker,” Victor said.
A group of victims sat stoically in the courtroom, some taking notes as the judge asked Soliman if he understood the proceedings. Several victims intended to make statements at Soliman’s sentencing but declined to do so in court Thursday, Assistant U.S. Attorney Melissa Hindman told the court.
Soliman is to be sentenced in January
Colorado U.S. District Judge John Kane said he would review sentencing guidelines before deciding whether to accept or reject prosecutors’ sentencing recommendation. He noted the guidelines are not binding.
“Sometimes I follow that advice and sometimes I don’t,” Kane said.
Soliman’s federal sentencing was set for Jan. 7.
Boulder residents, particularly the Jewish community, have described being unnerved by the attack in their city northwest of Denver that’s home to the University of Colorado.
The group “Run for Their Lives” had been demonstrating weekly downtown. Soliman got near the demonstration on the Pearl Street pedestrian mall of shops and restaurants by posing as a gardener.
Federal authorities alleged Soliman planned the attack for a year. After his arrest, Soliman told police he sought “to kill all Zionist people,” a reference to the movement to establish and protect a Jewish state in Israel, according to an FBI affidavit.
Federal officials said he was in the U.S. illegally. He entered in 2022 on a tourist visa that expired the following year, then filed for asylum.
He was granted work authorization, but it too expired, federal officials said.
Soliman worked a series of low-paying jobs and was living with his wife and their five children in a Colorado Springs apartment at the time of the attack.
The couple divorced in April. Soliman recently dropped his opposition to removing his family from the U.S.
Prosecutors say Soliman planned even more harm
Prosecutors in Soliman’s state case argued he planned for even more harm. He tried twice to buy a gun and was denied, they said.
He threw two Molotov cocktails — bottles filled with flammable liquid that are lit, thrown and burst into flames when they shatter — but brought 18 to the demonstration in a box.
Of the 29 attack victims identified by state prosecutors, 13 were physically injured. Prosecutors considered the rest victims because they could have been hurt.
An injured dog led to a state animal cruelty charge.
While in court to plead guilty to the state charges in May, Soliman said he has known and respected Jewish people but questioned the deaths of innocent people in Israeli attacks on Gaza.
“Yes, I am against Israel and I can’t deny that. And that is my right,” Soliman said.

title: Christa Pike says she feels constant pain in her first statement since failed Tennessee execution
text:
Christa Pike said she is in constant pain since surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee last month but thankful for the love and support she has received.
Pike issued her first public statement through her attorneys on Friday. She said she went into the execution chamber prepared to die in peace and woke up alone and confused in a hospital bed.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” Pike said.
Pike, 50, said she had not contemplated a life beyond her execution date.
“I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position. I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured,” Pike said.
Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 when she tortured and killed Slemmer with her boyfriend, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death.
She said she is thankful for the medical workers who saved her life and the people who showed her kindness.
“I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone,” she said.
Pike’s attorneys have urged Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to reduce Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment. Lee told reporters this week that, “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”
Lee called for an investigation into what happened during the failed execution and postponed the state’s other lethal injection scheduled this year.
Friday’s statement was dictated to her legal team from the infirmary at the prison where she is housed.
Pike was hospitalized in the immediate aftermath of the failed execution and then moved back to prison at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center.

title: Dyslexia expert offers steps to improve reading fluency
text:
Dyslexia expert explains how five-minute daily drills can improve reading fluency
The ability to read is one of the strongest predictors of success for students, but the latest national testing shows only 29% of California fourth graders are proficient at reading.
Bonnie Terry, M.Ed., BCET, founder of Scholar Within, said short, consistent reading drills can help struggling readers make significant progress.
During Dyslexia Awareness Month, Terry explained how her evidence-based program works. She first explained the signs of dyslexia, which impacts an estimated one in every five people. It is widely recognized as the most common learning disability.
Signs of dyslexia include:
- Struggling to sound out simple or unfamiliar words
- Difficulty remembering letter sounds
- Spelling the same word different ways
- Reading slowly or in a choppy manner
- Skipping/substituting words while reading
- Repeating words / entire sentences
Terry developed a program that involves just five minutes of daily practice using drills that are carefully designed to address 17 different processing challenges.
"A short amount of time of repeatedly doing something makes you proficient," she said. "Sometimes parents will say, well, can't we just do like three days' worth of practice in one day? And you're not going to get near the progress, as if you just spend five minutes three, four, five times a week."
Terry's book version of the "Five Minutes to Better Reading Skills" program includes one version for the child, and another with the same drills that the parent can use to count words and track progress. The drills use various spacing in the letters and lines to train the brain to process words smoothly and improve visual tracking.
Video below: Dyslexia Awareness Month
"The words are specifically separated out because that's working on a couple of areas of visual processing," Terry said.
Reading the words aloud helps with other areas of processing.
"Sometimes it's a tongue twister," Terry said, laughing.
Even adults with dyslexia have used her program to improve their reading skills.
There's evidence of the program's success. Terry's own data show first and third-grade students with reading difficulties nearly doubled their fluency rates after one to two years of use, while the rates more than doubled for fourth through sixth-grade students. An independent study in Trinity County replicated those results using Terry's program, and the University of Florida showed similar results with similar short, consistent fluency training.
Edie Lambert shared her personal experience with the program, saying it helped her daughter catch up to grade-level fluency numbers in seven weeks. She also used it as a volunteer in a local elementary school, where she worked with dozens of fourth through sixth-grade children and tracked their progress.
"It just feels pretty amazing when you see the strides that they can make," Lambert said.
The program costs $100 for both books, which Terry noted is more affordable than traditional tutoring, which can range from $60 to $150 per session.
"This is something that you can be doing for a whole year," she said.
Terry's son Nick, who co-owns Scholar Within, recently put the Five Minutes to Better Reading Skills program into an online format as well, with expanded help with note-taking and text reading.
For parents unsure whether their child is reading at grade level, Terry offers an assessment tool through her Scholar Within website. The online version has a $1 verification fee, or there's a printable version for free.

title: Maine set a deer harvest record last year. So where should you hunt this fall?
text:
Maine hunters registered a record 55,876 deer in 2025. With rifle season beginning Saturday, last year’s numbers offer clues about where hunters found success and what to consider when choosing where to hunt this fall.
Nathan Bieber, deer biologist for the Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, expects another good season but doesn’t anticipate a harvest on par with last year’s record.
Some conditions that may have contributed to the unusually high harvest could persist this fall, including a relatively mild winter and drought conditions affecting green forage and the availability of acorns and other mast. These conditions may influence deer movement, while favorable hunting weather may also contribute to hunter success.
Last year’s harvest was 32% higher than the 42,259 deer registered in 2024. Buck harvest increased 16%, while doe harvest rose 59%.
Wildlife Management District 17 had Maine’s highest deer harvest in 2025, with 8,025 deer registered, up from 5,618 in 2024. District 23 followed with 5,108 deer, compared with 3,881 in 2024. District 26 had 4,399 deer, up from 3,082, followed closely by District 16, with 4,395, up from 2,941.
By town, Buxton led the state with 474 deer registered, followed by Sidney with 433, Corinna with 417, St. Albans with 412 and Bucksport with 406.
But the places with the highest harvests aren’t necessarily the best choice for every hunter. Harvest totals reflect both deer abundance and hunting pressure. Southern Maine supports high deer densities, while some coastal islands have substantial deer populations but fewer residents and hunters. In northern Maine, deer are spread across large forested areas, offering a different type of hunting experience.
Rather than focus solely on harvest totals, hunters should consider what they want from the experience, whether that’s seeing more deer, tracking them through big woods or finding a place away from crowds.
Hunters hoping to avoid pressure may need to put in more scouting time. Bieber recommends looking for large public parcels or private land where hunters have permission, then getting away from convenient access points that tend to draw more traffic.
For hunters hoping to harvest a mature buck, Maine’s 2025 deer age report offers another factor to consider. In Region E, 10.8% of sampled adult bucks were at least 5 years old, compared with 6.9% in Region F and 4% in Region B. Yearlings made up 62.6% of sampled adult bucks in Region A and 45.7% in Region B, but just 24.5% in Region E.
Maine’s resident-only deer hunting day is Saturday, Oct. 31. The regular firearms season runs Nov. 2-28.

title: Trump cancels rallies in Kansas and Iowa, opting for telerallies
text:
Trump cancels rallies in Kansas and Iowa, opting for telerallies to reach more voters, RNC says
President Donald Trump on Thursday canceled weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas, opting instead to support Republican candidates with telerallies that his party said could reach more voters in nearly two dozen states in the final days of a midterm election that could cost the GOP control of Congress.
Video above: President Trump blasts reporter over question about canceled Kansas trip
The president traveled to South Carolina Thursday for the second time in a month, a sign of Republican anxiety about Darline Graham's ability to fend off a robust challenge from Democrat Annie Andrews for a critical U.S. Senate seat.
Voters in South Carolina have not sent a Democrat to the Senate in nearly three decades. But Andrews, a pediatrician who previously ran unsuccessfully for Congress, is urging voters seeking change to “try something new for once.”
That message could resonate in an election year defined by voter frustration with the economy, gas prices and the war in Iran, putting Trump's Republican Party on defense in territory where they have rarely had to compete in recent years.
Beyond South Carolina, Republicans are entering the final days of this year's midterm elections navigating tight contests in Texas, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska. Both parties are also closely following developments in the Mississippi Senate race.
The president projected confidence as he returned to the White House, saying, “We're going to have a strong Tuesday night.”
Trump was scheduled to hold a rally in Kansas on Saturday and in Iowa on Sunday. But the Republican National Committee announced Thursday evening that he would instead spend a “72-hour sprint” doing rallies by phone rather than in person, a move the RNC said would maximize Trump's ability to speak to voters nationwide. The RNC said telerallies are planned for nearly 20 states, and more may be announced.
It was an abrupt shift in Trump’s pledge to push through the final days of the campaign doing rally after rally to galvanize his supporters. As of Thursday, he had done 25 rallies during the month of October, falling short of a goal he had once placed north of 30.
Trump says he doesn't need to go to Kansas
There were signs the travel and long speeches have caught up with him. On Monday, in Corinth, Mississippi, Trump — whose voice has grown raspy — told the crowd, “God didn’t make your vocal cords to do a rally every day.”
But he bristled Thursday when a reporter asked whether he had canceled plans to travel to Kansas because of his health.
“You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect,” Trump snapped.
The president said he’s not traveling to Kansas, where GOP Sen. Roger Marshall faces Democrat Adam Hamilton, "because he’s doing very well,” an apparent reference to Marshall.
“I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas,” Trump said.
A campaign strategist with Republican Senate leadership said there was widespread curiosity about why the schedule was changing to telerallies. The strategist spoke on condition of anonymity to share the content of private conversations.
Trump, who revels in big crowds, has this month held rallies in smaller venues than many he once filled. The decision to switch to telerallies means he will be expected to speak for about 10 minutes instead of more than 90, as he does at in-person events.
Trump plans to travel to Daytona Beach, Florida, for a rally Friday. It’s not clear whether he will hold additional in-person events after that. The White House has not published his schedule for Monday, the final day of the campaign.
Video below: President Trump highlights economic growth as inflation accelerates
Democrats took notice.
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan who's in a tight race against Republican Mike Rogers, said Thursday night that the president's goal of trying to gin up GOP voters has backfired and he has “given up." “He’s an old man, he’s a loser,” El-Sayed continued. “He now understands that he has fully lost the midterms for his party."
Graham has struggled to connect with voters
In South Carolina, Graham has struggled to quickly build connections with voters. The sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, she was appointed in July by Republican Gov. Henry McMaster to fill the remaining months of her brother’s term after his sudden death. In August, she became the party’s nominee to succeed him for a full six-year term.
“He was a great politician,” Trump said of Lindsey Graham, before promoting Darline Graham as his elected successor. “She’s got the gene.”
Darline Graham commended the president for having “delivered what Washington promised for decades.” She warned that Andrews “would just throw it all away."
Andrews appeared in nearby Fort Mill on Wednesday, where she said that if voters elect her and become unhappy with her performance on Capitol Hill, “you can fire me in six years.”
Video below: Midterms 2026: the Balance of Power
South Carolina Rep. Ralph Norman, who lost to Graham in the GOP Senate primary runoff, has criticized Graham as unqualified. Norman, who has refused to campaign with Graham, said the race is closer than it would have been had he been nominated.
Lonnie Dean Johnson of Sumter, South Carolina, supported Norman in the primary and was voting Graham out of party loyalty, albeit unenthusiastically.
“She’s on a Republican ticket. I, by and large, support the Republican platform," he said. "So, I support her and wish her well.”
Democrats are bullish about Senate races across the US
Democrats, meanwhile, are optimistic about their chances of booting GOP incumbent senators, including in Ohio, with an American public frustrated by continued high costs.
“Families see more money going out the door and not enough money coming in,” said Sherrod Brown, the Democratic Senate nominee who's competing against Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted. At a rally in Toledo Thursday, Brown said Husted is “looking out for data centers and Wall Street."
Farther north, Alaska's Republican governor has ordered an investigation after The New York Times reported Wednesday that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting another candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
The Justice Department escalated the investigation Thursday, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
The Justice Department also issued subpoenas to California officials in the latest effort to scrutinize local election administration. A federal judge in California earlier Thursday appointed a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that the state has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls.
Trump called the development in Alaska a “conspiracy” and called for Peltola to be removed from the ballot. He has cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election.
Peltola’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a message Thursday seeking comment on the governor's order. But during a campaign stop in Soldotna, Peltola, a former congresswoman, suggested the Times’ report was a “distraction” from issues such as Sen. Sullivan’s support of the war in Iran.
The revelation in Alaska was a reminder of the volatility of the midterm campaigns' final days as both parties make decisions about how to spend time and money with control of Congress on the line.
Sloan reported from Washington. Associated Press writers Thomas Beaumont in Des Moines, Iowa, Jesse Bedayn in Austin, Texas, Hannah Fingerhut in Clive, Iowa, John Hanna in Topeka, Kansas, Mike Householder in Kalamazoo, Michigan, and Meg Kinnard, Collin Binkley and Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Maine Senate candidates make final pitches days away from the midterms
text:
Maine Senate candidates make final pitches days away from the midterms
Five days out until Election Day, all eyes are on Maine’s Senate race between Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson.
Both candidates are making the most of the little time they have left to campaign. Jackson spent the morning in Westbrook, and Collins made a federal stop at the Winthrop Police Department.
The senator's office says Collins secured more than $1.1 million for the town of Winthrop to support public safety improvements as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Her high spot in the Senate has been a large part of her most recent campaign.
"I'm still going to be effective because of my seniority and my position," Collins said. "If the voters of Maine send me back to Washington, I will be fifth in seniority in the United States Senate."
Since 2021, the Senator says she's secured about $1.5 billion since 2021.
Seniority in the Senate has been a major talking point for both candidates. Collins has said Jackson will have low seniority if he’s elected, but Jackson said the senator isn’t using her power enough to benefit Maine.
“It doesn’t seem like she's doing that great a job anyways,” Jackson said. “In the end, she's going to be in the minority. Democrats are going to take this back over with or without me.”
If Collins keeps her seat but the majority flips to blue, the senator would become vice chair of the appropriations committee.
Jackson seeks to unseat a senator who has held the position for nearly 30 years with just around three months to campaign. He was selected to be the new Democratic nominee in late July after the previous nominee, Graham Platner, dropped out due to a sexual assault allegation he denies.
Jackson picked up support Thursday from Gov. Janet Mills, who said she voted for him on Thursday. Mills went months without saying who she would vote for in this race and never gave a formal endorsement for Jackson. The governor suspended her campaign for Senate before the primary election.
Thursday marked the last day for early voting in person. Election Day is Nov. 3.

title: 'He has nothing to lose': Murder victim's sister fears for safety after killer escapes from prison
text:
'He has nothing to lose': Murder victim's sister fears for safety after killer escapes Tennessee prison
A manhunt continues for an escaped murderer in Tennessee.
Jacob Morley escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee, late Sunday.
Morley was serving a life sentence for killing his co-worker, Cody Birchfield.
Birchfield's sister, Carrie Norman, is now speaking out, saying she fears for her life and her family's lives.
"We were close. I was a big sister. Always big sister to my brother," Norman said.
It didn't matter when, where or what you needed, Norman said Birchfield was always there for his friends and family.
"If you ever needed anything, he was there," she said.
Birchfield was killed by his co-worker, Morley, in 2022. His body was found in a box under Morley's Carter County home after weeks of searching.
Morley was convicted and was serving a life sentence for the murder.
Norman and her family thought the ordeal was over, until Monday, when they found out through a friend about Morley's escape from the prison.
"You feel sick to your stomach," Norman said. "It opened up everything that you thought that you were able to grieve and process. It's-- it's all those feelings come rushing back."
Norman says she fears for her family's safety.
"Having to prepare yourself and your family and let them know, you know, we have to be alert," she said.
Norman said she has not received any threats or communication from Morley, but just as she fears for her family's safety, she's worried about everyone else.
"He is a dangerous man," Norman said. "Everyone needs to be aware. He has nothing to lose."
Authorities say a white 2008 Ford F-350 that Morley allegedly stole after escaping the facility was found abandoned Tuesday in Marion, Illinois.
Morley has been added to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation's Most Wanted list. A reward of up to $15,000 is being offered for information leading to his arrest.

title: New study reveals 43% drop in childhood peanut allergies over last decade
text:
(Aging Untold) — Recent research suggests that the long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach. New studies indicate that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy.
According to a study released in October 2025, peanut allergy rates in children under 3 have dropped by roughly 43% over the last decade.
Dr. David Hill, lead author of the study, believes the reversal in guidance is a major factor in this decline.
“It’s safe to say in all likelihood, there are tens of thousands of kids today that don’t have food allergy that may have if we hadn’t made these recommendations about early allergen introduction,” Dr. Hill said.
For many families, the change in medical guidance has been transformative.
Kristie Herring, whose son Parker suffered from a severe peanut allergy, said the diagnosis was a “total surprise” given their family history.
Parker has been undergoing oral immunotherapy, a treatment involving slowly increasing doses of peanut protein, which has allowed him to safely consume peanut butter again.
However, experts caution that oral immunotherapy is not without risks and that early introduction is not a guaranteed cure for everyone. Food allergy remains a complex condition with multiple causes.
The American Academy of Pediatrics now recommends early introduction of peanut products for all infants without a history of prior reaction, provided they are already eating other solid foods. Pediatricians advise starting small and feeding peanut foods regularly—at least twice a week—through the first year and beyond. Importantly, whole peanuts should never be given to infants due to the significant risk of choking.
For those whose children have already developed a peanut allergy, specialists recommend consulting an allergist about available treatment options and maintaining vigilance in managing the condition.

title: Bobby Charles hosts one-on-one discussions with Democrat and undecided voters
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bobby Charles hosts one-on-one discussions with Democrat and undecided voters
"You are only a good leader if your door is open, and people bring you their problems." | Charles answered questions from Democrat and undecided voters on race, reproductive rights, healthcare and education.
Bobby Charles hosts one-on-one discussions with Democrat and undecided voters
"You are only a good leader if your door is open, and people bring you their problems." | Charles answered questions from Democrat and undecided voters on race, reproductive rights, healthcare and education.
Republican candidate for governor Bobby Charles sat in the middle of the Auburn Mall on Thursday for an unfiltered conversation with voters. The purpose of the event was to hear from voters who disagree with his policies and beliefs. The crowd was partially made up of supporters, but there were questions from Democrat and undecided voters.
"Things like this, I give Bobby a lot of credit for, they really make you see the human," said Margaret Ranaldi, a Lewiston resident voting for Hannah Pingree.
Ranaldi came to ask Charles about his stance on abortion. She suffered two miscarriages and wanted to know what stance Charles would take on Maine's existing abortion laws if elected. Charles responded by saying he is against late-term abortion, but there should be exceptions for rape, incest, or the life of the mother. His response received a round of applause. Ranaldi said she was disappointed, as she wanted Charles to commit to not changing anything about Maine's existing laws.
Race was also a topic of discussion. A Lewiston resident of Jamaican descent asked Charles about some of his Facebook posts and if he would "have the backs" of people of color in Maine.
"For you to sit here and say that you will have my back and people of color's back, that means something," said the voter.
"There is no basis ever ever ever for racism in the state of Maine," Charles said.
Charles also spoke on the cost of healthcare and retaining healthcare workers in Maine. He proposed forgiving the loans of doctors and nurses if they plant roots in Maine. The Trump administration's Department of Education recently deemed nursing as not being a "professional" graduate degree.
"I don't really care what (President Donald) Trump says. I am involved right now in saving Mainers," Charles said.
He also added that he breaks with the president on certain issues related to the environment, like lowering mercury levels in Maine's lakes.
Energy costs for Maine families were also a hot topic for Charles supporters. Charles said he would build a natural gas pipeline from Pennsylvania and end subsidies for wind and solar power. He also talked again about phasing out Maine's income tax, overhauling Maine DHHS, and expanding addiction treatment services.

title: Letter: Troy Jackson won’t be nearly as effective as Susan Collins
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
James G. Blaine, Hannibal Hamlin, Margaret Chase Smith, Edmund Muskie, George Mitchell, Bill Cohen and Susan Collins. These Republicans and Democrats have all served Maine and the United States in the U.S. Senate with honor and distinction. If you can’t imagine ever seeing the name Troy Jackson on this distinguished list, you must vote to reelect Sen. Susan Collins this Nov. 3.
I think a vote for Mr. Jackson is a vote for Mr. Irrelevant. He will essentially be No. 100 in the line of seniority. I believe he will be relegated to whatever insignificant committee assignment he is given. He will immediately drop Maine to near the bottom of the list for consideration for any federal funding.
Compare that to Collins who is chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, fifth in the line of seniority, and ranked multiple times as the most non-partisan member of the Senate. I believe those facts put Collins in the best position to deliver for Maine. Her long list of federal funding for important Maine projects proves that.
Please vote, but don’t let disdain for President Donald Trump overshadow your good sense for what you know to be true. I believe a vote for Jackson is a vote against Maine’s best interests. You will be electing someone with no seniority, no proven federal legislative successes, and, I believe, little possibility of effectively advocating for legislation benefiting Maine.
And Trump will continue to be president for the next two years. What will you have accomplished by voting for Troy Jackson? Respectfully, reelect Susan Collins.
Richard Sprague
Trenton

title: Bobby Charles says he quit his federal job. Condoleezza Rice told a different story.
text:
Not long after she’d taken over for Secretary of State Colin Powell in 2005, Condoleezza Rice’s chief of staff walked into her office late one evening with a message about one of her bureau leaders.
Bobby Charles, the assistant secretary for international narcotics and law enforcement, had gone behind her back to complain to allies on Capitol Hill after resisting overhauls she wanted to implement, Rice wrote in her 2011 memoir.
“I decided that the bureau needed new leadership,” she wrote. “The message had to be clear that I encouraged open disagreement but that this kind of behavior was unacceptable.”
Now Maine’s Republican gubernatorial nominee, Charles has staked much of his bid on his State Department tenure. Rice’s account, an earlier book and a former colleague who delivered news of Charles’ ouster to staff offer a portrait of his exit that hasn’t been reported during the governor’s race. The candidate disputed both accounts.
Charles has often cited his State Department record as the brand of leadership he’d bring to the Blaine House. He faces frontrunner Democrat Hannah Pingree and independent state Sen. Rick Bennett in five days. The attorney and former naval intelligence officer became assistant secretary in October 2003, overseeing counter-narcotics efforts and police-training programs in Afghanistan and Iraq.
Rice’s account echoes one published nearly 20 years ago by former Washington Post reporter Glenn Kessler. In his 2007 book on Rice, Kessler wrote that she fired Charles, a former aide to House Speaker Dennis Hastert, after learning he “had tried to drum up support on the Hill for a position he was advocating on Afghanistan.”
Kessler also wrote that the firing came “within days” of Rice becoming secretary. But Charles stayed until March 15, 2005, seven weeks after Rice was sworn in, according to his State Department biography.
Charles disputed those accounts. In a statement, he said he was not fired “within days” of Rice taking office and that Powell had asked him in December 2004 to stay through the transition.
When differences with Rice over programs he’d built under Powell became clear, he resigned in mid-March 2005 after consulting Powell and then-Deputy Secretary Richard Armitage, he said. He denied going behind Rice’s back, saying lawmakers reached out with questions and the bureau “had an obligation to be transparent with them.”
“When you disagree with the direction of a new boss, you have two choices: change your views to keep your job, or leave,” he said. “I left. Integrity comes before position.”
Neither Rice nor her former chief of staff, Brian Gunderson, responded to requests for comment. Powell died in 2021, and Armitage died last year.
Rice’s memoir did not name Charles or specify their disagreements. But she wrote that his bureau was overseeing huge expenditures to train police in Afghanistan and Iraq.
“The recordkeeping, though, and thus the accountability for that work was less than adequate,” she wrote. “The serving assistant secretary was resistant to the changes that needed to be made.”
More than a dozen federal audits criticized the bureau during Charles’ roughly 18 months in charge, finding poor management, billions spent without accountability and failure to accomplish primary foreign policy goals, the BDN reported in May. Charles has said the BDN cherry-picked the audits. Supporters have credited him with bringing fiscal responsibility to the bureau.
“While his aggressive push for accountability may have ruffled the feathers of those comfortable with the old way of doing things, his results were undeniable,” William E. Todd, a career diplomat and former ambassador to Brunei and Cambodia who worked with Charles from 2003 to 2005, wrote in a public letter.
A retired longtime official in Charles’ bureau who told staff he had been asked to step down, granted anonymity because family members feared retaliation for weighing in on a political campaign, said “nobody was terribly surprised” at the news.
The official described Charles as charming and well liked by staff and credited him with standing up for the State Department as Gen. David Petraeus’ role in Iraq grew, but he was a disorganized manager and “kind of a loose cannon.”
Charles said the race is about Maine’s future, not a 2005 personnel decision.
“I’ve led a global bureau, managed large teams and budgets, served in the armed forces and made hard decisions under pressure,” he said. “Among the candidates running for governor, I am the only one who has done that.”

title: Suspect in killings of Oberlin professor, wife held on $3 million bond
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — An Oberlin College professor and his wife are dead, and the educator’s 31-year-old child is being held on a $3 million bond and facing murder charges in their deaths.
The bodies of Pipo Nguyen-Duy, 64, a studio art and photography professor and acclaimed fine art photographer, and his wife, Tran Thi Nam Phong, 56, were found shot in their home a few blocks off campus on Wednesday, according to police. The professor was on the first floor of the home, his wife on the second.
Asia Nguyen-Duy, previously known as Daniel Jones, of Ashland, Oregon, was arraigned Thursday on charges of murder, felonious assault and tampering with evidence, according to court filings. A motive has not yet been released.
The younger Nguyen-Duy, face tattooed and bloodied, was initially carried into the municipal courtroom before later being wheeled in a chair. The suspect said they are gender neutral and no longer go by the name Daniel Jones. Identification found in a car that police found set afire near the college’s conservatory of music, which led them to the scene of the crime, listed the name Daniel Jones.
Oberlin City Prosecutor Zachary Simonoff told the judge that the accused had offered a confession to the crimes and led them to the father and stepmother’s address.
Simonoff also told Oberlin Municipal Court Judge Farah Emeka that the defendant’s mother had been in touch with police to let them know that her child was “currently psychotic” and needed medication. A message was left with Asia’s attorney.
The case has been bound over to Lorain County Common Pleas Court, where it will next go before a grand jury. The suspect is being held in the Lorain County Jail.
The deaths have rocked the private liberal arts college, where students had just returned this week from fall break.
Studio art classes were paused or modified in the wake of the professor’s death. An exhibit of his internationally acclaimed photography was placed on display at the campus art museum to provide students, alumni and collaborators a place to gather and reflect. A memorial tribute for Nguyen-Duy, who arrived at Oberlin in 1998, also is being planned.
Digital forums for sharing condolences and memories also were set up by Oberlin and some regional institutions, including the Museum of Contemporary Art Cleveland.
Carmen Twillie Ambar, president of Oberlin College and Conservatory, called it “a deeply challenging moment for our community.”
“Tragedies such as this one intrude upon our lives in jarring ways,” she wrote in an open letter. “I am simply overwhelmed with sadness, and I am deeply concerned about the impact of the devastating loss of Pipo to our community.”
Pipo Nguyen-Duy was also mourned by the Guggenheim Foundation, where he was a 2011 photography fellow. The foundation said he immigrated to the U.S. from Vietnam in 1975 and took up photography in his late 20s. He had a bachelor’s degree in economics from Carleton College and both a master of arts and a master of fine arts degrees from the University of New Mexico at Albuquerque.
“In his wide-ranging body of work, Nguyen-duy considered immigration and emigration, intimacy, abandonment and decay, cultural assimilation, and the cost of war,” the foundation said on Instagram.

title: Trial date set for man charged with attacking White House correspondents’ dinner
text:
September 2027 trial date set for man charged with attacking White House correspondents’ dinner
A federal judge on Thursday set a September 2027 trial date for a man charged with attempting to kill President Donald Trump at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner earlier this year.
Video above: President Trump criticizes Maine Senate candidate during White House press dinner
Cole Tomas Allen's trial is scheduled to start with jury selection on Sept. 7 in Washington, D.C., and is expected to last approximately three to four weeks. Prosecutors had recommended starting the trial in May 2027, but U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden set the later date after one of Allen's attorneys asked for more time to prepare.
Allen, of Torrance, California, is accused of storming the WHCA dinner while armed with guns and knives and firing a shotgun at a Secret Service officer who tried to stop the April 25, 2026, attack at the Washington Hilton hotel.
The officer, who was struck once in a bullet-resistant vest, fired five shots but didn’t hit anybody, authorities said. Allen was injured but not from gunfire.
The attack led to an early end to one of the highest-profile annual events in the nation’s capital. President Donald Trump returned to speak at the rescheduled dinner three months later.
In writings that he sent to relatives before the attack, Allen railed against Trump administration policies and referred to himself as a “Friendly Federal Assassin,” authorities said.
Allen faces an attempted assassination charge that carries a maximum possible sentence of life in prison. He is also charged with assaulting a federal officer with a deadly weapon and two additional firearm counts.

title: 21-year-old woman arrested for social media post threatening to assassinate Trump
text:
VOLUSIA COUNTY, Fla. (Gray News) - A 21-year-old woman was arrested after allegedly posting a photo of herself with a caption that she was going to shoot President Trump.
“We are not going to tolerate threats to assassinate the president,” the Volusia County Sheriff Mike Chitwood wrote in a social media post on Oct. 30.
Allison Albro was charged with written threats to kill and unlawful use of a communications device after allegedly writing, “Going to the trump rally in my city so I can shoot him with my Glock! Wish me luck guys!!” the night before.
President Trump was scheduled to hold a campaign rally on Oct. 30.
According to Chitwood, the department’s Domestic Security Unit and U.S. Secret Service went to Albro’s home. She reportedly told officers she did not have access to weapons.
“I would strongly advise anyone else thinking of posting a “joke” along these lines to think twice,” Chitwood wrote.

title: Dom Burgess, Dani Pelletier Win Week Eight Athlete Honors

The votes are in, and two postseason performances have earned the Fall Week Eight Athlete of the Week honors.

Both came through with important tournament goals during a Week Eight ballot that featured 14 Aroostook County athletes from soccer and cross country.
