title: Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
text:
U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM said a North Korea hacking unit was likely behind the theft of more than $6 billion on the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance.
Binance said late on Thursday that approximately $6.3 billion was impacted, which its founder described as “like a hack.”
The company said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, and roughly $3 billion was frozen.
The cryptocurrency exchange added that it had temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed.
TRM, in a post on its website Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea’s elite hacking unit. “We make this judgment with high confidence,” the firm said.
“An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes,” TRM said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.
In February last year, another cryptocurrency exchange Bybit suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.
“Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack,” TRM said.
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was “likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor,” its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. DPRK stands for the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name.
Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is “working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice.”
Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.
In December 2022, South Korea’s spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea’s capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.
Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform, and stepped down as the company’s CEO. U.S. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.
Zhao posted Thursday on X that “User funds are safe!” but added that the theft “does look like a hack on Binance.” He added that while he doesn’t manage Binance anymore, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered.”
On Thursday, Binance said it would cover the losses from the apparent hack.
The event, meanwhile, also raises questions on why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.
“This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet,” he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users’ “private keys,” or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.
Binance said on X it had “found no evidence of any wallet private key leak” and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

title: Trump will rally in Kansas and Iowa after initially canceling weekend trips
text:
Trump will rally in Kansas and Iowa after initially canceling weekend trips before midterms
President Donald Trump has rescheduled campaign rallies in a pair of critical Midwestern states that he had previously canceled, according to a person familiar with the plans.
The person said Friday the Republican president will now visit Iowa and Kansas for back-to-back campaign rallies on Sunday. The person insisted on anonymity to discuss Trump’s schedule.
The Republican National Committee initially said in canceling the rallies that Trump would do telerallies instead to reach more voters. But the person familiar with the latest plans said the Iowa and Kansas rallies have been rearranged to accommodate the new telerallies added to Trump’s schedule.
The RNC announced Thursday evening that Trump would spend a “72-hour sprint” doing rallies by phone rather than in person, a move it said would maximize his ability to speak to voters nationwide. The RNC said telerallies were planned for nearly 20 states, and more may be announced.
The initial cancelation was an abrupt shift in Trump’s pledge to push through the final days of the campaign doing rally after rally to galvanize his supporters. As of Thursday, he had done 25 rallies during the month of October, falling short of a goal he had once placed north of 30.

title: Early voting turnout is high. Election fatigue is building
text:
Mainers are turning out in high numbers to cast their ballots early as a controversy-ridden campaign season nears the finish line in Maine.
Nearly 245,000 Mainers voted early this year, either by mail or in-person, as of Oct. 28, according to data from the Maine Secretary of State’s office. Thursday was the last day to request an absentee ballot or vote in the presence of a clerk.
Some town clerks reported that the number of voters casting their ballots early are nearing presidential election turnout numbers. In the November 2024 general election, 388,815 people in Maine cast their ballots early or by mail.
It’s not possible to know yet which candidates are garnering the most early votes. It is possible to know, however, which party’s early voters are turning out the most.
More than 118,000 Democrats and 54,000 Republicans have voted absentee so far. More than 66,000 unenrolled voters have also voted absentee, according to data from the Secretary of State’s office.
Even before early voting began for the day at 8:30 a.m. on Oct. 28, a line of people had formed on the second floor of city hall in Portland to vote. More than 16,000 Portland residents have requested mail-in ballots, state numbers show.
One city hall worker told a reporter on Wednesday, “It’s like Six Flags up there.”
Portland resident Lydia Savage said she waited 40 minutes in line at city hall to cast her ballot on Monday. Others waiting were generally in a good mood and passed updates down the line about how many people were ahead, she said.
Savage said she was delighted to vote early for the first time.
“The campaigns have been harsher than I’ve ever seen,” Savage said. “I just wanted to be done with it.”
Other towns in Maine have also seen high turnout for early voting.
Auburn City Clerk Emily Carrington said the city has seen higher absentee turnout this gubernatorial election cycle. Of the 4,833 ballots that were issued, 4,330 ballots have been returned so far. During the last gubernatorial election in 2022, Carrington said there were 3,634 absentee voters.
Still, the turnout does not surpass presidential election data: In 2024, 6,120 people voted absentee in Auburn.
Some smaller towns are seeing more early voting than in past midterm elections. Litchfield, which has approximately 2,500 active voters, had received about 675 absentee votes as of midday on Oct. 29. Deputy Registrar of Voters and Deputy Clerk Libby Rodrigue expected that total to reach about 700 by the end of the day, which would be comparable to the 2024 presidential election.
Casco has about 2,600 registered voters. As of early afternoon yesterday, 741 absentee ballots had been requested and 624 brought back. For the last presidential election, about 1,000 ballots were submitted early, according to the town clerk’s office.
Other towns are seeing manageable turnouts in early voting. Brunswick Town Hall, which normally closes on Fridays, kept its doors open on Oct. 23 to accommodate voters. Though not as busy as other cities such as Portland, three temporary assistant town clerks had received a steady trickle of in-person absentee voters.
Some Mainers are feeling fatigued from a rocky campaign year, which included explosive revelations about former Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate Graham Platner and a steady trade of political attack ads between Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson.
For some Mainers, voting in a challenging political climate does not feel worth it.
“All of it is such rubbish,” said a retired Navy man from Portland who asked not to be identified by name.
He said he feels disillusioned with the political system and therefore does not vote. He specifically named former Republican Gov. Paul LePage, who is running to represent the 2nd District in the U.S. House; Collins; and Jackson as candidates who have disappointed him.
“It isn’t about politics anymore, it’s about belittling the next person,” said another man, from South Portland, who declined to provide his name; he said he hadn’t voted since President Jimmy Carter was in office.
Falmouth resident Rachel Doe, who dropped her mail-in ballot at her town hall ahead of election day, said she’s voted early ever since she had kids. It’s easier to manage the timing of voting that way, she said, and dropping her ballot off in person means there’s no risk of delays in the mail.
But she’s ready for the season of fierce campaigns for Senate, Congress and local seats to be over. She said door-to-door canvassers and campaign calls are frequent, and there is a lot of pressure in the current political climate.
“It feels intense,” she said. “[I’m] getting a lot of phone calls.”
Portland resident Darrel Williams waited in line at city hall to vote but ultimately left when he realized how long it would take. He had a meeting that he couldn’t be late for and planned to return to vote later on Thursday.
Williams said he hadn’t seen such long lines before in previous election cycles. Several issues might be drawing people out, he said: the cost of living, immigration enforcement and general dissatisfaction. Williams, who is Black, said he is seeing society revert backward on issues such as racism, xenophobia and classism.
“The next generation should not have to battle those things,” Williams said.
Reporters Delger Erdenesanaa, Sean Scott and Rose Lundy contributed reporting.

title: Maine state senator’s adopted son arrested by immigration agents, released into Canada
text:
A Burundi man whose adopted mother is a Maine state senator was detained this week by U.S. immigration officials as he was leaving the country, his family says.
Jessie Laurel Tepler-Mujambere, 28, had recently obtained his Canadian citizenship and was leaving the United States when immigration authorities apprehended him in New Hampshire, his family said.
The Department of Homeland Security confirmed Friday that Tepler-Mujambere had been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and that the agency planned to remove him to Canada.
He arrived in Canada later Friday, his family confirmed. Upon arrival, he texted family members, “I’m free!”
“He seems to be doing well,” his sister Maya Tepler said in a phone call.
She said his experience didn’t sound “too harrowing,” compared to stories she’s heard of other people’s encounters with ICE.
“I think we feel like, what a best-case scenario for a worst-case scenario,” Maya Tepler said.
She noted he had only recently obtained his Canadian passport and could have faced deportation to Burundi otherwise.
‘WE WERE VERY WORRIED’
Tepler-Mujambere was pulled over in New Hampshire by a law enforcement agency that works with ICE through the federal 287(g) program. Such agreements are illegal in Maine following a new law that took effect this year.
DHS said Tepler-Mujambere arrived in 2014 on a visa that expired the following year, and the agency said his pending asylum application “does not confer legal status in the United States.” Multiple immigration attorneys have said that asylum seekers had been allowed for decades to live and work in their communities until President Donald Trump’s second term began in 2025.
Tepler-Mujambere came to the United States as a teenager, according to a 2018 interview with The Forecaster. He told the paper he had fled violence in Burundi and came to the U.S. seeking a safer life.
State Sen. Denise Tepler, D-Topsham, and her husband, Sheldon, an attorney, agreed at the time to become his legal guardians. Tepler-Mujambere graduated from Mt. Ararat High School in 2018. His family said he had been seeking asylum for 10 years.
In a phone call Friday evening, the senator said Tepler-Mujambere attained Canadian citizenship in July and had been waiting on official documentation so that he could travel across the border.
“We were very worried,” Denise Tepler said of her son’s detainment. “We just didn’t know what would happen. … I was pretty upset this happened at all.”
She expressed frustration at her son being stopped “10 miles from the border” and taken south, only to be returned to his original destination.
“It’s wasting taxpayer dollars,” she said.
Denise Tepler also noted his detainment was through a local police department and said she believes it’s an example of those agencies not being equipped to handle immigration cases.
“I’m very glad that we don’t have a 287(g) agreements here in Maine,” she said.
Maya Tepler added that she was “angry that this government organization is blatantly violating people’s civil rights,” including “Canadian citizens going to the border.”
“This is an agency from which no one is safe,” she said.

title: Top federal prosecutor in Alaska says criminal probe underway over would-be spoiler Senate candidate
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — The top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed on Friday the existence of a criminal investigation related to an alleged scheme to confuse voters by putting a Senate candidate on the ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent.
The investigation has been ongoing for several months, but revelations this week from The New York Times that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan Jr. have resulted in a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska,” U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters.
“When credible information comes out, we are committed to pursuing that information to deceive voters and we will act on it. We are acting on it intensely and swiftly,” Heyman said.
Heyman would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into or the targets of the probe, but encouraged the public to come forward with tips that could help investigators.
Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot, where Peltola is challenging Republican Sen. Daniel Sullivan.
“I just want to clear the air,” she said at the top of a speech in a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”
Federal prosecutors this week issued dozens of grand jury subpoenas and requests to preserve records, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign. “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber.

title: Reject hate and violence by voting for Hannah Pingree
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Deqa Dhalac, a native of Somalia who has lived in Maine for 21 years, is a former mayor of South Portland and former state representative.
“Go back to your toilet country!!”
“U.S.-born citizens only.”
These are just a few of the comments instigated by the Republican nominee for governor of Maine, Bobby Charles, when he launched a social media assault against me last year. It was relentless.
Maine has been my home for 21 years. And when I was elected as the state and nation’s first Somali American mayor, I was honored to serve my community and proud to model the value immigrants bring. After, I was elected to the State House of Representatives where I advocated to improve worker protection and healthcare for all Mainers.
Still, I was harassed online by Bobby Charles and his emboldened, hateful supporters solely based on where I was born.
While I was the target of Bobby and his base’s harmful comments this time, these sentiments have similar effects on our communities of immigrants, Muslims, indigenous peoples and community members of color throughout the state.
Since President Trump deployed masked, armed and violent ICE agents across the country and specifically targeted Maine, I have fought to keep our towns safe and welcoming to immigrants who are not only working to start a new chapter for themselves, but who are also deeply committed to contributing to their communities. Nobody benefits when we are driven into hiding out of fear, captured on our way to work and faced with violence in front of our children.
Maine is known for its kindness, and for neighbors who show up for one another when it matters most. Bobby Charles is out of touch with that. Speaking about Maine’s immigrants in July, he said, “We need to be putting them in our own version of Alligator Alcatraz.” Just a short scroll through the comments on that post will give you a clear picture of the devastating effect his leadership would have on our state.
Charles has boasted about calling his pal, Trump’s border czar Tom Homan, to request that ICE agents come to Maine polling locations on Election Day, an illegal intimidation tactic targeting voters who are legal immigrants and people of color.
Instead of addressing the systemic, urgent issues across the state like homelessness, the opioid crisis, the rising cost of living and the impact of federal cuts to programs such as Medicare and food assistance on thousands of Mainers, Bobby pits people against one another and sees the worst instead of the best of the state.
But that approach won’t work here in Maine. His recent attempts to soften his stance don’t erase what he’s said or the climate he helped create. I haven’t forgotten and I know my fellow Mainers haven’t either.
For every person busy in the comment sections, many more Mainers are thoughtful, decent and ready to stand up for their neighbors. We see it in the broad coalition of support for Hannah Pingree for governor.
While in the Legislature, I worked with Hannah to create the Office of New Americans. I watched her listen to people and find solutions to their problems from housing to storm damage repair to energy efficiency.
Since the start of her campaign, she has laid out clear plans to address affordability across housing, healthcare and energy and has been outspoken against ICE activity in Maine. Hannah and her campaign reflect the needs of Maine people, and she has the experience and reputation to fight for all of us.
If you, like me, believe Maine can reject hate and violence and grow stronger for it, Hannah Pingree is your candidate this November.

title: Obituary: Regina (Picard) Minott
text:
SCARBOROUGH – Regina (Picard) Minott, 77, of Scarborough, passed away peacefully at home due to congestive heart failure with her family by her side on Sunday, Oct. 19, 2026.
Reggie was born on Nov. 16, 1948, to Aldric and Ida Picard of Bucksport, Maine. She attended Bucksport Schools and Farmington State College, graduating in 1971 with a teaching degree.
She dedicated her life to a teaching career working in Waterville, Brunswick and Windham, Maine schools. Reggie had a special skill in reaching out to all of her students, making them feel welcomed and respected. It is no wonder that she was honored by receiving a “Who’s Who Among America’s Teachers” award.
As a working Mom, she steadfastly ensured that her three daughters had the love and nurturance to allow them to thrive. Always present at their school functions, plays, speech tournaments and ball games, Reggie showed her unwavering support.
The sparkle in Reggie’s eyes really glowed when the grandkids came to visit. Memere always had just the right snack or meal ready for their arrival. The “Queen of the Kitchen” was regaled for her famous Chicken Vegetable Soup, Apple Pies and homemade Strawberry Jam. Her house was filled with love and fun times, family dinners, splashing in the pool, puzzle making and card games. Her perfect 29 point hand in a cribbage game with Jim will go unequaled!
Regina’s Catholic Faith was an important part of her life, and she was a long-time parishioner of St. Maximillan Kobe Church in Scarborough, Maine. For many years she sang in the church choir and taught classes in their religious education.
Survived by her husband, Jim, of 52 years. Regina also leaves her three daughters, Sarah Mogan and husband Nate of Windham, Maine, Laura Sanders and husband Ty of Huntington Beach, Calif., and Diana Minott of Shapleigh, Maine. Her grandchildren include Willow and Wyatt Washburn, Wesley Mogan, Kyla Hebert, Miya and Koda Sanders. She is also survived by her brother, Roger Picard and his wife Gayle of Abbot, Maine. Reggie leaves behind countless cousins and the extended Cloutier family.
Visitation will be held on Monday, Nov. 2, from 9 to 10:30 a.m. at the Hobbs Funeral Home, 671 US Rt 1, Scarborough. This will be followed by a Mass of Christian Burial at 11 a.m. at St. Maximillian Kolbe Church, Black Point Road, Scarborough. A reception will follow at the church. Burial will be at the Calvary Cemetery at a later date.
For those planning to attend Reggie’s services please feel comfortable wearing happy, vibrant colors rather than somber black. Her family wishes to celebrate the life she lived rather than to mourn her passing. Let’s make the “Wall of Love” we surrounded her with as colorful as possible!

title: Older adults who stop driving face transportation gaps, experts say
text:
KANSAS CITY (InvestigateTV) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. They are “more likely to be seriously hurt,” according to the agency. Most older drivers do not have a plan for when they can no longer drive, which aging experts say is critical.
A trip to the doctor without a car
Kennie Sandbothe, 77, stopped driving and now relies on a ride program for older adults.
Sandbothe was headed to a doctor’s appointment about 25 minutes from their home outside Kansas City.
“There’s no buses out here, not in this kind of rural area out here,” Sandbothe said. “It’s so expensive for Uber to take somewhere all the time.”
Sandbothe joked that they thought about improvising.
“Sometimes I thought about taking my lawn tractor, riding it to someplace I need to go. But you can’t put it out on the street because it’s not licensed,” Sandbothe said.
Sandbothe is the primary caregiver for their spouse and is managing serious health conditions, including Type 2 diabetes. Sandbothe also sees a psychiatrist for gender dysphoria, a condition that can happen when someone’s gender identity doesn’t match the sex they were assigned at birth.
“They’re the ones that saved my life,” Sandbothe told us.
Balance issues and blood sugar spikes made driving unpredictable, so Sandbothe stopped driving.
“I never know when I’m falling and stuff,” Sandbothe said. “I don’t want to get out there and black out and hurt somebody or kill somebody.”
Confidence and independence
There is no set age when someone should stop driving.
A February 2025 University of Michigan poll found 81% of drivers 65 and older feel very confident in their driving right now. That number drops to 43% when they are asked about driving safely five years from now.
Without a plan, experts say giving up the keys can mean losing control of their day, where they go and how they get there.
Rachel Ohlhausen of Jewish Family Services of Greater Kansas City said that uncertainty is why it can be hard to let go.
“It means a loss of independence in a new way,” Ohlhausen said. “Your time is no longer just yours. You don’t get to decide to do something on a whim.”
According to AAA, former drivers were less likely to get out, had smaller social networks and faced a higher risk of depression. A number of studies found that driving cessation appears to contribute to a variety of health problems, including declining cognitive function.
“What we know about loneliness and isolation is that loneliness is the equivalent of smoking a pack of cigarettes a day for your health,” Ohlhausen said.
Public transit and rideshare
Ohlhausen said public transportation often does not work for older adults with limited mobility or stamina.
“We do have some public transportation, but for an older adult who’s using a walker, walking to the bus stop isn’t always feasible,” she said.
The National Aging and Disability Transportation Center said public transit can be limited or nonexistent in rural and suburban communities.
Rideshares can fill some gaps, but there are barriers, Ohlhausen said.
“So even if you were able to and had the technological savviness to download the app, can you afford a smartphone? And can you afford the rideshare?” she said.
When people can’t find a ride, Ohlhausen said some stop asking for help.
“When those folks no longer drive, they really fall off the radar of society,” she said.
Sandbothe’s first backup plan was a next-door neighbor, but the arrangement did not last.
“My next-door neighbor, she was helping me for a while, but then decided, you know, she didn’t want to do it anymore,” Sandbothe said. “I don’t blame people, you know, they got their lifestyle. I don’t want to hinge on anybody to do anything for me.”
Sandbothe contacted the area office on aging and was connected with Jewish Family Services’ “Jet Express.” The program provides door-to-door service for adults 60 and older.
“We are the main source of transportation for 300 older adults in the Kansas City metro area,” Ohlhausen said.
Jet Express costs $5 each way and runs on a mix of volunteers, staff drivers and partner rides.
Staff driver Chip Ingram drove Sandbothe to the appointment. Ingram said that for some riders, it is not about driving, but about not feeling safe on the road.
“Some of them probably still drive to the neighborhood market, but they don’t want to take a ride on a highway it’s just too nerve-wracking for some people,” Ingram said.
Talking with a loved one about driving
For many families, the first step is having “the talk.”
According to AgingCare.com, experts say these are some red flags to watch for:
- Delayed responses, or getting lost or disoriented easily.
- Increased close calls and near misses.
- Difficulty seeing pedestrians, objects or other vehicles.
- Several dents or scrapes on the car or on surrounding objects where the person drives and parks at home.
Amy Cameron O’Rourke, an aging expert with Aging Untold, suggests asking a loved one questions before driving becomes a problem.
“Start before it’s a problem and just start lobbing some questions and make it part of a routine check-in,” she said.
Families can also talk with a doctor about any health issues or medications that can affect driving. State DMVs can provide information on driver evaluations and restrictions. Local agencies on aging can help families find transportation options.

title: Aging Untold: When health changes your sex life, intimacy doesn’t have to disappear
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we address how aging and illness can impact intimacy, sharing practical ways for couples to talk openly and safely navigate sex after a diagnosis.
Then, we discuss clinical trials, why older adults are frequently underrepresented and what questions to ask before participating in a study.
Plus, we meet a 91-year-old world record holder in track and field proving that staying active has no age limit.
Health can affect intimacy as we age and the Aging Untold experts are addressing questions many couples are afraid to ask out loud: When is it safe to resume sex? What if it isn’t? And what should you ask your doctor?
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first step is figuring out what’s behind the change. Competence and consent are the first things to consider, she said.
For physical issues, like erectile dysfunction, a doctor can often help.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said one of the biggest misconceptions couples carry is treating intimacy and sexuality as interchangeable — and they’re not.
Older adults are often left out of clinical trials, but they can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, according to the Aging Untold experts.
When considering a clinical trial, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the first step is to think about what the clinical trial is trying to answer.
Many people see clinical trials as a last resort, but one of the biggest benefits is access, Rogers said.
“You get great access to tomorrow’s medicines today — devices, therapies and other things that will not be available to everybody else for years.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said participants should know going into a trial that they might receive a placebo.
Read the full article for more on clinical trials, how to find them and which ones compensate participants.
The long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach, according to new research.
There are new studies indicating that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy.
According to a study released in October 2025, peanut allergy rates in children under 3 have dropped by roughly 43% over the last decade.
Flo Meiler’s home is filled with medals, and she holds two world records.
The Vermont woman started competing in track and field at 60, and she was hooked. She is now 91 and still competes.
“I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said.

title: How art therapy helps patients connect with caregivers
text:
WILMINGTON, N.C. (InvestigateTV) — Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected.
Mother and daughter paint together
June Lederle and her daughter, Cathie Lederle, create artwork at a table in their Wilmington home most days. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness.
Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. June said the first signs that something was wrong appeared in 2019, starting with forgetfulness and then repeating tasks. Cognitive testing later confirmed their fears.
Doctors diagnosed Cathie with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease at age 58. Early-onset Alzheimer’s is a rare form of dementia that can affect people in their 40s and 50s.
Five years after the diagnosis, June, now in her late 80s, became her daughter’s full-time caregiver.
“And so I’ve had the opportunity to bring her back into my life in some fashion, not necessarily as we planned,” June said.
Goal is connection
Elizabeth Gronke, an art therapist, said creating art gives families a way to be together, even when talking about the disease is hard.
“The art therapy goal in many ways is really more being able to find ways to connect and being able to be in community without having to necessarily talk about what’s going on directly, especially with diseases like Alzheimer’s disease,” Gronke said.
Art therapy is described as creative expression with purpose. It includes painting, sculpting and drawing, and it gives people a way to communicate when words are not working.
Researchers have found creative activities can engage multiple areas of the brain.
For some patients, that can mean more focus, less anxiety and more engagement.
“But I’m looking for that spark,” Gronke said. “I’m looking for that moment when a person gets curious and they lean in or they’re making a choice like, ‘Oh, I like that one better.’”
Signs of connection
Staff in memory-care communities say they see that “spark” turn into eye contact, a smile and sometimes a few words.
Kate Bellon, activities director at Sunrise Senior Living outside St. Louis, said the response is noticeable as a person’s memory declines.
“When the mind really starts to digress, it’s really magical when you can see them looking at it and engaging,” Bellon said. “Eye contact is just huge. Even a smile is huge because it’s hard to get out of them.”
Through “Meet Me at MoMA,” a program with the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the community is bringing artwork to its memory care unit.
“It sparks socialization and it helps with memory and reflection, so it’s really good to help their mind get going and provide a positive atmosphere for them,” Bellon said.
Marjorie Dixon and other Sunrise residents have worked on art for about a year. Dixon’s art will be featured in an exhibition to raise money for the Alzheimer’s Association. She said she feels it is important to help.
“I think we’ll get a lot of people out to see it. I hope we will anyway,” Dixon said.
In North Carolina, June helps Cathie reconnect with her lifelong interests. As Cathie’s Alzheimer’s progresses, June has set up an environment where Cathie can spend hours crafting.
“I love just coming through all these kinda things that you can make your own and then give it to people to do it,” Cathie said.
For June, each piece Cathie creates is proof her daughter is still there.
“When you know that maybe it’s not how it should be, but that’s kinda my job — to create a happy environment,” June said. “And it gives me a purpose.”
Tips for planning an art activity
For someone with middle-to-late-stage Alzheimer’s, Graf said to keep these tips in mind when planning an art activity:
- Make sure the project is on an adult level. Avoid anything that might be demeaning or seem childlike.
- Help the person begin the activity. If the person is painting, you may need to start the brush movement. Most other projects should require only basic instruction and assistance.
- Use safe materials. Avoid toxic substances and sharp tools. Avoid using anything that may be confused with food.
- Allow plenty of time. The person does not have to finish the project in one sitting.
Gronke said it is important to be flexible and have fun.
“I try to create an environment of play,” Gronke said. “And a lot of people have talked about the power of improv as well. The attitude of whenever you can safely say yes and so if I think I’m going to be doing a certain kind of project with a person, I brought it, I’m all set up for it, and they go off in a different direction with it, that’s fine.”
Gronke said art therapy also benefits caregivers by giving them an opportunity to recapture a connection with a loved one or friend.
More information about art therapy is available at dementiaarttherapyalliance.org . The Dementia Art Therapy Alliance includes more than 20 schools nationwide and more than 500 volunteers.

title: Obituary: Louis “Louie” Michael Savard
text:
SCARBOROUGH – Louis “Louie” Michael Savard, 82, passed away on Oct. 25, 2026, peacefully in his sleep at the Enclave in Scarborough. Louie was born on Dec. 28, 1943, in Portland, son of the late Lorenzo and Marian (Qualey) Savard.
Louie was born and raised in Portland’s Libbytown. After his father passed away, he stepped up to help care for his mother and three sisters. A homebody at heart, his favorite escape was just a 30-minute drive away to his camp on Highland Lake in Windham.
He worked as an industrial plumber and pipefitter and was fiercely proud of his over 50 year UA union membership. His trade often required long-distance travel away from home, working hard to support his family. Naturally handy, he helped maintain his home and camp, always puttering around and fixing things.
A man of deep faith, he was a lifelong member at St. Patrick’s Church until its closing, and a member of the Knights of Columbus. He was also deeply generous, frequently using his skills to help friends and neighbors with plumbing or everyday tasks, and he valued the close, lifelong friendships he kept over the years.
Outside of work, he enjoyed gardening and took pride in his garden. In his retirement, he took up baking, making yummy fruit pies to share with family and friends. While he was happiest close to home, his children eventually broadened his horizons with memorable trips to Ireland, Germany, and the Caribbean.
Though a man of few words, Louie loved his children and grandchildren immensely, and took a quiet, profound pride in their education and successes. He is remembered for his strong work ethic, union pride, unwavering faith, and his steadfast devotion to his family.
Louie was predeceased by his wife of 42 years, Loretta (Hamm) Savard; brother, Joseph Savard; and partner of 12 years, Ruth Bridges.
He is survived by his children, Michael Savard and his fiancé Elizabeth “Happy” Guibeb, Christine and her husband Jeff Hamm, and Lisa Savard; grandchildren, Sarah and her husband Zane Speece, Samantha and her husband Alex Michel, Jacob and his wife Jessica Savard, and Noah Savard; great-grandchildren, Theodore Speece and Elowyn Savard; sisters, Marie Solak, Anne Letourneau, and Jeanne and her husband Steve Silverman; and Ruth’s daughter, Cindy Bridges.
The family would like to extend a special thank you to The Enclave of Scarborough and Gentiva Hospice for their excellent care of Louie.
Visiting Hours will be held from 4 p.m. – 6 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, at the new Conroy-Tully Walker, Funeral, Cremation, and Gathering Center, 300 Allen Ave. Portland, ME. Herbal supplement sold on Amazon, at Whole Foods recalled amid salmonella concerns
A possible salmonella risk has prompted a recall of an herbal supplement sold online and in stores.
Vitality Works Inc. is recalling one lot of 365 Whole Foods Market ashwagandha capsules because they may be contaminated with salmonella, officials with the Food and Drug Administration announced Friday.
Related video above | Recalls explained: How to stay ahead of recalls
The recall covers 120-count bottles of Standardized and Full Spectrum Blend Ashwagandha with lot number 2025-26227 and expiration date Oct. 13, 2028, FDA officials said.
Both numbers are printed on the bottom of the bottle.
The bottles have a UPC of 9948252099 and were sold online through Amazon and at Whole Foods Market stores from Nov. 24, 2025, through Oct. 20, 2026.
The product was available online nationwide, and at stores in 30 states and the District of Columbia.
The states are Arkansas, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa, Illinois, Kansas, Massachusetts, Maryland, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, North Carolina, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Washington and Wyoming.
No illnesses have been reported, according to the company. The potential contamination was found during routine testing of a retail unit.
Salmonella can cause fever, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting and stomach pain. The infection can be especially serious for young children, older adults, frail people and those with weakened immune systems.
Customers should not take the capsules. They should throw them away and not return them to a store. Click here to view the full recall.

title: Here’s what’s on the ballot in Windham
text:
Windham residents will vote next week on three ballot referendums, two of the town’s six positions on the Regional School Unit 14 school board, as well as two state House seats and one state Senate seat.
In-person voting will take place on Nov. 3 at Windham High School from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Early voting ended Thursday.
Here’s what Windham voters can expect to find on their 2026 ballots.
BALLOT QUESTIONS
Windham residents will vote on three questions next week.
Question 1 pertains to an amendment to the town charter changing Windham’s town meeting format from an in-person meeting to a secret-ballot referendum. The amendment, if approved, will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027, with the option of returning to the in-person format should the budget fail at referendum.
Question 2, if approved, would amend the town charter to say that any appropriation of $500,000 or more, with the threshold being raised from $25,000, shall become effective only after adoption at a town meeting by a majority vote of those present and the town meeting shall not increase the amount of any appropriation or bond issue above what is recommended by the Town Council. The amendment will go into effect immediately if approved.
Question 3 asks residents to approve $19.5 million to convert Windham Middle School, set to close at the end of this year, into a community center, and to appropriate up to $2 million of the town’s fund balance as the Town Council deems necessary to reduce the borrowing amount. The proposed community center will house the town hall, library, and social services.
LOCAL RACES
Windham will vote to fill two of its six seats on the RSU 14 school board. Candidates running for the board include Marge Govoni, Joe Kellner, Megan Potter and Adam Zajac.
Town Council members Mark Morrison and Mark Cobb are running uncontested for the council’s East district and at-large seats, respectively.
STATE RACES
State Senate District 26, which covers Windham, Casco, Frye Island, Raymond, and part of Westbrook, features a race between incumbent Democrat Timothy Nangle and Republican challenger Kenneth Cianchette.
In State House District 106, incumbent Republican Barbara Bagshaw faces a challenge from Democratic challenger Bradley Youngs.
Joseph Campbell, a Democrat, is challenging Republican incumbent Mark Cooper for State House District 107.

title: Trump cancels rallies in Kansas and Iowa, opting for telerallies to reach more voters, RNC says
text:
ROCK HILL, S.C. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday canceled weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas, opting instead to support Republican candidates with telerallies that his party said could reach more voters in nearly two dozen states in the final days of a midterm election that could cost the GOP control of Congress.
The president traveled to South Carolina Thursday for the second time in a month, a sign of Republican anxiety about Darline Graham’s ability to fend off a robust challenge from Democrat Annie Andrews for a critical U.S. Senate seat.
Voters in South Carolina have not sent a Democrat to the Senate in nearly three decades. But Andrews, a pediatrician who previously ran unsuccessfully for Congress, is urging voters seeking change to “try something new for once.”
That message could resonate in an election year defined by voter frustration with the economy, gas prices and the war in Iran, putting Trump’s Republican Party on defense in territory where they have rarely had to compete in recent years.
Beyond South Carolina, Republicans are entering the final days of this year’s midterm elections navigating tight contests in Texas, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska. Both parties are also closely following developments in the Mississippi Senate race.
The president projected confidence as he returned to the White House, saying, “We’re going to have a strong Tuesday night.”
Trump was scheduled to hold a rally in Kansas on Saturday and in Iowa on Sunday. But the Republican National Committee announced Thursday evening that he would instead spend a “72-hour sprint” doing rallies by phone rather than in person, a move the RNC said would maximize Trump’s ability to speak to voters nationwide. The RNC said telerallies are planned for nearly 20 states, and more may be announced.
It was an abrupt shift in Trump’s pledge to push through the final days of the campaign doing rally after rally to galvanize his supporters. As of Thursday, he had done 25 rallies during the month of October, falling short of a goal he had once placed north of 30.
Trump says he doesn’t need to go to Kansas
There were signs the travel and long speeches have caught up with him. On Monday, in Corinth, Mississippi, Trump — whose voice has grown raspy — told the crowd, “God didn’t make your vocal cords to do a rally every day.”
But he bristled Thursday when a reporter asked whether he had canceled plans to travel to Kansas because of his health.
“You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect,” Trump snapped.
The president said he’s not traveling to Kansas, where GOP Sen. Roger Marshall faces Democrat Adam Hamilton, “because he’s doing very well,” an apparent reference to Marshall.
“I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas,” Trump said.
A campaign strategist with Republican Senate leadership said there was widespread curiosity about why the schedule was changing to telerallies. The strategist spoke on condition of anonymity to share the content of private conversations.
Trump, who revels in big crowds, has this month held rallies in smaller venues than many he once filled. The decision to switch to telerallies means he will be expected to speak for about 10 minutes instead of more than 90, as he does at in-person events.
Trump plans to travel to Daytona Beach, Florida, for a rally Friday. It’s not clear whether he will hold additional in-person events after that. The White House has not published his schedule for Monday, the final day of the campaign.
Democrats took notice.
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan who’s in a tight race against Republican Mike Rogers, said Thursday night that the president’s goal of trying to gin up GOP voters has backfired and he has “given up.” “He’s an old man, he’s a loser,” El-Sayed continued. “He now understands that he has fully lost the midterms for his party.”
Graham has struggled to connect with voters
In South Carolina, Graham has struggled to quickly build connections with voters. The sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, she was appointed in July by Republican Gov. Henry McMaster to fill the remaining months of her brother’s term after his sudden death. In August, she became the party’s nominee to succeed him for a full six-year term.
“He was a great politician,” Trump said of Lindsey Graham, before promoting Darline Graham as his elected successor. “She’s got the gene.”
Darline Graham commended the president for having “delivered what Washington promised for decades.” She warned that Andrews “would just throw it all away.”
Andrews appeared in nearby Fort Mill on Wednesday, where she said that if voters elect her and become unhappy with her performance on Capitol Hill, “you can fire me in six years.”
South Carolina Rep. Ralph Norman, who lost to Graham in the GOP Senate primary runoff, has criticized Graham as unqualified. Norman, who has refused to campaign with Graham, said the race is closer than it would have been had he been nominated.
Lonnie Dean Johnson of Sumter, South Carolina, supported Norman in the primary and was voting Graham out of party loyalty, albeit unenthusiastically.
“She’s on a Republican ticket. I, by and large, support the Republican platform,” he said. ”So, I support her and wish her well.”
Democrats are bullish about Senate races across the US
Democrats, meanwhile, are optimistic about their chances of booting GOP incumbent senators, including in Ohio, with an American public frustrated by continued high costs.
“Families see more money going out the door and not enough money coming in,” said Sherrod Brown, the Democratic Senate nominee who’s competing against Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted. At a rally in Toledo Thursday, Brown said Husted is “looking out for data centers and Wall Street.”
Farther north, Alaska’s Republican governor has ordered an investigation after The New York Times reported Wednesday that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting another candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
The Justice Department escalated the investigation Thursday, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
The Justice Department also issued subpoenas to California officials in the latest effort to scrutinize local election administration. A federal judge in California earlier Thursday appointed a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that the state has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls.
Trump called the development in Alaska a “conspiracy” and called for Peltola to be removed from the ballot. He has cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election.
Peltola’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a message Thursday seeking comment on the governor’s order. But during a campaign stop in Soldotna, Peltola, a former congresswoman, suggested the Times’ report was a “distraction” from issues such as Sen. Sullivan’s support of the war in Iran.
The revelation in Alaska was a reminder of the volatility of the midterm campaigns’ final days as both parties make decisions about how to spend time and money with control of Congress on the line.
__
Sloan reported from Washington. Associated Press writers Thomas Beaumont in Des Moines, Iowa, Jesse Bedayn in Austin, Texas, Hannah Fingerhut in Clive, Iowa, John Hanna in Topeka, Kansas, Mike Householder in Kalamazoo, Michigan, and Meg Kinnard, Collin Binkley and Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington contributed to this report.

title: BU hockey scores on first 3 shots, breezes to easy 7-2 win over UMaine
text:
The fans at Agganis Arena had barely settled in their seats for the game between Boston University and the University of Maine when it had already been decided.
The Terriers scored on their first three shots on net in the game’s first 1:31 and BU coasted to an easy 7-2 victory over the overmatched Black Bears.
It was BU’s ninth consecutive Agganis Arena victory over UMaine dating back to 2018.
BU, ranked 14th in one national poll and tied for 13th in another, improved to 5-2 overall and 3-2 in Hockey East. UMaine, ranked 19th in one poll, fell to 4-3 and 0-1.
The teams will play again Saturday at 6.
“That was our first humbling experience of the year,” said UMaine head coach Ben Barr. “There’s nothing you can really say outside of credit to them.”
“That was alarming. You feel like you got some traction over the last four games and now it’s back to square one,” the coach added.
He intended to make lineup changes for Saturday’s game, saying, “We have to get a spark from somebody. We didn’t really have that from anybody” Friday.
The Black Bears were simply outclassed in every aspect of the game by a far superior BU team, which boasts 18 National Hockey League draft choices including 11 first and second round selections.
Tynan Lawrence, Xavier Villaneuve and Ben Merrill staked BU to a 3-0 lead and Viktor Norringer’s power play goal at the 4:49 mark expanded the lead to 4-0.
UMaine’s Tanner Klimpke scored just 19 seconds after Norringer, but that would turn out to be UMaine’s only offense until Max Scott scored a late consolation goal on the power play.
Lawrence opened the scoring just 29 seconds into the game when he outmuscled a Black Bear for the puck along the left wing boards in the neutral zone and pulled away from him en route to a breakaway opportunity.
Tynan’s quick wrist shot cleanly beat Petter Wickstrom Stumer for his team-high fifth goal of the season.
Villaneuve, the reigning Hockey East Rookie of the Week, made it 2-0 31 seconds later by finishing off a highlight-reel passing sequence by tapping the puck into a wide open net off a great pass from Jack Harvey.
It was the first goal of his college career.
Merrill made it 3-0 31 seconds later when he got behind the UMaine defense, took a pass from Jonathan Morello and skated across the top of the crease before tucking the puck behind Wickstrom Stumer for his second of the campaign.
Freshman Norringer scored his first college goal with a one-timer from the left circle from a nifty cross-ice feed from Caleb Malhotra.
That ended the evening for Wickstrom Stumer, who was replaced by senior Albin Boija.
He finished with two saves on six shots.
Klimpke gave UMaine a tiny glimmer of hope when he swatted home the rebound of an Alexander Bales shot that came to him off the boards behind the net. It was Klimpke’s fourth of the season and first even-strength goal.
But BU continued its complete dominance in the second period and swelled the lead to 6-1 on goals 4:10 apart by Niklas Aaram-Olsen and Brandon Svoboda and Conrad Fondrk’s power play goal in the third period made it 7-1.
Scott scored his first of the season with 5:49 remaining.
Mikhail Yegorov made 28 saves in goal for BU and Boija stopped 28 of 31 after replacing Wickstrom Stumer.

title: For many, striped bass fishing is a way of life. But the iconic species could face collapse
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MONTAUK, N.Y. (AP) — Striped bass fishing has been Bill Jakob’s passion for more than 60 years, and he remembers an era when he’d spend all night casting his line into the crashing waves off Montauk and get eight or nine fish ranging up to 40 pounds (18 kilograms), a big catch by anyone’s standards.
Then, after years of heavy fishing, the big runs of stripers stopped.
“I’m part of the problem, back in the years. I ran party boats, we slayed fish with reckless abandon,” said Jakob, president of the Montauk Surfcasters Association on the easternmost tip of Long Island.
Increasingly, fishermen like Jakob fear the good days of catching striped bass are coming to an end. The fish aren’t showing up like they used to, and young stripers are becoming harder to find.
Scientists who study striped bass say anglers on the East Coast are right to be concerned, and they say years of overfishing are just part of the problem. The fish have experienced eight consecutive years of poor reproduction in their most critical habitat in the Chesapeake Bay, regulators said last week, and the population has declined along much of the Atlantic coast.
Factors like years of warming waters — a prime concern cited by many scientists — poor river flow, drought, pollution and possibly increased predation from seals and sharks have left experts and fishermen asking whether tighter fishing limits would even be enough for striped bass to recover. Losing these higher-level predators, which help regulate smaller fish, would threaten an $8 billion fishing industry and tens of thousands of jobs.
___
See a visual essay featuring anglers who were fishing the shores of Long Island earlier this month here.
___
Striped bass fishing is a long-standing East Coast tradition
“Stripers” are prized in part because they put up a fight and can be fished right from shore. From the slippery rocks of Maine’s coast to the warmer waters of the St. Johns River in Florida, anglers wearing headlamps can be seen casting into the predawn darkness, hoping for a bite.
Interstate regulators have made changes to the way the migratory fish are managed in recent years, including standardizing the way they’re measured against size requirements. But regulators have balked at reducing the level of recreational catch. Some fishermen say the current moves might not go far enough, and stricter action — including possibly a fishing moratorium, a strategy used in the 1980s — is needed to ensure that future generations of anglers can still catch striped bass.
“They are not replacing themselves at a sufficient level. That obviously has everybody concerned,” said Beth Versak, the striped bass program manager for the Maryland Department of Natural Resources. “People all up and down the coast are passionate about striped bass.”
Fishing guides, boat trips, gear, bait, hotel rooms — it all adds up to what members of the industry say is about $8 billion in economic impact and as many as 100,000 jobs in the U.S. alone.
And it relies on a fish whose future looks grim.
“Striped bass as we know it is going to collapse,” said Patrick Paquette, government affairs coordinator for the Massachusetts Striped Bass Association and a member of an interstate advisory panel about the regulations.
“Sometime around 2029, 2030 it’s going to go off a cliff,” he said, “and it’s going to be ugly.”
Scientists say a variety of factors, including warming waters, have contributed to poor spawning
Striped bass hatch in fresh or brackish water and then spend the early years of their lives in estuaries where the rivers meet the sea. Their ability to reproduce and bring new fish into the population is predicated on environmental conditions that favor them — specifically, cool, wet springs.
Scientists identify four major spawning stocks along the Atlantic. The Chesapeake Bay is where up to 90% of stripers spawn and grow. When freshwater flows are too low, such as in times of drought, or when spring or summer temperatures are too high, the fish suffer and populations can fall, said Toni Kerns, fisheries policy director with the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, which regulates striped bass.
Conditions have been poor in recent years, and fewer fish have entered the population going back to 2019, said Chris Batsavage, chair of the commission’s striped bass management board.
“Low precipitation and waters that warm quickly result in weak year classes,” Batsavage said. “It seems like it’s environmentally driven.”
The conditions have led to a “slump of bad years” that have made it especially difficult for the fish to maintain their population in the Chesapeake, Versak said.
Fishermen fear the loss of an iconic species if trends continue
John Skinner, who wrote a book about striped bass fishing and runs a YouTube channel on the subject that has more than 100,000 followers, has been fishing off Long Island for more than 50 years and says once-reliable spots have completely dried up.
“I’m not saying the fishing is bad. I’m saying when you go there in perfect conditions, you catch nothing,” Skinner said. “Absolutely nothing.”
Many other striped bass fishermen across the Northeast shared a recurring story this summer and fall — the fish’s once-plentiful schools are dried up, and the individuals that remain are clearly older, meaning years of reproduction failure are starting to take their toll.
Some fishermen said stricter rules or a fishing moratorium could be the only ways to prevent the fish’s population from becoming dangerously low. And they lament what they’re seeing on the waters — smaller schools of fish, many of them older and larger, with few young fish entering the population to provide a future.
They also see more factors than just the warming environment at play. Some see years of heavy fishing on striped bass becoming apparent today in the form of a lower population. Others blame the resurgence of sharks buoyed by years of conservation efforts, as a reintroduction of competition for the fish.
Regulators have taken steps, but some call for a moratorium
The Atlantic States commission considers the stock to be overfished, although it says overfishing is not occurring at the moment. The fish are caught commercially as well as recreationally, but recreational fishing is much larger.
Most of the recreational catch is tossed back into the ocean alive. Still, some fish don’t survive the encounter. Regulators have historically expected 9% to die after release, while newer data shows the number could be less than 5%.
Limits on how large a striped bass can be caught and kept are typically in the range of 28 to 31 inches (71 to 79 centimeters), with rules varying by state and location. Striped bass are popular with catch-and-release fishermen, and these days, it’s more common to catch larger bass, many well over 31 inches.
Paquette, the Massachusetts Striped Bass Association coordinator and a longtime angler himself, said that without drastic action he fears the end of striped bass fishing.
“If you’re a guy who thought he was going to retire and striped bass fish, and you’re planning on retiring soon, get a different plan,” Paquette said.
___
Whittle reported from Portland, Maine. Associated Press video journalist Mingson Lau contributed.

title: Keep Halloween Spooky, Not Scary: Vet shares essential pet safety tips
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Halloween festivities are expected to bring plenty of ghouls and goblins to neighborhood streets, but emergency veterinarians are reminding pet owners that the holiday excitement can quickly turn into a real scare for four-legged family members.
Experts at the Eastern Maine Emergency Veterinary Clinic warn that open doors, constant doorbells, and unfamiliar costumes often lead to panicked pets escaping.
Create a Quiet Safe Zone
Veterinarians advise setting up a quiet, comfortable room away from the front door during trick-or-treating hours. Frightened animals can easily bolt through an open door, and emergency clinics frequently see an uptick in pets struck by vehicles on busy Halloween nights.
If you are hosting a party, excitement and stress can also upset a pet’s stomach. A bland diet or veterinarian-recommended probiotics can help prevent stress-induced vomiting or diarrhea.
Candy Hazards and Intestinal Blockages
Sweet treats should be kept well out of paws’ reach:
- Toxicity: Chocolate and sugar-free candies containing xylitol are toxic to pets.
- Blockages: Dogs often eat candy wrappers and all, which can cause severe gastrointestinal blockages requiring emergency surgery.
Candles and Costumes
Holiday decor and festive outfits can also pose hidden dangers:
- Open flames: Curious pets and wagging tails can easily knock over open flame candles, risking burns or house fires.
- Scented candles: Strong aromas can trigger severe asthma attacks in cats.
- Costumes: Only dress pets up if they genuinely enjoy it. Outfits should fit comfortably without restricting breathing, vision, or movement.
If your pet ingests candy or shows signs of distress, contact your local emergency veterinarian clinic immediately.

title: First-ever BRES Cancer Walk fundraiser totals $1,500
text:
About 30 eighth graders and three of their teachers took a walk Friday morning, Oct. 30.
It wasn’t a gym class and they weren’t just enjoying the sunshine and 60F temperature.
The group was delivering a special package to Ray Ruby, executive director of the Maine Cancer Foundation.
Dressed in pink shirts, the Boothbay Region Elementary School students and teachers Cordelia Chase, Elizabeth Tilton and Soren Barker, walked from the school to Whale Park on Commercial Street in a show of solidarity and to present $1,500 to Ruby and the MCF.
Said Chase, “We have been collecting donations for the past few weeks during our Wildcat Wednesday (part of a new Middle School Advisory Program). We have had amazing support through parents, BRES/BRHS staff, and community. The eighth graders thank everyone for their sponsorship.”
One of the students, Sawyer Piercy, who personally raised $530 of the total, presented the money to Ruby following an introduction of the fundraiser by Barker and a round of applause from everyone.
“It is so wonderful to see young people engaged in projects like this,” said Ruby. “I thank you and the Foundation thanks you and I hope you continue to help others.”
“We aren’t always available to respond to such presentations but we couldn’t say no to this one with young people involved,” said Ruby.

title: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As midterm candidates begin to make their final pitches to voters, experts are speaking out about the impact of artificial intelligence on this election cycle.
Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI has become a major issue in several races in the last few months. He noted how different the rhetoric surrounding it has been compared to other new technologies.
“We like tech traditionally as part of our political economy. That’s really changed in the last year, where you see a much more neutral and sometimes negative political position on AI,” Borick said.
Borick said the political calculus surrounding AI has gone from positive to negative in both red and blue states after the backlash.
“That’s picking up on the broader public attitudes and concerns regarding AI, its effect on society, its effect on the economy and effects on their communities. And that’s really popped in this election cycle,” Borick said.
Differences between parties
Both Republican and Democratic candidates have tapped into concerns about AI. But some observers say they are still some noticeable differences in how the two sides discuss the issue.
“I do think that the Republicans have been over the last year plus, have been in a much more close position with the AI companies,” said Shobita Parthasarathy, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan. “And so what you find, I think in general, is that they are trying to talk more about the cost issue. They generally are not talking about the broader issues. They are trying to limit the discussion. They may or they may be less likely to talk about a moratorium.”
Potential for political realignment
Beyond policy discussions, AI has the potential to change politics entirely.
Borick said that at the local level, conservatives, liberals, Republicans and Democrats often align in opposition to data centers or express concerns about AI.
“And when that happens, you have the potential for some political realignments that we might be experiencing,” he said.
A recent poll of Iowa and Ohio voters published online for SEMAFOR found the vast majority of voters want greater regulation of artificial intelligence.

title: 5 Aroostook County theater groups team up for County Theater Season
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - Five theater groups in Aroostook County are teaming up to promote each other’s productions and give audiences a reason to attend more than one show.
County Theater Season begins Friday and runs through Nov. 22. It brings together community and high school productions from Houlton to Fort Kent. Organizers said having several shows on the calendar became an opportunity to build support for live theater across the county.
“We really saw it as a way to celebrate theater in Aroostook County. And it feels like we have our own little theater season that’s starting today going on,” said Shelby Pelletier, producer of “Come From Away.”
The lineup
The season includes:
- Halloween one-acts from the County Community Players
- “Anastasia” at Presque Isle High School
- Broadway After Dark’s “Come From Away”
- “Frozen” at Houlton High School
- “Les Misérables” at Fort Kent High School
Some performances overlap, and organizers wanted to encourage audiences to support multiple productions.
Darci Faye, director of “Come From Away,” said it is “actually possible to see all of the shows because we don’t have any matinees and other shows have matinees.” She said it is possible to see every show over the two weekends.
Digital punch card and raffle
Audience members can sign up for a digital punch card and scan a QR code at each production to track their visits. Attending three or more shows qualifies them for raffle entries.
Prizes include 100 gallons of heating oil donated by Mapleton Oil and a County Theater Season gift basket.
Organizers hope the collaboration becomes an annual tradition.

title: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
text:
(Aging Untold) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time.
The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead.
Why promises can create pressure
Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said.
“They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.”
She said the questions can be practical:
Can we afford the care?
What if you have care that takes heavy lifting and I can’t do it?
A resident’s needs changed
O’Rourke shared an example from her own work with a man who had significant memory impairment. He had told his daughter not to put him in “one of those places.”
“I talked to the daughter, and over time, this isn’t the only time it’s ever happened, we moved him into a memory facility,” O’Rourke said. “He became ‘the mayor.’ He’s the most popular guy. He was happy. And the daughter was blown away.”
O’Rourke said she has used that example with other families.
“What their needs were at one point might change,” O’Rourke said. “And so you have to change with how they change.”
Most family caregivers aren’t trained
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said most family members aren’t trained to be caregivers. Instead, the training usually comes from parenting children.
“Now you’re going to try and translate that level into an adult and understanding the complexities of the relationship, the history of the relationship, the disease progressions and what it’s like to change an adult versus changing someone much smaller,” Cradduck said.
What to say instead
Cradduck said caregivers need to be fair to themselves and suggested wording along these lines:
“Listen, I promise to do the best by you and keep you here as long as my skillset and the affordability allow. But if something changes along the way, I’m going to have to change the plan.”
“Staying at home is always going to be what you want, but it may not be the safest place and it may not be the best place.”
“We have to be honest with our family members and that’s tough,” Cradduck said.
Have the conversation early
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said to have the conversation ahead of time.
“The biggest thing to do is have that conversation early, not in the time of a crisis,” Rogers said. “Love is going to be tested by illness and caregiving and finances.”
And over the years, needs and views can shift, she said.
“The discussion that you have when you’re 35, your needs are going to change at 65,” Rogers said. “You may be at a different point in terms of medical history at that point too. So that conversation needs to change as things change.”
When a loved one asks for a promise
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said the request to make promises is common.
“This is not an uncommon promise to make,” Ambrose said. “I find many seniors will say, ‘Promise me you’ll never put me in one of those homes.’ But I think a lot of times that’s because they can’t imagine what might be coming down the pike.”
Ambrose said a community might work out well, as in O’Rourke’s example.
“When the scope of care changes, it may not be possible and then it’s OK to say we might need to adjust,” Ambrose said. “Sometimes the loved one might not be a part of that conversation anymore, but you can only do what you can do.”
Ambrose suggested asking: “Knowing where you’re at now, what is going on now? Is this what your mom or your dad would still want for you?”
Key takeaways
- Talk about the reality up front.
- Needs can change.
- Make a promise you can keep.
- Start early and revisit it.

title: Portland football uses big plays to win Battle of the Bridge
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SOUTH PORTLAND — Behind the big-play, power-running combo of Alex Martin and David Gomes, Portland High’s football team accomplished its goals Friday night.
The Bulldogs, with three touchdowns of 50-plus yards, beat South Portland 27-7 in the Battle of the Bridge. Portland improved to 7-2 and sewed up the No. 2 seed in Class A North, setting up a home semifinal next week against No. 3 Windham.
“It’s always great to win the Bridge game,” said Portland’s first-year head coach, Dylan Rottkov, a South Portland grad. “We’re 7-2. We cleaned up the penalties a little bit. We’ve been talking for a while about cleaning those up and having better execution. We’re moving in the direction of playing clean football.”
It was Portland’s sixth straight win in the regular-season rivalry game. South Portland holds a 56-51-3 all-time advantage.
South Portland (4-5) struggled offensively and lost its third straight game. Considering the Red Riots started the week in ranked fifth in the Class A South Crabtree points — one spot out of the playoffs — common sense would seem to indicate their season would be finished.
But the vagaries of the Crabtree system may have pushed South Portland ahead of Noble (also 4-5), even though Noble beat South Portland in the regular season.
South Portland coach Aaron Filieo said after the game he believes his team will finish fourth because the New Hampshire team that beat South Portland (Winnacunnet, with a 6-2 record) is better than the New Hampshire team that lost to Noble (Dover, which is 2-6).
“We’re in,” Filieo said.
If that’s the case, South Portland can start preparing for a semifinal at No. 1 seed and unbeaten Thornton Academy.
FIREPOWER
Martin took a direct snap on Portland’s first play on an off-tackle run behind an offensive line bolstered by extra linemen as blocking backs and went 69 yards for a touchdown.
That was it for scoring in the first half. South Portland was held to 66 yards in the half and 235 in the game, with Portland making it tough sledding for quarterback Shea Healy and top running back Chris Salamone, who didn’t have a gain over 10 yards until the outcome was decided.
“Well, obviously they played well defensively and we struggled,” Filieo said. “We struggled to do a lot of the things we have done well over the course of the year. We just had an off night.”
Portland went ahead 21-0 on a Wildes-to-Martin 73-yard touchdown and then a Gomes 56-yard scoring run on the Bulldogs’ next offensive play.
The touchdown pass was a deep ball that Martin hauled in before breaking tackles to cover the final 30-plus yards. Gomes took advantage of an extremely well blocked lane off left tackle, then used a stiff-arm to push down the last South Portland defender who had a chance to bring him down.
“Credit to the O-line for blocking, especially Bailey (Jordan) and Will (Lukoki),” Gomes said. Asked about the stiff-arm, Gomes pointed to Martin and said, “I got it from him, actually. From watching (Martin’s) film.”
South Portland got on the board with an 18-yard touchdown pass from Healy to Ronin Westin. Portland responded with a drive that lasted 7:29, with Gomes ripping off runs of 19, 12 and 20 yards before Martin scored from the 2.
Portland is the three-time North champion and won the state title in 2024.
“Obviously, we’d love to be the No. 1 seed, but we’re in an amazing spot,” Martin said. “We just need to take it day-by-day, win the practice, and it accumulates in the game.”
UNSUNG HERO
Justin Bouchard has made a name for himself as Portland’s kicker. As a senior, the very slender Bouchard (5-10, 130 pounds) has played more from scrimmage. He was a two-way starter Friday, making several tackles from his cornerback spot and one catch at wide receiver.
STATISTICS
Portland: Alex Martin (18 carries, 112 yards, 2 TDs; 2 catches, 76 yards, 1 TD), David Gomes (8 carries, 128 yards, 1 TD), Reece Wildes (9 of 12, 136 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT)
South Portland: Chris Salamone (18 carries, 107 yards) Shea Healy (6 carries, 13 yards; 6 of 19, 115 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT), Brady Dobson (2 catches, 42 yards; interception)

title: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As midterm candidates begin to make their final pitches to voters, experts are speaking out about the impact of artificial intelligence on this election cycle.
Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI has become a major issue in several races in the last few months. He noted how different the rhetoric surrounding it has been compared to other new technologies.
“We like tech traditionally as part of our political economy. That’s really changed in the last year, where you see a much more neutral and sometimes negative political position on AI,” Borick said.
Borick said the political calculus surrounding AI has gone from positive to negative in both red and blue states after the backlash.
“That’s picking up on the broader public attitudes and concerns regarding AI, its effect on society, its effect on the economy and effects on their communities. And that’s really popped in this election cycle,” Borick said.
Differences between parties
Both Republican and Democratic candidates have tapped into concerns about AI. But some observers say they are still some noticeable differences in how the two sides discuss the issue.
“I do think that the Republicans have been over the last year plus, have been in a much more close position with the AI companies,” said Shobita Parthasarathy, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan. “And so what you find, I think in general, is that they are trying to talk more about the cost issue. They generally are not talking about the broader issues. They are trying to limit the discussion. They may or they may be less likely to talk about a moratorium.”
Potential for political realignment
Beyond policy discussions, AI has the potential to change politics entirely.
Borick said that at the local level, conservatives, liberals, Republicans and Democrats often align in opposition to data centers or express concerns about AI.
“And when that happens, you have the potential for some political realignments that we might be experiencing,” he said.
A recent poll of Iowa and Ohio voters published online for SEMAFOR found the vast majority of voters want greater regulation of artificial intelligence.
