title: Trump to make final midterm stops in Iowa and Kansas Sunday
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump will make final campaign stops in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, two days before Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Trump won Iowa three times and Kansas twice. He is hoping to give Republicans a final boost in both states. He originally scrapped the stops but decided at the last minute to go through with them.
The Senate seats in both states are a must-win for Republicans to hold the chamber.
A recent Marist poll shows Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson trailing Democrat Josh Turek by three points in Iowa.
In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton holds a narrow lead over incumbent Republican Roger Marshall for the first time.
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said he is not worried.
“I’ve seen the voters on the ground. I’m telling you, the polls are wrong. They’re inaccurate. They’re underrepresenting Republicans,” Johnson said.
The last time Iowa sent a Democrat to the Senate was 2008. The last time Kansas did was nearly a century ago.
Trump’s approval rating is around 34% according to the latest Quinnipiac poll.
Whether his presence helps or hurts the Republican ticket will be determined Tuesday.
The Republican Party has confirmed, President Donald Trump will hold rallies starting at 3pm ET, 2pm Central at the Five Flags Center in Dubuque, Iowa and then 8pm ET, ypm CT at the Salina, Kansas regional airport.

title: How art therapy helps patients connect with caregivers
text:
WILMINGTON, N.C. (InvestigateTV) — Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected.
Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases.
Mother and daughter paint together
June Lederle and her daughter, Cathie Lederle, create artwork at a table in their Wilmington home most days. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness.
Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. June said the first signs that something was wrong appeared in 2019, starting with forgetfulness and then repeating tasks. Cognitive testing later confirmed their fears.
Doctors diagnosed Cathie with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease at age 58. Early-onset Alzheimer’s is a rare form of dementia that can affect people in their 40s and 50s.
Five years after the diagnosis, June, now in her late 80s, became her daughter’s full-time caregiver.
“And so I’ve had the opportunity to bring her back into my life in some fashion, not necessarily as we planned,” June said.
Goal is connection
Elizabeth Gronke, an art therapist, said creating art gives families a way to be together, even when talking about the disease is hard.
“The art therapy goal in many ways is really more being able to find ways to connect and being able to be in community without having to necessarily talk about what’s going on directly, especially with diseases like Alzheimer’s disease,” Gronke said.
Art therapy is described as creative expression with purpose. It includes painting, sculpting and drawing, and it gives people a way to communicate when words are not working.
Researchers have found creative activities can engage multiple areas of the brain.
For some patients, that can mean more focus, less anxiety and more engagement.
“But I’m looking for that spark,” Gronke said. “I’m looking for that moment when a person gets curious and they lean in or they’re making a choice like, ‘Oh, I like that one better.’”
Signs of connection
Staff in memory-care communities say they see that “spark” turn into eye contact, a smile and sometimes a few words.
Kate Bellon, activities director at Sunrise Senior Living outside St. Louis, said the response is noticeable as a person’s memory declines.
“When the mind really starts to digress, it’s really magical when you can see them looking at it and engaging,” Bellon said. “Eye contact is just huge. Even a smile is huge because it’s hard to get out of them.”
Through “Meet Me at MoMA,” a program with the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the community is bringing artwork to its memory care unit.
“It sparks socialization and it helps with memory and reflection, so it’s really good to help their mind get going and provide a positive atmosphere for them,” Bellon said.
Marjorie Dixon and other Sunrise residents have worked on art for about a year. Dixon’s art will be featured in an exhibition to raise money for the Alzheimer’s Association. She said she feels it is important to help.
“I think we’ll get a lot of people out to see it. I hope we will anyway,” Dixon said.
In North Carolina, June helps Cathie reconnect with her lifelong interests. As Cathie’s Alzheimer’s progresses, June has set up an environment where Cathie can spend hours crafting.
“I love just coming through all these kinda things that you can make your own and then give it to people to do it,” Cathie said.
For June, each piece Cathie creates is proof her daughter is still there.
“When you know that maybe it’s not how it should be, but that’s kinda my job — to create a happy environment,” June said. “And it gives me a purpose.”
Tips for planning an art activity
For someone with middle-to-late-stage Alzheimer’s, Graf said to keep these tips in mind when planning an art activity:
- Make sure the project is on an adult level. Avoid anything that might be demeaning or seem childlike.
- Help the person begin the activity. If the person is painting, you may need to start the brush movement. Most other projects should require only basic instruction and assistance.
- Use safe materials. Avoid toxic substances and sharp tools. Avoid using anything that may be confused with food.
- Allow plenty of time. The person does not have to finish the project in one sitting.
Gronke said it is important to be flexible and have fun.
“I try to create an environment of play,” Gronke said. “And a lot of people have talked about the power of improv as well. The attitude of whenever you can safely say yes and so if I think I’m going to be doing a certain kind of project with a person, I brought it, I’m all set up for it, and they go off in a different direction with it, that’s fine.”
Gronke said art therapy also benefits caregivers by giving them an opportunity to recapture a connection with a loved one or friend.
More information about art therapy is available at dementiaarttherapyalliance.org . The Dementia Art Therapy Alliance includes more than 20 schools nationwide and more than 500 volunteers.

title: Owner of St. Joseph Hospital agrees to pay $2M to settle data breach lawsuit
text:
The owner of St. Joseph Hospital in Bangor has agreed to pay $2 million to settle a class-action lawsuit over a major data breach last year.
In the 86-page settlement submitted to Penobscot County Superior Court, Covenant Health agreed to make two payments into an escrow account to cover claims stemming from the May 2025 infiltration of the system’s IT network.
Those affected by the data breach can receive a maximum payment of $5,000 for documented losses for which they haven’t already been reimbursed, according to the proposed settlement. But people can get a $75 cash payment without proving any losses. Covenant Health also will provide free credit monitoring for two years.
St. Joseph was hit by a cyberattack in May 2025, prompting the hospital to take its data systems offline.
That prompted a class-action lawsuit accusing the hospital and its parent company of negligence in protecting patient information. Among the information potentially compromised in the attack are Social Security numbers, dates of birth, names, phone numbers, emails and health information.
More than 500,000 patients, including nearly 300,000 in Maine, were affected by the data breach, vastly larger than the approximately 8,000 originally reported.
In addition to St. Joseph, Covenant owns St. Mary’s Health System in Lewiston and St. Andre Health Care in Biddeford.
As part of the proposed settlement, Covenant Health and its hospitals admit to no wrongdoing and patients participating in the settlement won’t pursue further legal action related to the data breach.

title: MaineHealth brings in 3rd party to reassess birthing unit closure
text:
MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital will host a public forum via Zoom on Wednesday to introduce independent experts reviewing the data and process behind the decision to close the labor and delivery unit at the hospital.
In a Monday press release, MaineHealth Vice President of Communications and Public Affairs Kathleen Taggersell said the review team will assess whether alternatives considered by the hospital’s management were “reasonable, feasible, and sustainable.”
On Aug. 6, MaineHealth voted to close the labor and delivery unit at Lincoln Hospital in Damariscotta on Friday, Dec. 18. The decision came after two other votes from the MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital Local Board and the Coastal Region Board.
In the announcement of the closure, MaineHealth said it will not close any additional labor and delivery programs anywhere in the health system during the next two years.
Under the new regional model, the Damariscotta and Brunswick-based hospitals would operate as “one coordinated regional OB-GYN and certified nurse midwife team,” hospital officials said in the announcement. Patients will be transitioned to MaineHealth Mid Coast Hospital in Brunswick.
Lincoln Hospital President Cindy Wade said in a Tuesday interview that the creation of the review team and forum is for transparency, as well as more input on the assessment and to see if there are any alternatives that can be approached. The research will consider if the decision to close the labor and delivery unit is reasonable and appropriate, she said.
“It’s really transparency, but also, because they have in-depth experience in rural maternity care, workforce sustainability, community engagement, and other things,” Wade said.
According to the press release, the five-member review team brings in knowledge from areas such as maternal-fetal medicine, family medicine, nurse midwifery, public health and healthcare operations.
Wade said the idea for the review came after the Legislature’s Health Coverage, Insurance, and Financial Services Committee held a hearing on Aug. 27, at which committee members suggested a third-party review of the assessment that led to the decision to close the unit.
She said after conversation at the senior team level of MaineHealth, the organization decided to move forward with creating a review team to see if all possibilities were looked at and considered.
At the Wednesday forum, community members will be able to meet who is on the team and can send in questions beforehand to a designated email.
Taggersell said reviewers are free to reach conclusions that differ from those of MaineHealth or other stakeholders. If the review team comes up with any opposing information, Wade said it would remain in the hands of MaineHealth’s three boards — local, regional and system — if there will be reconsideration of the closure.
“I’m appreciative of the fact that we’ve been able to have independent experts come in and take a look at this,” Wade said. “I think that is certainly, you know, something we welcome. So, we look forward to hearing what their feedback is.”
The review team is expected to have a full report by Dec. 11 and Wade said it will then be up to the MaineHealth system to make a consideration based on the results.
Conversation surrounding the closure started before the decision was made. For months, community members, including the grassroots Miles Delivers Action Coalition, pushed back against the closure, bringing in attention for local and state politicians. The coalition has since transitioned its work to focusing on reversing the decision and finding alternatives to the closure.
In a Sunday email from the coalition, members urged the community to submit public comments by Friday to support the state’s proposed maternity care closure rules and asking the Maine Department of Health and Human Services to “strengthen them further.”
The email references that Maine recently enacted a law that requires hospitals give a 120-day notice before closing labor and delivery services, pushing for the citizen-led petition to use the legislation in favor of reversing the decision.
On April 3, Gov. Janet Mills signed LD 2189, An Act to require Prior Notification of Closures of Labor and Delivery Units and Changes in Maternity or Newborn Care Services by Hospitals as Recommended by the Commission to Evaluation the Scope of Regulatory Review and Oversight over Health Care Transactions That Impact the Delivery of Health Care Services in the State.
“But advance alone isn’t enough,” the email said. “Patients need clear communication, continuity of care, and assurance that hospitals are prepared for obstetric.”
The independent review public forum is from 6-7 p.m. Wednesday. Questions for the review team can be sent in advance to lincolnfeedback@mainehealth.org.

title: More than 34 million people got new congressional districts
text:
Redistricting map: How mid-decade changes are shaping the 2026 midterm elections
A mid-decade congressional redistricting battle has played out for more than a year now, reassigning millions of people to new districts.
Our Get the Facts Data Team broke down what to know about redistricting ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
What is redistricting?
Redistricting is the process of redrawing congressional district boundaries every 10 years, which occurs after population counts come out following the decennial census.
Most recently, the regular redistricting process for states occurred after the 2020 decennial census. But ever since, nine states have new congressional districts for the 2026 midterm elections. Multiple other states have attempted to redraw districts.
Just two other states have voluntarily redrawn districts to give a party advantage in between census cycles since 1970, according to Pew Research Center.
What districts were targeted?
Both Democrats and Republicans targeted specific districts, starting with the five targeted in Texas when President Donald Trump asked the state to redraw boundaries.
California followed in response, redrawing boundaries in favor of Democrats to target five districts.
Several states didn't succeed in their redistricting battles, but ahead of the 2026 elections, nine states are using new congressional district boundaries. There were 15 districts redrawn potentially favoring Republicans, and six districts redrawn to favor Democrats, adding up to a net of nine districts favoring Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives.
Six of the 21 targeted districts were rated as a toss-up, according to race ratings from The Cook Political Report.
Some that were previously rated as a toss-up or as leaning Democrat are actually rated even more likely to sway Democrat now, including Ohio's 1st congressional district. In Ohio, the new districts were adopted last year to boost Republican chances in two districts.
How many people have new districts?
More than 34 million people were assigned to new districts, according to an analysis from Protect Democracy. That's about one in every 10 Americans.
Utah has the highest share of people reassigned districts at more than 69% of voters. The new congressional districts were court-ordered after state judges ruled that state Republicans violated anti-gerrymandering laws.
The representative of Utah's 1st congressional district is currently held by a Republican, but is rated by The Cook Political Report to shift from solid Republican to solid Democrat.
Other states, including Texas, Louisiana, Tennessee and Florida, have roughly a third of voters being reassigned districts.

title: The relationship between Christian nationalism and Americans’ views of democracy
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The number of Americans who identify with Christian nationalism is slightly declining, but religion remains a large part of politics for both candidates and voters ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
“We see where Americans fall on this spectrum of Christian nationalism, which really tells us a lot about what they think democracy is and how it’s functioning,” said Andrew Whitehead, a professor of sociology at Indiana University Indianapolis and a research fellow for the Charles F. Kettering Foundation.
Whitehead cited data from the Kettering Foundation and Gallup’s annual national survey of more than 23,000 adults. He said around 14% of the U.S. population strongly embraces Christian nationalism, with just over 16% at least sympathetic to it.
Christian nationalism is the belief that Christianity defines the nation and the government should take active steps to keep it that way.
“Even though there are fewer Americans who embrace Christian nationalism, there are Americans in positions of power in federal government and media who will take that rhetoric of Christian nationalism and really make it part of the national discourse,” Whitehead said. “So fewer Americans embrace it strongly, but it is much more a part of our national political discussions than it ever used to be.”
Among white Americans, 31% are at least sympathetic to Christian nationalism. A third of men are at least sympathetic, while 28% of women responded similarly.
Christian nationalism is also strongly associated with political party. More than half of Republicans, 55%, strongly embrace or sympathize with it.
Whitehead said Americans who embrace Christian nationalism and those who reject it view democracy differently.
“They’re more worried about certain threats, quote unquote, to democracy than are Americans who reject Christian nationalism,” he explained. “When we asked them about how democracy is functioning, Americans who strongly embrace Christian nationalism right now say democracy is doing great; for those that reject it, very few think democracy is doing well or even okay.”
Whitehead said the nearly 70% of respondents who resist or reject Christian nationalism are being driven to the polls this midterm cycle.
“Right now, they’re very motivated for Congress to check the power of the executive branch,” he added, “something that hasn’t been happening in these first two years of the Trump administration.”
It is far more common for Republicans to combine religion and politics, but this election cycle, five Democrats are on the ballot in Congressional races who are clergy or in training to become clergy.

title: Covenant Health reaches settlement in data breach lawsuit
text:
Covenant Health reaches settlement in data breach lawsuit
Covenant Health has reached a $2 million settlement in a class action lawsuit filed after a May 2025 data breach compromised sensitive patient information. More than 280,000 patients in Maine were impacted. Covenant Health owns St. Joseph Healthcare in Bangor and St. Mary's in Lewiston.
Plaintiff Michael McClain filed the complaint on behalf of himself and others whose personal and medical information was allegedly exposed during the breach. The lawsuit accused Covenant Health of failing to properly protect patients' private information.
It claimed the breach was preventable and resulted from the defendants' failure to implement standard cybersecurity practices. It also alleged that affected individuals now face an increased risk of identity theft and fraud.
In the settlement agreement, Covenant Health denies any wrongdoing. A spokesperson told Maine's Total Coverage, "We have agreed to the settlement so that our resources and attention are focused on what matters most in our ministry: the patients and residents who entrust us with their care and the communities we have the privilege of serving."
The impacted Maine patients may submit proof of documented losses related to the Data Incident for cash payments up to $5,000, or they can receive a $75 cash payment without documentation. That amount may vary based on the number of valid claims.
In addition to the cash payment, they will be automatically enrolled in a program for credit monitoring, dark web monitoring, real-time authentication alerts, high-risk transaction monitoring, lost wallet protection, and insurance coverage for up to $1,000,000 for identity theft.
Before the payout begins, the settlement must first be approved by a judge.

title: As a historic measles outbreak hits Pennsylvania Amish country, more show openness to vaccines
text:
EPHRATA, Pa. (AP) — Amish and Mennonite shoppers in conservative dress mingled with shoppers from the wider public on a recent Friday at a vast outdoor market here, where vendors sold colorful pumpkins and mums, fry pies and squash, sports jerseys and Barbie accessories.
Such interactions are common in Lancaster County in central Pennsylvania, home to the largest Amish population in the U.S. — and the epicenter of the nation’s worst measles outbreak in 35 years. While they avoid many types of civic engagement for religious reasons, the Amish — like many other groups vulnerable to measles across the nation — are not truly separate.
“We are all interconnected,” said Dr. Diego Hijano of St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital.
Robust vaccination rates once protected Americans much better.
But rates among the general public are now falling, and rates have long been low among the Amish, creating the perfect conditions for the contagious virus — officially considered “eliminated” from the U.S. since 2000 — to spread here and beyond.
Pennsylvania has the most U.S. cases, with over 1,350 this year, more than a third in Lancaster County alone, according to state figures. That’s a big undercount, community leaders say, since many people with measles never see a doctor.
The state has recorded three measles-associated deaths in Lancaster and two in other counties.
In Amish country, a measles surge poses questions about vaccine acceptance
The outbreak has especially hit the “Plain communities” of Amish and conservative Mennonites — so named for their modest dress and limited use of technology. Vaccination rates, and attitudes about vaccines, range widely. But overall, they are less likely to be vaccinated than the general population, due more to culture and habit than doctrine.
Many are now showing a new openness to vaccines, while members of the general public are also taking extra precautions.
All of this has underscored the interconnectedness of Plain and wider “English” populations.
The Plain People avoid such areas of civic participation as holding public office. Still, they regularly shop and do business with their neighbors in this growing county of half a million people, where an urban core is ringed by suburban subdivisions abutting Amish farms.
“There’s no way to imagine that this is going to be an isolated community,” said Dr. Anne-Marie Derrico, chief medical officer at the nonprofit Union Community Care. It has clinics in the city of Lancaster and outlying towns, along with a mobile unit operating a “Plain Healthy” outreach to the Amish and to Mennonites.
“We have Plain patients coming to the city, we have patients in the city who don’t vaccinate, who are going to school, going to other programs with other children,” Derrico said.
Pennsylvania’s measles rates have declined from their September peak, but some doctors expect them to rise as winter brings more indoor gatherings.
While most cases are mild, measles can cause serious and even fatal complications, such as pneumonia and encephalitis.
Union has held small-scale vaccine clinics to reach Plain populations, resulting in about 450 measles shots. “That’s hopefully made a significant impact,” Derrico said.
Union’s clinics are also offering vaccinations for infants earlier than normally scheduled, as health experts advise in areas experiencing measles outbreaks.
Lauren and Mason Spence brought their 10-month-old son, Bowen, to a clinic recently to get his first dose of the MMR vaccine, short for measles, mumps and rubella. The “English” family frequently goes to public places, including farmers markets.
“It’s scary,” Lauren Spence said. “It’s spreading quick.”
Vaccine views vary among Plain people
Attitudes toward vaccines in Plain communities have alternately warmed and cooled over time — most recently cooling in reaction to strict COVID-19 public health measures, according to community leaders and scholars. The measles outbreak is prompting many to accept the shots while reinforcing vaccine skepticism in others.
One Amish farmer, Ephraim Zook, still opposes vaccines even after he and his wife nursed their young twins through the illness. “We just felt that measles is a natural thing,” he said.
A Mennonite market vendor said his largely vaccinated community has had no infections.
One Plain farmer said he got vaccinated after his adult siblings began getting measles. With vegetables to harvest and tobacco leaves to pick, “I thought, if I get it, I’m going to be done,” he said.
Most interviewed by the AP asked not to use their names, in keeping with Plain traditions of not calling attention to themselves.
Those who avoid vaccines usually aren’t driven by ideology, community leaders and experts say.
“The overwhelming reason had nothing to do with being against vaccinations,” said Allen Hoover, an Old Order Mennonite and former administrator of the Parochial Medical Center in the town of New Holland. “It was simply, ‘Well, we never did before, and we came through all right.’”
Hoover said the most effective strategy for medical workers is to encourage vaccination — not to push it aggressively.
It takes time for outside professionals to build trust in Plain communities, he said.
About how long?
“Twenty years,” he said.
One cluster of Amish schools and individuals in New York is asking the U.S. Supreme Court to require their state to allow exemptions to school vaccine requirements on religious grounds, as Pennsylvania and most states do.
But the wider Amish leadership hasn’t presented this as a religious issue, according to Steve Nolt, director of the Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies at Elizabethtown College in Lancaster County.
“There’s nothing in Amish theology or historic documents that you can find that specifically addresses or is opposed to immunization,” he said.
About 45,000 Amish and 6,000 Old Order Mennonites live in and around Lancaster County, according to the Young Center. Many rely on traditional remedies and visit doctors infrequently, Nolt said.
This year’s outbreak follows ones in 2025 in Mennonite communities in Texas and elsewhere across North America.
Contagious virus is a rising threat to everyone
Measles spreads easily when people who have it breathe, cough or sneeze, or through contaminated surfaces.
“Measles is really the lion king of infectious diseases when it comes to transmission,” said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. “No one in the United States of America who is susceptible to the measles virus, either having not been vaccinated or not having previously had it, should feel safe from measles. No one.”
The risk grows as vaccination rates decline.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received the required MMR shots. That’s down from 95.2% in 2019-20.
“Though Plain communities are an easy and recognizable target, declining childhood vaccination rates in our county are not limited to the Amish,” wrote Berwood Yost, director of the Center for Opinion Research at Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster, in a recent commentary. “Kindergarten vaccination rates have declined in every central Pennsylvania county since 2020.”
A 2022 survey by the center found the vast majority of Mennonite families reported having their children vaccinated, compared to about 3 in 10 Amish families.
Yost urged the public not to blame the Amish, or any group, for the outbreak. “Every one of us is susceptible to misinformation and confusing messages,” he wrote.
Vaccine hesitancy that rose across populations during the pandemic still lingers.
That’s eroded “herd immunity,” which occurs when enough people in an area have immunity to measles that it no longer spreads easily. Although nothing short of 100% immunity guarantees the virus won’t spread, an outbreak is considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate.
Pennsylvania’s kindergarten MMR vaccination rate fell to 93.2% last year.
Lancaster County’s rate is 88%, with rates lower in the county’s religious and other private schools than in public schools, according to an AP review of state data.
Across the county and state, the percentage of students receiving religious or philosophical exemptions from at least one required vaccination has risen significantly.
Nolt said some anti-vaccine groups targeted the Amish with their messaging.
In 2021, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who helped lead the anti-vaccine movement for years, spoke at a Lancaster County fair, alleging the government was trying to force the Amish to vaccinate.
Now U.S. health secretary, Kennedy recently sparred with Pennsylvania’s Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, over the extent of the outbreak. Further controversy ensued when the county coroner attributed the death of a measles-infected infant to a ruptured spleen, not the disease itself.
After a decline in trust, some minds are changing
Lancaster County Commissioner Alice Yoder said public officials should unite behind the message that the vaccine is safe and effective and should encourage people to get it.
That approach succeeded during Pennsylvania’s last measles outbreak in 1991.
“There were lines of people in the Plain community that would come and get vaccinated,” she said.
Dr. D. Holmes Morton, who founded the Central Pennsylvania Clinic in Mifflin County — which treats Plain patients with genetic diseases — said the same is happening now.
“We are having more success at having vaccine days,” he said.
Ultimately, this will keep everyone safer, said Hijano of St. Jude.
Getting the shot is “an act of love to your community,” he said. “You will get protected yourself. But in truth, you are actually protecting everyone around you.”

title: Methylene blue: What to know about textile dye being used as a wellness supplement
text:
Methylene blue: What to know about textile dye being used as a wellness supplement
Name a substance that can disinfect your aquarium tank, dye fabric and treat a rare blood disorder.
Here's a hint: Social media users went bonkers last year when they surmised U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was stirring it into his drinking water. The answer is methylene blue.
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com's Well Informed.
This synthetic textile dye, created in 1876, has shown promise in treating and diagnosing a variety of medical conditions, but it’s also being misleadingly promoted and sold by wellness influencers as a cutting-edge anti-aging supplement.
It’s hard to find anyone who would not want to ward off Alzheimer’s disease and sharpen the mind, but only sparse data backs claims that methylene blue will help. Taking this substance without medical supervision is risky.
Related video above: Trump administration addresses health care price transparency
Here are the facts.
A textile dye used in medicine
Medical researchers began using methylene blue to stain microorganisms and, in 1891, discovered it could treat malaria.
Over the years, the medical uses for methylene blue grew. In the early 1930s, it was discovered as an antidote to cyanide poisoning, and it was also used as an early psychiatric medication.
Currently, the only Food and Drug Administration-approved use for methylene blue is to treat methemoglobinemia, a rare blood condition that restricts blood cells from delivering oxygen throughout the body. The condition can be genetic, or caused by specific chemicals, recreational drugs or pain medications. Patients with this condition receive methylene blue through an IV.
Doctors sometimes use methylene blue off-label to treat vasodilatory shock, neurotoxicity from the chemotherapy drug ifosfamide or to enhance light-therapy for skin conditions or cancers. It’s also used in diagnostics, for highlighting polyps during colonoscopies, staining tissue samples or detecting if cancer has spread to a nearby lymph node.
What all of these uses have in common is that they happen under medical supervision and a doctor's care.
Evidence of brain benefits is mostly from lab and animal studies
On TikTok, you’ll find countless videos of people putting drops of methylene blue on their tongues or in their water and attesting it boosted their energy and sharpened their thinking.
The purported benefits are numerous: improved cognitive function, slowed aging, Alzheimer’s prevention, cancer prevention and more.
These claims lack solid evidence. Some research shows it offers cellular benefits by assisting cells’ energy powerhouse — mitochondria. It’s unclear, however, how those benefits apply to humans.
That’s because most of the supportive evidence we have so far comes from laboratory or animal studies. One study in humans found that methylene blue reduced, rather than increased, blood flow and oxygen metabolism in the brain.
Raphael E. Cuomo, University of California San Diego professor of medicine, said methylene blue has the potential to support cellular energy production and, in some cases, reduce oxidative stress — an imbalance in the body’s antioxidants that can cause problems for cells and tissue.
“Small studies in healthy adults have explored memory and brain activity, but lasting cognitive benefits remain unproven,” Cuomo said.
A study of 26 people found that one dose of methylene blue improved accuracy on a memory retrieval task. Lorne J. Hofseth, a University of South Carolina pharmacy professor, said that finding gave researchers “preliminary support” to keep studying it, but didn’t establish that it would lead to sustained mental sharpness when used routinely.
Laboratory studies show that methylene blue or related compounds may affect certain proteins tied to Alzheimer's, but research is still needed before it can be a recommended treatment.
Based on current data, the claims that taking methylene blue will slow aging, or prevent cancer and Alzheimer’s "go beyond the clinical evidence," Cuomo said.
Taking methylene blue without medical supervision can be dangerous
Methylene blue is not just a fun way to turn your tongue (and urine) blue.
It can dangerously interact with other medications, including common antidepressants that increase serotonin levels. Methylene blue has a similar effect as the medications, so when they are taken together, it can cause serotonin syndrome, a medical emergency in which the body gets overloaded with serotonin.
Methylene blue is also dangerous for people with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, a common genetic disorder that can have no symptoms, which means people may not know they have it.
When someone with G6PD takes methylene blue, it can cause hemolytic anemia, a life-threatening condition that can cause your body to destroy red blood cells faster than they can be created.
It should also not be taken while pregnant.
Other worrisome interactions are more mundane. People taking methylene blue may want to avoid foods and drinks rich in tyramine, including red wine, beer, and aged cheeses and meats or otherwise risk uncontrolled high blood pressure.
And taking too much methylene blue can trigger methemoglobinemia — the condition it is FDA-approved to treat.
For these reasons, "methylene blue should be monitored in a medical setting by someone who understands the risks associated with the drug," said Dr. Mazie Tsang a hematologist at the Mayo Clinic. "If taken without medical supervision, people could be exposed to life-threatening events. The harms outweigh any potential benefits."
Unlike a prescribed medication, methylene blue purchased online may vary in dosage, purity, and contain unknown ingredients.
Plus, it is easy to buy the wrong version. Methylene blue is still sold online as aquarium treatment or dye, so someone may order methylene blue not safe for human consumption.
"Given the unproven benefits and established risks, I would not recommend routine use as a wellness supplement," Cuomo said.
This article originally appeared on PolitiFact.com's Well Informed.
It is republished here as part of a reporting and fact-checking partnership between PolitiFact and Hearst Television.

title: 'Time is the fire in which we burn': 2 major cast losses rock the passionate 'Star Trek' universe
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — One of the countless memorable lines that have tumbled out of the “Star Trek” universe over the years is this gem, originally from a 20th-century poet named Delmore Schwartz: “Time is the fire in which we burn.”
It was uttered as an existential warning to Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in the 1994 film “Star Trek Generations.” But it feels equally apt this week after a one-two punch of loss that is hitting hard for devotees of the epic, six-decade science fiction saga.
First, on Sunday, Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov in the original series during the 1960s, died at age 90. Then, on Thursday, the cosmos lost Patrick Stewart, a Shakespearean actor who in 1987 began to inhabit Picard, the poetic face of that show’s sequel, “Star Trek: The Next Generation,” and decades later the anchor of the darker streaming drama “Star Trek: Picard.”
For a fan base that has long signed on as acolytes of a brighter, more equitable future, recent days have given the present an unwelcome sting.
“What a heartbreaking week it has been,” said William Shatner, who played Capt. James T. Kirk in the original series from 1966 to 1969 and went on to star in six movie sequels. He is one of only two members of that long-ago cast still living; Leonard “Spock” Nimoy, his best friend on the show — and off and on in real life — died in 2015.
‘Star Trek’ has infiltrated modern mass culture in myriad ways
For all the characterizations of it as nerdy over the years — something many fans have come to accept cheerfully — “Star Trek” has long been at the vanguard of modern-day mythmaking. That has helped it seep into the culture in various ways, vacuuming up disciples as it goes.
The earliest space shuttle was christened “Enterprise” after the show’s flagship after a mass letter-writing campaign persuaded President Gerald Ford to rename it, and the cast attended the ship’s introduction. The handheld “communicators” from the show helped inspire early flip phones. Phrases like “Beam me up, Scotty,” “He’s dead, Jim” and “Make it so” have infiltrated society ad nauseam. (The first one was never actually spoken verbatim on the show.)
Today, as the end of a decade-long streaming run of “new Trek” approaches and the franchise’s longtime godfather, Paramount, rumbles into a new corporate era, Trek fans are legion and global and wondering what happens next.
They haunt online forums by the millions, discussing and arguing about themes, stories and minutiae — particularly “canon,” or how well the fictional universe adheres to or violates its own rules. Things can get contentious and aggressive for a fan base that has signed on for peaceful and utopian tomorrows.
This week, those same forums, now turned somber, are awash with tributes and laments — first for Koenig and now for Stewart. At the same time, the sense of mortality is palpable. “Bubble wrap George Takei and William Shatner ASAP,” one post on X said.
Fellow actors in the now-sizable cadre from various shows — and those behind the scenes, too — weighed in on the loss of two people who were, for them, legends.
“His Captain Jean-Luc Picard permanently expanded the universe of Star Trek without measure,” Akiva Goldsman, co-creator of “Star Trek: Picard,” said of Stewart.
Planting the roots of a diverse future
Koenig was introduced in the show’s second season for two key reasons. First, his character was a Russian in an era of U.S.-Soviet Cold War tension, part of creator Gene Roddenberry’s effort to build a diverse cast that was groundbreaking for its era and featured, among others, a Japanese helmsman and a Bantu communications officer — not to mention the then-progressive presence of women in authority. Second, Koenig’s Beatle-like looks, complete with mop-top, were calibrated to entice younger fans vibing at the time to the Monkees.
Koenig, oddly, was the first Chekov to exist but is not the first to die. His young counterpart in the lightly rebooted “Kelvin” universe series of “Star Trek” movies that began in 2009, the Soviet-born Anton Yelchin, was killed in 2016 when his car pinned him against a gate outside his Los Angeles home.
With Koenig’s death, only two members of the original cast remain: Shatner and Takei, who played helmsman Hikaru Sulu. The two, who have had an occasionally prickly relationship across the decades, both remain active at ages 95 and 89 respectively. Shatner, a raconteur who has seemingly boundless energy, recently unveiled his latest project — front man for a heavy-metal band. Takei remains in the public eye on social media with his “Oh, Myyyy” content.
Takei and Koenig, who sat together on the Enterprise bridge as helmsman and navigator, were close in real life. On Monday, Takei said his “heart was heavy.”
“He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend,” Takei said of Koenig. “Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course.”
Optimism amid the mourning is very ‘Trek’
Ever since the early 1980s, when Capt. Kirk said bitterly that “Galloping around the cosmos is a game for the young,” the “Star Trek” universe has embraced aging and mortality. It became a theme in many productions, perhaps most prominently from 2020 to 2023 in “Star Trek: Picard.”
Even so, the ethos of “Star Trek” has always been optimism and life. Even its darkest iterations, like “Star Trek: Deep Space Nine,” have been suffused with the notion that humanity — which has always, in the show’s universe, meant far more than humans — would endure and thrive.
“Spock, you want to know something?” Kirk once said to his first officer. “Everybody’s human.” Responded Spock, dryly: “I find that remark … insulting.”
That exchange came in “Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country,” a 1991 end-of-the-Cold War political thriller that was the final film to feature the entire original cast. The story focused on the idea of the undiscovered country being the future, and the journey ended in the galactic equivalent of what John F. Kennedy once called “a hard and bitter peace.”
In truth, though, Shakespeare — whose work has infused not only the various incarnations of “Trek” but the careers of its two most prominent actors, Shatner and Stewart — meant something else when he coined the phrase. “The undiscover’d country, from whose bourn no traveller returns,” he writes in “Hamlet.” In short: death.
But with “Star Trek,” as with Shakespeare, the show must go on. That’s exactly what Shatner, then at the ripe old age of 77, told this writer when they spent the day together in 2008: “None of us will be around forever,” he said, “but ‘Star Trek’ will.”
___
Ted Anthony, director of new storytelling and newsroom innovation at The Associated Press, has been watching “Star Trek” since he was 18 months old. His younger son’s middle name is Kirk, which is not a coincidence.

title: Two Westbrook restaurants listed for sale
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Two downtown Westbrook restaurants, Stockhouse Restaurant and Sports Pub and Brea Lu Cafe, are on the market.
Stockhouse, which opened in 2005 at 506 Main St., is listed on buybizsell.com for $800,000. Brea Lu Cafe is listed on the same site for $275,000. The Brea Lu listing notes that the seller is “motivated” and hopes to sell by the end of the year.
The owners of both restaurants could not be reached for comment before deadline.
Brea Lu originally opened in 1989 on Forest Avenue in Portland. The restaurant moved to Cumberland Street in Westbrook after a devastating 2016 fire at the Portland property. It moved to Main Street in 2024.

title: Mariners score in overtime to earn 3rd straight win
text:
Linus Hemstrom scored in overtime and the Maine Mariners beat the Trois-Rivieres Lions, 3-2, in an ECHL game Friday in Trois-Rivieres, Quebec.
Kalle Vaisanen scored in the second period, with assists from Ben Allison and Mason Primeau, to give Maine a 1-0 lead. Anthony Beauregard tied it later in the period.
The Mariners regained the lead when Robert Cronin scored 3:12 into the third peirod, but the Lions tied it with 19 seconds left in regulation on a goal by Mathieu Bizier.
Luke Cavallin made 34 saves for Maine. Francesco Lapenna stopped 30 shots for Trois-Rivieres.
The teams face off again at 1 p.m. Saturday.

title: Covenant Health reaches settlement in data breach lawsuit
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WMTW) - Covenant Health has agreed to a $2 million class-action settlement following a data breach that affected more than 280,000 patients in Maine.
The system operates St. Joseph Healthcare in Bangor and St. Mary’s in Lewiston.
The lawsuit accused the provider of failing to maintain proper cybersecurity. Covenant denies wrongdoing, saying the deal allows them to refocus on patient care.
Impacted patients can claim up to 75 dollars in cash without documentation, or up to $5,000 for documented losses.
They’ll also receive free credit monitoring and up to $1 million in identity theft insurance.
A judge must still approve the settlement.

title: She says she was abused by a Maine priest 60 years ago, but wasn’t invited to church settlement process
text:
When she was 8 years old, Kimberly Watkins Stevens said, she was sexually abused by a Catholic priest in Windham.
More than a dozen other adults have reported they were abused by the same priest, the Rev. Lawrence Sabatino, in the 1950s and 1960s. They recently resolved their civil claims against the Roman Catholic Bishop of Portland through a settlement process — except for Stevens, now 68, whose attorney says she was not invited to participate.
“There is unfortunately nothing unique to this claim from Ms. Stevens,” her attorney Mitchell Garabedian said Friday.
He said he brought her case to the Roman Catholic bishop of Portland in 2021, when the state changed its law to allow anyone to sue for child sexual abuse, regardless of previous statutes of limitations. The Maine Supreme Judicial Court overturned that law last year after an appeal by the diocese.
Stevens, a Maine resident, can’t sue the diocese for child sexual abuse under current law. Garabedian said the diocese has refused to engage with settlement requests for more than five years.
A spokesperson for the Roman Catholic bishop of Portland declined to comment on Friday.
Stevens said she met Sabatino when she was a child through friends who were Catholic. Standing outside the chancery in Portland on Friday morning, with Garabedian on the phone, she recalled how Sabatino used to pick the children up and bring them to St. Peter’s Parish. She said she would wait until he finished Mass, and then he would take them to get a treat from a bakery.
She said Sabatino hung on to the treats until he took them to a property in Windham, where he would play “hide and go seek” with Stevens and the other children. During the visits to the property, she said, he would sexually abuse her. Stevens said she was abused five times before Sabatino invited her to a sleepover, which is when her parents said she couldn’t see him anymore.
Garabedian, a Massachusetts attorney who specializes in sexual abuse cases, said the diocese should have known at the time that Sabatino had been accused several times of abusing children. In 1958, a girl’s mother tried reporting him to police. Sabatino was assigned to nine different parishes over more than 30 years before he died in 1990, according to previous reporting.
He was later included on a list of 20 “credibly accused” clergy that the Office of the Maine Attorney General released following an investigation into the diocese in 2004.
The diocese recently resolved more than 100 claims against the church, involving allegations against several different clergy. Some of the claims were filed as lawsuits, others were never made public. Many included claims that were no longer able to be brought following the high court decision in 2025.
Attorneys for some of the plaintiffs said the diocese only agreed to settle the older claims if all of their clients with active claims agreed to participate. At least one woman also had to agree she wouldn’t sue a different religious order, the Brothers of the Sacred Heart, which employed a priest who pleaded guilty in 1988 to two counts of unlawful sexual contact with a 15-year-old girl.
Attorneys who were involved in the settlements declined to say how much was paid, but one attorney said it was a seven-figure amount.
Garabedian said he had asked the diocese for $2 million for Stevens.
Stevens said on Friday she learned about the settlements from news coverage. She said she wanted to share her story to bring attention to how that diocese has treated her case. She sought help through counseling and has struggled through many low periods, she said. Stevens said she was recently baptized and is a practicing protestant and has found some comfort in her faith.
She said she prays daily.
“But I did go through a time where it was like, how can a priest do this to me?” she said. “And how can I believe in anything?”

title: Early voting turnout is high. Election fatigue is building
text:
Mainers are turning out in high numbers to cast their ballots early as a controversy-ridden campaign season nears the finish line in Maine.
Nearly 245,000 Mainers voted early this year, either by mail or in-person, as of Oct. 28, according to data from the Maine Secretary of State’s office. Thursday was the last day to request an absentee ballot or vote in the presence of a clerk.
Some town clerks reported that the number of voters casting their ballots early are nearing presidential election turnout numbers. In the November 2024 general election, 388,815 people in Maine cast their ballots early or by mail.
It’s not possible to know yet which candidates are garnering the most early votes. It is possible to know, however, which party’s early voters are turning out the most.
More than 118,000 Democrats and 54,000 Republicans have voted absentee so far. More than 66,000 unenrolled voters have also voted absentee, according to data from the Secretary of State’s office.
Even before early voting began for the day at 8:30 a.m. on Oct. 28, a line of people had formed on the second floor of city hall in Portland to vote. More than 16,000 Portland residents have requested mail-in ballots, state numbers show.
One city hall worker told a reporter on Wednesday, “It’s like Six Flags up there.”
Portland resident Lydia Savage said she waited 40 minutes in line at city hall to cast her ballot on Monday. Others waiting were generally in a good mood and passed updates down the line about how many people were ahead, she said.
Savage said she was delighted to vote early for the first time.
“The campaigns have been harsher than I’ve ever seen,” Savage said. “I just wanted to be done with it.”
Other towns in Maine have also seen high turnout for early voting.
Auburn City Clerk Emily Carrington said the city has seen higher absentee turnout this gubernatorial election cycle. Of the 4,833 ballots that were issued, 4,330 ballots have been returned so far. During the last gubernatorial election in 2022, Carrington said there were 3,634 absentee voters.
Still, the turnout does not surpass presidential election data: In 2024, 6,120 people voted absentee in Auburn.
Some smaller towns are seeing more early voting than in past midterm elections. Litchfield, which has approximately 2,500 active voters, had received about 675 absentee votes as of midday on Oct. 29. Deputy Registrar of Voters and Deputy Clerk Libby Rodrigue expected that total to reach about 700 by the end of the day, which would be comparable to the 2024 presidential election.
Casco has about 2,600 registered voters. As of early afternoon yesterday, 741 absentee ballots had been requested and 624 brought back. For the last presidential election, about 1,000 ballots were submitted early, according to the town clerk’s office.
Other towns are seeing manageable turnouts in early voting. Brunswick Town Hall, which normally closes on Fridays, kept its doors open on Oct. 23 to accommodate voters. Though not as busy as other cities such as Portland, three temporary assistant town clerks had received a steady trickle of in-person absentee voters.
Some Mainers are feeling fatigued from a rocky campaign year, which included explosive revelations about former Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate Graham Platner and a steady trade of political attack ads between Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson.
For some Mainers, voting in a challenging political climate does not feel worth it.
“All of it is such rubbish,” said a retired Navy man from Portland who asked not to be identified by name.
He said he feels disillusioned with the political system and therefore does not vote. He specifically named former Republican Gov. Paul LePage, who is running to represent the 2nd District in the U.S. House; Collins; and Jackson as candidates who have disappointed him.
“It isn’t about politics anymore, it’s about belittling the next person,” said another man, from South Portland, who declined to provide his name; he said he hadn’t voted since President Jimmy Carter was in office.
Falmouth resident Rachel Doe, who dropped her mail-in ballot at her town hall ahead of election day, said she’s voted early ever since she had kids. It’s easier to manage the timing of voting that way, she said, and dropping her ballot off in person means there’s no risk of delays in the mail.
But she’s ready for the season of fierce campaigns for Senate, Congress and local seats to be over. She said door-to-door canvassers and campaign calls are frequent, and there is a lot of pressure in the current political climate.
“It feels intense,” she said. “[I’m] getting a lot of phone calls.”
Portland resident Darrel Williams waited in line at city hall to vote but ultimately left when he realized how long it would take. He had a meeting that he couldn’t be late for and planned to return to vote later on Thursday.
Williams said he hadn’t seen such long lines before in previous election cycles. Several issues might be drawing people out, he said: the cost of living, immigration enforcement and general dissatisfaction. Williams, who is Black, said he is seeing society revert backward on issues such as racism, xenophobia and classism.
“The next generation should not have to battle those things,” Williams said.
Reporters Delger Erdenesanaa, Sean Scott and Rose Lundy contributed reporting.
This story was originally published by The Maine Monitor, a nonprofit civic news organization. To get regular coverage from The Monitor, sign up for a free Monitor newsletter here.

title: Protester thrown out at Trump rally after heckling president about Epstein
text:
(AP) - Early in his remarks as he took the stage Wednesday during a campaign rally in Chillicothe, Ohio, President Donald Trump was interrupted by a protester shouting about Jeffrey Epstein.
Trump rarely brings up Epstein, his former friend, but remarked on it Wednesday at the Shoemaker Center at Ohio University Chillicothe. He repeated comments he made last year saying that he threw Epstein out of his Florida club about two decades ago.
“That was a great thing I did, I must tell you,” Trump said.
He added: “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago.”
After he was interrupted by two more protesters, Trump returned to his remarks and pivoted immediately into praising Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s physique.

title: Obituary: Virginia “Ginny” McQuarrie
text:
BATH – Virginia “Ginny” McQuarrie was born in Bath, Maine, on June 1, 1923. It is hard to put into words all that encompassed her 103 years, except to say her focus and joy was always her family, as she was theirs. She was the only child of Lucille Donnell and Everett Stilphin.
Ginny was educated in the Bath School system and was a member of the Morse High class of 1942. Very much in love, she married her childhood sweetheart James McQuarrie. She was employed at Belangers Gift and Music Shop in the 40s & 50s until she and Jim started a family and raised their two children, Janis and Jeffrey. Ginny and Jim were happily married for nearly 50 years, being active members of Knights of Columbus and Daughters of Isabella and frequently visiting Boston to see daughter Janis’ three children, Sheila, Barbara, and Michael, and attend Red Sox games.
Ginny volunteered at the soup kitchen and beano at the Bath Nursing Home. She was a communicant at St. Mary’s Church and a member of the Bath Senior Citizens Center. To all who knew her, Ginny was a sweet, impish, funny, and vibrant force who brightened any room with her smile.
She was the strong, beloved matriarch of her family, who knew her as Mimi, and her love and nurturing were gratefully reciprocated by her family who were privileged to return to her to provide care and allow her to spend her final years in her home on Dummer Street.
She was predeceased by her husband Jim; her son Jeffrey McQuarrie; grandson Michael Bramer; as well as a special cousin, Mary Elliott.
She is survived by daughter Janis McQuarrie; granddaughters Sheila McQuarrie and Barbara Bramer; cousins Sandy Elliott, Marnie Kaler, Katahdin Staples and Steve Vachon.
Visiting hours will be held at Desmond’s Funeral Home, 638 High St, Bath, on Monday, Nov. 2, from 1 to 3 p.m. Funeral services will be held at St Mary’s Church, 144 Lincoln St, Bath, on Tuesday, Nov. 3, at 11 a.m.
To share your thoughts and condolences with the family, please visit http://www.desmondfuneralhomes.com.

title: Opinion: Susan Collins is a champion for broadband connectivity, and for Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Drew Petersen is senior vice president of corporate affairs for TDS Telecom.
High-speed internet has become essential for Maine communities and is keeping the economy moving. Across the state, high-speed internet enables farmers to use precision agriculture, rural residents to access telehealth specialists, small businesses to sell Maine-made products worldwide, and tourism operators to manage reservations and attract visitors.
This is what drives TDS Telecom (TDS) to deliver better internet for businesses and residential customers. TDS has served Maine since 1971 and today operates seven local telephone companies serving more than 30 communities from Swan’s Island and Isle au Haut to rural areas such as Kingfield and North Anson. Every new connection unlocks new opportunities, especially in rural and historically unserved parts of the state.
That’s why we are grateful for the leadership of Sen. Susan Collins. As the first Mainer in nearly a century to serve as the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, we believe Collins has consistently advocated to improve the quality of life for Mainers, including broadband. Her bipartisan leadership has helped create a policy and funding environment that has allowed experienced providers like TDS to invest, build, and connect some of Maine’s hardest-to-serve communities.
As a longtime champion of rural connectivity, Senator Collins has said, ”broadband is not a luxury, but a necessity” and we applaud her work in this area. She helped shape one of the most significant broadband investments in our nation’s history. She was a lead negotiator for the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, which allocated $65 billion for broadband deployment including $42.5 billion for the Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) Program in 2021.
At the same time, her support has been critical for programs such as the federal Enhanced Alternative Connect America Cost Model, E-ACAM, which is enabling providers like TDS to make long-term network commitments in rural communities. By pairing federal support with private investment in E-ACAM, TDS is currently extending faster service to thousands of rural Maine locations.
Her support extends beyond funding; she has advocated for broadband programs to be implemented efficiently with flexibility to allow providers to use the technologies best suited to the communities they serve. In addition, she has supported efforts to reduce regulatory barriers and accelerate broadband deployments.
Collins has a proven record of bridging the political divide to get things done. As a result, her advocacy has helped create lasting benefits for Maine communities.
TDS is proud of its more than 50-year history in Maine and the investments we continue to make across the state. No single company or program can close the digital divide, but when effective federal policy, state partnerships and regulatory reforms work together, providers like TDS can upgrade networks, improve lives, and strengthen communities. Collins has helped make that work possible.
Throughout her career, she has been a tireless advocate for Maine communities, fighting to bring resources home. We believe Maine is stronger because of her, and we are grateful for her continued leadership.

title: Doctor says time outdoors can support physical and mental health
text:
(Aging Untold) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine.
Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it.
“Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Our genetic roots are in the outdoors and the surroundings that we see around us right now,” Mann said.
Doctor cites human history outdoors
Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments.
Asked whether people should be prescribed time outside the way they are prescribed medicine, Mann said, “I absolutely think we should.”
He said he is personally an advocate for holistic health.
Sunlight and physical health
Mann said sunlight benefits the body, including through vitamin D development.
“Sunlight is beneficial for your body for vitamin D development and has links to improved cancer rates and decreased infections, and a whole host of other medical problems that are directly connected to your interaction with the sun,” Mann said.
Exercising outside can also have physical benefits.
Outdoor time and mental health
Mann said there is a lot of data and research on the psychological effects of being outdoors.
Mann said people spend a lot of time on screens, including phones, tablets and TV, and screen time is directly linked to anxiety and other psychological conditions.
Time outdoors does not require a long hike
Mann said time outdoors does not have to involve a long hike.
“It doesn’t have to be a hike seven miles in the woods,” Mann said. “We know that based on literature and data that even just 10 or 15 minutes outdoors, working in your garden or mowing your lawn or spending time on your back porch can equally yield significant benefits.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers discusses benefits of outdoor time
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said that when people get less sunlight, vitamin D levels go down and people start to see affective disorders.
“Sometimes one of the simplest prescriptions for the body and the brain is to step outside,” Rogers said.
