title: Some addiction treatment services in Maine aren’t financially sustainable, provider warns
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Staff at a Wabanaki Public Health & Wellness drug recovery center in Bangor said they helped save a man who overdosed outside the facility on Tuesday. The same day, the organization’s leadership told the staff it plans to cut some of its addiction recovery services.
Those services have been built up over the past few years to help address drug and alcohol abuse around the state, but they are not financially viable, said co-CEO Lisa Sockabasin.
“I know that lives will be impacted by this, and it breaks my heart,” she said in an interview.
Her organization is one of several that expanded with encouragement from Gov. Janet Mills. Opioid-related deaths had been rising for six years when Mills was elected, and she made addressing it one of her top priorities. A Maine Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson said the state has put $6.8 million toward residential recovery treatment.
Sockabasin said when her organization started additional recovery services in 2023 with $1 million from the state, she thought they would be self-sustaining, but that has not turned out to be the case. Their two recovery homes in Bangor are losing money, she said, and the service that helps people go through withdrawal is an even bigger drain.
Several leaders in the recovery field in Maine said providing detox is precarious. They said they lose hundreds of dollars a day for each person they help manage through withdrawal who is on MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, because it does not pay the full price of what the service costs.
Ever since Wabanaki Public Health & Wellness opened its detox facility in 2023, it has cost the organization about $1.5 million more per year to deliver the service than MaineCare will reimburse for it, Sockabasin said. It has covered the losses with fundraising and grants but she said those grants were less available in 2025 and 2026, and covering the cost of drug and alcohol treatment hasn’t left enough money for the organization’s other services like food and water delivery to tribal members.
On Friday, she said the organization plans to close its detox services as soon as current patients finish receiving care.
“The closure of detox beds would be a critical loss on the front lines of the opioid crisis in the state,” said Courtney Gary-Allen, executive director of the Maine Recovery Action/Access Project, a nonprofit advocacy organization.
She said medically supported detox like what Wabanaki Public Health & Wellness has provided is an essential first step for people to end dependency on drugs and alcohol. Sockabasin said she raised an alarm with the state six months ago and has been fundraising in the hope she could avoid having to close detox beds or additional recovery services.
She said her “excruciating” last few months are a warning signal.
“There were many partnerships built to create a statewide system to catch people no matter what. And there are many of us within that statewide system today that are struggling to keep the lights on,” Sockabasin said.
At the same time, a few new facilities for detox and other residential recovery services plan to open soon, though some will be primarily for people with private insurance who can pay more.
Gordon Smith has led the state’s opioid response since Mills took office and in an interview on Tuesday said he’s optimistic recovery services built up on his watch will survive, but he’s not surprised to hear some providers are struggling.
“The sustainability of our entire healthcare system is at risk, so of course our addiction treatment facilities are fragile,” he said.
HARD MATH
Gary-Allen said Wabanaki Public Health & Wellness is one of the first three places she calls when she meets someone who is ready to detox. Another is Milestone Recovery in Portland, which also primarily serves people who have MaineCare or are uninsured.
The fact that MaineCare can open the door to medical detox is an improvement, advocates say. Mills expanded Medicaid in 2019 and nearly 40,000 people on MaineCare got substance use treatment in 2025, according to the state health department.
But Milestone loses $210 a day per bed for someone on MaineCare who is going through withdrawal because of insufficient reimbursement rates, said Executive Director Jayme Villanueva.
With high demand for detox, Milestone tried to expand its offerings in 2024. Mills cut the ceremonial red ribbon on a new facility to go from 16 beds to 30, but Milestone couldn’t keep it going. A little over a year later, they scaled back to 10 spots while converting 16 beds to a less costly recovery service for people who have already gone through withdrawal.
“We really tried hard to answer the call for more detox beds,” Villanueva
Detox requires 24-hour medical staffing, and Villanueva said Milestone couldn’t maintain the number of nurses and other personnel needed.
MaineCare last significantly increased its rates for residential substance use treatment in 2021. The rate for detox went up 77% and the Mills administration has added yearly cost-of-living increases. MaineCare currently pays $449, about $150 less than New Hampshire’s daily rate.
In 2025, the Maine Legislature considered raising the rate to match its neighbor.
Madison Birch was one of more than a dozen people who testified in favor of the proposal. She said her sister had been addicted to heroin and when she was ready to get help detoxing, there wasn’t room for her. She died about a week later, Birch said in an interview.
“I truly believe that if she had been given access to detox, she would still be here today,” Birch said.
Representatives for Wellspring also testified. Along with Milestone and Wabanaki Public Health & Wellness, Wellspring is one of the few substance use treatment providers in the state primarily helping people on MaineCare. Wellspring said it was losing nearly $3,000 a day.
“Detox centers, such as the one I run, will struggle to maintain their current operations, and may be forced to reduce their capacity or even shut down altogether,” Wellspring’s Mary Ellen Dunfield testified. The organization did not respond to an interview request.
Lawmakers decided not to increase the MaineCare rate in 2025. The Mills administration said at the time the state would revisit it within a few years as part of the normal review cycle, and there wasn’t enough justification to make an exception.
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services did not make anyone available for an interview. It pointed to the opening on Tuesday of Guardian Recovery Pine Tree in Westbrook as a sign that the landscape of substance use treatment providers in Maine continues to expand. Pine Tree is adding dozens of beds for people at various stages of drug recovery and moving a lot of its current operation from Portland.
A majority of their clients are not typically on MaineCare and Executive Director Kerry MacDonald said that is essential to its financial viability. Guardian Recovery is a nationwide company and has the infrastructure to be able to accept private insurance plans, which pay higher rates than MaineCare.
“The breadth of services and level of care we provide would be difficult to sustain on MaineCare,” MacDonald said.
The same is true in York County, said Manager Greg Zinser. The county is getting ready to open a recovery facility in Alfred this winter. He said of the 12 new detox beds, he anticipates the county will be able to have about five people with MaineCare. In Augusta, Housing For God’s Children is planning a detox center for MaineCare recipients, Gary-Allen said.
Smith said the Mills administration is encouraging Milestone and Wabanaki Public Health & Wellness to set up the private insurance infrastructure, but Sockabasin said it’s not a simple process and her team would need support to do it.
Villanueva said Milestone is seeking to get credentialed with one private insurance company, though she worries that if she uses a bed for someone with private insurance, that’s one less MaineCare patient who would have access.
“It would end up meaning that we would not be able to serve as many of the underserved population,” she said.
People in the Bangor area who work in recovery say Wabanaki Public Health & Wellness has been crucial in part because it serves the northern part of the state, which was particularly hard hit in the opioid epidemic. It’s also the only one offering Wabanaki ceremonies and values to native and non-native people in Maine, Sockabasin said.
She said her organization created services like detox and recovery homes in order to be part of a statewide solution to make sure that people with substance use disorders had a place to go. Now she’d like to see more of a statewide response to the organization’s funding shortage.
“It should be the strategic solutions that we’re creating together,” she said.
NO FUNDING LINED UP
Many recovery services in Maine have received temporary funding from opioid settlement funds, which are being paid by pharmaceutical companies and retailers that helped fuel the crisis. In 2024, Wabanaki Public Health & Wellness was awarded $1 million split over two years to provide treatment services.
Patricia Kimball, chair of the Maine Recovery Council that hands out half of the state’s opioid settlement funds, said its mission “is not to rescue organizations in financial trouble.” Though she said in her opinion as a private citizen, “the state needs to figure out a way to support detox,” because the MaineCare rate isn’t high enough to provide proper staffing.
Sockabasin said federal grants that her organization has gotten in the past to fund recovery services are less available in the Trump administration. A federal grant that helped pay for two recovery houses ended in July, she said.
The result, she said, is that Wabanaki Public Health & Wellness has had to focus its fundraising on addiction treatment services that can’t pay for themselves. That means they have less money for basic human needs work like maternal-child healthcare and regular bottled water deliveries to hundreds of homes on the Passamaquoddy Reservation, where the tap water is rarely safe to drink.
“There are many people who think we can figure our way out of this dilemma. We can’t. Recovery services that don’t have a solid financial footing will go away,” Sockabasin said.
She added,
Some small recovery providers have closed or suspended some services, including the Together Place in Bangor and a Volunteers of America community center in Belfast.
Smith, the state opioid response director, said as he ends his tenure this winter, he worries about sustainability but he believes people in Maine’s recovery movement won’t let it fall apart. Gary-Allen, the statewide advocate, said she hopes the next governor will focus on stabilizing services that were built up under Mills, including small community recovery centers.
One of them, the Coastal Recovery Community Center, said it has no funding lined up for 2028.
“It’s a great big question mark,” said Director Erin Hustus. She said it’s possible the organization will have to go back to relying solely on volunteers and scale back the hours it’s open.
“Drugs will always be available,” she said.
Editor’s note: Lisa Sockabasin serves on the community board for the Maine Trust for Local News, which owns the Portland Press Herald.

title: Older adults who stop driving face transportation gaps, experts say
text:
KANSAS CITY (InvestigateTV) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. They are “more likely to be seriously hurt,” according to the agency. Most older drivers do not have a plan for when they can no longer drive, which aging experts say is critical.
A trip to the doctor without a car
Kennie Sandbothe, 77, stopped driving and now relies on a ride program for older adults.
Sandbothe was headed to a doctor’s appointment about 25 minutes from their home outside Kansas City.
“There’s no buses out here, not in this kind of rural area out here,” Sandbothe said. “It’s so expensive for Uber to take somewhere all the time.”
Sandbothe joked that they thought about improvising.
“Sometimes I thought about taking my lawn tractor, riding it to someplace I need to go. But you can’t put it out on the street because it’s not licensed,” Sandbothe said.
Sandbothe is the primary caregiver for their spouse and is managing serious health conditions, including Type 2 diabetes. Sandbothe also sees a psychiatrist for gender dysphoria, a condition that can happen when someone’s gender identity doesn’t match the sex they were assigned at birth.
“They’re the ones that saved my life,” Sandbothe told us.
Balance issues and blood sugar spikes made driving unpredictable, so Sandbothe stopped driving.
“I never know when I’m falling and stuff,” Sandbothe said. “I don’t want to get out there and black out and hurt somebody or kill somebody.”
Confidence and independence
There is no set age when someone should stop driving.
A February 2025 University of Michigan poll found 81% of drivers 65 and older feel very confident in their driving right now. That number drops to 43% when they are asked about driving safely five years from now.
Without a plan, experts say giving up the keys can mean losing control of their day, where they go and how they get there.
Rachel Ohlhausen of Jewish Family Services of Greater Kansas City said that uncertainty is why it can be hard to let go.
“It means a loss of independence in a new way,” Ohlhausen said. “Your time is no longer just yours. You don’t get to decide to do something on a whim.”
According to AAA, former drivers were less likely to get out, had smaller social networks and faced a higher risk of depression. A number of studies found that driving cessation appears to contribute to a variety of health problems, including declining cognitive function.
“What we know about loneliness and isolation is that loneliness is the equivalent of smoking a pack of cigarettes a day for your health,” Ohlhausen said.
Public transit and rideshare
Ohlhausen said public transportation often does not work for older adults with limited mobility or stamina.
“We do have some public transportation, but for an older adult who’s using a walker, walking to the bus stop isn’t always feasible,” she said.
The National Aging and Disability Transportation Center said public transit can be limited or nonexistent in rural and suburban communities.
Rideshares can fill some gaps, but there are barriers, Ohlhausen said.
“So even if you were able to and had the technological savviness to download the app, can you afford a smartphone? And can you afford the rideshare?” she said.
When people can’t find a ride, Ohlhausen said some stop asking for help.
“When those folks no longer drive, they really fall off the radar of society,” she said.
Sandbothe’s first backup plan was a next-door neighbor, but the arrangement did not last.
“My next-door neighbor, she was helping me for a while, but then decided, you know, she didn’t want to do it anymore,” Sandbothe said. “I don’t blame people, you know, they got their lifestyle. I don’t want to hinge on anybody to do anything for me.”
Sandbothe contacted the area office on aging and was connected with Jewish Family Services’ “Jet Express.” The program provides door-to-door service for adults 60 and older.
“We are the main source of transportation for 300 older adults in the Kansas City metro area,” Ohlhausen said.
Jet Express costs $5 each way and runs on a mix of volunteers, staff drivers and partner rides.
Staff driver Chip Ingram drove Sandbothe to the appointment. Ingram said that for some riders, it is not about driving, but about not feeling safe on the road.
“Some of them probably still drive to the neighborhood market, but they don’t want to take a ride on a highway it’s just too nerve-wracking for some people,” Ingram said.
Talking with a loved one about driving
For many families, the first step is having “the talk.”
According to AgingCare.com, experts say these are some red flags to watch for:
- Delayed responses, or getting lost or disoriented easily.
- Increased close calls and near misses.
- Difficulty seeing pedestrians, objects or other vehicles.
- Several dents or scrapes on the car or on surrounding objects where the person drives and parks at home.
Amy Cameron O’Rourke, an aging expert with Aging Untold, suggests asking a loved one questions before driving becomes a problem.
“Start before it’s a problem and just start lobbing some questions and make it part of a routine check-in,” she said.
Families can also talk with a doctor about any health issues or medications that can affect driving. State DMVs can provide information on driver evaluations and restrictions. Local agencies on aging can help families find transportation options.

title: Justice system reform is paying off in Cumberland County
text:
Jacqueline Sartoris is the district attorney of Cumberland County, completing her first term.
Voters chose change that was pragmatic, measurable and modern when they elected me in 2022, the first Democrat to become Cumberland County DA in over 30 years.
That change began when I arrived, when I restored accountability for street crimes. Within two years I increased charges for drug possession by 285% (116 to 331 cases) and criminal trespass by 137% (107 to 254 cases). County numbers continue to rise from the 2022 pandemic low.
But because I ran to deliver pragmatic, progressive reform, I built partnerships and programs so that our power as prosecutors moves people toward recovery and rehabilitation rather than the decades-old revolving door between the jail and the streets.
It’s working. Encampments have shrunk. Over 400 people have been housed in just a few years. Repeat offending is falling, not rising. Crime rates are lower. Our partnership with the Portland Recovery Community Center has helped many struggling with addiction choose recovery.
Yet over 100 people in Portland remain persistently homeless, refusing or unable to engage with help, affecting neighborhoods and businesses, schoolchildren and visitors. I track them by name. They are almost all products of a decades-long failure to create appropriate treatment.
As a person whose family is affected by substance use disorder, I know recovery programs are critical to change. But our county lacks adequate pathways to sobriety and recovery. Our 30-year-old Treatment Court is tiny, and only serves those steeped in addiction and convictions — there isn’t capacity for minor cases. Even as jail-based and bail-based programs sprung up from 2000 on, our jail offers no program like that available where I worked previously, in Kennebec County, and we’ve never tried the in-community options commonplace elsewhere.
I have built support for this critical need with leaders and community members, many of whom have endorsed my work. I’ve convened nonprofit and law enforcement partners to advocate for a residence for people on bail, where treatment would be a release condition.
I’ve also demanded better in our approach to mental health. I am the first DA in the state to use our civil code to request that a chronically psychotic — often dangerous — individual stay on medication. But my groundbreaking efforts in this area have shown that our existing laws cannot keep people safe. Given the ongoing absence of community-based facilities, promised when AMHI closed, I’ve proposed long-needed, pragmatic changes to Maine’s mental health laws for legislators to consider in the next session. My leadership on this issue is one reason why Speaker of the House Ryan Fecteau and former Maine CDC Director Nirav Shah believe I deserve a second term.
Finally, I also needed to focus on more serious crimes. I’ve overhauled our prosecution of sex assault crimes. I obtained a $2.5 million federal grant to end the backlog of sex assault kits and prosecute cases. This grant has been available for over 10 years, but I am the first DA in Maine to apply.
We’ve found that up to 2,000 kits entrusted to law enforcement by traumatized victims were routinely discarded for decades. Victims of sex assault deserved better, and I am keeping my promises to them. My deputy, Christopher Coleman, brings a stellar trial and appellate track record to his leadership of our new Sex Crimes Prosecution Division.
Resistance to any change, even pragmatic reform, was always going to be strong after 32 years of concentrated power. This election is about whether we modernize or go back, about whether the people or the attorney insiders, backed by conservatives, decide.
Cumberland County leaders know how important it is that we bring our justice system into the 21st century, which is why I have the trust and support of over 30 local leaders from school boards to unions, emeritus law professors to the Legislature.
We were ready for change. We are seeing results. And I believe we want to continue to move forward.

title: 4 hospitalized after lightning strike at elementary school
text:
EL MIRAGE, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — Authorities in Arizona say several adults were injured by a lightning strike at an elementary school bus drop-off Friday morning.
First responders said they were called just after 8:30 a.m. for reports of a lightning strike at El Mirage Elementary School.
Four people, all identified as adults, were conscious and taken to a nearby hospital for treatment, according to the El Mirage Police Department.
El Mirage Fire Captain Joseph Rivera said one woman was holding an umbrella when lightning struck in the vicinity. The woman reported feeling pain in both of her arms.
Capt. Rivera said none of the people were directly struck by the lightning.
Carrie, a librarian at the El Mirage Library across the street, said she was doing her morning duties before the strike.
“The lightning and the thunder were right on top of each other, so loud that it made me jump,” she said. “It felt like the building almost shook.”
Carrie said the strike was followed by a wave of “at least a dozen” car alarms going off across the street.
“It’s wild,” she added. “Then the rain just came down in buckets.”
The strike happened during the first round of storms that began passing through the Phoenix area Friday morning.
Around 8 a.m., fast-moving storms began passing through the area, with viewers reporting hail and heavy rain in Peoria, Sun City and Buckeye.

title: The three-legged cat and dog duo that are best friends
text:
WALDORF, Md. (InvestigateTV) — A 1-year-old dog named Blueberry and a 10-month-old cat named Meadow were adopted together after they met at the veterinary hospital run by Last Chance Animal Rescue in Waldorf, Maryland.
Rachel Clarke, who adopted both animals, said Blueberry “loves to play, and she loves to snuggle.” She said Meadow is “a little more independent, but Blueberry goes where Meadow goes.”
Laurie Jenkins, assistant director of Last Chance Animal Rescue, said both animals arrived with wounds to their extremities that required amputations.
Hospital Manager Lauren Webb said she got a call about Blueberry on Christmas Eve.
“We’ve got to help this dog. It’s Christmas Eve. We’ve got to pull out a miracle,” Webb recalled.
Blueberry had been found on the street in bad shape. The hospital saved her life. “You could see in her eyes that she was a fighter.”
A month later, Meadow was transferred from a shelter in West Virginia. Jenkins said Meadow “came in with her own leg issues, but also had upper respiratory.”
Another month passed before the two met at lunchtime. Webb said staff typically spend their lunch breaks snuggling with animals that need extra care. She said staff had laid a blanket on the floor.
Jenkins said Blueberry came out, and Meadow came out and laid on top of her. “They were together ever since,” Jenkins said.
“It was magic,” Webb said.
After the two had healed and were ready for adoption, Last Chance posted the pair on its Facebook page. The post requested that they be adopted together.
Clarke said her partner, Kevin, saw the post while scrolling on Facebook. The couple also has a “tripod cat,” she said.
“Even though they had a lot of attention, we’re like, let’s just throw our hat in the ring,” Clarke said.
Clarke said the animals “will hang out together. They’ll sleep together. They have been such great additions to the family.”
“We could not have asked for a better home,” Webb said.
Clarke said that “even if they stumble and they fall down, it doesn’t, you know, deter them from getting back up.”
Clarke said hearing “bad news one week and worse news the next” made the story stand out to her.
“It’s nice to have kind of something that was a very sad story that has a happy ending, and to kind of see that there is hope,” she said.
Jenkins said seeing the animals with their family makes her “unbelievably happy.”

title: Sombr surprises riders with pop-up performance at New York City subway station
text:
Sombr surprises riders with pop-up performance at New York City subway station
Singer-songwriter Sombr performed his pop hit "My Body Isn't Ready" during a pop-up performance at a New York City subway station on Thursday.
See a clip of the performance in the video above.
The "Back to Friends" singer and New York native told the Metropolitan Transportation Authority ahead of his impromptu performance, which also included a keyboard player and a group of harmonizing backup singers, that he grew up riding the subway.
"The MTA is my childhood. It was how I got around," he said.
The performance took place at the 14th Street-Union Square station, the MTA said.
"When I was in high school, I took four trains to school every day," he added.
After his performance, he had a simple message: "Keep taking the subway," he said, giving a smile and a thumbs-up.

title: Ex-Husson employee under police investigation, school says
text:
Editor’s note: Ex-professor Jonathan Houck has been charged with possession of child sexual abuse material and violation of privacy. Read the latest story here.
A now-former Husson University employee is being investigated by police, the school said.
The university is aware of the police investigation into the person, who is no longer employed at the school, spokesperson Sarah Walker Caron said Thursday. She did not name the employee.
Husson learned about the investigation early on Sept. 21, Walker Caron said. The employee was escorted from campus and fired within an hour, she said.
Bangor police said there is an active investigation and declined to provide additional details.
A TikTok video from a Husson student, posted hours before the school issued its statement, outlines allegations against a school employee. It’s unclear if the video is directly related to the school’s statement.
In the video, she describes a fall 2025 exercise science class where the students’ body weights were needed. In a lab for the class, they were supposed to undress and weigh themselves, she said. She undressed to her bra and underwear, weighed herself, got dressed and went back to class.
She said she learned this week that there were hidden cameras near the scale taking footage of the weigh-ins. Police showed her three pictures of herself that were on the professor’s devices but they were blurry, so she said it could have been screenshots from a video.
She said she is “one of God knows how many victims” of the employee. The Bangor Daily News does not name victims of crimes without their permission. The student did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“I’m disgusted, I don’t really have words,” the student said in the video.
She said the Husson employee was her adviser, and that she had classes and conversations with the employee in the year since that class.
The employee the student names is not included on the school’s online staff directory, and a page about the person as an assistant coach for the university no longer exists.
The BDN is not naming the employee because the person has not been charged with a crime.

title: What’s really behind Bucksport’s famous witch’s foot
text:
Downtown Bucksport is lined with the legacy of its founder, Colonel Jonathan Buck: the mill site whose predecessors he helped develop, a stone chiseled with words of affection for his town, the stately library bearing his name.
And, where Main Street becomes Route 1, a granite monument that’s fueled the myth of a curse for more than a century.
That’s because of an outline resembling a woman’s leg that appears on the monument, which legend says appeared as a curse from a witch Buck had condemned to death — never mind that witch trials never happened in Maine, and the last one in New England was decades before his birth.
“It’s very popular among tourists, I can tell you that, even though the stories behind the foot on the stone are not true,” said Larry Wahl, a member of the town’s cemetery committee.
He doesn’t buy in, “but a lot of people do,” he said. “And they love it.”
Since the early 1900s, the monument has attracted variations on the legend, fed real suspicions and drawn many spectators. But the leg shape’s appearance may well have begun long before Buck, or anyone, lived along the shores of the Penobscot where the granite likely formed.
Buck, who settled the town in 1762, was buried with a simple headstone when he died in 1795. His grandson had the monument installed in 1851 to honor Buck’s role as father of the town, according to Gary Bagley, president of the town’s historical society.
Almost 50 years later, the story of the curse appeared in a newspaper and spawned more articles in following years that fed the myth.
“It’s totally poetic license,” Bagley said. Some people in town still believe it, he said, though he doesn’t think it’s discussed much these days.
Growing up in Bucksport in the 1950s, he was told that the monument was thrown into the river and replaced three times, only for the leg to reappear each time on the stones — though there aren’t purchase records for additional monuments.
The answer could lie across the river itself.
The leg shape facing out over Route 1 looks similar to patterns of circular, “amorphous-looking blobs” in the granite of Mt. Waldo, a quarry across the river in Frankfort, according to Myles Felch, a curator at the Maine Mineral and Gem Museum in Bethel. Its color and texture also resemble Mt. Waldo granite.
Historical society members believe Mt. Waldo was the source of the monument’s stone, though records don’t say for sure.
Such “blobs” can form when molten material ascends through the Earth’s crust, according to Felch. It sometimes gets stuck in place, exerting force on non-molten material around it and dislodging pieces. In the hot magma, these other rocks can begin melting.
The leg looks like such a rock that broke down “considerably” and diffused into the molten material around it, Felch said. The dark outline of the foot appears to be many small grains of mica.
He’s not certain, but sees a familiar pattern to other rocks in the area west of Bucksport, he said. Stone was generally quarried locally at that time.
Some tales say the foot only appeared after the monument was installed, or disappeared when washed and then reemerged.
One of the first widely circulated national stories, published in the New England Magazine in 1902, described the woman turning to Buck at the gallows to prophesize its appearance.
“You will soon die,” part of her speech reads. “Over your grave they will erect a stone, that all may know where the bones of the mighty Jonathan Buck are crumbling to dust. But listen! Listen all ye people — tell it to your children and your children’s children — upon that stone will appear the imprint of my foot, and for all time long, long after your accursed race has perished from the earth, the people will come far and near and the unborn generations will say, There lies the man who murdered a woman.”
More recently, local historian Emeric Spooner countered in a retelling that the tale was penned by a bored newspaper reporter waiting for news in a local murder case, then picked up by the Associated Press.
A 2019 BDN story said it wasn’t noticed for several decades, emerging as the stone weathered.
“I don’t know,” Felch said of the leg appearing or reappearing. “That seems like lore.”
Based on his observations, it doesn’t seem like something that would appear later, he said. He hasn’t sampled the stone, but the pattern likely continues inside it, he said.
It doesn’t appear to be polished, either, he said, though that process can enhance how colors appear.
The monument isn’t just attractive to the paranormally curious. Felch has visited it on local geology field trips, where groups have drawn similar conclusions about its likely origin.
“I would be a little skeptical of the myth, but it is nonetheless kind of an interesting story,” Felch said. “Except for the young woman, of course.”
Not everyone enjoys the myth and the historically unsupported shadow it attempts to cast on the town’s founder, whose descendants still live in the area.
In 2007, the local Daughters of the American Revolution rededicated the monument to help reclaim the Revolutionary War hero’s image, and a plaque beside the monument described him as “honorable and industrious,” highlighting his role in founding and growing the town.
Earlier this summer, another historical society member declined to discuss the myth with a reporter.
“We get a lot of interest in that, but it’s simply a flaw in the granite,” said Bagley, the society’s president. “But that’s kind of boring compared to the idea of a witch’s curse, I guess.”

title: Maine adopts $600K mental health safety net for people affected by PFAS
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine has approved a $600,000 program to offer free clinical therapy, peer support and community health services to farmers and residents dealing with the repercussions of forever chemical contamination.
The money comes from the state’s $65 million PFAS relief fund.
“In addition to being a financial and health issue, PFAS is an emotional issue that affects the whole family,” said Beth Valentine, executive director of the fund. “We hope to offer people the support needed to navigate through their crisis.”
The PFAS Fund Advisory Committee unanimously approved the program design Thursday.
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, are called forever chemicals because they don’t break down in nature and build up in the human body over time. Exposure can cause serious health conditions, including liver dysfunction, thyroid disease and kidney cancer.
In Maine, the toxic compounds spread across farmland through decades of state-sanctioned application of industrial sewage and paper mill sludge as fertilizer. State testing has revealed dangerous chemical levels in the soil and drinking water of almost 100 Maine farms.
As a profession, agriculture has a suicide rate three and a half times higher than the general population, according to the National Rural Health Association. State health studies show forever chemicals compound that job stress with acute anxiety, financial ruin and social stigma.
The new program was designed to lower the financial and social barriers to mental health treatment.
Digital campaigns will deploy micro-targeted “Can’t sleep?” ads during late-night web searches, directing residents to trained operators at state helplines 211 and 988. Out in the fields, facilitators will hold farmer-to-farmer talk sessions.
The program will assemble a roster of agriculturally trained social workers. To break through rural isolation and stigma, the state will enlist everyday figures — including milk truck drivers, feed store clerks and large-animal veterinarians — to make warm referrals.
The program operates as a payer of last resort, covering remaining costs for about four to six sessions after private insurance or MaineCare. If needed, the therapists could recommend a longer-term care plan.
The mental health initiative complements the Maine PFAS Fund’s broader mitigation efforts, which already provide financial relief and technical assistance to farms, land purchases, blood testing for affected residents and an array of PFAS research projects.
Individuals will qualify if their soil or water exceeds state screening thresholds or if their farm products were put under a stop-sale order. Non-farm residents qualify if their well water tests above the state’s interim safety threshold of 4 parts per trillion for PFOS or PFAS.
Program leaders will start recruiting clinicians and conducting farmer training early next year, with referrals and funds for therapy sessions projected to be available to those who qualify by next summer.

title: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
text:
(Aging Untold) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time.
The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead.
Why promises can create pressure
Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said.
“They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.”
She said the questions can be practical:
Can we afford the care?
What if you have care that takes heavy lifting and I can’t do it?
A resident’s needs changed
O’Rourke shared an example from her own work with a man who had significant memory impairment. He had told his daughter not to put him in “one of those places.”
“I talked to the daughter, and over time, this isn’t the only time it’s ever happened, we moved him into a memory facility,” O’Rourke said. “He became ‘the mayor.’ He’s the most popular guy. He was happy. And the daughter was blown away.”
O’Rourke said she has used that example with other families.
“What their needs were at one point might change,” O’Rourke said. “And so you have to change with how they change.”
Most family caregivers aren’t trained
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said most family members aren’t trained to be caregivers. Instead, the training usually comes from parenting children.
“Now you’re going to try and translate that level into an adult and understanding the complexities of the relationship, the history of the relationship, the disease progressions and what it’s like to change an adult versus changing someone much smaller,” Cradduck said.
What to say instead
Cradduck said caregivers need to be fair to themselves and suggested wording along these lines:
“Listen, I promise to do the best by you and keep you here as long as my skillset and the affordability allow. But if something changes along the way, I’m going to have to change the plan.”
“Staying at home is always going to be what you want, but it may not be the safest place and it may not be the best place.”
“We have to be honest with our family members and that’s tough,” Cradduck said.
Have the conversation early
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said to have the conversation ahead of time.
“The biggest thing to do is have that conversation early, not in the time of a crisis,” Rogers said. “Love is going to be tested by illness and caregiving and finances.”
And over the years, needs and views can shift, she said.
“The discussion that you have when you’re 35, your needs are going to change at 65,” Rogers said. “You may be at a different point in terms of medical history at that point too. So that conversation needs to change as things change.”
When a loved one asks for a promise
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said the request to make promises is common.
“This is not an uncommon promise to make,” Ambrose said. “I find many seniors will say, ‘Promise me you’ll never put me in one of those homes.’ But I think a lot of times that’s because they can’t imagine what might be coming down the pike.”
Ambrose said a community might work out well, as in O’Rourke’s example.
“When the scope of care changes, it may not be possible and then it’s OK to say we might need to adjust,” Ambrose said. “Sometimes the loved one might not be a part of that conversation anymore, but you can only do what you can do.”
Ambrose suggested asking: “Knowing where you’re at now, what is going on now? Is this what your mom or your dad would still want for you?”
Key takeaways
- Talk about the reality up front.
- Needs can change.
- Make a promise you can keep.
- Start early and revisit it.

title: Acadia’s first Bark Ranger dog dies
text:
The poster dog for Acadia National Park’s Bark Ranger program passed away in mid-October.
Drift, a skilled tracking dog who worked with a statewide, volunteer search and rescue nonprofit and helped solve two missing persons cases, died Oct. 20 at age 12, according to the group’s Facebook page.
Acadia is one of only a few national parks that permit dogs. Drift was the park’s first Bark Ranger.
The border collie is featured on the park’s Bark Ranger activity checklist.
Throughout his eight years as a tracking and trailing dog for the Maine Search and Rescue Dogs group, which was formed in 1983 in collaboration with the Maine Warden Service, the accomplished search dog was involved in locating two important clues that helped nearby teams find missing people.
“Drift was also a slayer of vacuum cleaners, a mentor to foster border collies and a great traveler,” his obituary says. “He will be missed by his handler and other members of his human and K9 family.”
Drift and his handler, Kelly Pontbriand, a former park ranger, held public search and rescue demonstrations throughout the state, including at Bradbury Mountain State Park in Cumberland County and Camp Beech Cliff on Mount Desert Island.
The Bark Ranger program, launched in 2018, encourages canine owners to clean up after their dogs, use a leash no longer than 6 feet long, respect wildlife and know which areas of the park are off limits to dogs, including all visitors centers, the park’s six cliff ladder trails and Echo Lake and the Sand Beach between May 15 and Oct. 15.
To become a Bark Ranger, owners must review the program’s rules and participate in one of three activities with their pet: hiking a park trail, exploring a carriage road and strolling along a body of water.
Upon completion of the checklist, the pet can be sworn in as a Bark Ranger, and their owners will be eligible to purchase a specialized dog collar at the Hulls Cove Visitor Center, according to the park’s website.
The park sells $20 plushies that look like Drift, and are named after him, at the Hulls Cove Visitor Center.
Neither the search and rescue dog group nor park officials responded to inquiries from the Bangor Daily News.

title: Paul LePage has failed to make the case
text:
Janet T. Mills is the 75th governor of Maine, and former District Attorney for Androscoggin, Franklin and Oxford Counties.
Nearly eight years ago I took office as the 75th governor of the State of Maine.
Immediately it became clear that I had inherited an office my predecessor left rudderless and dysfunctional.
Paul LePage had decimated the Department of Education, calling teachers “a dime a dozen” and labeling the thousands of men and women who worked for the state “corrupt.”
LePage ruthlessly ignored the state’s obligation to pay its fair share of the costs of education. He left our premier mental health institution broke and beholden to the federal government.
Heartlessly, he had allowed hundreds of people to die from drug overdoses, deprived of the one life-saving medication that could save them and put their lives back on track again.
He denied our towns and cities millions of dollars in revenue sharing funds legally due to them.
LePage refused to follow the will of the people, even as they voted overwhelmingly to fund senior housing and to provide vital healthcare to thousands of citizens.
In dealing with lawmakers and the general public, secrecy, hostility and insults were his daily bread.
He fought with legislators, teachers, public health nurses and sheriffs. Even youngsters who wrote to him became the target of his spite.
LePage ignored the City of Lewiston and blamed the city’s ills on newcomers, even as those newcomers opened new stores and businesses and brought the downtown back to life.
Now Paul LePage wants to represent us in the U.S. Congress. Why?
During this campaign, he has still had nothing good to say about our state or the good people of Lewiston-Auburn. He offers no positive ideas or vision for the future, promising only to vote in lockstep with Donald Trump — as he did as governor.
Paul LePage has failed to make the case for a seat in Congress. Please vote for Matt Dunlap on Nov. 3.

title: Boston Celtics and Owners Give More Than $200 Million to Boston Children's Hospital
text:
Boston Celtics and Owners Give More Than $200 Million to Boston Children’s Hospital
New England’s basketball team and its ownership group have made a sizable donation to Boston Children’s Hospital.
👇 KEEP READING: Look Inside Boston Celtics Jayson Tatum's Massachusetts Home Worth $4 Million 👇
Boston Children’s Hospital announced Oct. 29 that the Boston Celtics and their ownership group, in association with the Boston Celtics Shamrock Foundation, donated more than $200 million.
The gift is the largest in the hospital’s history. The announced total includes a $100 million gift from Celtics co-owner Rob Hale and his wife, Karen, first announced in December 2025. Their contribution supports the hospital’s new pediatric behavioral health campus.
Part of the funding will help build a children’s mental health facility on the Franciscan Children’s campus in Boston’s Brighton neighborhood.
A groundbreaking ceremony was held Oct. 8th for the project, whose first phase includes a planned 116-bed psychiatric hospital. The expansion is expected to nearly double Boston Children’s inpatient psychiatric capacity.
The donation will also support research into new treatments for childhood diseases and help establish an innovation fund for new approaches to children’s health care.
Additional funding will go toward advanced training for pediatric nurses and family programs that promote healthy lifestyles.
Founded in 1869 as a 20-bed hospital, Boston Children’s has grown into a 491-bed medical center serving children and adolescents.
It is also a pediatric teaching affiliate of Harvard Medical School.
And there you have it! The Boston Celtics and their ownership group have donated more than $200 million to Boston Children’s Hospital.

title: Market Basket to open 4th Maine store in Scarborough next week
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SCARBOROUGH, Maine (WMTW) - Market Basket’s new Scarborough store is scheduled to open Nov. 6, according to the company’s website.
The store is at 70 Market St. in The Downs development and will serve as the first anchor retailer at the heart of the Town Center project.
“It is very rewarding to start delivering long-awaited amenities that residents and visitors want here in Scarborough,” said Peter Michaud, a managing partner of The Downs. “Market Basket is an excellent grocer, and we are confident this marks the beginning of exciting things to come at The Downs,” Michaud said.
It will be the grocery chain’s fourth location in Maine, joining stores in Biddeford, Westbrook and Topsham.
The 80,000-square-foot store is expected to create about 300 jobs.
“The Downs presented a vibrant opportunity for Market Basket to be located within a true Town Center, with people and supporting services all within walking distance,” said Joe Schmidt, Director of Operations for Market Basket. “The whole team is very much looking forward to bringing Market Basket and ‘more food for your dollar’ shopping to Scarborough and the surrounding communities,” Schmidt said.

title: Voters weigh opposing views of Susan Collins' power and influence
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine’s U.S. Senate race has been a 15-month odyssey of twists and turns, all driven by its potential to reshape power in Congress and alter President Donald Trump’s final two years in office. The attendant national media spotlight has tracked all the plotlines of micro and macro importance.
But the race could turn on a simple question: Are Maine voters angry enough at Trump that they’ll part with Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, the state’s longest serving senator in more than a century?
Democrat Troy Jackson, the candidate hastily drafted by Democrats in late July, is hoping that they will, and he has spent the past 90 days trying to nationalize the contest by framing Collins as an enabler of Trump’s unrestrained second term. Collins, meanwhile, has sought to rekindle the election magic that lifted her to a resounding victory six years ago, running a hyperlocal race that focuses on her seniority and ability to direct federal dollars to Maine.
The candidates’ divergent approaches were crystalized on the same in late August.
Collins dropped in to Kenduskeag, just northwest of Bangor, to celebrate the fruits of her seniority and influence: a new library funded in part by a slug of federal cash that she secured through a congressional earmark. While she was there, she also made note of the new fire station that will one day sit right next to it.
“I have been able to secure funding for 45 fire stations all over the state to be rebuilt or renovated, and today we see what an important role they play,” she said.
It wasn’t an official campaign stop, but it allowed Collins to advance her central argument for why she deserves a historic sixth term: That as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, she brings home federal money that might otherwise go to other states.
Jackson was making a different case at an event in Brunswick: That Collins has refused to leverage her influence in Congress to stop Trump.
“You know, tariffs, the Iran War — all these things Susan Collins, I believe, could stop,” he said. “But she doesn’t want to stop them because that’s who her master is.”
On Tuesday, Maine voters will decide whether Collins, the only Republican member of Congress in New England, should return to Washington or be replaced by Jackson, a former logger and longtime state legislator and former Maine Senate president who has firmly aligned himself with organized labor and the wing of the Democratic Party led by independent U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont.
With so much at stake, Democratic and Republican political groups, many with secret donors, have spent accordingly — more than $200 million so far.
It’s the costliest race per capita in the country, and the majority of the ads, mailers and the nonstop barrage of text messages have been negative, if not downright nasty. The persuasion value is debatable, but the investment by monied interests, corporations, billionaires — even trillionaire Elon Musk — reveals what they believe is on the line.
Jackson was drafted by Democrats when progressive firebrand Graham Platner succumbed to scandal. His win at the nominating convention was largely attributed to his affiliation with organized labor and a volunteer network that quickly secured commitments from delegates.
But his platform — Medicare for All, taxing the wealthy — also largely mirrors Platner’s focus on the struggles of working class Mainers, an approach that helped the oysterman win more primary votes than any other Democratic Senate candidate in state history.
Jackson is no stranger to those same issues. He was drawn to Sanders after losing a Democratic primary for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District race in 2014.
“I’m nothing extraordinary,” he told the audience in Brunswick. “But I’ve worked with a lot of hardworking people in my life and a lot of families that were holding on hope that they were going to have somebody that was actually going to step up for them.”
Jackson didn’t enter the Senate race until late July, and the campaign scrambled to channel Platner’s populist message, but without the force of its charismatic messenger.
“I owe Donald Trump nothing. I owe the billionaires nothing. I owe the people of Maine everything,” Jackson said during a stump speech with Sanders in October.
Jackson’s embrace of the progressive platform was not decisive in the race he originally wanted to win. He placed third in the Democratic primary for governor in June.
Lisa Eaton, a Democratic voter from Kennebunk, was among the primary voters who didn’t choose Jackson first during the ranked-choice election. She showed up to an event headlined by historian Heather Cox Richardson to get a better look at the candidate taking on Collins.
“It was an enthusiasm thing, totally. When he was running for governor, I voted for him, but I ranked him. He wasn’t in the top,” Eaton said.
To boost Jackson’s profile, particularly among women, the campaign has tapped a parade of high-profile surrogates, including New York U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
“He has stood up for our equal pay. He has stood up for our rights. And the most important thing for us as women to do, is to elect this man to the U.S. Senate,” Ocasio-Cortez said during an event with Jackson in Portland.
Collins, meanwhile, has toiled in the long shadow of Trump. His war in Iran and trade war with Canada have made him even more unpopular in Maine than he was when he lost the state by seven points two years ago.
And his cowing of the Republican Congress has complicated Collins’ claims of independence, a key piece of her political identity that has long won over Maine’s fickle but determinative block of unenrolled voters.
“I vote very independently,” she said during a debate hosted by Maine Public. “We need more people in the center. We don’t need more people who are going to vote a straight party line.”
To bolster this narrative, Collins campaigned with former West Virginia U.S. Sen. Joe Manchin, a one-time Democrat who left the party to become an independent.
“So when I hear all this stuff on TV, she’s not bipartisan. That’s a lie. She’s the most bipartisan person we have in the Senate today. And I have said this publicly, she is the soul of the Senate,” Manchin said at one of two events he held with Collins.
Even the White House has tried to reinforce that image. In late August it dispatched Vice President JD Vance to Maine to campaign for Republican candidates on the ballot.
Collins did not attend, but Vance made sure to mention her.
“She does an amazing job so please give it up to our very independent friend, Susan Collins,” Vance said.
But in that same rally Vance also defended the president’s trade war with Canada, using rhetoric sharply at odds with Collins’ stance that the White House is alienating Maine’s leading trade partner.
It also undercut Collins’ efforts to keep the race local and Trump an abstraction.
Instead, Collins has had to ask the Trump administration for carve-outs on Canadian tariffs. She also made a direct plea to the administration for the release of New England home heating oil reserves to mitigate the effects of the war in Iran in a state where more than half the homes use it as a primary heat source.
“This is good news, by increasing the amount of supply we should see some price relief,” she said after the administration granted her request.
Collins has framed these favors as evidence of her influence. Jackson says it wouldn’t be necessary if she would only stand up to Trump.
Maine voters will now resolve these dueling views of Collins’ power.
For the past 30 years Collins has prevailed by playing to their local interests. Jackson is hoping voters will see those interests as directly tied to the direction of the entire country.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: LA Metro Chamber, Bates College to host entrepreneurship expert
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Lewiston Auburn Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce, in partnership with Bates College, will host a session with investor and author Allison Byers to discuss startup fundraising, access to capital and the forces that shape opportunities for entrepreneurs.
“Who Gets Funded?” is a free event to be held Wednesday, Nov. 4, at Bates College.
Sponsored by the Maine Technology Institute, the program will bring together business leaders, entrepreneurs, investors, students and community members for a conversation about the future of innovation.
Byers is the founder and CEO of Scroobious, a relationship-first capital access platform, and the author of “Fundraising for the Rest of Us,” a guide to building a compelling pitch, navigating bias and raising capital.
Through her work, Byers examines the structural barriers that can influence early-stage investing and advocates for approaches that broaden access to funding. She co-authored California’s Fair Investment Practices by Venture Capital Companies Act and has spoken at conferences, accelerators and universities around the world.
“There’s no shortage of good ideas or entrepreneurial talent in our region,” said Susan Ruhlin, president and CEO of the LA Metro Chamber. “But having a great idea and having access to the resources to build a business are two very different things.
“We want to help close that gap by connecting entrepreneurs with the people, knowledge, and opportunities that can help them succeed,” Ruhlin added. “Bringing conversations like this to Lewiston Auburn is part of that effort.”
The Nov. 4 event, from 7 to 8:30 p.m., will be at Bates College’s Olin Arts Center. It marks the launch of the Chamber’s Business & Innovation Speaker series.
Registration is required; information is available on the chamber’s website.

title: High schools Friday: Scarborough girls soccer nips South Portland in OT
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Wren Bodah knocked in the rebound of a long free kick by Josie Duncan at 12:37 of overtime, lifting top-seeded Scarborough to a 2-1 win over fourth-seeded South Portland in a Class A South girls soccer semifinal Friday in Scarborough.
Duncan’s kick from nearly 40 yards almost eluded South Portland keeper Maizie Savage, who had to leap and stretch to keep the ball from slipping into the goal just under the crossbar. The ball caromed of the crossbar and landed right in front of the net, and Bodah dashed in to score the winner.
Scarborough (15-0-1), the four-time defending regional champion, took lead in the 10th minute when Scarlett Floyd stole the ball from a defender and sent a shot from the top of the box into the lower right corner.
The Red Riots (11-3-2) tied it, however, which just six seconds remaining in the first half. With time running out, Mackie Ramsell delivered a perfect corner kick that was headed into the net from cross range by Sasha Neff.
Savage finished with 15 saves. Scarborough’s Vera DiSotto stopped two shots.
Scarborough will play at home against Tuesday in the regional final against No. 3 Kennebunk.
KENNEBUNK 2, WINDHAM 1: Ava McCourt scored a spectacular go-ahead goal with 4:46 remaining as the third-seeded Rams (12-3-1) rallied past the second-seeded Eagles (11-4-1) in a Class A South semifinal in Windham.
McCourt gained control of a loose ball in the left side of the penalty area, and with her back to the goal lofted an overhead shot into the upper far corner, just inside the post.
Windham broke a scoreless deadlock at 24:39 of the second half when Logan Curry converted a cross from close range.
The lead lasted only 46 seconds, however, as Natalie Elia quickly answered for Kennebunk.
MT. ABRAM 2, TRAIP ACADEMY 1: Evelyn Pepin scored on a penalty kick with one second left in the second overtime to send the top-seeded Roadrunners (15-1) to the Class C South final with a win over the fourth-seeded Rangers (10-4-2) in Salem Township.
Pepin scored in the first half, assisted by Lya Pepin. Lucy Gingras tied it in the second half, with an assist from Jacqueline Diallo.
Edna Bilodeau made 12 saves for Mt. Abram, which will face No. 2 Maranacook in the regional final. Traip’s Rose Dembele stopped nine shots.
BOYS SOCCER
THORNTON ACADEMY 2, SOUTH PORTLAND 1: Matthias Sunderland scored on a penalty kick with 36 seconds left in the first overtime to lift the top-seeded Golden Trojans (13-1-2) to a berth in the Class A South final with a win over the fourth-seeded Red Riots (9-4-2) in Saco.
Thornton Academy will face Falmouth in the regional final on Tuesday.
South Portland took a 1-0 lead with 16:21 left in regulation when Isaac Arey headed in a direct kick by Cam Willis. Sunderland sent it to overtime when he scored with 2:02 remaining.
FALMOUTH 3, SCARBOROUGH 2: The 11th-seeded Navigators (7-8-2) converted all five of their attempts in the penalty kick tiebreaker to upset the second-seeded Red Storm (11-3-2) in a Class A South semifinal in Scarborough.
After winning only four games during the regular season, Falmouth has posted three straight road victories to earn a return trip to Scarborough for the regional final Tuesday against top-seeded Thornton Academy.
The defending state champion Red Storm twice erased one-goal deficits.
Kian Long put Falmouth ahead in the 13th minute when his corner kick from the right went directly into the net off the far post. Nsimba Ilunga tied it in the 23rd minute, putting in a header off a corner kick during a scramble in front of the goal.
Moments later, Falmouth’s Jack Verville struck a low left-footed shot into the right corner. But Scarborough pulled even again early in the second half, as Andrew LeFebvre scored off another corner kick.
In penalty kicks, Penn Giard, Long, Verville, Clayton Hickey and Ewan Tennent all scored for Falmouth, and Navigators keeper Wyatt Binnette stopped Scarborough’s second attempt with a diving save to his left.
PINE TREE ACADEMY 8, TEMPLE ACADEMY 0: Rhett Tyson scored three goals, Fitzroy Hakizimana recorded two goals and an assist, and the top-seeded Breakers (14-0) earned a mercy-rule win over the fourth-seeded Bereans (7-6-3) in an eight-person South semifinal in Freeport.
Camden Brace, Rio Soram and Lucky Kabeya were the other goal scorers as Pine Tree advanced to the regional final Tuesday against second-seeded Telstar at Gardiner High.
MT. ABRAM 3, WAYNFLETE 1: Will Swain scored twice to lift the second-seeded Roadrunners (9-5-2) to a Class C South semifinal win over the sixth-seeded Flyers (8-8) in Salem Township.
Mt. Abram advances to face No. 1 Hall-Dale on Tuesday at Edward Little High School.
Chase Ross contributed a goal and an assist for Mt. Abram. Cayden Bate added an assist and Ben Beauliuer stopped 12 shots.
Omari Brent scored and Lila Fremont stopped five shots for Waynflete.

title: Shifting shadows, stories, haunt Boothbay Opera House
text:
On Oct. 29, ninety-seven living souls dragged their bones across the creaky old floors of the Opera House of Boothbay Harbor (OHBH) to behold the magic of community spirit and the terror of storytelling.
Ghostly shadows waltzed throughout the grand room. Flickers of candlelight cast spells. Friends dressed in their Halloween bests amassed in clusters around the potluck, as skeletons peered down from the balcony, evoking a sense of Camille Saint-Saëns’ “Danse Macabre.” Twice, something unseen brushed against my leg.
Kevin Kiley, the evening’s ghastly master of ceremonies, summoned attention for the evening’s first story: "Click-Clack the Rattlebag" (Gaiman, 2012). The story plays on the power of suggestion, turning a mundane act into genuine horror. The narrator walks a young boy up a drafty flight of stairs in an old, presumably haunted house, to his bedroom in the attic. Along the walk, the boy tells the man about the Click-Clacks, creatures of the darkness who prey on people by biting them, liquifying their internal organs and sucking out the milky goo from their eye sockets. The creatures then hang the lifeless bodies on a hook. As they dry, they rattle in the wind. The man reassured the boy that no Click-Clacks are lurking in the house before realizing that the boy is a Click-Clack and he has just walked into a trap.
Mary Boothby amped the tension of the first story with her rendition of “The King o' the Cats,” a British folk tale (earliest citation in 1481, most common citation, William Baldwin, 1553). Tom, with his one yellow eye and one green, a beloved tuxedo cat and family pet, lounges on his pillow beside the fireplace. But Tom has a dark history. When a stranger announces a villager has died, and he has just witnessed a group of cats holding a royal funeral, Tom announces, "Now I am the King of the cats!" and rushes up the chimney to the funeral to claim his crown and is never seen again.
Frances Mercanti-Anthon delivered a spectacular performance of her own writing, an all-too-familiar haunt. A middle-aged woman tormented by a supersized Italian supernatural woman. She is a crass, menacing and intimidating ghost, first name: Peri, last name: Menopause. More comical than terrifying, the story lightened the atmosphere, but not for long.
Ending the evening, Honora Boothby questioned reality vs. illusion, blurring the line between a manufactured fantasy world and the harsh consequences of the subconscious mind. She read Ray Bradbury’s "The Veldt," originally published in a September 1950 issue of The Saturday Evening Post. What starts as a happy, futuristic home life turns the world of virtual reality into an African killing field for little Peter and Wendy, who use the room to trap their parents. Let’s just say, it doesn’t end well. Some event guests scanned the room for exits, wondering if perhaps they, too, had been called forth to their final room.
“Selecting the stories to be read was a joint effort,” said Kiley. “I like letting the readers pick the stories they can really get into.” About the event, he said, “The bars have their parties, and there are tons of stuff for young children at Halloween, but what about the people that don’t fit into either of those groups? This is what tonight is about at the Opera House, a place for them, an event for them.”
“People look forward to this event every year. And Kevin (Kiley) does a wonderful job decorating the house and creating the perfect mood,” said OHBH Board President Kari Smith. With a wink in her eye, she would neither confirm nor deny whether the grand old building is haunted.

title: 2 helicopters carrying a total of 3 people collide midair in Oregon
text:
3 people killed after 2 helicopters collide in Oregon, shutting down a highway
Two helicopters collided and crashed into a farm field Thursday near a small airport southwest of Portland, Oregon, killing all three people on board and forcing the closure of a key highway, authorities said.
The crash killed 22-year-old Maddie Aasbo, a Texas flight instructor, 38-year-old Tyler Sturdevant, a pilot from Oregon, and a student pilot from the United Kingdom, whose name has not been released, Yamhill County Sheriff Sam Elliott said during a news conference.
In the video player above: Listen to scanner audio
Emergency crews responded around 2:15 p.m. following reports of a crash a few miles east of the McMinnville Airport, according to the sheriff’s office. By Thursday evening, officials were continuing their recovery efforts.
Photos posted by the sheriff's department show a green helicopter upside down in a field, while a red helicopter lies in pieces.
One of the aircraft came from the aviation school Jerry Trimble Helicopters, which is located at the airport.
“Our hearts and thoughts are with the individuals involved, their families, and everyone affected by this event,” the school said in a statement posted on social media.
The school, which offers everything from demo flights for first-time flyers to advanced training, said it is cooperating with law enforcement along with the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board to secure the site and determine the cause of the collision.
The FAA said the collision was between a Robinson R22 and an Airbus H125.
Two people were on board the Robinson, and the Airbus was carrying just the pilot, according to the sheriff.
The Oregon Department of Transportation said Highway 233 is closed 1 mile (1.6 kilometers) west of Dayton because of the crash. There was no estimate for reopening.
Local roads were also closed. The sheriff's office urged the public to stay clear of the area.
The FAA and NTSB will investigate.
The R22 is a two-seat aircraft, and the H125 can carry up to six passengers, depending on the configuration.
McMinnville, about 35 miles southwest of Portland, is home to about 34,000 people.
The small airport, situated on 650 acres, has two paved runways and remained open Thursday, according to its website. It’s partially bordered by homes and near the North American Aerospace Museum.

title: Midterms 2026: The final message to voters
text:
Midterms 2026: The final message to voters
With the 2026 midterm elections just days away, Democrats and Republicans are focused on driving more voters to the polls with the issue of affordability top of mind.
Midterms 2026: The final message to voters
With the 2026 midterm elections just days away, Democrats and Republicans are focused on driving more voters to the polls with the issue of affordability top of mind.
With just days to go until the 2026 midterms, candidates are making their final pitches to voters, where the issue of affordability is taking center stage.
Both parties agree that the final days before Election Day are critical to driving voter turnout.
"Midterms are historically bad for the incumbent party. We're trying to defy history," Joe Gruters, chairman of the Republican National Committee, said. "It's all about turnout, turnout, turnout."
Gruters argues the key to lowering prices is advancing President Donald Trump's legislative agenda, pointing to the administration's focus on tax cuts, job creation and reduced prescription drug costs.
"We have to continue to give the president the tools that he needs, the majorities that he needs, so he can continue to pass good legislation and get Americans back to work and get the economy back up and going," he said.
But Democrats are pushing back with a different economic message, highlighting plans to gain control of both chambers of Congress and bringing the cost of living down for Americans.
"We're going to make sure that we harness the enthusiasm that voters have for Democrats all across the country," Kendall Witmer, deputy communications director for the Democratic National Committee, said. "While Americans have been forced to pay more for everything, Trump and Republicans have been selling the White House to the highest bidder."
Witmer added a Democratic majority would likely signal a major shift in foreign policy and a crackdown on tax cuts for the wealthy, among other priorities.
While affordability is the leading concern for voters, other issues are also shaping the midterm landscape. A recent Gallup poll found that healthcare and foreign policy are among the top priorities for voters, along with crime, immigration and the construction of AI data centers.
In the wind-up to Election Day, Republicans are hosting tele-rallies in more than a dozen states, while Trump is holding in-person rallies in states like Iowa and Kansas after initially canceling stops there.
Witmer says Democrats remain focused on direct voter outreach, including door-knocking and rallies, right up to Election Day.

title: Author Rylan Hynes discusses recently released novel ‘Grafting’
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Author Rylan Hynes recently released their novel “Grafting.”
Book summary from publisher
“When Eben Turner returns to his family’s apple orchard in rural Maine after his parents’ death, he faces more than just the weight of inheritance—he confronts the love he left behind. A decade has passed since he and Chris Hartley, the Methodist minister’s son, were torn apart in their final year of high school, their secret relationship severed by the forces of faith and small-town judgment. Now, as adults navigating the crossroads of identity and belonging, they must reckon with both their buried past and an uncertain future.
“Set against the Edenic beauty of New England, Grafting unfolds through dual perspectives in a lyrical narrative that mirrors the delicate art of joining two trees to create something stronger. As Eben and Chris work to understand how they came to be parted, they discover that healing requires more than forgiveness—it demands the courage to cultivate love in hostile ground.
“This exquisite debut explores the cost of forbidden desire and the resilience required to claim one’s authentic self. With prose as rooted and enduring as the heritage apple trees that anchor the story, Grafting asks whether two people can truly come home to each other after being forced apart by the very communities that shaped them.
“A voice-driven and unforgettable tale of queer love and rural identity, Grafting will resonate with readers who were moved by the sweeping emotion of Brokeback Mountain, the luminous prose of Ocean Vuong’s On Earth We’re Briefly Gorgeous, and stories that find the sacred in the profane, the universal in the deeply personal.”
Inspiration for the book
Hynes said they wanted to write about the queer experience of living and belonging in a rural area.
“So often in media we associate the LGBTQ+ community with urban spaces—big cities like NYC or LA, yet queer people have always lived beyond those metropolises. I wanted to write about characters closer to home who intend to put down roots and stay in a place like rural Maine, even though it might come with friction—politically, culturally, and personally. There’s a lot of tension in that, and also joy to be found in claiming space for your authentic self,” Hynes said.
The title comes from the practice of cloning apple trees, which is how most apple trees are bred. Hynes said they even took a grafting class and created a few trees that now live in their yard.
“I fell in love with apples while writing the book. I read a ton of books on horticultural and orcharding, and took some hands-on classes through Fedco, the University of Maine, and the Viles Arboretum in Augusta,” Hynes said.
About the author
Hynes is a Maine Literary Award winner, former writer-in-residence at Monson Arts and Tin House Workshop alum.
They are the Communications & Editorial Director of The Telling Room, a nationally-recognized youth serving literary arts nonprofit in Portland, Maine. Hynes lives in Central Maine.
Where to buy “Grafting”
To purchase locally, visit The Briar Patch in Bangor. it is also available anywhere books are sold as well as Islandport Press’ website.
For more information, visit their website.

title: Morning Update: What you need to know in Maine today
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A version of this story first appeared in the Morning Update newsletter. Sign up here to receive the Morning Update and other BDN newsletters directly in your inbox.
Happy Friday!
Unfortunately, there’s not much to be happy about heating oil prices reaching yet another record high this week.
The Maine Department of Energy Resources announced that the statewide average is now $6.05 a gallon, up 82% from this time last year when a gallon went for $3.32.
In eastern and Down East Maine, prices range from a low of $5.71 to a high of $6.40.
Mainers will now have to spend an additional $750 to fill a standard 275-gallon tank.
Global energy prices have spiked since President Donald Trump launched his surprise war against Iran in February. That war entered its eighth month this week with no clear end in sight, especially as Trump has mused about more military action after the midterms.
In the run up to the election, his administration has rolled out a number of actions in an attempt to tamp down on voter angst over high energy prices. The Trump administration released low-income heating assistance early, tapped the Northeast heating oil reserves and made available one-time payments to farmers and fishermen to offset rising diesel prices.
But you can at least take it easy on the heat the next few days, because we have a stretch of seasonable weather ahead with highs in the low 60s. The only exception is Halloween, when the high may not even get into the 50s.
Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles has leaned heavily on his State Department experience as the brand of leadership he’d bring to the Blaine House. But a 2011 memoir by his former boss, Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, contradicts a key detail of his tenure.
Rice claimed that she fired Charles after learning that he’d gone behind her back to allies on Capitol Hill after resisting overhauls she wanted to make. Charles says he resigned over differences with Rice on programs he’d built under her predecessor, Colin Powell.
The truth may remain unknown, but no one disputes that Rice and Charles held different views.
When Charles left the State Department, a retired longtime official in Charles’ bureau said “nobody was terribly surprised” at the news.

title: Controversial attack ad featuring Democrat’s estranged mother is off the air in Ohio
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Ohio governor candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton, is off the air after the Republican spent about a quarter of what his campaign initially said it would invest to run it.
Ramaswamy said during a campaign appearance in Vandalia, Ohio, on Thursday that the ad’s planned run was over. His campaign originally said it would spend $4 million to air the ad, but data from the ad-tracking firm AdImpact showed it spent roughly $1 million.
The divisive spot had provoked backlash in Ohio and among politicians of both parties across the nation. It featured Donna Arthur calling her daughter a lifelong liar. That was despite the two having not seen each other for nearly 50 years. Arthur lost custody of her children in 1978 after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12.
Ramaswamy had defended the ad, though a later version trimmed some portions.
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance said they supported the decision to air the ad. The president said he told Ramaswamy to leave it on the air, adding “she’s fair game.”
Ohio governors past and present, alumni of Ramaswamy’s Catholic high school in Cincinnati and others had urged him to pull it down.
Acton’s campaign said the ad was “despicable” and should never have run and that Ramaswamy should have apologized.
___
Associated Press reporter Thomas Beaumont contributed from Des Moines, Iowa.
