title: Youth sports coach sentenced for sexually assaulting 12-year-old girl he coached
text:
PEORIA, Ill. (25News Now/Gray News) - A youth sports coach has been sentenced to 26 years in prison for sexually assaulting a 12-year-old girl he coached.
Aydan Trueblood was sentenced Wednesday after pleading guilty to predatory criminal sexual assault in August, according to the Peoria County State’s Attorney’s Office.
Assistant State’s Attorney Dave Gast argued for the 30-year maximum permitted under the plea agreement, emphasizing the victim’s age.
Chief Judge Katherine Gorman acknowledged Trueblood’s lack of criminal history but said he needed to take accountability for his actions.
“This is the nightmare of every parent with a daughter in a sport,” Gast said.
Bartonville Police received a tip on Nov. 9 that Trueblood had behaved inappropriately with the victim. According to the state’s attorney’s office, the victim said in a forensic interview that they communicated on Snapchat and that she snuck out to meet him. Trueblood admitted to the assault and to sending her explicit photos, the state’s attorney’s office said.

title: Conservationists are buying 2 large midcoast blueberry barrens
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Two large tracts of wild blueberry land in the midcoast that have been the focus of local conservation efforts since 2025 will soon go to new owners as of this week.
The Wild Blueberry Collective, a grassroots nonprofit, announced Thursday it had purchased a 138-acre barren parcel in Searsport. Coastal Mountains Land Trust separately said Friday that it’s under contract to buy Blueberry Hill, a 248-property in Belfast.
Both were once commercial fields owned by Allen’s Blueberry Freezer, an Ellsworth-based company that sold its facility and most of its midcoast and Hancock County land to Milbridge grower and processor Wyman’s in 2021.
The Milbridge company is now selling off hundreds of acres of less productive land to help fund investment for responding to increasingly unpredictable weather that’s challenging the industry, a spokesperson said this summer.
That decision has drawn alarm in several communities when scenic fields with histories of public access go up for possible development, presenting a change to a historical part of the landscape in coastal Maine.
Wild blueberry land can be relatively expensive to purchase and requires regular maintenance to keep it from reverting to forest, making it more challenging for land trusts to take on. Larger-scale efforts haven’t emerged to preserve the land in the area, but this week’s developments suggest efforts to preserve individual properties are gaining traction.
Blueberry Hill stayed under ownership of a member of the Allen family, the BDN previously reported, while the Searsport land was sold by Wyman’s.
“We’ve heard from so many community members who care deeply about the future of this property, and we’re excited about the opportunity to permanently protect Blueberry Hill and keep community access open,” Camden-based Coastal Mountains Land Trust said in a Friday post on Facebook announcing it was under contract for Blueberry Hill.
It described the property as holding a special place in the community, with panoramic views of Penobscot Bay from the highest point in the city.
When the property went up for sale last August, residents worried a developer would bar public access from the property, the BDN reported at the time.
Ian Steward, the trust’s executive director, said this summer that “blueberries are second only to lobsters” when it comes to emblems of local culture, but it was hard to react to so much blueberry land going on the market at once. The land trust already manages large blueberry barrens at its Beech Hill Preserve in Rockport and hears frequently from people worried about such land being lost to development, according to Steward.
The Wild Blueberry Collective, meanwhile, purchased its land with a loan and needs to raise another $310,000 toward the $650,000 purchase cost, the group posted on Facebook Friday.
“138 acres of wild blueberry land, forests and wetland will be a protected space for our community [that’s you!]” the group said on social media last week.
Another grassroots effort to purchase wild blueberry land out of fear of development met with success in Blue Hill last year. Residents in Northport pushed back this summer on a proposal for an RV resort on another hill of wild blueberry land and in June passed a moratorium on new RV parks in response.

title: The police said Sandra Birchmore's death was a suicide. Then the FBI accused a cop of murder
text:
BOSTON (AP) — When Sandra Birchmore was found dead in her Massachusetts home, police quickly decided it was a suicide. From the start, her friends didn’t believe it.
The 23-year-old had recently learned she was pregnant — and was thrilled about it, they told police. The person upset about the pregnancy, they said, was the married police detective she’d been seeing, Matthew Farwell.
Five years later, Farwell, 40, is on trial in federal court, charged with killing Birchmore and staging her death to look like a suicide to hide that he had begun sexually abusing her when she was 15.
Also on trial, in a sense, is the original police investigation.
State police troopers working in the Norfolk County district attorney’s office never wavered from their judgment that Birchmore’s death was a suicide, according to federal prosecutors. Farwell was interviewed for just 15 minutes in a parking lot, they said. Investigators didn’t take notes, examine him for injuries or sample his DNA. Police did look at Farwell’s phone, but only after he’d deleted his texts with Birchmore.
“Not only did they not investigate, they very quickly told others, including the medical examiner, that this was definitively a suicide and there was no foul play,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Torey Cummings told jurors.
Among those they reassured was Farwell’s twin brother, Billy Farwell. He testified that the lead investigator — a longtime family friend — told him he wanted the case closed. Billy Farwell recalled the investigator saying that he needed the investigation like he needed a “bullet in the head.”
One of Farwell’s attorneys, Kimberly Stevens, acknowledged to jurors Farwell “had an affair” but insisted he is no killer.
“He has made regrettable mistakes. He is human,” Stevens told jurors. “Matthew did not kill Sandra Birchmore.”
The FBI took up the case after a deputy chief raised concerns
The FBI began looking into Birchmore’s death in 2023, partly at the urging of a former deputy chief at the Stoughton Police Department, where Farwell worked.
Deputy Chief Brian Holmes had led an internal affairs investigation, but Farwell resigned before Holmes released findings that concluded Farwell had a sexual relationship with Birchmore.
An expert brought in by federal authorities, Dr. William Smock, concluded Birchmore was strangled with a duffel bag strap and that she struggled before dying.
Birchmore dreamed of becoming a police officer
Birchmore was 12 when she participated in a police mentoring program in Stoughton for children interested in careers in law enforcement. Farwell, who was 24, soon friended her on Facebook.
Years later, they would exchange 40,000 texts, some of which were read at the trial. In one 2020 text, Birchmore told Farwell she would never forget the day they first had sex: April 10, 2013, when she was 15 and Farwell was 27.
“Best day of my life,” Birchmore wrote.
“Me too,” Farwell replied.
Over time, the communications showed Farwell engaging in sexting that involved strangling or choking.
“I’ll grab your throat and say you won’t say a word to anyone or you will be sorry,” Farwell wrote in one message.
She wanted a baby and it led to fights
In 2020, prosecutors said Birchmore pressed Farwell to get her pregnant — and threatened to tell his wife about their relationship if he didn’t. After she became pregnant late that year, she texted Farwell an image that read, “Congrats, we are going to be parents.”
Farwell responded that he had “nothing to say.”
When Birchmore suggested in a text that Farwell should be present when the baby was born, he replied: “You are truly the worst person on the face of the earth.”
One of Birchmore’s friends, Leslie Davis, testified that the two fought. She said Birchmore told her about one fight where Farwell pushed her to the ground. Birchmore had wanted Farwell to promise to identify himself as the baby’s father on a birth certificate.
“He wouldn’t sign it and said, ‘That’s not my baby,’” Davis said.
A tipster contacted the police
In January 2021, a woman called Stoughton police and reported Farwell’s relationship with Birchmore.
Farwell was incensed, saying in a text to Birchmore, “You have no idea how bad what she did is.”
Twelve days later, on Feb. 1, 2021, Farwell texted Birchmore, asking to stop by her apartment. She said he was welcome.
Security camera video showed Farwell entering the building at 9:14 p.m. A digital forensics expert testified that Birchmore’s phone stopped moving at 9:40 p.m., three minutes before the lobby security camera recorded Farwell leaving.
Prosecutors say that during that time, Farwell killed Birchmore to prevent her from revealing their relationship. She was about eight weeks pregnant.
“It was no longer a matter of whether his crimes would be exposed; it was a matter of when,” Cummings, the prosecutor, told jurors. “He had lost control of Sandra. He had a real problem. He needed a way to silence her permanently.”
Farwell’s lawyer says Birchmore was suicidal
Farwell’s lawyer, Stevens, told jurors that Birchmore was a troubled woman who started taking psychiatric medication at age 6, attempted suicide as a teenager and was desperate after becoming pregnant. Birchmore was alone for the holidays and had less than $3 in the bank, Stevens said.
“She is worried. She is stressed. She is freaking out,” Stevens said.
Farwell, she said, went to Birchmore’s apartment to break up with her, not kill her.
The state’s medical examiner, relying partly on information from police, initially determined Birchmore died by suicide. The office has since changed the official cause of death to “undetermined.”
A paternity test revealed Farwell was not the one who impregnated Birchmore. It was Army recruiter Jason Pickard, who said he met Birchmore in 2019, when she was considering enlisting, and soon after started a sexual relationship. He testified that Birchmore told him Farwell was the father and that their relationship began when she was underage.
Prosecutors finished presenting their case Wednesday.
The defense was expected to call witnesses for a third day Friday before the case goes to the jury as early as next week.

title: Top federal prosecutor in Alaska says criminal probe underway over would-be spoiler Senate candidate
text:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — The top federal prosecutor in Alaska confirmed on Friday the existence of a criminal investigation related to an alleged scheme to confuse voters by putting a Senate candidate on the ballot with the same name as the Republican incumbent.
The investigation has been ongoing for several months, but revelations this week from The New York Times that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan have resulted in a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska,” U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters.
“When credible information comes out, we are committed to pursuing that information to deceive voters and we will act on it. We are acting on it intensely and swiftly,” Heyman said.
Heyman would not say what potential crimes authorities are looking into or the targets of the probe, but encouraged the public to come forward with tips that could help investigators.
Peltola denied Thursday that she knew anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot, where Peltola is challenging Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
“I just want to clear the air,” she said at a campaign rally at a downtown bar in Juneau, Alaska’s capital. “I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters.”
Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola’s campaign. “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.
The race is among a handful of Senate contests this year expected to determine control of the chamber.
Trump had previously directed his Department of Justice to sue to block certification of the Senate race should Peltola defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
State attorneys have asked a court to rule on the Justice Department’s lawsuit by Monday, saying the case could “cast a cloud over Alaska’s election that is contrary to the public interest.”
Separately, Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation into Peltola, saying the newspaper’s reporting “reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes.”
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” Dunleavy added, noting that the reporting “substantially supports” earlier findings by the state’s elections board into the matter.
Trump on Thursday cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election. “Well, you’re going to have to see what happens,” the president told reporters on his way to a rally in South Carolina. “It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run.”
___
Durkin Richer reported from Washington. Bohrer reported from Juneau, Alaska.

title: 2 earthquakes have shaken Maine this week
text:
A pair of earthquakes have rattled Maine this week.
The first temblor, a magnitude 1.6, shook the ground at a depth of 3 miles about 7.5 miles north-northwest of the Piscataquis County town of Brownville about 11:11 p.m. Monday, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.
That was followed by a magnitude 1.5 quake that hit nearly 4 miles deep about 4 miles west-northwest of the Kennebec County town of Windsor at 9:19 p.m. Wednesday, the U.S. Geological Survey reported.
Since 1997, there have been more than 170 recorded earthquakes in the state, according to the Maine Geological Survey.
The strongest quake in recent memory occurred on Oct. 16, 2012, when a 4.5 magnitude earthquake shook the ground in East Waterboro, according to the Maine Geological Survey. But Maine has felt the impact of much larger earthquakes that hit as far away as Plattsburgh, New York, and Quebec City.
Recorded quakes tend to be clustered near Passamaquoddy Bay, the Dover-Foxcroft-Milo area and southwestern Maine. Of course, earthquakes have been felt across Maine, even as far north as the St. John Valley, according to a Maine Geological Survey report.
Every so often quakes happen in clusters. That happened off York Harbor between Jan. 27 and Feb. 2, 2024, when three quakes ranging from magnitude 2 to 3.8. It happened again near Jonesboro between Aug. 11 and Sept. 1, 2022, when about nine earthquakes ranging from magnitude 1.7 to 3 shook the ground. Before that there was the cluster of six quakes east of Cadillac Mountain on Mount Desert Island from Sept. 22 to Dec. 29, 2006, the strongest of which measured a magnitude 4.2.

title: InvestigateTV+: Prison program helping veterans
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ takes you inside a peer-led prison program helping incarcerated veterans rebuild purpose through discipline and mentorship and talk to the supporters who say it’s breaking the cycle.
Plus, how art is helping dementia patients reconnect and communicate.
Then, an unlikely dog-and-cat friendship brings comfort to one family.
Helping veterans rebuild
American Legion Veterans Memorial Post 432 at Elayn Hunt Correctional Center was the first prison-based American Legion post in Louisiana, helping incarcerated veterans heal and rebuild their lives.
The program is recognized for a zero percent recidivism rate. No one from the post comes back to prison.
The benefits of art therapy
Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected.
Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases.
Cancer conversations
Do you only go to the doctor when you have an ache or feel sick? For many women that answer can be “yes.”
A 2025 survey said that every one in six women say they missed or may have missed a routine cancer screening within the past year.
A South Carolina salon is partnering with a statewide health initiative to have important conversations about cancer screening with clients.
Three-legged besties
A 1-year-old dog named Blueberry and a 10-month-old cat named Meadow were adopted together after they met at the veterinary hospital run by Last Chance Animal Rescue in Waldorf, Maryland.
Rachel Clarke, who adopted both animals, said Blueberry “loves to play, and she loves to snuggle.” She said Meadow is “a little more independent, but Blueberry goes where Meadow goes.”

title: The best way to hunt ducks in Maine if you only have an hour
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
I’ve used a duck hunting tactic for decades that’s effective, exciting and possible to pull off in an hour before or after work. Jump shooting neighborhood waterways is a blast, literally and emotionally.
Sneaking the first 50 yards toward the water’s edge wasn’t too tough. Bending over and duck-walking through tall grass and brush kept us hidden. The last 25 yards through sparse cover, over rocks, roots and brambles, required slow progress on our hands and knees, followed by belly crawling.
The venture proved far more rigorous than my first outings 50 years ago, resembling a military obstacle course. But my camo-clad companions, keeping pace 25 feet to either side, and I persevered.
At my signal, everyone surged to their feet and stepped through the underbrush onto the raised bank of a remote farm pond. With a rush of wings, splashing water and raucous quacking, more than 20 ducks of several species took flight as a barrage of shotgun blasts sounded.
In the autumn hush that followed, six colorfully accented ducks floated on the rippling water.
When October arrives, so do multiple hunting opportunities. Moose, deer, grouse, woodcock and waterfowl seasons are all underway.
Duck hunting tops my to-do list because local species are still around. Many smaller varieties will head south by late November, including blue-winged and green-winged teal, wood ducks and wigeon.
Another reason to hunt ducks in the coming weeks is that other hunting seasons draw attention away from them, reducing competition and hunting pressure.
Traditional duck hunting methods include setting decoys in a field and shooting from layout blinds or placing floating decoys on a lake and hunting from a camouflaged boat or shoreline hide. Hunters can also float a canoe down a river or stream, switching between paddling and shooting as ducks flush.
These methods can be effective, but they often require multiple hunters, plenty of equipment and several hours.
For working men and women with limited time, there’s a simpler option.
Maine is dotted with thousands of waterways, many of them small and easy to overlook. Swamps, farm ponds, marshes and bogs attract puddle ducks throughout the state.
Hunters can scout gravel back roads, farm-field tracks, ATV trails and old logging roads to find these hidden spots.
Many are surrounded by trees, brush, reeds and cattails that provide cover for hunters to creep within shotgun range before suddenly appearing and flushing the ducks.
Full camouflage helps hunters stay concealed, especially a face mask and gloves. Waders can protect the knees during crawls and allow hunters to retrieve downed ducks from shallow water.
A 12-gauge shotgun is popular for duck hunting, but I’ve switched to a synthetic-stocked, camouflaged 20-gauge. It’s lighter and shorter for crawling through brush, and it works well with bismuth No. 4 shot on small ponds and streams.
Some of my most exciting and memorable hunts have involved sneaking up on streams and ponds to jump-shoot ducks.
One of the most unforgettable happened one morning when I shot four ducks from a flushed flock with four shots, and each bird was a different species. It was a rare feat, especially since a semiautomatic shotgun can legally hold only three shells while hunting.
Three of us crept through the woods to a cove and back eddy on Prestile Stream, where ducks congregate every fall. I crawled to the opposite shoreline while two friends positioned themselves 50 yards upstream and downstream, giving us a chance to shoot regardless of which direction the birds flew.
When I popped into the open, at least three dozen waterfowl exploded in every direction.
I picked a duck and fired, then selected another as the first tumbled. I swung and dropped a third bird as it headed downstream.
As I started wading out to retrieve the closest duck, my upstream hunting buddy fired a couple of shots. Then I heard ducks quacking as they came my way.
I quickly pulled a shell from my pocket, jammed it into the open breech and snapped the action closed as a pair of mallards rounded the bend.
Fourth shot, fourth bird.
I ended up with a black duck, wood duck, green-winged teal and drake mallard. To this day, I can close my eyes and see the entire scene play out in my mind.
That’s why I’m still jump-shooting ducks all these decades later.
Scouting is key to finding secluded ponds and backwaters where ducks gather. I use a mapping app on my phone or a GPS to mark dozens of productive locations.
It’s best to visit each spot only two or three times at most. Ducks quickly relocate under hunting pressure and may not return.
Jump shooting is more fun with a partner, but groups should be limited to three hunters to keep things safe and controlled along small streams and ponds.
A well-trained retrieving dog makes recovering downed ducks easier, particularly in reeds and thick brush. When I don’t have a dog, I use my 17-foot Old Town Kevlar canoe, which weighs just 57 pounds and is easy to transport and maneuver.
With a little planning, it’s possible to visit several neighborhood duck ponds before work and even more on a day off.
So far, it’s been a banner year. Despite dry weather shrinking or drying up some wetlands, a strong hatch has produced plenty of puddle ducks in a wide variety of species.
Get out before cold weather arrives. It’s time to get a “jump” on duck hunting.

title: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
text:
(Aging Untold) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love.
The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates.
Step away before things escalate
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room.
“You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.”
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help.
“If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said.
Treat communication as behavior
Caregivers should consider what the person they care for is going through, Cradduck said.
“Their communication is really behavior,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to figure out what’s going on that’s causing the frustration.”
She said unspoken expectations can also cause conflict.
“You expecting something from somebody oftentimes turns into spoken resentment,” Cradduck said. “So then, you’re frustrated and you’re yelling and they have no idea.”
A person may be cognitively whole and still not know what a caregiver wants if the caregiver has not said it, she said.
Choose words and tone with care
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke listed words that can escalate a conversation:
- No
- You
- Always
- Never
- Don’t
- You can’t
In addition to the words, tone affects how a caregiver is perceived, Cradduck added.
“It’s not just what you say, it’s how you say it,” Cradduck said.
“If you want to have a better day, have a better tone,” Ambrose said.
She said miscommunication is often the source of conflict.
“All drama and conflict comes from one thing, and that’s miscommunication,” Ambrose said.
She said the way a person communicates is a cue to how that person is feeling, and caregivers should have the emotional maturity to manage themselves.
Meet people where they are
O’Rourke described a visit to her father in a nursing home. He was upset about a missing key for his wheelchair, and staff members were upset with him for being upset. She said she took out a key, turned it on the arm of the chair and got it to work.
Her heart rate went up in that moment, despite her training.
“But then I realized, I don’t have to be right,” O’Rourke said. “I can let go and be with him where he is.”
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said that when communication is off and there’s a misunderstanding, people begin to second-guess themselves and things can spiral toward anger.
A caregiver can be as distraught as the person receiving care, she said.
Check negative self-talk and name the fear
The Aging Untold experts also addressed negative thoughts and venting to others.
Ambrose said she sees “low-level energy” in Facebook groups where people complain about the person they care for or about others involved — and that kind of drama will make the caregiver more miserable.
But Cradduck said she likes that such groups exist because caregivers can vent in a safe place before they walk into the room.
Negative thoughts, such as “she just never listens to me,” lead to negative and hurtful words, she said.
O’Rourke said venting about fears, frustrations and stress to someone else helps a caregiver feel more balanced going into another conversation.
Rogers addressed underlying fear and said it is something caregivers do not talk about enough.
Go in without a set outcome, and treat adults as adults
How a caregiver goes into the conversation matters too.
O’Rourke said that a caregiver who goes into one with a specific outcome in mind “will lose.” BUt a caregiver who goes in with no outcome, aiming for a successful connection, can build on that.
Cradduck cautioned that caregivers should not treat an adult like a child.
“When you’re trying to parent or you’re trying to correct them like you would a child, then you’re creating a conflict because they’re not going to be happy,” Cradduck said.
The caregiver has to be “the peaceful adult” and keep the calm, but that it is not always easy, she said.
Key takeaways
- Step away to calm down. Remove yourself or get help when you notice signs such as feeling hot, shaky or tense in the jaw.
- See communication as behavior. Consider what the person you care for is going through and what is causing the frustration.
- Say what you expect. Unspoken expectations can turn into spoken resentment.
- Watch your tone and your self-talk. Tone affects how you are perceived, and negative thoughts can lead to hurtful words.
- Ditch the “dance of normalcy” and reclaim your agency. Let go of old relationship dynamics and choose who you want to be now, even when the past is complicated.
- De-escalate to prevent burnout.

title: Ground cinnamon recalled ahead of holiday season due to elevated lead risk, FDA says
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - Ground cinnamon is being recalled in 14 states ahead of the holiday season.
SLR Food Distribution Inc said it’s voluntarily recalling Wise Wife Brand Ground Cinnamon because it could be contaminated with elevated levels of lead, according to a recall alert.
The affected cinnamon was sold in retail and grocery stores between Sept. 8, 2025, and June 28, 2026, in Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Nebraska, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin.
According to the recall notice, lead exposure can impact nearly every bodily system, with effects depending on dosage, duration, and an individual’s age and weight. Low-level, short-term exposure may not produce immediate symptoms, and no illnesses have been reported to date.
Here’s what to check for:
- Description: 110 grams (3.88 ounces) clear plastic container with a black screw-top cap.
- Best-before date: April 25, 2027.
- UPC: 0688474302754 (printed on the back label)
Short-term exposure to very low levels of lead may not cause any symptoms, and so far, no illnesses have been reported as a result of the potentially contaminated cinnamon, according to the recall alert.
Consumers are advised not to consume the recalled product and to throw it away or return it to the place of purchase for a full refund.

title: Ian McKellen pays tribute to co-star, lifelong friend Patrick Stewart
text:
Ian McKellen pays tribute to co-star and lifelong friend Patrick Stewart
As fans and colleagues mourn the death of Sir Patrick Stewart, the legend of the stage and screen who died Thursday at the age of 86 from complications with Alzheimer's and Lewy body dementia, perhaps no reaction was more anticipated than that of Stewart's lifelong friend and co-star, Sir Ian McKellen.
Related video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
McKellen, who starred alongside Stewart in the "X-Men" film franchise and shared the stage with Stewart for countless productions, shared his memories of his lifelong friend on his Instagram account.
"We first met as ambitious young actors with the Royal Shakespeare Company half a century ago but we weren't in the same productions," McKellen said. "My first strong memory was a few years later, meeting him in the street in central London when he told me about an offer to take over a leading part in 'Star Trek.'"
McKellen goes on to describe how he tried to discourage Stewart from taking the role.
"'But Patrick, think of your stage career in the UK. Do you really want to risk—getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?'" McKellen wrote. "Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did."
According to NBC News, their first performance together was in Tom Stoppard's 1977 play, "Every Good Boy Deserves Favour," which was produced in collaboration with the Royal Shakespeare Company.
"I had admired him from the start of his career," Stewart told The Guardian in 2019 when speaking on McKellen. "When he joined the RSC, I was frankly intimidated."
Stewart and McKellen's friendship has been well documented over the years, with the two first sharing the screen in 2000's "X-Men," where they played friends-turned-rivals Charles Xavier and Magneto, respectively. Both actors are reprising their roles 26 years later in this year's "Avengers: Doomsday," which McKellen references in his tribute as Stewart's "farewell performance."
"We have to thank 'X-Men' for the two of us really getting to know one another, because every day on an 'X-Men' movie you spend far more time sitting in your trailer than you do on the set doing a drop of work — and those trailers are extremely luxurious. And we had adjoining ones, so we sat around and talked and reminisced," Stewart said on a 2014 SAG-AFTRA Foundation panel that the two appeared on together. "And I discovered a lot about this chap and he about me, and we found that there were many, many overlaps in our careers and many areas where we had little in common."
In total, the two starred together in six movies and three plays, with two of those plays — "Waiting for Godot" and "No Man's Land" — running concurrently for part of their duration.
"That I get to spend six nights a week and three afternoons on stage with this chap is still—," Stewart said in the 2014 panel before being overcome with emotion. McKellen, next to him, held his hand. "Because I was a fan!"
McKellen officiated Stewart's 2013 wedding to his wife, Sunny Ozell, whom McKellen said "has cared for [Stewart] through sickness and health, through thick and thin."
McKellen, like so many of Stewart's other co-stars, shared what the late actor meant to so many people.
"He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and, in my case, love," McKellen said.

title: 10-bed detox program in Bangor is closing
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness is closing its 10-bed detox program in Bangor due to lack of funds, according to co-CEOs Lisa Sockabasin and Rebecca Petrie.
The closure will cut the number of detox beds in the region in half, further straining a network of addiction recovery services that is already stretched thin. It’s a sign that more sweeping changes are needed statewide to support the recovery infrastructure that has grown during Gov. Janet Mills’ tenure.
Detox is a multi-day inpatient program, often the first step someone takes toward recovery from substance use disorder. The nonprofit’s Cedar Road Detox Facility on Mt Hope Avenue accepted people, including those on MaineCare, who wished to detox from opiates, alcohol and stimulants, and offered counseling alongside 24/7 withdrawal management. Clients typically stayed between three and seven days, according to Petrie.
Cedar Road served about 500 people last year, Petrie said. Its closure will leave Wellspring’s 10-bed New Horizons center in Hampden as the only detox program within an hour of Bangor.
“Detox Beds historically have been very difficult to find,” she said. “There’s a significant gap, and we’re extremely heartbroken that it’s due to financial reasons that we had to close.”
Cedar Road opened three years ago but has struggled to maintain funding since President Doanld Trump took office and his administration slashed many federal grant programs.
“Over the past year, we’ve been working really hard to address a shortage in funding for the detox center,” Petrie said, noting that reimbursements for the detox program only cover about one third of its operating expenses. That gap forced the organization to rely on federal grants, but those grants were frozen last year and several ended more recently.
That left the nonprofit with a $2 million gap, Sockabasin said. “It’s math. It’s that simple,” she added.
Funding a detox program can be tricky because many health grant programs restrict how funds can be used. For example, Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness was a recipient of rural health transformation funds, the federal program that was created as part of the Trump administration’s “big beautiful bill” — but those funds cannot be used for detox. Instead, the nonprofit plans to put them toward behavioral health case management and crisis management services.
Mills has touted her administration’s work to expand addiction services, which she made a priority when she took office amid record-high overdose deaths. Recovery advocates hope her successor will work to stabilize the services established during Mills’ tenure.
In Sockabasin’s view, the detox center’s closure represents an opportunity to “critically interrogate the system” that supports recovery services in Maine and shows that ensuring access to addiction treatment requires more sweeping legislative change. Wabanaki Public Health and Wellness cannot fix the system alone, she said, emphasizing that solutions must take into account flaws in the reimbursement model and the high costs associated with employing medical staff.
It’s not just detox centers that struggle to find adequate funding, Sockabasin added, pointing to rural recovery centers that lack a sustainable funding stream.
“People are going to be harmed in the meantime, while we’re all trying to figure it out. And that, to me, is unacceptable,” she said.
Thirty-one people staffed Cedar Road, and 24 have been laid off, Petrie said. The remaining workers will continue to provide medication-assisted treatment and substance use counseling at the facility on an outpatient basis.
The facility is no longer taking new clients, and the inpatient program will officially end when current clients finish treatment next week.
In addition to Wellspring, there are three detox programs in the Portland area and three hospital-based programs elsewhere in the state: Maine General Medical Center in Augusta, St. Mary’s Center for Recovery in Lewiston and Pen Bay Hospital in Rockport.
Wellspring’s executive director, Rick Gwinn, was not immediately available for comment Friday afternoon.

title: The three-legged cat and dog duo that are best friends
text:
WALDORF, Md. (InvestigateTV) — A 1-year-old dog named Blueberry and a 10-month-old cat named Meadow were adopted together after they met at the veterinary hospital run by Last Chance Animal Rescue in Waldorf, Maryland.
Laurie Jenkins, assistant director of Last Chance Animal Rescue, said both animals arrived with wounds to their extremities that required amputations.
Hospital Manager Lauren Webb said she got a call about Blueberry on Christmas Eve.
“We’ve got to help this dog. It’s Christmas Eve. We’ve got to pull out a miracle,” Webb recalled.
Blueberry had been found on the street in bad shape. The hospital saved her life. “You could see in her eyes that she was a fighter.”
A month later, Meadow was transferred from a shelter in West Virginia. Jenkins said Meadow “came in with her own leg issues, but also had upper respiratory.”
Another month passed before the two met at lunchtime. Webb said staff typically spend their lunch breaks snuggling with animals that need extra care. She said staff had laid a blanket on the floor.
Jenkins said Blueberry came out, and Meadow came out and laid on top of her. “They were together ever since,” Jenkins said.
“It was magic,” Webb said.
After the two had healed and were ready for adoption, Last Chance posted the pair on its Facebook page. The post requested that they be adopted together.
Clarke said her partner, Kevin, saw the post while scrolling on Facebook. The couple also has a “tripod cat,” she said.
“Even though they had a lot of attention, we’re like, let’s just throw our hat in the ring,” Clarke said.
Clarke said the animals “will hang out together. They’ll sleep together. They have been such great additions to the family.”
“We could not have asked for a better home,” Webb said.
Clarke said that “even if they stumble and they fall down, it doesn’t, you know, deter them from getting back up.”
Clarke said hearing “bad news one week and worse news the next” made the story stand out to her.
“It’s nice to have kind of something that was a very sad story that has a happy ending, and to kind of see that there is hope,” she said.
Jenkins said seeing the animals with their family makes her “unbelievably happy.”

title: Former Husson University assistant professor facing child sex abuse materials, violation of privacy charges
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) — A former Husson University assistant professor was arrested Friday on charges of possession of child sexual abuse material and violation of privacy, according to the Bangor Police Department.
Jonathan Houck, 33, of Bangor, was taken into custody on an arrest warrant and transported to the Penobscot County Jail. He is charged with six counts of possession of child sexual abuse material and four counts of violation of privacy.
Investigation sparked by cybertip from Dropbox
Court records show Dropbox alerted the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children that an account associated with Houck’s username had uploaded four sexually exploitative images involving children under 16. The report alleges the uploads took place between late 2020 and June 2026.
Investigators who reviewed the material said they discovered videos featuring an adult male performing sex acts with young girls. Prosecutors said the man was not Houck.
Investigation and searches of Bangor home, campus
On Sept. 21, as part of an investigation into Houck for dissemination or possession of sexually explicit material, Bangor police searched his Pearl Street home and his campus office at Husson University. Court documents say investigators seized dozens of items from both locations.
Police say the searches led to evidence of additional violation of privacy crimes.
At the time of the search, Houck was working as an assistant professor of exercise science and assistant cross country coach at Husson. His biography has been removed from the university’s website.
Prosecutor, university officials weigh in
“This is a person who was in a position of trust. And I think that really elevates things because victims are not suspecting someone like a professor,” Deputy District Attorney Chelsea Lynds said. “It really shakes the confidence of the community when someone in a position like this commits such a predatory act. And that is just very unfortunate. And it really elevates the seriousness of this case.”
University communications director Sarah Walker Caron said the faculty member involved in the investigation was escorted from campus and “relieved of his duties” within an hour of their learning of the investigation on Sept. 21. She said the university will continue to comply with all law enforcement.
“Husson University is deeply disturbed by Jonathan Houck’s alleged conduct,” Walker Caron said.
In an email obtained by WABI, Husson President Lynn Coy-Ogan said the university was “made aware of a small group of students who were believed to be impacted, and they have been notified and provided appropriate support.”
Alleged victim speaks out
One of those students came forward in a TikTok.
“He already took all of that from me. I’m not going to let him take my name, too. So, that being said, my name is Abigail Dudley, and I am one of God knows how many victims of Jonathan Houck.”
Abigail Dudley said she learned this week that her images were among those found on Houck’s devices. She said that as part of an assignment last year, Houck asked students to undress and weigh themselves in a room with an apparent hidden camera.
“Just know that I feel disgusted every time I wake up in the morning,” Dudley said in the video. “I am terrified to walk into school. I look everywhere for cameras. I can’t even use the bathroom here. [...] I wouldn’t say that I expected it from him, you know, he was my advisor, professor, someone I looked up to and trusted,” she said.
Dudley’s attorney, Star Wagner with Bigos Law, issued a statement to WABI on her behalf. Wagner said Houck “could not have carried out this betrayal without being placed in a position of authority within the classroom.”
Wagner’s statement continued: “Husson caused an unfathomable breach of trust against Abigail Dudley, other Husson students, and the broader community. Students place their trust in educational institutions to provide a safe learning environment, and that trust was violated here.
“Serious questions must be answered regarding Husson’s role in allowing this abuse to occur. We are grateful to law enforcement for the investigation that brought this atrocity to light and will continue to cooperate in their efforts.”
“As always, our primary concern is that the needs of our students are met and that the continuity of the education is maintained,” Walker Caron added.
What’s next for the case
Houck is being held at the Penobscot County Jail. His profile on the jail’s website shows bail is set at $50,000 cash.
He’s expected to make his first court appearance next week.

title: Trump cancels rallies in Kansas and Iowa, opting for telerallies to reach more voters, RNC says
text:
ROCK HILL, S.C. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday canceled weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas, opting instead to support Republican candidates with telerallies that his party said could reach more voters in nearly two dozen states in the final days of a midterm election that could cost the GOP control of Congress.
The president traveled to South Carolina Thursday for the second time in a month, a sign of Republican anxiety about Darline Graham’s ability to fend off a robust challenge from Democrat Annie Andrews for a critical U.S. Senate seat.
That message could resonate in an election year defined by voter frustration with the economy, gas prices and the war in Iran, putting Trump’s Republican Party on defense in territory where they have rarely had to compete in recent years.
Beyond South Carolina, Republicans are entering the final days of this year’s midterm elections navigating tight contests in Texas, Kansas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska. Both parties are also closely following developments in the Mississippi Senate race.
The president projected confidence as he returned to the White House, saying, “We’re going to have a strong Tuesday night.”
Trump was scheduled to hold a rally in Kansas on Saturday and in Iowa on Sunday. But the Republican National Committee announced Thursday evening that he would instead spend a “72-hour sprint” doing rallies by phone rather than in person, a move the RNC said would maximize Trump’s ability to speak to voters nationwide. The RNC said telerallies are planned for nearly 20 states, and more may be announced.
It was an abrupt shift in Trump’s pledge to push through the final days of the campaign doing rally after rally to galvanize his supporters. As of Thursday, he had done 25 rallies during the month of October, falling short of a goal he had once placed north of 30.
Trump says he doesn’t need to go to Kansas
There were signs the travel and long speeches have caught up with him. On Monday, in Corinth, Mississippi, Trump — whose voice has grown raspy — told the crowd, “God didn’t make your vocal cords to do a rally every day.”
But he bristled Thursday when a reporter asked whether he had canceled plans to travel to Kansas because of his health.
“You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect,” Trump snapped.
The president said he’s not traveling to Kansas, where GOP Sen. Roger Marshall faces Democrat Adam Hamilton, “because he’s doing very well,” an apparent reference to Marshall.
“I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas,” Trump said.
A campaign strategist with Republican Senate leadership said there was widespread curiosity about why the schedule was changing to telerallies. The strategist spoke on condition of anonymity to share the content of private conversations.
Trump, who revels in big crowds, has this month held rallies in smaller venues than many he once filled. The decision to switch to telerallies means he will be expected to speak for about 10 minutes instead of more than 90, as he does at in-person events.
Trump plans to travel to Daytona Beach, Florida, for a rally Friday. It’s not clear whether he will hold additional in-person events after that. The White House has not published his schedule for Monday, the final day of the campaign.
Democrats took notice.
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan who’s in a tight race against Republican Mike Rogers, said Thursday night that the president’s goal of trying to gin up GOP voters has backfired and he has “given up.” “He’s an old man, he’s a loser,” El-Sayed continued. “He now understands that he has fully lost the midterms for his party.”
Graham has struggled to connect with voters
In South Carolina, Graham has struggled to quickly build connections with voters. The sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, she was appointed in July by Republican Gov. Henry McMaster to fill the remaining months of her brother’s term after his sudden death. In August, she became the party’s nominee to succeed him for a full six-year term.
“He was a great politician,” Trump said of Lindsey Graham, before promoting Darline Graham as his elected successor. “She’s got the gene.”
Darline Graham commended the president for having “delivered what Washington promised for decades.” She warned that Andrews “would just throw it all away.”
Andrews appeared in nearby Fort Mill on Wednesday, where she said that if voters elect her and become unhappy with her performance on Capitol Hill, “you can fire me in six years.”
South Carolina Rep. Ralph Norman, who lost to Graham in the GOP Senate primary runoff, has criticized Graham as unqualified. Norman, who has refused to campaign with Graham, said the race is closer than it would have been had he been nominated.
Lonnie Dean Johnson of Sumter, South Carolina, supported Norman in the primary and was voting Graham out of party loyalty, albeit unenthusiastically.
“She’s on a Republican ticket. I, by and large, support the Republican platform,” he said. ”So, I support her and wish her well.”
Democrats are bullish about Senate races across the US
Democrats, meanwhile, are optimistic about their chances of booting GOP incumbent senators, including in Ohio, with an American public frustrated by continued high costs.
“Families see more money going out the door and not enough money coming in,” said Sherrod Brown, the Democratic Senate nominee who’s competing against Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted. At a rally in Toledo Thursday, Brown said Husted is “looking out for data centers and Wall Street.”
Farther north, Alaska’s Republican governor has ordered an investigation after The New York Times reported Wednesday that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting another candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
The Justice Department escalated the investigation Thursday, issuing a raft of new grand jury subpoenas, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
The Justice Department also issued subpoenas to California officials in the latest effort to scrutinize local election administration. A federal judge in California earlier Thursday appointed a special master to evaluate claims by the Trump administration that the state has some 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls.
Trump called the development in Alaska a “conspiracy” and called for Peltola to be removed from the ballot. He has cast doubt on whether Peltola would be seated in the Senate even if she won the election.
Peltola’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a message Thursday seeking comment on the governor’s order. But during a campaign stop in Soldotna, Peltola, a former congresswoman, suggested the Times’ report was a “distraction” from issues such as Sen. Sullivan’s support of the war in Iran.
The revelation in Alaska was a reminder of the volatility of the midterm campaigns’ final days as both parties make decisions about how to spend time and money with control of Congress on the line.
__
Sloan reported from Washington. Associated Press writers Thomas Beaumont in Des Moines, Iowa, Jesse Bedayn in Austin, Texas, Hannah Fingerhut in Clive, Iowa, John Hanna in Topeka, Kansas, Mike Householder in Kalamazoo, Michigan, and Meg Kinnard, Collin Binkley and Alanna Durkin Richer in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Chadbourne Road Crash In Standish Highlights Dangers Of Drowsy Driving On Maine Roads
text:
Maine State Police Say Drowsy Driver Hit Maine DOT Trailer In Standish After Falling Asleep At The Wheel
Maine DOT workers at a job site in Standish got quite a scare Thursday afternoon, after a man allegedly fell asleep behind the wheel and hit a trailer.
Read More: Halloween Safety In Eastern Maine This Weekend
According to the Maine State Police, the incident happened just before 2 PM on the Chadbourne Road.
"The preliminary investigation indicates that 32-year-old Merlin Maston of New Gloucester was traveling southbound in a Chevrolet Cruze when he fell asleep at the wheel and struck the rear of a MaineDOT trailer. At the time, MaineDOT employees were conducting roadway work. One MaineDOT employee who was outside the truck was struck by the vehicle but reported no injuries."
There was another Maine DOT employee who was also impacted by the crash. Both individuals were evaluated at the scene.
Authorities say they are still looking into the incident.
According to the Maine Driver Handbook, drowsy drivers account for a significant number of crashes each year.
"Drowsiness is tied to as many as 240,000 crashes a year...Micro-sleeps last only 4 to 5 seconds, but at 55 mph even that can be fatal."
They suggest that drivers should take periodic breaks if they start to feel sleepy.
"Take a break every 2 hours or 100 miles, and a 15 to 20 minute nap if you feel danger signs of fatigue."
The National Sleep Foundation echoes the concern about drowsy drivers on Maine roadways.
"Just like drunk, drugged, and distracted driving, drowsy driving is a real public health issue, causing thousands of car crashes each year and killing an estimated 6,400 people in the U.S. alone according to the AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety. 95% of Americans recognize that drowsy driving is dangerous yet nearly two-thirds of Americans report that they have driven while drowsy."
They say younger drivers between the ages of 16 and 25 and shift workers are in a high-risk category for falling asleep while driving.

title: Ex-band director facing molestation charges critically injured after shooting self during arrest
text:
BOSSIER PARISH, La. (KSLA/Gray News) - A former high school band director facing dozens of sex offense charges is in critical condition after shooting himself during an arrest Thursday, authorities said.
Bossier Parish Sheriff’s deputies were serving an arrest warrant for 56-year-old Kevin Williams at his Bossier City home when he resisted, according to officials. During a physical struggle, Williams pulled a handgun from his waistband and shot himself.
Deputies immediately administered first aid until emergency medical personnel arrived. Williams was transported to an area hospital, where he remains in critical condition.
Williams, a now-former band director at Haughton High School, was previously arrested Sept. 22 on 50 counts of molestation of a juvenile and 50 counts of felony carnal knowledge of a juvenile.
Authorities said those charges stemmed from an investigation into the alleged abuse of a former student in the school’s band program.

title: A colder weekend despite the sunshine
text:
A colder weekend despite the sunshine
A colder weekend despite the sunshine
A warm evening will give way to colder weather overnight as a cold front moves through. Expect scattered rain showers, some snow showers in the mountains, plenty of clouds, and gusty west-northwest winds into early Saturday.
Saturday will start breezy, with winds gradually easing during the day. It will also be much colder, with highs 10 to 15 degrees lower than today. Temperatures will drop into the 30s Saturday evening.
Dry weather looks likely through at least the middle of next week, with temperatures bouncing around but averaging above normal. Our next chance for meaningful rain may come late next week, but the timing and track of that system remain very uncertain.

title: US approves a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine after alleged holdup
text:
US approves a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine after alleged holdup
The Trump administration said Friday that it has approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot air defense interceptors for Ukraine after Kyiv had accused the Pentagon of delaying delivery of the vital munition needed to stop Russian ballistic missiles.
The State Department said 500 Patriot missiles are being purchased for Ukraine with donations from Canada, Germany and Norway through a U.S. program and that no American funds were involved.
Related video above: Ukraine-U.S. relations strain amid renewed Russian strikes
“This proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe,” the department said in a press release.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned this month that his country had nearly run out of the vital military munition it needs to combat Moscow's attacks as tensions with President Donald Trump's administration escalated.
The Ukrainian leader had accused the Pentagon of delaying the delivery of the missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine. He also said U.S. intelligence that warns of incoming Russian attacks had been interrupted and the Starlink satellite internet service had been throttled. Ukraine says Starlink speeds and intelligence have been restored.

title: Hong Kong's housing minister resigns after fire investigation finds inadequate oversight
text:
Hong Kong's housing minister resigns after fire investigation finds inadequate oversight
Hong Kong leader John Lee apologized Thursday and said his housing secretary resigned after an investigation into the city’s deadliest fire in decades found inadequate regulatory oversight.
The massive fire that broke out last November engulfed seven buildings in an apartment complex in a northern suburban district, killing 168 people and displacing thousands of others.
Many former residents of Wang Fuk Court have spent nearly a year waiting to see how the government will address accountability for the disaster that claimed their loved ones and their homes, which were undergoing building maintenance work at the time.
Related video above: Residents take shelter in Hong Kong community center after deadly high-rise fire
At the opening of the news conference, Lee and seven other top officials bowed in apology. Lee said the death toll deeply saddened him.
“As the chief executive, I apologize to the disaster victims and the public, and commit to fulfilling my responsibilities to lead the government with full force in resolving problems,” he said. “Comprehensive reforms will also be carried out. Similar incidents will never be allowed to happen again.”
Lee said Housing Secretary Winnie Ho “should bear political responsibility,” although no personal wrongdoing was found. He said Ho resigned Wednesday.
An independent committee found that the Housing Bureau’s independent checking unit, the Buildings Department, the Fire Services Department and the Labour Department had deficiencies in their supervision work, Lee said. A three-month investigation will now determine whether government employees were derelict in their duties.
Lee also announced a series of measures, including criminalizing bid-rigging in building maintenance projects, overhauling the system for handling complaints, and establishing a cross-departmental data system to share information such as violation records. A new organization would also be set up to better support residents in building maintenance projects.
Behind the fire were substandard materials and deception
The committee's report said evidence indicated that a lit cigarette end likely caused the fire, which started on the flat roof between two apartments on the first floor of Wang Cheong House. The committee heard substantial evidence that construction workers had smoked on site, and several cigarette butts and some partially burned materials, such as cardboard boxes, were found on the flat roof.
Experts found that the use of foam boards, non-fire-retardant scaffolding nets and canvases contributed to the fire’s spread, the report said.
Most of the deaths were caused by smoke inhalation. Some staircase windows were replaced with movable aluminum composite panels or wooden boards for workers’ convenience, allowing smoke to infiltrate escape routes. Opaque foam boards covered the windows, blocking sightlines and delaying evacuation. The shutdown of the fire alarm system was also a factor in the heavy death toll.
The committee said evidence clearly demonstrated that Will Power Architects Company, the consultant for the maintenance project, and Prestige Construction & Engineering Co., the main contractor, cut corners.
“There is no doubt that they are the main culprits responsible for the occurrence of the inferno and the high fatalities in the tragic incident,” the report said.
It said the evidence also revealed an array of registered contractors and building professionals who conducted no substantive work and were only asked to lend their names to “rubber-stamp” statutory forms in return for a fee. The private contractors and consultants had deceived the regulators, it said.
“Deception succeeded because the regulators’ own practices enabled it,” the report said. “The regulator’s reliance on the good faith of the regulated parties left obvious fire hazards uninvestigated.”
An agency under Ho's bureau is among those found with shortcomings
The committee found the Housing Bureau’s independent checking unit and the Buildings Department, the two agencies primarily responsible for supervising the maintenance work at Wang Fuk Court, had failed in their supervisory duties.
But the checking unit should bear a greater share of responsibility, the committee said. Among its shortcomings was the lack of proper investigations into the use of the foam boards and the fire-retardant quality of the scaffolding nets despite multiple complaints, it said.
It added the agency notified consultants and contractors of site inspections in advance.
The report also noted many features indicating the presence of bid-rigging and other associated misconduct at Wang Fuk Court.
The committee's work is separate from criminal investigations. Police and anti-corruption authorities previously charged seven people and two companies, Will Power and Prestige, with offenses including manslaughter and conspiracy to defraud over the fire.
Authorities alleged that the two companies and some defendants conspired to defraud the apartment owners by concealing previous litigation records of the company later awarded the renovation project, a contract worth more than 300 million Hong Kong dollars (over $38 million).
Beijing praises the government's handling, but some residents are not satisfied
China's Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office said the Hong Kong government’s handling fully demonstrated its sense of responsibility and its governing vision of putting people first and upholding the rule of law. Beijing's liaison office in Hong Kong also praised the government.
However, Phyllis Lo, who lost her mother in the fire, said she saw progress made but that justice had yet to be served. Lo said the criminal trial still has not begun, and it's not enough to see just one top official step down.
“She was not being sacked. She resigned herself,” Lo said.
She added the officials' apology was late, though it was better than nothing.
Dorz Cheung, who was displaced by the fire, was angry, saying he felt the news conference focused mostly on the future.
He said if the government wanted residents to move on, it should first resolve some matters they were facing, including the tax issues in their purchase of new homes.
“The feeling is just like what a fellow resident said — the press conference only had three takeaways: Sorry. I’ll do better, and it won’t happen again. A minister has stepped down … What more do you want?” he said.

title: Yarmouth woman’s haunted garage invites Halloween spirit and neighborliness
text:
YARMOUTH — In October, entering Karen McKenna’s garage feels like stepping between the pages of a Halloween “I Spy” book.
A bookshelf displays jars of witchy “ingredients” like bat wings and dodo feathers. A mad scientist’s lair in the corner features laboratory equipment and Frankenstein’s head in a jar. A potion-making table holds dozens of bottles and liquids for visitors to mix, and several decorated dollhouses are inhabited by bats, owls and mice. Above it all hangs a canoe — which is always in the garage and not particularly spooky — as well as twinkling lights and floating candles that illuminate the hundreds of different pieces of carefully crafted Halloween paraphernalia.
“The more you look, the more you see,” said McKenna, 65.
The collection of delicately placed items were either handmade by McKenna, found at thrift stores or gifted to her over the years. The retired senior caregiver gives visitors lists of items to find in a scavenger hunt — three ways to tell a fortune, white ghosts made from canned whipped cream caps, or Snow White’s poisoned apple.
“Some kids are so into it, they really want to get the challenge. And others just want to soak up the magic,” she said.
For the past three years, McKenna has invited the community into her transformed garage on Newell Road. The display takes her a steady week to set up, and she opens it to visitors on Friday and Saturday evenings throughout October, plus Halloween. Last Halloween, over 200 people wandered through.
“It’s always something to look forward to,” said McKenna’s neighbor Mark Priceman, whose young daughters are bringing a party of friends to visit the garage this year. “People will congregate here.”
New this year in the yard is “Witch’s Wood,” complete with a full-size goblin and witch and many more hidden details for those brave enough for a scarier experience.
McKenna has loved Halloween since she grew up trick-or-treating in the Cleveland suburbs, and she began throwing parties at her Yarmouth home even before her younger son was born on Halloween 31 years ago. Over the decades, as her children grew up, she collected and crafted more and more spooky decor for their front yard.
Setting everything up always delighted her, and her husband was her biggest cheerleader, McKenna said. After he died unexpectedly several years ago, she kept the tradition going, expanding the setup into a newly built garage four years ago.
“In a way I do this to indulge myself, and in a way I also do it kind of to honor the fact that he enjoyed that so much,” she said.
McKenna runs a donation drive alongside her experience, offering visitors a chance to drop personal hygiene items — because they’re not covered by the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program — into the mouths of monsters. McKenna will later take the donations the Yarmouth Community Food Pantry and Maine Needs.
“What’s really scary is not being able to afford the necessities,” said McKenna.
Wearing her simple ghost costume, McKenna plans to welcome her neighbors into her homemade Halloween project on Saturday. She says seeing children — and adults — delight in the details of her haunted scene is her favorite part of her favorite holiday.
“Connecting with your neighborhood is really priceless,” said McKenna. “It’s a labor of love.”

title: DEA approvals could bring big tax benefits for medical marijuana businesses
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration has for the first time issued registrations to medical marijuana dispensaries, a bureaucratic maneuver under President Donald Trump’s historic rescheduling of the drug that could pave the way for the businesses to receive tax benefits long denied the industry.
The agency issued the registrations Friday to more than 900 state-licensed dispensaries in Alabama, Florida, Mississippi, South Dakota, Texas, Virginia and West Virginia, the Justice Department said in a news release. The department did not immediately identify the approved businesses.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said in the statement that the regulated distribution of cannabis for medical use from those shops “will help ensure broader access to chronic pain treatment and the safety of the American people.”
In April, Blanche signed an order shifting the classification of state-licensed medical marijuana from Schedule I — reserved for drugs without medical use and with high potential for abuse, like heroin — to the less strictly regulated Schedule III.
The decision largely legitimized medical marijuana programs in the 40 states that have adopted them, and it set up an expedited system for state-licensed medical marijuana producers, manufacturers and distributors to register with the DEA. Businesses must undergo a pre-registration investigation and have security, recordkeeping, inventory controls and other safeguards governing the handling of controlled substances.
Registering with the agency is also expected to ensure immense tax benefits. Historically, state-licensed cannabis businesses haven’t been able to deduct normal business expenses — like advertising, rent or labor costs associated with sales — on their federal taxes because they were dealing with a federally illegal, Schedule I drug. Many in the industry have found that financially crippling.
Nearly 7,000 other cannabis dispensaries, manufacturers and distributors across the country have similarly applied for registration, according to a list published by the DEA on Friday.
Steph Sherer, the founder of the medical cannabis organization Americans for Safe Access, noted that the registrations were issued just days before the 30th anniversary of California becoming the first state to legalize the medical use of marijuana.
“For the first time, the federal government is recognizing and registering the medical cannabis dispensaries that patients fought to establish,” Sherer said in a written statement. “This is a tremendous victory for patient access and an opportunity to build on 30 years of progress.”
But questions abound. The way state-licensed medical marijuana businesses are regulated is vastly different from how most companies dealing with Schedule III drugs are overseen, and it remains unclear exactly what requirements the DEA may seek to impose on medical cannabis.
For example, some cannabis industry attorneys have noted, state regulators have often sought to mitigate the effects of the drug war by allowing people with some criminal history to run licensed marijuana businesses. It isn’t certain whether the DEA will adopt that approach with the businesses it registers.
Furthermore, many states have merged their recreational and medical marijuana industries. While the Trump administration has sought to reschedule marijuana more broadly, it remains unclear how the DEA will treat businesses that handle both adult-use and medical cannabis.
Two dozen states plus Washington, D.C., have authorized adult recreational use of marijuana, 40 have medical marijuana systems, and eight others allow low-THC cannabis or CBD oil for medical use. Only Idaho and Kansas ban marijuana outright.
“It’s obviously a positive step to see the program taking shape,” said Chris Lindsey, vice president of policy and state advocacy at the American Trade Association for Cannabis and Hemp. “What everybody’s watching for is, what can we expect to see now that we have companies that are going to be operating in this class? What are they going to have to start to do?”
___
Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press writer Jennifer Peltz in New York contributed.

title: Cooper Flagg scores 33 points as Mavs hand Rockets their first loss
text:
DALLAS — Kyrie Irving scored 35 points, Newport native Cooper Flagg added 33 and the Dallas Mavericks rallied for a 116-111 victory over Houston, handing the Rockets their first loss of the season in an NBA Cup opener Friday night.
Irving scored 26 of his points in the second half, including a jumper that put Dallas ahead for good at 102-100 and set up a tense final two minutes.
Houston’s loss left idle Memphis (5-0) as the only remaining unbeaten team in the league.
Kevin Durant scored 28 points, but the career 88% free-throw shooter missed a pair with the Rockets trailing by two with 1:53 remaining. Amen Thompson did the same thing with 42 seconds to go after Dallas’ P.J. Washington threw the ball directly to him for a turnover.
After each pair of misses, Flagg converted a clutch bucket on the other end, including a three-point play. Irving was 12 of 19 from the field, including 5 of 8 from 3-point range, and Flagg was 13 of 19.
Daniel Gafford scored 18 points, including two clutch free throws with Dallas leading by one with 11 seconds remaining.
The Mavericks held on down the stretch by fouling on purpose twice with a three-point lead in the final 10 seconds, and Irving hitting the free throws each time on the next possession.
Irving finished 6 of 6 from the line, extending the NBA’s longest active streak of made free throws to 54 going back to before he was sidelined for 19 months by a torn ACL in his left knee.
Jabari Smith Jr. scored 10 points of his 22 points in the second quarter, when Houston outscored Dallas 31-17 to turn a seven-point deficit into a seven-point lead.
Fred VanVleet scored 16 points, and Thompson had 15 for Houston, which was just 24 of 33 on free throws.
Up next
Rockets: Host Thunder on Saturday night
Mavericks: Host Kings on Monday night

title: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
text:
SHELBURNE, Vt. (Aging Untold) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump.
Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver.
How she started
Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked.
Jordan died a decade ago.
“I miss her so much,” Meiler said.
Still competing at 91
Meiler continues to compete.
“I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said.
Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them.
“I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.”
Inspiring others
One of the people Meiler has inspired is University of Vermont freshman Jason Lei.
“I want to be moving like you when I’m older as well,” he told Meiler.
“It makes me feel like 60 again,” she said with a smile.
Meiler has also inspired Gene Meiler, her husband of 65 years.
“She’s impressed me, that’s for sure,” Gene Meiler said. “That’s why I married her. She impressed me.”
Flo Meiler said she is happy to continue running the track. When she feels like she is slowing down, she adds a few more exercises.
“I’m very happy,” Flo Meiler said. “The good Lord has given me my health and my talent.”

title: InvestigateTV+ Weekend: Plane crashes near airports
text:
(InvestigateTV) — For millions living in the shadow of an airport, the danger isn’t hypothetical. For one mother, it cost her everything.
Plus, not every danger comes from above, sometimes it’s sitting right outside your window.
Danger Zone
When a UPS plane crashed just seconds after taking off in Louisville, Kentucky last year, the incident killed not just the three crew onboard but a dozen people on the ground in an industrial area near the runway. That crash is now shining a light on millions of Americans who live or work in “Danger Zones” in close proximity to airports. Although the FAA has established minimum buffers designed to avoid worst-case scenarios when aviation disasters occur, experts say more needs to be done to protect homes and businesses.
Our national investigative team examined federal crash data to see where these accidents are happening and how often, and found examples from across the country of plane crashes into homes and neighborhood streets — often injuring and killing not just those onboard the aircraft, but people on the ground.
Senior National Investigative Reporter Joce Sterman sat down with some of those pushing for change industry wide — including a Florida mayor whose city has seen a series of close-proximity crashes - and the grieving mother of a 4-year-old boy killed in one of those crashes when a plane hit the family’s car just feet from the airport. We also hear from a retired airline pilot and safety advocate about potential solutions on both sides of the runway fence.
Generator carbon monoxide dangers
When the power goes out during a hurricane or storm, many families turn to generators to stay safe. But a new federal report finds that same backup power can create a hidden danger of its own.
Investigators spent four years studying carbon monoxide poisonings in southeast Louisiana — and now they’re calling for a major change in how close generators can be to your home.
Electric aircraft & EMS response times
When seconds matter in a medical emergency, getting help there fast can mean the difference between life and death.
Now, some rural communities are testing a new way to close that gap — a one-person aircraft that can carry a paramedic and full life-saving gear straight to a patient, skipping the roads altogether.
Photojournalist Greg Simpson in Charlotte introduces us to the woman flying it.
Tips to tackle credit card debt
Many of you are focused on credit card bills right now as rates stay high and prices keep climbing. In this Watching Your Wallet, Consumer Investigator Rachel DePompa lays out a plan to tackle your credit card debt between now and the end of the year.
