title: Appeals court rejects Justice Department request for California to set aside disputed ballots
text:
Appeals court rejects Justice Department request for California to set aside disputed ballots
The 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday rejected the Justice Department’s request for California to set aside disputed ballots received in the midterm election.
The panel’s 2-1 ruling is the latest setback for the Trump administration’s efforts to assert control over state-run elections.
The administration has alleged California sent ballots to some 20,000 people who may not be U.S. citizens. It wants the state to set those ballots aside and not count them until citizenship can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens.
Related video above: Maryland officials prepare for DOJ election monitors
A district court judge already forcefully denied that request and warned that the Justice Department’s demands could disenfranchise citizens.
“As the district court found — and we discern no clear error — there is no feasible way to identify and segregate the ballots of specific individuals without potentially catastrophic effects on the entire system,” the appeals court wrote.
The ruling is the latest in an expansive legal battle between the federal government and the state before Election Day in the midterms on Tuesday. Millions of people in California have already voted.
The majority opinion was authored by Judge Mark J. Bennett, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, and Judge Gabriel P. Sanchez, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden.
The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling.
Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. Elections officials have said that processed votes are completely anonymized and can’t be matched back to the voters who submitted them.
The ruling comes during broader federal scrutiny of local elections, with the Trump administration issuing a raft of subpoenas in Alaska in a spoiler-candidate controversy. The Justice Department has also provided a list of alleged noncitizen voters to officials in Washington state.
Outside groups sued for access to the disputed list
Earlier on Friday, a federal judge in Washington ordered the Trump administration to share the disputed list of names with lawyers for the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights and the UCLA Voting Rights Project. They want the list so they can examine who is on the list and assess its impact on eligible voters.
It will be the first time that a nongovernment organization will have the opportunity to evaluate the merits of the list of some 20,000 names.
Prosecutors with the Trump administration have argued that there is just as much to lose from noncitizens illegally voting, arguing that to tally those votes would dilute the voice of citizens.
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra is an adviser to the UCLA Voting Rights Project.
The two groups sued the Homeland Security Department in early October to prevent it from using federal immigration data to challenge state voter rolls. The lawsuit cited examples in other states where the federal government’s data has been proven to mistakenly include thousands of citizens. It argued that the data-matching methods risk disenfranchising or deterring citizens from voting. On top of that, plaintiffs argued, the lists could disproportionately target naturalized citizens who are legally entitled to vote.
Another suit seeks to defend election workers
A coalition of unions on Friday also joined the growing list of groups challenging the federal government’s efforts.
The unions, including the A.F.L.-C.I.O. and the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, are asking a federal judge to temporarily block the Justice Department from demanding that local officials stop counting ballots and to drop threats to criminally prosecute officials who do not comply with its demands.
The top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, Bill Essayli, has warned that “any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy.”
On Thursday the Associated Press obtained subpoenas issued to election officials in Los Angeles County. The subpoenas request any documents and communications related to letters sent in July and October by federal officials to state election officials outlining the allegations about noncitizen voters. They also seek any information about efforts to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted. At least three L.A. County election officials have been asked to appear before a grand jury on Nov. 4, the day after the election.
The lawsuit accuses the Justice Department of issuing threats against election officials that could interfere with their ability to process votes.
It is unclear whether the Justice Department intends to bring criminal charges against anyone. The department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury.

title: Dating again? What older adults should know about sexual health and protection
text:
(Aging Untold) — Dating, intimacy and connection can be an important part of emotional and physical well-being for older adults. That includes people who are divorced, widowed, remarried or dating again for the first time in decades.
The Aging Untold experts are addressing the topics of sexual health, how it has changed over the years and how to stay protected.
You can’t tell by looking
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said appearances do not show whether someone has a sexually transmitted disease.
“You can’t tell by looking at someone if they have a sexually transmitted disease,” Rogers said. “You say, ‘Oh, they look healthy.’ You can’t tell by that.”
She said age does not change that risk.
“Getting older does not make you immune to getting a sexually transmitted disease,” Rogers said. “Just because you retired, your sexual health didn’t.”
Rogers said older adults have to take precautions to protect themselves against several diseases.
Condoms are about more than preventing pregnancy.
Over the decades, prevention options have changed, including for HIV.
And human papillomavirus, or HPV, is the most common sexually transmitted disease, Rogers said. The virus can cause cancer later in life, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Menopause is not protection
Having gone through menopause does not mean you do not need protection, the Aging Untold experts said.
“A lot of people think, ‘Well, I’ve been through menopause, I can’t get pregnant. I don’t need to protect myself,’” gerontologist Sam Cradduck said. “Menopause doesn’t protect you from gonorrhea or syphilis or HIV or HPV.”
Cradduck also said syphilis contracted at a younger age can show up later in life, and it shows up in communities where older adults live.
“That lives forever in you,” Cradduck said. “We’ve seen neurosyphilis in communities.”
Start the conversation
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said prevention starts with getting tested and having a conversation with your partner.
It can be awkward to ask a new partner whether they have been tested, especially for people who were married for many years before dating again, but the conversation still matters, she said.
One approach is to start by saying that an active sex life is important to you, then ask how the other person feels about getting tested and what the two of you will do to prevent infection, O’Rourke said.
Talk to your doctor as well, get tested and know what your risk factors are because you might have some and not know it, Rogers added. And protect yourself.
“That test might have been one month ago and things have changed,” Rogers said.
One of the risk factors that Rogers noted is a weakened immune system.
“If your immune system is not strong, you can’t fight off what you get exposed to,” Rogers said.
Protection details that matter
Cradduck added that people should check to see if the products they plan to use can be used together.
“Wearing a condom is important, but a lot of condoms and a lot of lubricants don’t go well together, and so you will impair the integrity of the condom with certain lubricants,” she said.
She also said people with a latex allergy should not use a latex condom.
Rogers said that it is easy for someone who has one disease to get another.
“When we treat people for chlamydia or gonorrhea, we treat for the other one as well,” Rogers said.
She added that PrEP, pre-exposure prophylaxis, a medication taken to prevent HIV infection, does not provide protection against other sexually transmitted diseases.
Couples who are dating after being widowed, each with one sexual partner, should still use protection, Rogers said.
“They only had one sexual partner that they know about,” Rogers said. “I used to get this all the time. ... You only know what the person told you. You don’t really know, so still protect yourself.”
Rogers said people should talk to their health care provider, talk to their partner and know whether they have risk factors that put them at risk for other things.
Name the diseases
To address the topic of sexually transmitted diseases, O’Rourke said she thinks it helps to name specific diseases instead of using the term “STDs.”
“STD seems like a distancer, like you don’t really hear syphilis. When I hear syphilis, my ears perk up. I think it’s important to really say what those diseases are, and then what do we get if we have it and it progresses and you’re older? I want to say the word cancer,” O’Rourke said.
Key takeaways
Be mindful of diseases, including gonorrhea and syphilis
Close the education gap: The three Ps are partners, practices and protection
Use today’s prevention tools, such as advanced screenings, immune supports and daily PrEP

title: Coach June Jones dies at 73
text:
June Jones, whose run-and-shoot offense dazzled at Hawaii and in the NFL, dies at 73
June Jones, the cutting-edge coach who brought the run-and-shoot offense to Hawaii and led the Rainbow Warriors to their greatest era and an undefeated regular season that catapulted them all the way to the Sugar Bowl, died on Thursday. He was 73.
Video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
Hawaii's football program in a statement did not list a cause of death for Jones, who coached the Atlanta Falcons for three seasons in the 1990s before his stint at Hawaii. The Honolulu Star-Advertiser cited a close family friend as saying Jones had entered hospice two weeks ago in his native Oregon.
“Coach Jones was a father figure, a mentor, and a visionary who revolutionized the game," said Timmy Chang, the current Hawaii coach who set the NCAA record for career passing yards (since broken) under Jones. "He believed in a young kid from Hawaii and gave me the opportunity of a lifetime to run his offense.”
Hawaii was one of three schools where Jones played quarterback in college, but it was his decision to transfer to Portland State that shaped the rest of his football career.
He played under Mouse Davis, who is largely credited with bringing to the big-time an offense that featured four receivers who adjusted their routes on the fly, rarely ran the football and, most of all, moved fast.
It was dubbed the run-and-shoot. Jerry Glanville, Wayne Fontes, Jack Pardee and Kevin Gilbride were among the few willing to throw out convention and use it. Jones might have had the most success.
After spending time in the 1980s with the Falcons, mostly as the third-string quarterback, Jones worked his way through assistant coaching jobs, landing with Glanville (and QB Warren Moon) of the Houston Oilers in 1987. In 1991, Jones joined Glanville with the Falcons, then took over when Glanville got fired.
“A visionary in the passing game,” the Falcons called Jones in a statement Thursday.
Sticking with the run-and-shoot, Jones briefly thrived and took Atlanta to one playoff trip with the help of quarterback Jeff George. But the Falcons fired Jones after three years. Jones also had a brief stint as an interim with the San Diego Chargers, replacing Gilbride after he was let go.
Jones returned to Hawaii in 1999 after the Warriors had gone 0-12, and he produced a remarkable turnaround. Hawaii capped off a 9-4 season with a win in the Oahu Bowl.
His most memorable season, though, ended at the Sugar Bowl. It came in 2007, when Colt Brennan ran the offense well enough for a 12-0 regular-season record that got Hawaii into the Bowl Championship Series — the precursor to today's playoffs. In New Orleans, the Rainbow Warriors ran into Georgia and lost 41-10.
Over nine seasons in Honolulu. Jones became the winningest coach in Hawaii history at 76-41. His run-and-shoot dazzled at Aloha Stadium, but also provided entertainment deep into the night on Saturdays (and into Sunday morning) when Hawaii games started late on the East Coast.
Jones' success landed him a job on the mainland, at SMU, where he went 36-43 over six-plus years.
But even after he left, Jones, a towering figure on the islands, remained among the most popular sports celebrities in a state where surfing, golf and even basketball often grabbed more headlines than football.
Gov. Josh Green called him “an exceptional human being.”
“He was a motivator of young people and he was a winner,” Green said. “He won big moments for us, and that put us into the spotlight.”

title: Cuba welcomes home diplomat expelled from US after unusual altercation at the UN
text:
Cuba welcomes home diplomat expelled from US after unusual altercation at the UN
Cuba on Friday welcomed home a diplomat expelled by the United States after an unusually heated confrontation between the two countries’ representatives at the United Nations this week.
Cuban Deputy Foreign Minister Gerardo Peñalver posted a photo of Richard Tur de la Concepción, first secretary of Cuba’s U.N. mission, alongside Foreign Ministry officials holding a Cuban flag at Havana’s airport. It was Cuba’s first public response since the U.S. State Department announced it would take action against Tur after he tried to knock a phone out of a U.S. diplomat’s hand.
“We welcomed the young diplomat home,” Peñalver wrote on X, saying Tur had “firmly and with dignity confronted the disrespectful and provocative behavior” of the U.S. delegation.
Related video above: Island-wide blackout hits Cuba
Peñalver accused U.S. officials of trying to disrupt a vote on a resolution condemning the U.S. embargo on Cuba and undermine Tur’s candidacy for a position on a U.N. body.
Tur’s expulsion was announced by U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz and later confirmed by the U.S. State Department.
U.S. officials accused Tur of shoving an American diplomat and trying to snatch the phone he was using to record their confrontation Tuesday during a General Assembly session on the embargo.
The encounter escalated into a shouting match between Waltz and Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez.
Cuba said Tur was defending himself after his personal space was invaded.
The confrontation came as tensions between the two countries have deepened since President Donald Trump imposed an energy blockade on Cuba in January in a bid to force changes to its government and political system. Washington has also threatened military action against the Caribbean nation.
Peñalver said the U.S. delegation’s behavior was part of a strategy to obstruct the vote against what he called the “genocidal blockade.”
Tur thanked Cuban officials for his reception in a post on X on Friday.
“Cuba will prevail over Yankee arrogance and anyone who seeks to intimidate us,” he wrote.
The General Assembly approved Cuba’s resolution Wednesday by a vote of 130-17, with 25 abstentions. The nonbinding measure calling for an end to the U.S. embargo is introduced annually.

title: ICE officer has been charged after striking a man with a car in Houston
text:
HOUSTON (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston was indicted by a grand jury Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, prosecutors said.
The officer, Mario Alberto Morales, was driving an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10 when he struck and ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, who was running away during a pursuit through a parking lot, according to the Harris County District Attorney’s Office. Parra Hernandez broke his leg and remains in federal custody at a rehabilitation facility, said District Attorney Sean Teare, who announced the indictment at a news conference that included body camera video of the encounter and a recording of Morales calling 911.
ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that Teare said is contradicted by video.
“The evidence we have in this case is as clear as any that I’ve ever prosecuted or investigated,” Teare said.
Morales, 33, is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, although other encounters have come under investigation, including a fatal shooting by an ICE officer this summer in Houston.
Morales’ attorney, David Lindenmuth, said his client didn’t commit a crime and he accused Teare of indicting Morales “for political gain.” Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth said.
“Mr. Morales is truly a good man, a former member of our military, who has given his entire life to public service either for his country or in or adjacent to law enforcement,” Lindenmuth told The Associated Press. “To have him charged for what was so clearly just an accident — the DA’s office, the DA himself, has invented a crime out of thin air.”
Teare hinted at concerns over Morales’ background but would not provide details.
Morales, who is charged with a second-degree felony, was not in custody Friday and a warrant will be issued for his arrest, according to Teare.
ICE asserted that local officials do not have the authority to investigate federal officers acting in the course of their duties.
“Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE,” the agency said in a statement.
The district attorney played Morales’ body camera footage
Teare has said video clearly contradicts the ICE account. Surveillance video shows a Jeep Cherokee speed over a median and drive toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away. During a news conference Friday, he played Morales’ body camera footage, which shows him driving and talking about pursuing someone.
The video shows Morales making a few sharp moves with the steering wheel before the SUV shakes. Morales stops the vehicle, then gets out and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is several feet away. The video then shows Parra Hernandez on the ground and grabbing his leg, and yelling in pain.
Morales is heard saying, “He got hit with a car, bro.” It is not clear to whom he is talking.
“I was coming in and I hit him with the car,” Morales says.
Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation
Parra Hernandez has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years and did not have a deportation order or criminal background, according to Teare.
Other aspects of ICE’s account have also been called into question.
After Parra Hernandez was taken into custody, ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day. ICE said he was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him. FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston that has been working with the family, said Mendoza-Cervantes’ daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017.
Teare’s office has previously said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE’s statement.
ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for years.
Fatal summer Houston shooting also under investigation
Teare has said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence “either intentionally or through gross negligence.” He has said Morales left the scene before the vehicle could be impounded.
In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his requests for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his van. DHS has said Salgado Araujo had “weaponized his vehicle” before the shooting and that an officer fired in self-defense. Other passengers in the van have disputed that account.

title: 10 Directors Famous for Making Terrible Movies
text:
10 Directors Known for Making Terrible Movies
Like anyone else, we love good movies, but truly terrible films hold a special place in our hearts as well, reminding us that for all of cinema’s high art merit, there are few things more fun than settling in for 90 minutes of pure schlock. While the landscape of Hollywood and beyond is scattered with bad and so-bad-it’s-good movies here and there uncovered occasionally by the real purveyors of terrible taste, there’s something to be said for those directors who can pretty reliably be expected to churn out nonstop slop.
You would think that a “bad” director would be immediately blacklisted from the industry, but the overwhelming evidence shows that this is not so. Maybe it says something about the lack of oversight in Hollywood, or perhaps the indomitability of the human spirit, but all of the directors on this list have managed to make more than one movie, so congrats to them (and woe to the rest of us). Some of these directors are bad at it on purpose, or at least didn’t exactly set out to make the next Citizen Kane. Some of them are truly sincere in their pursuit of art, yet something perpetually stands in their way.
Whatever the case, we love to hate these guys — or at least the work they produce. But that disdain is also tinged with a little bit of love, because it does take a certain amount of talent to make something really, really, really bad. Maybe art doesn’t need to be good to be “good.” Maybe it just needs to entertain our lizard brains.

title: Friday’s high school football: Biddeford bounces back against Cheverus
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Stanley Richerson rushed for three touchdowns as third-seeded Biddeford got revenge for a lopsided loss just a week earlier, rolling to a 35-20 victory over sixth-seeded Cheverus in a Class B South football quarterfinal Friday night in Biddeford.
The Tigers (6-3) took control quickly in the rematch, starting with a 79-yard run by Richerson. He added 12-yard TD run on the first play of the second quarter, and Estevao Lembissa extended the lead to 21-0 with a 6-yard run.
Richerson struck again on the opening drive of the second quarter, breaking several tackles on the way to a 24-yard touchdown.
Colton Jewett of Cheverus (3-6) returned the kickoff 80 yards for a touchdown, but Lembissa answered with a 44-yard TD run.
Nick Deschambault and Igor Bitencourt had touchdown runs in the fourth quarter for Cheverus, which qualified for the playoffs by beating Biddeford 44-8 in the regular-season finale. That resulted prevented the Tigers from getting a bye into the semifinals.
Biddeford will visit second-seeded Kennebunk next weekend.
FRYEBURG ACADEMY 48, MESSALONSKEE 7: Lars Bruhn scored three touchdowns and the fourth-seeded Raiders (5-4) rolled to a Class B North quarterfinal win over the fifth-seeded Eagles (4-5) in Fryeburg.
Fryeburg advances to face No. 1 Lawrence in the semifinals next week.
Bruhn scored on runs of 6 and 5 yards in the second quarter and caught a 35-yard touchdown pass from Marcus Sutton in the third.
Sutton scored on a 1-yard run and threw a 2-yard touchdown pass to his brother, Darryl, in the first quarter as Fryeburg jumped out to a 13-0 lead. Marcus Sutton added a 3-yard run in the third quarter and Connor Hollis scored on a 80-yard run in the fourth quarter.
Fin Minkel scored on a 1-yard run for Messalonskee.
OLD ORCHARD BEACH 42, MARANACOOK 0: Brayden Koelker scored three touchdowns, Matthew Charron threw three TD passes, and the top-seeded Seagulls (9-0) advanced to their fifth straight eight-man Small South final by defeating the fourth-seeded Black Bears (3-5) in Old Orchard Beach.
Koelker rushed for the game’s first two TDs, then caught a 23-yard pass from Charron early in the second quarter.
The Seagulls added a backbreaking touchdown on the final play of the half, as Charron connected with Scout Schilling for a 27-yard reception that made it 26-0.
Jackson Stanton caught a 25-yard scoring pass in the third quarter, and Cooper Gallant plunged in from the 1 early in the fourth.
WINDHAM 19, DEERING 0: Aiden Rinaldi broke a scoreless tie a 58-yard interception return midway through the third quarter, sparking the visiting Eagles (6-3) to a win over the Rams (1-8) in a Class A regular-season finale in Portland.
Windham quarterback Patrick Davenport connected with Landon Wyman for an 86-yard touchdown later in the third. Davenport also had a 42-yard pass to Dre O’Neil to set up Windham’s final score, a 7-yard run by M.J. Imran in the fourth.
Ryan Stultz had an interception and made 10 tackles for Deering.
THORNTON ACADEMY 35, MASSABESIC 0: Brennan Tabor scored two third-quarter touchdowns, and the defending Class A champion Trojans (9-0) capped an undefeated regular season with a win over the Mustangs (6-3) in Waterboro.
Josiah Blain scored on a 2-yard run and Logan LeBlanc returned a punt 49 yards for a score as Thornton, the No. 1 team in the Varsity Maine poll, took a 14-0 lead into halftime.
Tabor then scored on a 3-yard run and an 85-yard run in the third quarter to make it 28-0.
Chase Paquette added a 1-yard touchdown run in the fourth.
YARMOUTH 52, GRAY-NEW GLOUCESTER 6: Stephen Connolly rushed for four touchdowns and four 2-point conversions to lead the top-ranked Clippers (9-0) past the Patriots (5-4) in an eight-man Large South semifinal in Yarmouth.
Connolly scored on runs of 2, 69, 48 and 44 yards for Yarmouth, which advances to face Spruce Mountain in the regional final.
Iggy McGrath threw two touchdown passes to Jack Flanagan (65 and 56 yards) and one to Jackson Jabar (26 yards).
Cole Prescott scored on an 81-yard kick return for Gray-New Gloucester.
MORSE 42, MOUNTAIN VALLEY 6: Dylan Root rushed for two touchdowns and passed for another as the third-seeded Shipbuilders (6-3) beat the sixth-seeded Falcons (2-7) in a Class D South semifinal in Bath.
Logan True, Jack Trask and Nathan Marlow also had rushing TDs and Colton Aucoin caught a touchdown pass for Morse, which advances to play defending state champion Winthrop in the semifinals.

title: ‘Star Trek’ and ‘X-Men’ Stars Pay Tribute to Patrick Stewart
text:
‘Star Trek’ and ‘X-Men’ Co-Stars Pay Tribute to Patrick Stewart
Tributes continue to pour in for the late Patrick Stewart, the beloved star of the Star Trek and X-Men film and television series, who passed away earlier this week after the age of 86 after a brief battle with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.
William Shatner, Star Trek’s original captain (and Stewart’s co-star in the film Star Trek Generations) wrote on Instagram: “What a heartbreaking week it has been. Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.”
Shatner’s Star Trek colleague George Takei shared “As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.”
Ian McKellen, who shared the screen with Stewart in the X-Men film as the Magneto to his Professor Xavier, posted a beautiful tribute to his late friend on his own Instagram account. He wrote, in part:
We first met as ambitious young actors with the Royal Shakespeare Company half a century ago but we weren’t in the same productions. My first strong memory was a few years later, meeting him in the street in central London when he told me about an offer to take over a leading part in 'Star Trek'. “But Patrick think of your stage career in the UK. Do you really want to risk—getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?”. Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did for not just his devoted Trekkies but film and theatre audiences, who marvelled at his using international celebrity to star in a string of cinema successes ('X-Men' of course) and in great classical plays by Shakespeare, Ibsen, Arthur Miller, Peter Shaffer, Pinter and Beckett at Stratford-upon-Avon, in London’s West End and on Broadway.
McKellen’s fellow X-Men alumnus Hugh Jackman wrote “We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”
The Next Generation’s Doctor Crusher, Gates McFadden, wrote on Instagram “great memories, unforgettable man. Rest in Peace.”
The Next Generation’s Commander Riker, Jonathan Frakes, posted a simple "Rest in peace my friend” to his Instagram story, while LeVar Burton — who played Geordi La Forge on the series, wrote “He was family ... I am lucky to have known and loved so many of the facets of a soul so rich in talent and generous of heart. Of all the Dames and Knights I’ve known he was deep down-the silliest.”
Stewart’s Star Trek: The Next Generation co-star Wil Wheaton might have summed it up best when he simply posted a photo of the two together with a single emoji: “💔”

title: Letters: Susan Collins could have done more as chair of Appropriations
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
Some voters say they are considering voting for Sen. Susan Collins because of her position as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Collins herself has used that as a selling point in her campaign. What voters must understand is that I believe she has not fully used that power to the advantage of Maine, the country, or the world for that matter. One might say she has squandered it.
Although her heavily publicized ads showcase projects she has obtained funding for in Maine, our state ranks only 22nd in the nation for federal grants. In 2025, excluding programs such as Social Security and Medicare, Maine received an average of $1,066 per person in federal grants, just over the national average of $979, but Alaska received $3,252, New Mexico $2,558, and Virgin Islands $3,265! Yet “Maine’s Senator” Collins is the chair of the committee that has control over those funding sources.
She has allowed funding of rampant ICE operations, and cuts to healthcare funding. Through her failure to stand up against more unqualified and unscrupulous cabinet appointments, she has facilitated the degradation of the strength and character of our country, and essentially turned her back on clean air, water, public lands, climate change, clean energy, and public health.
She could be using the power of the purse to pressure the Trump administration to stop aligning with Russia, to end his tariff wars, and abide by the law and Constitution. I think Susan Collins is no longer working for the people who elected her. It’s time for a change.
Paul Potvin
Hampden

title: Spain’s latest deadly train crash puts human error and systemic failure under scrutiny
text:
Spain’s latest deadly train crash puts human error and systemic failure under scrutiny
Was Spain’s second major train collision in nine months caused by human error, or did it stem from deeper problems in its once-vaunted high-speed rail network?
Spain's transport minister Óscar Puente has blamed a traffic controller’s poor judgment for much of what went wrong in Wednesday’s collision in Toledo province, which has killed at least 69 people.
Railway unions have pushed back, citing deteriorating working conditions. They say too few controllers are handling growing workloads, making it increasingly difficult to ensure the safety of millions of passengers.
As the country sought answers on Friday, police with sniffer dogs continued searching the wreckage. Regional authorities warned that the death toll could rise.
Related video above: Oklahoma City man missing after train crash in Spain, family says
It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January, more than two hours farther south along the route, a train derailed and struck another traveling in the opposite direction, killing 46 people. That crash remains under investigation.
“It is unacceptable that a country like Spain with such a strong high-speed railway has two accidents of this type in the same year,” Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said Friday at the crash site near Urda.
Spain’s high-speed rail network, the world’s second-largest after China’s, has long been regarded as a success of state industrial policy. Until this year, it had recorded no fatal crashes since entering service more than three decades ago.
Japan’s high-speed rail, in contrast, has not had a derailment or collision resulting in a fatality since it started in 1964.
The timeline of the catastrophe given by the government
The chain of events that ended in disaster started at 8:31 a.m. on Wednesday, when the communication system key to the functioning of the security system on the Madrid-Seville line went down. The system, called LZB, monitors the position of trains with digital sensors and can automatically apply their brakes to prevent a collision.
The backup safety system, which is the primary system on older, low-speed commuter lines, didn't help out because the trains were both inside the same stretch between two analog sensors.
That meant that traffic controllers based at a control post in Madrid took over full responsibility for monitoring the positions and safety of the trains on a stretch of 39 miles. At the time of the accident, there were 16 controllers in the control post and two monitoring the Madrid-Seville line.
At 8:36, a controller told one train, belonging to state-owned RENFE, that it could start running again at normal speed. The other train, operated by privately owned IRYO and located 15.5 miles down the line, also tried to restart, but the engineer was unable to restart the train. The IRYO conductor told the control center, but the RENFE train was not told to stop.
Recordings leaked to Spanish media contain snippets of apparently hectic conversations between the engineers on the trains and the traffic controllers in Madrid in the minutes before the accident.
At 8:53, the collision occurred, derailing carriages and shredding parts of the trains to bits.
The independent investigators said their initial findings indicated that the RENFE train was moving at between 100mph and 125 mph when it struck the IRYO train.
Transport minister points the finger at traffic controllers
Puente, who is under pressure to resign, called the controller's decision to let one train restart at full speed while the other remained stationary “inexplicable” and “erroneous” when he spoke to the media in the immediate aftermath of the crash.
“I won’t use a worker as a shield,” Puente told reporters in a 2-hour-long news conference Friday, but added that “the information points to a mistake in the control center.”
Unions say controllers have too many trains to supervise
Unions, however, say working conditions must also be considered.
Raquel Ayllón, spokesperson for SCF, Spain’s railway traffic controllers’ union, told The Associated Press that workloads regularly exceed what current staffing levels can safely support.
“We believe (the minister) is blaming a mere worker who was working under increasingly poor conditions,” Ayllón said. “Human error isn’t incomprehensible. What is incomprehensible is that the safety system is regularly failing.”
The liberalization of Spain’s high-speed rail market and the arrival of private operators have driven a sharp rise in passenger numbers. Rail journeys rose from 35 million in 2019 to 49 million in 2024, according to the Spanish National Markets and Competition Commission.
Both collisions this year involved a RENFE train and an IRYO train.
“We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines,” said Joan Rodríguez of Spain’s train workers’ union.
Puente defended his ministry, saying the number of rail traffic controllers had risen from 1,000 in 2016 to 1,700 today.
Questions over safety systems
The SEMAF train engineers’ union said the three-decade-old LZB train safety system, which is being phased out but remains in use on the Madrid-Seville line, repeatedly goes offline.
“The LZB system should have been replaced some time ago,” said union spokesperson Diego Martín.
Puente acknowledged that the German-made system regularly goes offline for reasons including infrastructure damage caused by vandalism, maintenance work and bad weather. He said it had gone offline 170 times this year, describing that figure as “normal” and in line with recent annual averages.
The minister said Spain was ahead of most other European countries in replacing LZB with a new system required by the European Union.
Investigation continues as families await news
Investigators from a specialist rail accident committee removed the trains’ black boxes late Thursday and handed them to the Civil Guard for examination. A judge is also investigating the crash.
Seventy families have filed missing persons reports with police for passengers still unaccounted for. Only five bodies have been identified so far. Of the more than 200 people injured, 39 remained hospitalized Friday.

title: Christa Pike says she feels constant pain in her first statement since failed execution
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WVLT/AP) - Christa Pike said she is in constant pain since surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee last month but thankful for the love and support she has received.
Pike issued her first public statement through her attorneys on Friday. She said she went into the execution chamber prepared to die in peace and woke up alone and confused in a hospital bed.
“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” Pike said.
Pike said she had not contemplated a life beyond her execution date.
“I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position. I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured,” Pike said.
She said she is thankful for the medical workers who saved her life and the people who showed her kindness.
“I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone,” she said.
Pike was convicted in 1996 in the “Jobs Corps Murder,” a name that came about because both Pike and the victim — 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer — were members of the Jobs Corps at the time of the girl’s 1995 killing.
Prosecutors and testimony have said Pike conspired with two others, 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson, to kill Slemmer over relationship issues.
It was discovered throughout the case that the offenders had carved a pentacle into Slemmer’s chest and taken a piece of her skull as a souvenir of the grisly murder.

Trump to make final midterm stops in Iowa and Kansas Sunday
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump will make final campaign stops in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, two days before Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Trump won Iowa three times and Kansas twice. He is hoping to give Republicans a final boost in both states. He originally scrapped the stops but decided at the last minute to go through with them.
The Senate seats in both states are a must-win for Republicans to hold the chamber.
A recent Marist poll shows Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson trailing Democrat Josh Turek by three points in Iowa.
In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton holds a narrow lead over incumbent Republican Roger Marshall for the first time.
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said he is not worried.
“I’ve seen the voters on the ground. I’m telling you, the polls are wrong. They’re inaccurate. They’re underrepresenting Republicans,” Johnson said.
The last time Iowa sent a Democrat to the Senate was 2008. The last time Kansas did was nearly a century ago.
Trump’s approval rating is around 34% according to the latest Quinnipiac poll.
Whether his presence helps or hurts the Republican ticket will be determined Tuesday.
The Republican Party has confirmed, President Donald Trump will hold rallies starting at 3pm ET, 2pm Central at the Five Flags Center in Dubuque, Iowa and then 8pm ET, ypm CT at the Salina, Kansas regional airport.

title: Troy Jackson wants to revive Searsport wind project
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson wants to revive Maine’s stalled offshore wind ambitions if elected, saying in an interview with the Midcoast Villager that the Waldo County-based project could help lower energy costs and create economic opportunities for generations to come.
Jackson, a former Maine Senate president who helped advance the state’s offshore wind plan before President Donald Trump torpedoed it, said he is increasingly inclined to favor building the port to service offshore wind turbines at Mack Point rather than on nearby Sears Island, the controversial site selected by Gov. Janet Mills’ administration.
“I think I would tend to lean towards that,” Jackson said of Mack Point in an interview with the Villager on Thursday. “More and more people are telling me that Sears Island is something they would rather not do. So get it at Mack Point, even though I guess it could cost more and maybe have some environmental issues.”
Still, he said the final decision should be made closer to the ground: “It’s a local issue that I think should be determined by the people there.”
After a lengthy and contentious review process, the Mills administration determined that state-owned Sears Island would be a better and cheaper place to build the wind port than privately owned Mack Point, about half a mile away and already home to a major oil and gas terminal.
But some environmentalists and local grassroots groups have rallied to stop further development on Sears Island, which has some infrastructure from previous, abandoned port construction projects.
The Trump administration has effectively halted Maine’s offshore wind plans, including the proposed Searsport port that would serve offshore wind development. But Jackson said the groundwork laid during the Biden administration could allow the project to move forward again.
“The roadmap is there,” Jackson said. “We will be doing offshore wind sometime in the future.”
Jackson said he was proud of efforts during his time in the Maine Legislature to bring environmentalists, labor unions and lobstermen together to develop an offshore wind plan that would protect Maine’s fishing grounds, even if lobstermen remain skeptical of the industry.
He argued that offshore wind, combined with a proposed massive wind project in Aroostook County and other renewable energy projects, could make Maine a net energy exporter, generating revenue and lowering electricity costs for residents.
“We’ve got a real chance here with offshore wind and onshore wind to set ourselves up for generations to come,” he said.
In another matter of considerable local interest, Jackson confirmed — with a small caveat — that his son Camden is indeed named after the Midcoast town.
“I want to check with Lana 100%, but I’m almost positive,” Jackson said, explaining that his partner had more say in naming their second son after he took the lead in naming their first, Chace.
Jackson recalled that Camden and Rockport came up during the naming process and that he and Lana liked the area.
The interview came as Jackson and Republican Sen. Susan Collins entered the final days of an extraordinarily close and expensive election.
Jackson continued to criticize Collins over a campaign advertisement featuring longtime Maine television personality Bill Green, who seemed to mock Jackson’s past work as a logger by saying that while Jackson might know how to sell a cord of wood, he “doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective” in the U.S. Senate.
Collins has distanced herself from the ad’s tone, saying she does not look down on anyone and pointing to her own experience picking potatoes as a young person in Aroostook County. Jackson was unmoved.
“I don’t care how many potatoes she picked when she was a kid,” Jackson said, arguing that Collins and Green were out of touch with the economic struggles of working-class Mainers, including high heating costs. “This election, I mean, it is about a cord of wood right now.”
Jackson also pushed back on Collins’ argument that her seniority and position as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee allow her to deliver federal funding and jobs to Maine.
“What she brings in, I’m not gonna discredit, but it’s a pittance to what we’re losing,” Jackson said, pointing to tariffs on Canadian goods, high fuel prices caused by the Iran War and other Trump policies that he argued are harmful to Mainers.
With Election Day approaching, Jackson predicted an extremely close race that could take until late Tuesday night or early Wednesday morning to decide, but said he would be surprised if write-in votes forced a ranked-choice voting tabulation.
“I feel like the enthusiasm is like nothing I’ve ever seen before,” he said.
And Jackson said he hoped to bring that same independent streak to Washington.
“I want to push the Democratic Party because I haven’t always agreed with them,” he said.
Mills, who had been mum on the Senate race since dropping out of the Democratic primary earlier this year, announced Thursday that she had voted early for Jackson and other Democrats.
Jackson and Mills have a somewhat strained relationship, dating back to clashes during their time in state government.
Jackson said he appreciates Mills’ support and noted that they “worked on a lot of things together,” adding that he wants a “big coalition” behind him.
But have Mills and Jackson spoken since he became the Democrats’ replacement nominee after Graham Platner dropped out?
“I mean, I made a call, but we haven’t actually talked,” Jackson said.
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: Students learn the power of giving through painting pet portraits
text:
WINNECONNE, Wis. (InvestigateTV) — Seventh graders at Winneconne Middle School are painting pet portraits for a community project.
Students in Susan Meunier’s new leadership class are tracing and painting portraits of pets. Vaughn Wurtz and her classmates are working on the project at the school.
“We had to do a project for something to do with the community that benefits the community,” Wurtz said.
Aubrey Salm and Paul Reinke helped come up with the idea.
“We’re doing pet portraits for Go Fetch and we’re going to donate all of the money to the humane society,” Salm said.
Meunier said the students are working hard on the portraits.
“They are putting so much effort into it,” Meunier said.
She said the students told Go Fetch in an interview, “It might not be the best painting but we’ll try our hardest.” Meunier said they are trying hard on everything.
Meunier said the value of the project is in the lesson.
“I’m glad they’re seeing the work it does, but really the reward for that work, it’s definitely worth it to go out and be the positive light to see that carry on to other people,” Meunier said.
Meunier said she teaches math by trait.
“Even when I’m teaching math, we just want to teach good humans,” Meunier said. “I always tell them, our goal for you is to go out in the world and do good and be on your own, and in math, sometimes that’s hard to connect those, but this is really showing them we want them to be the positive.”
Reinke said he plans to continue the work.
“I’m going to keep doing this all the way through high school, maybe college,” Reinke said. “It feels amazing, helping people in general.”
Salm said the project has an effect on her classmates.
“Seeing how everyone, even in my class, it makes everyone so happy, knowing that it will make other people happy, it’s just amazing to know,” Salm said.
Wurtz said the school has a set of guidelines called the Winneconne Way.
“We have this thing called the Winneconne Way, it’s PAW: Practice Kindness, Always Show Respect and Work to do your Best,” Wurtz said. “I feel like this class really tries to follow those rules.”

title: Woman who killed best friend’s newborn said she had a years-long compulsion to hurt children, reports say
text:
ALLEGHENY COUNTY, Pa. (Gray News) - A woman admitted to killing her best friend’s 6-week-old son and injuring his twin brother while babysitting in Pennsylvania, prosecutors said.
Nicole Virzi, 32, pleaded guilty Wednesday to third-degree murder and other charges, avoiding a potential death penalty trial. She was sentenced to 35 to 80 years in prison.
In 2024, Virzi was visiting Pittsburgh to assist her longtime friend, Savannah Roberts, with newborn twins Leon and Ari Katz, NBC News reported.
When the parents took Ari to a hospital to treat unexplained injuries, Virzi offered to watch Leon.
Later that night, Virzi called 911 claiming Leon fell from a baby bouncer. He was rushed to a children’s hospital, where he died.
An autopsy revealed Leon died from blunt force trauma to the head, with investigators concluding the catastrophic injuries could not have resulted from a bouncer fall.
Detectives also determined Virzi caused Ari’s initial injuries. Prosecutors revealed in court that Virzi told investigators she “always had a compulsion she could not control to harm kids.”
In a letter to Allegheny County Common Pleas Judge Jill E. Rangos, Roberts said Virzi’s betrayal shattered her trust, writing, “I could’ve never imagined that a person, let alone my best friend, was capable of the cruelty or violence Nicole displayed.”

title: Maine can Make America Good Again

text:
Kindness and compassion are public goods. This Republican president, aided by a do-nothing Republican Congress, has focused on faithlessness, greed, bellicosity and cruelty. Nothing in that formula is faithful to the purposes of good government as laid out in the preamble to the Constitution.
There is nothing “radical” about having an affordable home, being able to feed our families and having affordable access to healthcare. There is nothing “radical” about promoting the general welfare, as the Constitution mandates.
What is radical is a Republican administration that undertakes unwise and unnecessary offensive aggression, rather than merely providing for the common defense, as the Constitution stipulates; and unjustifiably kills people in our own streets with an unaccountable agency.
If we want to secure the blessings of liberty, namely peace, prosperity and justice, we must vote Democratic. Make America Good Again, by voting for Troy Jackson, Hannah Pingree and Matt Dunlap.

Auburn

title: This family runs a distillery in an old fire station
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
DALE, Wis. (InvestigateTV) — A Wisconsin family runs a distillery in an old fire station along Highway 96 in Dale, with a business designed to support the fire departments that keep them safe.
Volunteer firefighter Alex Hopfensperger works at the family business, Old Station 31 Spirits.
“Right now we’re distilling in-house vodka and gin, so we have the four vodkas and two gins,” Alex Hopfensperger said.
“We wanted to become a part of the community, and 20-plus years ago, part of becoming part of the community was joining the volunteer fire department,” Rob Hopfensperger said.
Alex’s father, Rob, is also a volunteer firefighter. He and his wife, Tavia, decided to honor the fire service when they created Old Station 31 Spirits.
“You start to do it and, you know, I’m on it, then your sons get on it, your daughter-in-law gets on it, and it’s just, and we have that,” Rob said.
“Living in a small town, people just pop in and you get to meet so many different people and people that have memories of this place,” Tavia said. “We’ve heard hundreds of fire station stories. That fire service connection, when they come in the building, it’s a brotherhood.”
The tasting room and museum feature artifacts and memorabilia honoring local departments and those who gave their lives.
“We have a memorial for the 9/11. We do the stair climb every year at Lambeau Field and then they give you badges with the firefighters that perished there, and we are starting our collection of those badges,” Tavia said.
Old Station 31 Spirits makes its products grain to glass.
“We take a department every month and sell a particular drink for that department, and then those proceeds we donate back to that department,” Rob said.
The family business plans to expand its reach when the time is right.
“We’re going to be filling up our own barrels with whiskey and then in five-ish years with the barrel age process we’ll be able to enjoy that ourselves,” Alex said.
The business has stayed in the small town where it started.
“There’s a lot of our fellow distillers or distilleries in Wisconsin that is either in a bigger city or they’re in a tourist area. And as you probably know, Dale is neither,” Rob said.
